papers.title: Survival-Time Risk Beyond Low-Order Channel Models: Identifiability and Scheduling
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether low-order packet-loss statistics suffice to assess survival-time risk under bursty packet losses, i.e., the probability that no update succeeds for a prescribed number of consecutive slots. Conventional models, such as the Gilbert model, characterize packet losses using the loss rate and mean burst length, but channels sharing these statistics may exhibit substantially different failure risks. We characterize the Markov channels one order above a given low-order fit that share its statistics and analyze their risks under acknowledgment-based scheduling with transmission budgets. We show that, with dense transmission attempts, risk is primarily governed by loss persistence beyond the modeled memory, and the worst-case channel need not be the most persistent one. Under limited budgets, retry spacing makes loss relapse probabilities important and can reverse the risk ordering of compatible channels. Numerical and measurement results show that low-order models can substantially underestimate the risk, highlighting the need for scheduling-dependent channel statistics.

papers.intro:
Industrial control and human-in-the-loop applications of the Tactile Internet, such as teleoperation, require timely and reliable information updates [1]. A prolonged interruption in successful packet delivery may violate the application’s survival-time requirement [2], even when the average packet-loss rate is low. Assessing reliability therefore requires accounting for temporal correlations in packet losses rather than their average rate alone. In practice, bursty communication channels are commonly represented by low-order models, such as the Gilbert model [3] and first-order Markov models of fading [4], which provide tractable descriptions of packet losses using a small number of statistics, including the loss rate and mean burst length. However, different channels may share these statistics while exhibiting substantially different probabilities of survival-time violations.

However, different channels may share these statistics while exhibiting substantially different probabilities of survival-time violations.

The temporal structure of packet losses and its effect on reliability have been widely investigated [5, 6, 7]. Previous studies have examined Markov models of different orders using measured loss traces [8] and queueing analysis [9], as well as scheduling and remote estimation over Markovian channels with acknowledgment feedback [10, 11, 12]. Related work has also characterized information freshness, age violations, and estimation stability under correlated losses [13, 14]. Robust verification and control methods [15, 16] and reliability bounds under unknown dependence [17] can account for channel-model uncertainty. However, these approaches assume a given model or uncertainty set, not the set of channels a low-order fit cannot resolve. A fundamental question remains: to what extent can survival-time risk be determined from low-order channel statistics, and which additional statistics are needed for reliable risk assessment?

This paper addresses this question by considering channels that share the same low-order packet-loss statistics but differ in their higher-order dependencies. We investigate their survival-time risks under acknowledgment-based scheduling with a finite transmission budget. The key observation is that the relevant channel statistics depend on the transmission schedule. When transmissions are attempted in every slot, consecutive packet losses primarily determine the failure risk. Under a limited transmission budget, however, successful channel opportunities during idle slots cannot reset the age of information. Consequently, the spacing between transmission attempts introduces additional dependence on loss relapses, potentially changing the relative reliability of channels with identical low-order statistics.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows. (i) We characterize the Markov channels one order above a low-order fit as an explicit box whose maximum-entropy point is the fitted model. (ii) We bound the risk of every channel in this box and show that, with dense attempts, loss persistence beyond the modeled memory governs the risk to first order, while the worst case need not be the most persistent channel. (iii) We show that under a budget, retry spacing makes loss relapses matter, and construct two compatible channels whose risk order the budget reverses. (iv) We show by exact computation, fading simulations, and measured IEEE 802.15.4 links that low-order models can substantially underestimate the risk, even with a second-order fit. Full proofs, code, and data are available in [18].

papers.title: A Universal Raw-IQ Radar Encoder for Cross-Sensor Human Sensing
papers.abstract: Radar-based human sensing typically relies on end-to-end task-specific models trained on hand-chosen signal projections, which generalize poorly across unseen users, tasks, and hardware. We argue that the dominant signal processing choice, the micro-Doppler spectrogram, is a poor starting point for transfer because it keeps the Doppler axis, which carrier frequency rescales, and discards the angular axis, which carrier frequency leaves unchanged. We instead pretrain a convolutional beta-VAE without labels on clutter-removed raw radar measurements from four platforms spanning 60 and 77 GHz and 4 to 12 virtual antennas, aligned by a unified spectral interpolation grid. For every downstream benchmark the encoder stays frozen, and only a small supervised temporal classifier is trained on its embeddings. We compare against supervised models trained end to end on each benchmark and a pretrained radar foundation model across ten settings covering activity, gesture, sign-language, and gait recognition. When the test users and the radar are seen during training, our encoder is best on all five benchmarks. For users never seen in training, it leads on three of four benchmarks, by 4.8 to 23.2 points. On subject-disjoint gait recognition, it is best for each of the four held-out subjects and 8.3 points above the strongest baseline on average, even though its pretraining excluded every recording of this radar. Excluding the test radar from pretraining costs at most 5.3 points on any benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/jonasmueler/UniversalRadarEncoder_WACV.

papers.intro:
Radar-based contactless human sensing is gaining interest, from biomedical monitoring [8] to human pose estimation [10, 16, 13, 2, 15, 14] and activity recognition [28, 29, 30, 20, 21]. Most models in this literature are trained and tested on one sensor. Radar hardware, however, differs substantially in antenna configuration, field of view, carrier frequency, and signal characteristics [3, 6], and representations do not carry over directly from one radar to another. Spectrogram classifiers for activity classification, for example, degrade severely when the test sensor differs from the training sensor [3], so transfer between sensors is a hard, open problem. We therefore pretrain one encoder across several radars, freeze it, and train only a small classifier on each benchmark’s labels (Fig. 1), so that what transfers to a new sensor is the representation rather than the classifier itself.

Before learning, the signal is usually tailored to the task. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) MIMO radar delivers a complex-valued multi-dimensional tensor, the radar cube, that combines range, velocity, and angular information from multiple synchronized transmit–receive antenna pairs [8]. Most pipelines collapse this cube early into a lower-dimensional, task-specific representation, and these representations differ in density and in the information they preserve [8]. Activity recognition sits at the dense, heavily projected end, where most models classify a single 2D time–frequency projection, above all the micro-Doppler spectrogram [29, 21, 20, 3], which preserves the Doppler dynamics of human motion but collapses range and angle entirely. Pose-estimation and automotive pipelines usually sit at the sparse end, reducing the signal to point clouds via constant false alarm rate (CFAR) detection and angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimation [2, 26], which keeps an explicit representation suited to localization. Only a few systems operate close to the original tensor [36, 13, 16, 10]. For the input of such an encoder, new evidence favors data close to the raw signal. On a 3D occupancy-prediction task, omitting the Doppler FFT raises the test loss by 22.5%, replacing dense antenna measurements with AoA estimates by 28.0%, and applying CFAR thresholding by 31.5%, each as large a degradation as training on more than ten times less data [6]. Operating on the raw complex tensor [16] improves pose estimation by 19% over the CFAR point-cloud pipeline of Engel et al. [2], and in activity recognition the spectrogram yields 86.49% accuracy, the range–time map 95.25%, and fusing multiple views of the cube 95.80% [28]. In general, a gradient in performance gains can be observed by including more of the raw data in the input to the encoder.

papers.title: MAGIC's interferometric diameters of $\theta$ Ophiuchi and $\beta$ CMa and comparison with asteroseismic modelling
papers.abstract: $\beta$ Cephei type stars are massive ($8-25$M$_{\odot}$) and known to have several pulsation modes with periods typically of a few hours. Despite a better understanding of their physics since 1992, the inner structure of these stars involves key stellar physics processes that are still uncertain. Asteroseismology offers insights into these variable stars by analysing pulsation modes, helping to probe their inner layers and understand their structure and mixing processes. We measure the angular diameter of two $\beta$ Cephei stars, $\theta$ Oph and $\beta$ CMa, using the MAGIC Stellar Intensity Interferometer and compare them, together with the Gaia and Hipparcos parallaxes, to the predictions of the asteroseismic model. The latter are based on Levenberg-Marquardt local minimisation of stellar evolution model parameters to fit observed pulsation modes. In the case of $\theta$ Oph, the observed angular diameters are compatible with the asteroseismic model. For $\beta$ CMa, the radius derived from the angular diameter and the Hipparcos parallax is in tension, at the $2.5\sigma$ level, with the asteroseismic prediction. We show that this tension mirrors a pre-existing conflict between independent spectroscopic determinations of the surface gravity of the star, that percent-level systematics of the stellar models are quantitatively insufficient to explain it, and that it most likely points to a bias of the Hipparcos parallax. In the frame of this paper, the statistical uncertainty on the interferometric results is similar to the systematic uncertainty on the parallaxes. With the already implemented addition in early 2024 of the first Large-Sized Telescope (CTAO-North LST-1) to the setup, the uncertainty in the angular diameter of these stars is expected to decrease by an order of magnitude, allowing to further constrain stellar evolution models and parallaxes.

Asteroseismology is one of the few methods that can constrain the inner structure of stars. Analogously to how seismologists analyse sound waves from earthquakes, asteroseismology allows us to determine the density and composition of the stellar medium through which the oscillations propagate.

Asteroseismology is one of the few methods that can constrain the inner structure of stars. Analogously to how seismologists analyse sound waves from earthquakes, asteroseismology allows us to determine the density and composition of the stellar medium through which the oscillations propagate.

Hence, this method is especially useful in the study of pulsating stars such as β\beta Cephei variables. These stars are massive, and their brightness can change by 0.01 to 0.3 magnitudes over timescales of a few hours. Cox et al. (1992) explained the pulsation phenomenon with the κ\kappa mechanism, which is the preferred scenario to date. Usually, the opacity κ\kappa of a star decreases as it contracts and heats, following Kramers’ law κ∝ρ/T3.5\kappa\propto\rho/T^{3.5}. However, in β\beta Cephei, inner layers have a high iron density and at a temperature of ∼200 000\sim 200\,000 K, partial ionisation zones can form. As a result, less energy passes through the layer, increasing the opacity. Hence, the pressure rises, and the layer overshoots its equilibrium position. It follows that the pressure and temperature decrease, which also decreases the opacity, and the star starts a new cycle (Goss 2012). These processes are challenging to model and their understanding could refine stellar evolution models as they depend on quantities such as the overshooting parameter (Pedersen et al. 2018), which impacts the mixing of layers, providing more fuel to the stellar core (Claret and Torres 2016).

The MAGIC telescopes are two Cherenkov Telescopes located in the Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, La Palma, Spain. While they were originally built to perform very-high-energy gamma-ray observations, they were slightly modified to also perform as a stellar intensity interferometer (MAGIC-SII) (Abe et al. 2024). In this mode of observation, the setup is used to measure stellar angular diameters of the order of 1 milliarcsecond in B-band with a ∼10\sim 10 % precision in about 2.5 h for stars up to magnitude 4. Thus, these measurements, together with distance estimates from other experiments (Gaia/Hipparcos), can be compared with the stellar radii predicted by asteroseismic models, hence testing the models themselves.

papers.title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
papers.abstract: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) (Johnson et al., 2023a) has enabled thousands of peer-reviewed publications (Zhang et al., 2025). This leads to a fragmented ecosystem of “individual preprocessing” where, in the absence of a standardized pipeline, each project must build its own scripts to extract the specific variables needed for its use case. These isolated preprocessing pipelines are rarely shared or unified, resulting in duplicated engineering effort and inconsistent extraction quality across the community. But even if such an effort were made, the resulting datasets are typically tailored so closely to individual projects that they lack the generality needed to support broader research questions. papers.title: Boundary determination from the anisotropic elastic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
papers.abstract: We show that the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map of the elastic wave equation determines the density and the anisotropic stiffness tensor on the boundary for generic density and stiffness tensor fields. The proof builds on an interplay between microlocal analysis and algebraic geometry. Microlocal analysis yields a construction of special solutions, valid for many real principal type systems, that concentrate near a boundary point. Generic conditions ensure that this construction holds and allow for extraction of information about stiffness tensor and density at the boundary. We also describe the generic sets through algebraic conditions.

papers.title: In-situ azimuthal sample rotation within a horizontal-field cryomagnet for small-angle neutron scattering
papers.abstract: We present an in-situ azimuthal rotation stage for small-angle neutron scattering measurements. The stage provides an azimuthal rotation range of $315^\circ$ about the stage normal. At the reference sample-stick orientation, the stage normal is parallel to the incident neutron beam, so that the sample rotates in the plane perpendicular to the beam. Combined with a sample stick rotation about a second, orthogonal axis, the stage provides control of the magnetic-field direction relative to the crystal axes, while the field remains fixed in the laboratory frame. For a 5 mm diameter incident beam, sample-stick rotations of approximately $\pm315^\circ$ are accessible with negligible additional attenuation from the holder. The commercial rotator is specified for operation between 1 and 373 K and in magnetic fields up to 35 T, making the stage nominally compatible with the full temperature (1.8 to 320 K) and field (0 to 6.8 T) ranges of the used cryomagnet. As a working example, we characterize its performance on a spherical single crystal of MnSi between 20 and 35 K and in fields up to 183 mT, observing local sample heating during operation of $\sim$20 mK per $5^\circ$ step. We illustrate the design considerations behind the holder construction, with specific notes for mounting spherical samples, and discuss the resulting performance and limitations.

papers.intro:
Neutron scattering and magnetic fields are among the most important experimental tools in condensed matter research. The coupling of a magnetic field to orbital and spin degrees of freedom provides the ability to directly manipulate electron states. Neutron scattering then provides a microscopic probe of the magnetic structures, dynamics, and electron correlations, which in many cases are markedly anisotropic [28]. Examples include orientation-dependent magnetic phase diagrams in rare-earth systems [19], quantum phase transitions in Ising magnets [8, 31, 10, 43], exotic magnetic structures [25, 33, 9, 30, 11], and anisotropic interactions in chiral helimagnets [1, 24, 39, 4, 5]. Small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) is the primary method to resolve mesoscale magnetic behavior, where the precise orientation of the magnetic field can be consequential [43, 9, 30]. Typically, SANS measurements use cryomagnets, in which the sample orientation is aligned ex-situ, using a Laue camera or test diffractometer, and fixed during an experiment. Resolving misalignments, or changing the experimental geometry, can consequently waste valuable beam time and limit the feasibility of an experiment. The ability to precisely control the sample alignment or magnetic field orientation in-situ is therefore beneficial.

Controlling the sample alignment is commonly achieved by dedicated goniometer inserts. For example, inserts have been developed for nuclear magnetic resonance [36, 12, 41], electronic transport[34, 42], quantum oscillations [29, 45], and measurements in pulsed magnetic fields [44], all of which utilize the sample rotation to access multiple crystal directions and map angular-dependent physics. These concepts have also been developed for neutron scattering [35, 15, 38, 23, 16]. However, the angular range is often limited, with the insert developed primarily to correct sample misalignments rather than as an experimental variable.

Vector magnets provide an alternative that enables precise control of the magnetic field with respect to the sample. These systems use multiple coil sets to control the net field orientation with respect to a fixed sample, and, given their complexity, are often designed for specific use cases [13]. Such designs are more constrained for scattering techniques, in which beam access over a wide angular range is required [40, 6, 27]. Consequently, vector magnets designed explicitly for neutron scattering are rare [18, 22]. Furthermore, manipulation of the sample orientation in such systems is typically limited, and so the problems of misalignments or orientation changes persist.

In this paper, we report the development of an in-situ azimuthal rotation stage for SANS measurements in a horizontal-field cryomagnet. Alongside the sample stick rotation, the stage offers the ability to precisely tune the sample orientation along two orthogonal axes. The combined rotations enable controlled variation of the field direction relative to the crystal axes. This provides an alternative to a vector magnet for measurements within the accessible angular range, with the changing sample orientation accounted for in the data treatment. We subsequently demonstrate this potential by controlling the skyrmion lattice orientation in MnSi during a precession of the magnetic field. Although designed with SANS in mind, we anticipate that our developments may aid in the design of further rotation stages for other neutron scattering techniques where precise control of the sample orientation is either useful or imperative.

Finally, we summarize the main developments and discuss future applications in Sec. IV.

papers.title: 3D dark matter map of the JWST COSMOS-Web field using diffusion-based generative priors
papers.abstract: Mapping the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter is key to tracing the growth of cosmic structure. Two-dimensional weak lensing mass maps recover its projected distribution, but they blend structures at different distances along the line of sight. We reconstruct the three-dimensional matter distribution in the 0.54 deg$^2$ COSMOS-Web field using deep James Webb Space Telescope imaging, with an effective source density of 121 galaxies arcmin$^{-2}$ We combine a physical weak lensing forward model with a diffusion-based Bayesian generative prior learned from cosmological simulations, yielding a posterior distribution of the matter field across 20 lens planes to $z \simeq 2$, doubling the redshift reach of previous Hubble Space Telescope-based 3D reconstructions and approaching cosmic noon, an epoch of rapid galaxy growth. The reconstruction separates structures that overlap in projection and recovers non-Gaussian matter structure across a range of spatial scales, including over-densities associated with independently identified galaxy clusters that were not detected in earlier weak lensing maps. Posterior sampling quantifies the range of three-dimensional matter distributions allowed by the data, enabling a probabilistic visualization of the cosmic web while propagating uncertainties in its inferred structure. Null and simulation-based tests show that the recovered structures are supported by the lensing signal and are consistent with expectations from the fiducial $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. These results extend three-dimensional weak lensing mapping into the high-redshift, non-Gaussian regime and establish a route towards probabilistic mapping of the evolving cosmic web with current wide-field lensing surveys.

papers.title: Isophotal signatures of the brightest cluster galaxy - intracluster light transition
papers.abstract: The distinction between brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) and intracluster light (ICL) remains ambiguous, with inferred cluster properties depending strongly on the adopted definition and measurement methodology. We report the presence of a common inflection feature in the radial profiles of surface brightness, ellipticity, and position angle of BCG+ICL systems, indicative of a structural transition in the underlying stellar distribution. Using a combination of low redshift clusters (z < 0.1) observed with the Wendelstein Wide Field Imager, deep Hyper Suprime-Cam observations of clusters at 0.2 < z < 0.4, and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations from Horizon-AGN and Hydrangea, we consistently identify a common inflection at radii of 60-85 kpc. We interpret this feature as a characteristic transition in the combined BCG+ICL light distribution, that may reflect the hierarchical assembly of the cluster. The persistence of this feature across multiple photometric bands, redshift ranges, and simulations supports its robustness. To identify these transitions, we employ an automated second derivative based approach that does not rely on parametric decompositions or arbitrary surface brightness thresholds. This framework provides a physically motivated and scalable means to characterise the BCG-ICL transition, and it will be of paramount importance for forthcoming large scale surveys such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the European Space Agency's Euclid mission.

The formation of this diffuse stellar component is primarily driven by hierarchical structure assembly. Both minor and major mergers involving central and satellite galaxies (Monaco et al., 2006; Murante et al., 2007; Gerhard et al., 2007; Contini et al., 2014; Jiménez-Teja et al., 2018; Jiménez-Teja et al., 2019; Groenewald et al., 2017; Joo and Jee, 2023), as well as tidal stripping processes (Rudick et al., 2009; Rudick et al., 2011; Contini et al., 2014; DeMaio et al., 2015; Montes and Trujillo, 2018; Jiménez-Teja et al., 2018; Jiménez-Teja et al., 2019), are widely regarded as the dominant channels contributing to its build-up. Pre-processing within infalling galaxy groups can also play a significant role (Willman et al., 2004; Mihos et al., 2005; Rudick et al., 2006). Other mechanisms, such as in-situ star formation (Puchwein et al., 2010) and dwarf galaxy disruption (Murante et al., 2007; Purcell et al., 2007; Conroy et al., 2007; Martel et al., 2012; Giallongo et al., 2014; Annunziatella et al., 2016; Morishita et al., 2017; Raj et al., 2020), are thought to contribute only to a small degree (Melnick et al., 2012; Contini et al., 2014; DeMaio et al., 2015; Montes and Trujillo, 2018, e.g.,). Isophotal analyses of the ICL have further revealed radial trends in ellipticity (Gonzalez et al., 2005; Kluge et al., 2020; Montes et al., 2021, see e.g.,) and a close alignment with the cluster large-scale structure and dark matter (DM) distribution (Despali et al., 2014; Montes and Trujillo, 2019; Alonso Asensio et al., 2020; Deason et al., 2021; Lau et al., 2021; Montes and Trujillo, 2022; Diego et al., 2023; Contreras-Santos et al., 2024; Yoo et al., 2024; Asensio and Contreras-Santos, 2025; Butler et al., 2025; Ellien et al., 2025; Fernandez et al., 2026, e.g.,). (in preparation)), making their separation challenging. papers.title: The STARfall pathway: forging intermediate-mass black holes through stellar collisions in dense star clusters
papers.abstract: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, $10^2 < m_{\rm BH}/\mathrm{M}_{\odot} < 10^5$) are elusive objects bridging the gap between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes, whose origin remains uncertain. They may form from the collapse of very massive stars (VMSs, $m_*\geq150\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$) assembled through repeated stellar collisions in compact and fast evolving star clusters. We investigate the formation of VMSs and IMBH seeds via repeated mergers and collisions as a function of cluster initial conditions, assessing the implications for globular clusters and dense high-redshift system. We develop STARfall, a semi-analytic tool that follows the evolution of a massive stellar binary via binary-single interactions, mergers, collisions, and stellar evolution, while consistently accounting for the host cluster evolution. Our results show that clusters with central densities above $10^6\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}\,\mathrm{pc}^{-3}$ can undergo a catastrophic sequence of stellar collisions, or "starastrophe", within $3$ Myr. Through this process, VMSs rapidly grow in mass and collapse into IMBHs with masses of up to $10^3-10^4\,\mathrm{M}_{\odot}$, despite the effects of intense stellar winds. Applying our models to observed systems, we find that compact clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arc and Milky Way globular clusters could have hosted VMSs that collapsed into IMBHs in this mass range. Despite their longer core-collapse timescales, the inferred central densities of Little Red Dots may also support IMBH formation in the same mass interval. Our models show that VMS assembly requires two essential ingredients: short core-collapse times and large central densities. Compared to observed systems, our models suggest that clusters in the Cosmic Gems Arcs and several Galactic globular clusters could have nurtured VMSs that directly collapsed to IMBHs with masses $10^3-10^4\,\text{M}_{\odot}$.

papers.title: Towards Self-consistent Modeling of Quasi-Stars and their NLTE Spectra: Implications for Little Red Dots
papers.abstract: Quasi-stars, massive envelopes surrounding rapidly accreting black hole (BH) seeds, are promising candidates for explaining the rapid formation of supermassive black holes in the early Universe and may account for some of the JWST-discovered Little Red Dots (LRDs). We present a self-consistent framework combining stellar evolution calculations with non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) spectral synthesis to test this connection. Our models drop the polytropic assumptions of previous work: the envelope is described entirely by mixing-length theory, with saturated convection and radiative energy setting the luminosity at an inner boundary a few hundred Schwarzschild radii from the BH. This removes the BH-mass limits of earlier models, and we follow the evolution up to BH-to-total mass ratios approaching unity. We then use TLUSTY to compute the first converged NLTE atmospheric models for the surface conditions and primordial hydrogen-helium composition expected in quasi-stars. Our models produce cool photospheres, prominent Balmer breaks, and Balmer and Paschen absorption features. NLTE effects substantially modify line strengths, increasing Balmer absorption depths by $\sim 35-55\%$ relative to LTE models, while having a minor effect on the continuum. Comparison with observed LRD spectral energy distributions shows broad agreement in continuum shape, although our models do not reproduce their commonly observed strong emission lines. Under the quasi-star interpretation, comparisons with individual LRDs suggest characteristic quasi-star masses of approximately $10^5-10^7 M_\odot$. These results establish a physically motivated connection between quasi-star evolution and observable spectra, providing a framework for testing quasi-stars as progenitors of LRDs while identifying limitations of current atmospheric models.

papers.intro:
The existence of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) with masses exceeding 109​M⊙10^{9}M_{\odot} within the first billion years of the Universe remains an important open problem [14, 1]. The conventional pathway of Eddington-limited accretion onto stellar-mass black hole (BH) seeds struggles to account for such rapid growth, motivating the exploration of alternative SMBH seed formation channels. Among these, quasi-stars — massive, radiation-pressure-supported envelopes surrounding accreting BH seeds formed through direct collapse — have long been recognized as a promising mechanism for rapid early BH growth [7, 6]. In quasi-stars, the central BH accretes at highly super-Eddington rates while the liberated energy is transported outward primarily by convection and radiated near the Eddington luminosity of the entire (BH + envelope) system. Since the envelope is initially much more massive than the BH, this configuration enables the BH to grow rapidly to intermediate masses (∼103\sim 10^{3}–104​M⊙10^{4}\,M_{\odot} or larger) on Myr timescales, thereby providing plausible progenitors for the SMBHs powering high-redshift quasars.

The observational motivation for the quasi-star paradigm has been revitalized by recent discoveries from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Deep extragalactic surveys, including CEERS [15], JADES [37], and related programs, have revealed a population of compact, red, high-redshift sources colloquially referred to as “Little Red Dots” (LRDs) [25, 30, 4, 17, 24, e.g.,]. These objects are typically found at redshifts z∼4−10z\sim 4-10 and are characterized by compact morphologies, red rest-frame optical colors, and unusual spectral energy distributions (SEDs). In several cases, their SEDs exhibit a pronounced rest-frame optical excess and a steep ultraviolet-to-optical slope, producing a characteristic “V-shaped” continuum with a minimum near ∼3500\sim 3500 Å in the rest frame [25, 30, 17].

Spectroscopically, many LRDs display broad Balmer emission lines, including Hα\alpha and Hβ\beta, with full widths at half maximum (FWHM) of order 103−5×10310^{3}-5\times 10^{3} km s-1 [28, 17]. These line widths suggest the presence of dense, rapidly moving gas analogous to the broad-line regions (BLRs) of active galactic nuclei (AGNs). At the same time, LRD spectra differ significantly from those of classical unobscured quasars: high-ionization ultraviolet lines are often weak or absent, forbidden lines appear suppressed, and some objects exhibit strong Balmer breaks and Balmer absorption features [28, 17]. These properties point toward environments characterized by high gas densities, substantial obscuration, and potentially large optical depths.

A variety of interpretations have been proposed for the LRD population. One class of models identifies LRDs as rapidly accreting, dust-obscured AGNs in which emission from the accretion disk and BLR is partially reprocessed by surrounding gas and dust [28, 17]. Alternative explanations invoke extremely compact and intense starbursts with strong nebular emission contributing substantially to the rest-frame optical flux [25]. However, purely stellar models face difficulties in reproducing the observed broad Balmer line widths and equivalent widths without invoking an accreting BH component. Hybrid scenarios involving both star formation and BH accretion have also been considered [17].

Quasi-stars have emerged as particularly intriguing candidates for at least a subset of the LRD population [5]. Their predicted properties — large photospheric radii, cool extended envelopes, dense ionized interiors, and high luminosities powered by rapid BH growth — naturally produce compact, red spectra with strong hydrogen recombination features. Additional support for this interpretation comes from observations of the gravitationally lensed LRD R2211-RX1 [42], which exhibits century-scale photometric variability and a hysteresis loop in the luminosity–temperature plane suggestive of a pulsating stellar-like photosphere. Quasi-star models have been shown to reproduce several of the principal characteristics of this variability [8].

papers.title: LaplaceDiag: Fault Diagnosis through Changes in Learned Actuator Effects
papers.abstract: Identifying faulty components from sensor anomalies is difficult because fault effects can propagate through a plant and different faults can produce similar observations. Detailed component models and labeled fault examples may also be unavailable. We introduce LaplaceDiag, a data-driven method that uses changes in actuator effects to narrow the search for faulty equipment. Actuators act on specific devices and mechanisms, so their changed effects can provide clues to root causes. LaplaceDiag learns a healthy plant model with LaplaceNet, a neural network that operates in Laplace space. It separates nonlinear prediction based on measured history from an explicit matrix that describes how actuator values affect sensor values. Keeping the history predictor fixed allows current actuator effects to be estimated by linear regression without retraining the neural network. Comparison with a healthy reference accounts for estimation uncertainty and normal variation to detect changes and generate actuator-related diagnostic hypotheses. The method supports online and offline diagnosis, providing an intermediate step between anomaly detection and identifying faulty components. We successfully evaluate LaplaceDiag on two datasets.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz for the Toda chain from inverse scattering transform
papers.abstract: The Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) procedure developed by Yang-Yang provides the free energy functional to be minimized via a variational problem. Their result not only gives the correct thermodynamics, but it also sets the framework for Generalized Hydrodynamics. Originally developed for quantum systems, this procedure has been recently successfully applied to (integrable) classical particle systems. However, this has never been done for classical field theories: no classical derivation has consistently accounted for solitons, breathers, radiation (dispersive modes), and their mutual interactions. We here derive the TBA equations for the Toda chain directly from its inverse scattering transform. This results in solitonic modes interacting with radiation, extending the soliton gas picture. We provide numerical verification of our equations against well established TBA equations in terms of particle modes. We expect the same procedure should apply to KdV, and pure radiative models as defocusing NLS and Sinh-Gordon, while we discuss current limitations in other models such as focusing NLS (and Ablowitz-Ladik) and Sine-Gordon.
papers.intro:
In recent years we have witnessed a large amount of scientific production in the field of integrable many-body systems [13, 30, 4, 58, 24]. This is mainly about one-dimensional Hamiltonian systems, and there are very good reasons for such interest. Integrable systems are, exceptionally, exactly solvable, and they allow to explore strongly interacting physics beyond approximations. This, combined with numerical accessibility of one-dimensional systems and experimental realizability [69, 71, 56, 52] creates the perfect conditions for a fruitful physical program. Although the early work of Yang–Yang goes back more than 50 years [72, 59], and Generalized Hydrodynamics [6, 15] has by now a decade of history, the subject is far from being exhausted.

The Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) is the central framework for many-body integrable systems [38]. These are described by stable modes that scatter elastically, and the TBA connects the macroscopic density of these modes with the stationary states, the generalized Gibbs ensembles (GGEs). Generalized Hydrodynamics is naturally formulated in the same language. The TBA was originally derived for quantum systems. However, its interpretation is simple and not specifically quantum, and this makes it reasonable that the same description applies to classical systems. The difficulty is practical: in the quantum case the Bethe ansatz quantizes the spectrum, and this provides a way to count the modes and obtain their entropy, while for classical systems there is no quantization, and it is not obvious how the counting should be done. For classical particle systems this has been achieved, first for the Toda fluid [57, 29] and then for integrable particle systems with arbitrary scattering shift [25], and even for more exotic systems, as the box-ball system [50].

Different is for integrable nonlinear wave equations, or classical field theories, such as Korteweg de Vries, nonlinear Schrödinger, sine-Gordon, Landau-Lifshitz (as well as their lattice versions). Since the late 1960s, the deterministic evolution of integrable nonlinear waves has been described via the inverse scattering transform (IST) [2, 55, 35], obtaining exact profiles in terms of solitons and dispersive radiation. Much less is understood when the initial conditions are random [76, 34]. They feature as excitations solitons, breathers and dispersive radiation, and the obstacle to a TBA formulation is the counting of the modes of a wave field, in particular for delocalized modes as the dispersive radiation and extended solitons. It is not even clear whether radiation enters the thermodynamics at all, since in some semiclassical limits it is found to be replaced by extended solitons [46, 45]. Existing approaches are indirect or partial. The Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz has been obtained for some models through semiclassical limits of quantum ones [19, 23, 46, 45, 5], but not from first-principles. Soliton gas theory [74, 33, 32] works instead at the hydrodynamic level: it provides a kinetic equation for large numbers of solitons, with the same structure of Generalized Hydrodynamics [27, 8], but it excludes the dispersive modes, and whether it is complete is not settled.

Since the TBA from the fluid side is very well understood, the Toda chain is an ideal setup to understand how to construct the TBA for nonlinear waves. In addition, it features a single species of solitons interacting with radiation, and no breathers, which makes it a minimal model for the soliton-radiation interaction.

In this paper, we give the first derivation of the TBA for the Toda chain in terms of solitons and radiation, based on the inverse scattering transform. We will refer to this as chain TBA, to distinguish it from the fluid TBA above. Within this approach, the key object is the Lax operator, whose spectrum encodes the excitations: the discrete spectrum corresponds to solitons, the continuous spectrum connects to radiation. The main new ideas we introduce are essentially two. The first one is a criterion to decide whether radiation is extensive or not. We show that the extensivity of the radiation is related to the localization of the absolutely continuous spectrum of the Lax operator, due to the randomness of the generalized Gibbs ensemble. In the case of Toda, the Lax operator takes the form of a random Jacobi operator, so this is really Anderson localization. Then, we propose a calculation that counts the entropy of the radiative modes, similar in spirit to the one of Doyon for classical particles, obtaining a Rayleigh-Jeans type of statistics.

papers.title: Time to AC-t: When AC-transmission changes capacity expansion planning
papers.abstract: Capacity expansion models often dramatically simplify the physics of how power flows through a transmission network in order to preserve computational tractability. However, with the rapid growth of electrification, large loads, renewables, and storage, increased realism in planning future grids is imperative. We extend the open-source capacity expansion model GenX with AC optimal power flow physics, and analyze generation, storage, and transmission investment decisions for 20-zone, hourly models of Germany and Texas. We compare our results against those using two common approximations, the transport model and DC optimal power flow. We find that total costs and emissions largely agree across all formulations. However, we find substantial differences in outputs related to transmission, generation siting, storage, and reactive-power support between the approximate formulations and the true AC physics formulation. We identify where AC physics changes planning decisions and discuss how to potentially capture these effects without the full computational cost.

papers.intro:
Electricity systems worldwide are undergoing rapid transformation. On the supply side, the falling cost of low-emission generation and storage1 along with fuel price volatility is changing the generation mix. On the demand side, rising electricity consumption in emerging markets,2 increasing electrification of end-use sectors,3, 4 and the emergence of new large loads such as data centers8 are reshaping demand profiles and peak-load patterns. The transmission and distribution networks that connect supply and demand are also challenged by rising congestion and investment barriers.6, 7 Against this backdrop, balancing supply and demand reliably and affordably requires careful long-term system planning alongside regulatory and policy frameworks to align market incentives with broader system-wide objectives.

Capacity expansion models (CEMs) are a central tool for long-term planning, identifying the least-cost combination of generation, storage, and (in some cases) transmission investments needed to meet projected demand.8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 Like any model, CEMs must balance fidelity with computational tractability. While spatial and temporal resolution are classic dimensions of this trade-off,14, 15, 16 the representation of the power transmission network also affects both model results and runtime.12 At the high-fidelity end is AC optimal power flow (ACOPF). This representation captures all steady-state network physics, including how reactive power must be supplied to keep voltages within their limits. The resulting constraints are nonlinear and nonconvex, making any CEM that incorporates ACOPF rather expensive to solve in long-term planning contexts.17, 18 CEMs therefore use simplified transmission representations that reduce the computational burden. These include DC optimal power flow (DCOPF),19, 20 which neglects reactive power and voltage magnitudes, and the transport model,21 which only limits power flows by per-line capacities. Today, the transport model is the default in many open-source planning tools.22, 23, 24, 25

Although simplifying the network representation improves tractability, an important question remains unresolved: to what extent does it distort planning outcomes? Previous studies in both generation expansion and, separately, transmission expansion have found varying results. On the generation side, Weng et al. Super compare the transport model against ACOPF, finding significant differences in generation capacity investments for a 3-zone model of ISO New England. Wogrin et al. Super add reactive power constraints to generation expansion planning through a second-order cone approximation of AC power flow; they show that omitting these detailed transmission constraints can distort optimal resource allocation and cause infeasibilities. On the transmission side, Bent et al. Super find that DC transmission expansion plans substantially underestimate expansion costs and violate AC line and voltage limits when evaluated on the full network. Zhang et al. Super, who augment a transmission expansion model with a linearized representation of reactive power and losses, similarly find that DC-based plans can require additional network reinforcements. In their model of Egypt’s transmission network, Farrag et al. Super find that AC selects fewer lines than DC formulations. In contrast, Cameron et al. Super report close agreement between AC- and DC-based transmission investment costs. These generation and transmission expansion studies provide important insights, but most focus on small test networks, and none model renewables-rich systems where generation, transmission, and storage all compete for investment.

We systematically compare three power flow formulations of increasing physical realism – the transport model, DCOPF, and full ACOPF – across two 20-zone systems representing Germany and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT).

To conduct this study, we extend the open-source CEM GenX22 with full AC power flow constraints. Our experiments co-optimize generation, storage, and transmission investment under AC power flow across 20 zones and a year of hourly operation. In our framework, we develop a representation of reactive power for CEMs, deriving each resource’s reactive capability from grid-code power factor requirements. We also extend GenX’s DCOPF formulation to allow for transmission expansion, updating impedances as line capacity is added, consistent with ACOPF. Finally, while neither the transport model nor DCOPF inherently represents losses, common practice is to approximate them linearly as a fixed fraction of flow;22, 24 we adopt this approach for both approximate formulations to allow a more fair comparison with ACOPF.

To conduct this study, we extend the open-source CEM GenX22 with full AC power flow constraints. Our experiments co-optimize generation, storage, and transmission investment under AC power flow across 20 zones and a year of hourly operation. In our framework, we develop a representation of reactive power for CEMs, deriving each resource’s reactive capability from grid-code power factor requirements. We also extend GenX’s DCOPF formulation to allow for transmission expansion, updating impedances as line capacity is added, consistent with ACOPF. Finally, while neither the transport model nor DCOPF inherently represents losses, common practice is to approximate them linearly as a fixed fraction of flow;22, 24 we adopt this approach for both approximate formulations to allow a more fair comparison with ACOPF.

We find that the three formulations agree on total system cost to within 1.2%, but differ considerably in where generation is built and how much storage and transmission are installed. In Germany, total generation capacity differs from ACOPF by only 2.1% under transport and 1.2% under DC, yet the median zonal capacity differences are 37.5% and 12.0%, respectively. Some of these differences arise because the transport model does not capture competition between renewable generators for shared transmission capacity, allowing more investment at sites whose output would otherwise contribute to congestion. Reactive power requirements also affect investment decisions. Under our baseline assumptions, ACOPF builds more battery power capacity, with shorter storage duration, to supply reactive power alongside batteries’ use for energy arbitrage. The size of this effect depends on how we model reactive capability and which technologies can provide it. These results suggest that simplified transmission models can give similar system-wide results while selecting quite different investments, an important distinction when using CEMs to inform generation siting and network expansion.

papers.title: The vertical distribution of molecular gas in the fourth quadrant of the Milky Way
papers.abstract: The vertical distribution of molecular gas in the Milky Way disk is poorly studied, especially in the 4th quadrant and the far side of the Galaxy. While surveys over 20 years ago suffered from coarse beam and non-Nyquist sampling, most of the recent surveys are limited to $|b|<1^\circ$ and/or focus on the Northern Galactic plane. We examine the molecular gas's vertical distribution and properties in the fourth quadrant to check the impact of Galactic structure on current star formation. We mapped two arm tangent regions ($l=[329^\circ.0,327^\circ.0]$ for the Norma-Outer arm, and $l=[310^\circ.0,308^\circ.5]$ for the Scutum-Centaurus arm) with the $^{12}$CO 3-2 line using the 7-pixel LASMA receiver of the APEX 12 m telescope, covering up to $b=[-2^\circ,+2^\circ]$ (or $|z|\sim200$ pc near the tangent points). The noise level of the $^{12}$CO 3-2 line is about 0.4 K [$T_{MB}$] in velocity channels of 0.5 km s$^{-1}$. The vertical distribution around the tangent regions of the spiral arm is fitted with two Gaussian components, the narrow one with an FWHM thickness of 25 pc and the wide one of about 100 pc. Two explanations are proposed: they are two sub-components of the thin disk (the narrowest tracing the spiral arm and the other the inter arms components), or they trace both thin and thick disks that show a smaller thickness when observed with CO 3-2 than when observed with CO 1-0. The latter indicates that the density distribution of the interstellar medium exhibits a steeper gradient at larger heights above the plane. Clumps in the two tangent regions are searched and divided into groups by relative height. Compared with the low relative height clumps ($|z|<50$ pc), the median relative height clumps ($50~\mathrm{pc}<|z|<100~\mathrm{pc}$) have lower excitation temperature and surface density, with fewer high values in the distribution. A similar tentative trend is found for the mass.

The Galactic disk is a composite of stars and interstellar medium (ISM) formed primarily of H I gas and H2 gas. All of them can be further divided into two components, namely the thin disk and the thick disk. The vertical distributions of the stellar disk and the H I disk are better understood than the H2 disk, as we summarize in the following.

This study shows that one can still identify thin and thick molecular disks with high-resolution observations, although with a relatively high RMS noise at 0.5 K for 0.16 km s-1 channel rather than the old 0.1 K data of Dame & Thaddeus (1994) in which the thick molecular disk was discovered. In addition, they found that the FWHM and midplane displacement of the thin disk have a variability depending on the longitude of tangent regions. This MWISP study is limited to the tangent regions in the first quadrant, where the distance can be well determined. However, due to their 50″ resolution, the MWISP study had to include both clouds on the spiral arms and inter-arm clouds for better statistics, but the authors did not compare their high-latitude clouds with the low-latitude sample. In addition, their samples had a large range of Galactocentric distances, which may include other environmental effects rather than the height of targets.

With this higher resolution, we are able to resolve a linear scale of about 0.5 pc at two tangent positions (distances about 5 kpc), which allows us to detect a statistically significant number of molecular structures and to examine the vertical distribution of their physical parameters for dense structures rather than large clouds for the first time to our knowledge. Across this work, we call a structure as a clump when it is a hierarchical, connected region of CO emission bounded by an iso-intensity surface and without sub-structure in our our 0.5 pc beam (see Sect. 4.2 for details).

papers.title: LINDA: Low Resource Foot Ulcer Segmentation using Local Similarity and Iterative Neural Dynamics
papers.abstract: Foot ulcers are a leading cause of lower limb amputation, and the highest burden often falls on low and middle income regions where specialists and computing hardware are both scarce. Wound monitoring tools are most useful there when they are accurate yet small enough to run on ordinary devices, but accuracy usually comes from heavy networks. We present LINDA, a compact model that grounds segmentation in an explicit structural prior instead of raw intensity. A Local Self-Similarity (LSS) map, computed directly from the image and stable under local lighting changes, is fused into a ResNet-34 encoder, and a small Liquid Time-Constant module refines the boundary over four iterative steps. With every model trained under one protocol on the FUSeg 2021 dataset, LINDA obtains the best Dice (86.68\%), IoU (79.67\%), and boundary accuracy (HD95 6.37 pixels) in our comparison while using only 25.70M parameters, fewer than the U-Net and transformer baselines. As the LSS map is a fixed function of the input, it exposes the structural cues the model follows in a readable form. Together this makes LINDA an accurate, inspectable, and lightweight option for wound assessment in resource-constrained care.

papers.intro:
Foot ulcers are a primary cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation [1], and precise delineation of the wound bed is needed to track healing and plan treatment [2]. Manual planimetry, the clinical gold standard, is subjective, slow, and varies between observers, so automated segmentation has become a priority. In many settings, and especially in low and middle income regions, this must run with limited specialist time and limited computing hardware, which favors models that are accurate yet small enough for modest devices.

Foot ulcers are a primary cause of non-traumatic lower-limb amputation [1], and precise delineation of the wound bed is needed to track healing and plan treatment [2]. Manual planimetry, the clinical gold standard, is subjective, slow, and varies between observers, so automated segmentation has become a priority. In many settings, and especially in low and middle income regions, this must run with limited specialist time and limited computing hardware, which favors models that are accurate yet small enough for modest devices.

Despite recent advances [3], automated foot ulcer segmentation remains a hard problem. Ulcers vary widely in scale, lighting, and texture. The transition zones between necrotic tissue, granulation tissue, and healthy skin are often ambiguous, with low contrast and diffuse gradients [4]. Widely used architectures such as U-Net variants [5] and Vision Transformers (ViTs) [6] perform well on many medical segmentation tasks, yet wound boundaries can remain imprecise when ulcer shapes are irregular and contrast with healthy skin is low. Convolutional encoders have a limited receptive field, while the patch tokenization in ViTs can blur fine boundary detail and lead to oversmoothed masks [7]. Most of these models also predict the mask in a single forward pass, unlike the way a human reader traces a boundary, revisiting and adjusting it as local and global cues are weighed.

To address these limitations, we propose LINDA, a boundary aware architecture for foot ulcer segmentation. First, a Local Self-Similarity (LSS) map is computed directly from the input image and fused into a pretrained ResNet-34 backbone, giving the early layers explicit local texture awareness. Second, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) network [8] at the bottleneck acts as an iterative refinement loop that resolves boundary ambiguities. Finally, the structural prior stays visible: because the LSS map is computed before encoding and used as the target of the boundary loss, it offers a concrete, readable view of the cues the network follows, in the spirit of explainable AI in clinical imaging [9, 10, 11].

Second, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) network [8] at the bottleneck acts as an iterative refinement loop that resolves boundary ambiguities. Our contributions are as follows. (1) An additive LSS fusion module injects local patch-correlation statistics into the early encoder features, anchoring the network to tissue boundaries without disturbing the pretrained weights. (2) An LTC-driven refinement loop at the bottleneck uses iterative dynamics to refine a global spatial token that conditions the decoder. (3) A Boundary Alignment Loss ties the prediction to the LSS map, giving the lowest boundary error in our comparison together with strong overlap accuracy at a low parameter count. Overall, these components form a compact, interpretable foot ulcer segmentation model that matches the strongest baselines on region overlap and clearly improves boundary precision, while using far fewer parameters, a good fit for resource-constrained clinical settings.

papers.title: Constraining Dust Properties Along the Minor Axis of Andromeda
papers.abstract: Previous studies of dust emission in M31 based primarily on Herschel data have reported inconsistent radial trends in the dust emissivity index ($\beta$), partly due to limited wavelength coverage and the intrinsic $T_{\rm dust}$-$\beta$ degeneracy. We aim to improve the constraints of $\beta$ determinations and obtain the spatial surface density and temperature distributions at GMC scales in M31 by extending the spectral coverage into the millimeter regime and by quantifying the impact of wavelength coverage on the $T_{\rm dust}$-$\beta$ degeneracy. We present new IRAM 30m NIKA2 1.15 mm observations along the minor axis of M31 at an angular resolution of 11 arcsec, corresponding to $\sim 40$ pc at the distance of M31. These data are used with Herschel and JCMT SCUBA-2 maps to perform pixel-by-pixel single-component modified blackbody fitting. Including the 850 $\mu$m and 1.15 mm data helps reduce the $T_{\rm dust}$-$\beta$ degeneracy and yields an average emissivity index of $\beta \approx 1.8$, systematically lower than values derived from far-infrared-only analyses. Radial analysis shows higher $\beta$ values in the 5 kpc ring compared to the 10 kpc ring. The elevated $\beta$ values in the inner 5 kpc may be linked to changes in dust composition, potentially associated with enhanced starlight heating in this region. Millimeter wavelength coverage is important for improving $\beta$ constraints in M31. The lower $\beta$ values inferred from the 250--1150 $\mu$m SED fitting suggest possible variations in dust emissivity and highlight the importance of sampling the long-wavelength SED slope in nearby galaxies.

papers.title: Reconstruction-Based Diagnosis through G\"odel-Regularized Virtual Observability
papers.abstract: Not every component in a technical system can be equipped with sensors. Hence, when a fault occurs, available sensors often detect it only after its effects have propagated. This makes the isolation of faults difficult. We approach this problem by introducing virtual sensors. For each combination of component and fault type, we let external knowledge describe the fault-sensitive variables. We introduce a novel neural observer that is only trained on normal data. For fault isolation, it uses available sensor measurements where it is possible and reconstructs missing variables as virtual sensors to predict normal behavior. It detects deviations between current values and nominal predictions and computes local symptoms, which are then compared by onset time. The result is a set of root causes describing the faulty behavior. We use G\"odel logic to encode physical knowledge and guide training. We evaluate our approach on synthetic networks, the Tennessee Eastman Process, and datasets of two modular production plants.

papers.intro:
Fault diagnosis supports the safe and reliable operation of technical processes. But not all behaviors within a system can be observed at all times. A fault may hence appear at an unobserved location and its effects then propagate through material, energy, and control connections before a sensor can detect them. Noise and delays can change the order of symptoms. Model-based methods address this with residual and structural models (Isermann, 2005; Krysander et al., 2008), while data-driven methods learn normal or faulty behavior from observations (Qin, 2012). Both must infer the cause from indirect and delayed evidence.

Suppose that every possible root cause had a fault-sensitive local sensor that reacts before all propagated symptoms. The first persistent local symptom would then identify the root cause, and fault isolation would reduce to comparing symptom onset times. However, no real-world plants offer such complete coverage, and learned estimates remain uncertain. In this article we address how machine learning can close the observation gaps without hiding this uncertainty.

We propose Reconstruction-Based Diagnosis through Virtual Observability (ReDiVO) which employs virtual sensors to make the whole system observable. We use available a-priori knowledge to determine the components within the system and associate these with known sensor locations. We then identify locations that contain components but have no direct sensors monitoring the specific components. For instance, if some pump performance is not measured, we reconstruct it from related process measurements like downstream flow and control signals. Measured and virtual sensors together create virtual observability, this means that every fault candidate has at least one observed or virtual root-cause variable. We propose a neural observer which compares the current value of each variable with a nominal prediction learned from normal data, both as uncertainty ranges. A persistent separation of these ranges is a local symptom. We compare the onset times of these symptoms and return a set of candidate diagnoses.

We pursue a hybrid approach fusing data-driven modeling of normal behavior with a-priori knowledge. Without reference values, normal data alone may not determine a reconstruction uniquely. A shifted or rescaled estimate of the pump performance, for example, can predict the measured flows equally well. We therefore add physical knowledge about topology, qualitative dependencies, balances, and operating constraints, expressed as rules in Gödel logic. During training, rule violations penalize the reconstructions and nominal predictions. For example, a higher pump performance should not reduce downstream flow when all other influences stay fixed. Such a rule favors plausible estimates without forcing the pump to stay nominal.

papers.title: Variational Learning with Lie Group Exponential Families
papers.abstract: Variational Bayesian learning for deep neural networks offers many potential benefits. The difficulty in implementation arises from constraints on the parameters of the variational distributions, as well as the need for low-variance gradient estimators. Our recent work proposes Lie group methods for multiplicative or affine groups that naturally overcome such difficulties. Lie groups are essentially parameter spaces with a binary operator such as addition or multiplication, which allows for natural updates within the parameter space. In this article, we streamline and extend our Lie group framework to any general Lie group, and give an explicit relation to standard natural-gradient variational learning methods such as the Bayesian learning rule (BLR). In particular, we prove that linear approximations of the Lie group algorithm give generalizations of the BLR. The key ingredient is the harmonic exponential family, a general class of Lie group exponential families associated to representations of Lie groups. Our work provides a systematic method to construct from such representations efficiently implementable algorithms for variational learning.

papers.intro:
Variational learning for neural networks (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011) offers many potential benefits over standard empirical risk minimization and can be used to motivate various deep-learning algorithms (Khan and Rue, 2023). Some of the benefits of variational learning are improved regularization and reduced overfitting, as suggested by the minimum description length principle (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011; Blier and Ollivier, 2018; Grünwald, 2007) and PAC-Bayesian bounds (Alquier, 2024). Depending on the form of the variational posterior, different deep learning algorithms can be obtained, for instance, Adam-like methods (Shen et al., 2024) for diagonal Gaussians, algorithms for binary neural networks for Bernoulli distributions (Meng et al., 2020) and biologically plausible multiplicative dynamics for log-normal distributions (Nishida et al., 2026). The Bayesian viewpoint also offers a fruitful framework for thinking about model adaptation and model understanding, for example, federated and continual learning (Nguyen et al., 2018; Ashman et al., 2022), model merging (Matena and Raffel, 2022; Daheim et al., 2024) or sensitivity analysis to perturbations in both the model and data (Nickl et al., 2023).

Variational learning for neural networks (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011) offers many potential benefits over standard empirical risk minimization and can be used to motivate various deep-learning algorithms (Khan and Rue, 2023). Some of the benefits of variational learning are improved regularization and reduced overfitting, as suggested by the minimum description length principle (Hinton and Van Camp, 1993; Graves, 2011; Blier and Ollivier, 2018; Grünwald, 2007) and PAC-Bayesian bounds (Alquier, 2024). Depending on the form of the variational posterior, different deep learning algorithms can be obtained, for instance, Adam-like methods (Shen et al., 2024) for diagonal Gaussians, algorithms for binary neural networks for Bernoulli distributions (Meng et al., 2020) and biologically plausible multiplicative dynamics for log-normal distributions (Nishida et al., 2026). The Bayesian viewpoint also offers a fruitful framework for thinking about model adaptation and model understanding, for example, federated and continual learning (Nguyen et al., 2018; Ashman et al., 2022), model merging (Matena and Raffel, 2022; Daheim et al., 2024) or sensitivity analysis to perturbations in both the model and data (Nickl et al., 2023).

The de-facto standard approach for variational learning in neural networks is to update the distribution parameters using gradient-based methods to leverage backpropagation training (Graves, 2011). Khan and Rue (2023), for example, use a natural gradient method on the natural parameters of an exponential family. This method has two main difficulties. First, one needs to satisfy constraints on the parameters of the distribution, for example, positivity of the covariance matrix in the case of Gaussians (Lin et al., 2020). Secondly, the objective functions involve integrals with respect to the variational distribution, and obtaining low-variance stochastic gradients is a major challenge. Reparametrization tricks provide such estimators, but it is not clear whether they are available for the variational family at hand and they have to be derived case by case (Mohamed et al., 2020).

Recently, Kıral et al. (2023) proposed a learning algorithm which addresses the above difficulties by parametrizing the probability distribution through Lie groups. The constraints on the parameters are naturally handled through the group’s closure and lower variance gradients are available by default as the Lie group automatically enables the reparametrization technique. In this work we establish the connection between the Lie group updates and existing methods on exponential families (EFs) such as the Bayesian Learning Rule (BLR) by Khan and Rue (2023). The Lie group update rule does not require the family to be an EF, however many useful families are EFs. EFs are especially well suited to the Bayesian framework, which relies on multiplication and division of distributions to add, remove or modify information. This corresponds to simple addition and subtraction on the natural parameters of the family, connecting the Bayesian framework to optimizing on natural parameters. EFs come with a rich structure, such as dually flat coordinate systems of natural and expectation parameters studied in information geometry (Amari, 2016). As EFs have many desirable properties, the aim of this paper is to further study the Lie group learning rule of Kıral et al. (2023) when specialized to EFs and to understand its relation to the Bayesian learning rule (Khan and Rue, 2023) which is derived for EFs and gives a unifying and simplifying view of many other algorithms.

Those EFs which also have a Lie group structure are families of distributions which combine the best of both worlds, and it should therefore not be surprising that most of the eponymous EFs named after a mathematician share this property. They have the above desirable properties of EFs, but the additional group structure gives easy reparametrization tricks and allows for updating without breaking constraints. Developing a recipe to construct exponential families on homogeneous spaces from real representations of Lie groups, Tojo and Yoshino (2021) redefine the term harmonic exponential families subsuming the earlier definition coined by Cohen and Welling (2015) for homogeneous spaces of compact Lie groups via unitary representations. These families characterize all exponential families closed under a Lie group action. Using this characterization we establish a general and concrete connection between the Lie group update and BLR. Our main contribution is to prove that the linearization of the update proposed by Kıral et al. (2023) always recovers the Bayesian learning rule for exponential families with Lie group structure, see Theorem 13. Altogether, our work supplies the theoretical foundations for efficient algorithms for variational learning using Lie groups and exponential families.

papers.title: Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models
papers.abstract: This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets.

The aerodynamic design of front wings for automotive applications relies heavily on computational fluid dynamics (CFD), which, while accurate, demands substantial computational resources and turnaround time. In motorsport applications, for example, fast-paced design cycles require hundreds of geometry iterations within months, making the computational cost of fluid simulations a significant bottleneck.

The reason for this cost is that a direct analytical solution to the equations which describe the motion of viscous fluids, such as air, has not yet been discovered. The equations in question are known as the Navier-Stokes equations [1], which CFD software aims to resolve iteratively through finite volume methods. Even with these strategies, however, simplified modeling of the most complex flow behaviors has to be employed in order to keep the simulation time within reasonable limits. One such simplification, used in this paper, is the usage of the RANS (Reynolds Averaged Navier Stokes) [2] equations instead, whose solution provides the time-averaged flow field across the simulation domain, while using models [3] to calculate the effects of instantaneous turbulence. In addition, to allow for these methodologies to produce meaningful results, newly designed geometries require extensive preprocessing even before the simulation itself can start. CAD surfaces need to be made perfectly watertight, discretization of the airflow volume needs to be obtained through meshing, and boundary conditions for all relevant surfaces need to be set, all of which require a combination of manpower and computational effort.

By learning a mapping from geometric inputs directly to flow field solutions, they can provide predictions of flow variables by avoiding the iterative residual minimization of traditional CFD solvers altogether. They also do not require a mesh to produce a result, as they can operate on simpler representations of the objects of interest, such as simple 3D point clouds, sampled directly from a CAD geometry. This reduces the need for resource intensive meshing pipelines. By leveraging architectures such as Neural Operators [4] they feature the possibility for predictions on arbitrarily (i.e. distinct from the training setup) dense grids.

papers.title: A general sharp-interface simulation framework for microstructure evolution
papers.abstract: Simulating microstructure evolution requires tracking many moving grain and phase boundaries coupled to thermodynamic and mechanical fields. We present Gaussian-projected kinetics (GPK), a sharp-interface framework in which every cell stores an integer grain or phase label. Near a boundary, a temporary Gaussian projection of the label map provides the interface normal and curvature and is then discarded. Capillarity, chemistry, stored energy, transport and elasticity move the boundaries through one topology-preserving update. Because the Gaussian measurement length is fixed in physical units, mesh refinement keeps a consistent capillary scale without a diffuse interface. GPK models grain growth, recrystallisation, multiphase evolution and elastic-coupled solidification in two and three dimensions. It is verified on analytical benchmarks and compared grain by grain with phase-field simulations, running 8.5 to 96 times faster at matched accuracy in our tests. An Al-Cu application with CALPHAD thermodynamic data connects it to measured recrystallisation and precipitation data.

papers.intro:
Microstructure evolution determines many structure–property relationships in metals and alloys. Important examples are isotropic and anisotropic grain growth, recrystallisation and multiphase boundary migration 1; 2. All of them combine capillarity with chemical, stored-energy or mechanical driving forces. Computational methods differ mainly in how they represent the interfaces and how they enforce the local force balance at them 3; 4.

Microstructure evolution determines many structure–property relationships in metals and alloys. Important examples are isotropic and anisotropic grain growth, recrystallisation and multiphase boundary migration 1; 2. All of them combine capillarity with chemical, stored-energy or mechanical driving forces. Computational methods differ mainly in how they represent the interfaces and how they enforce the local force balance at them 3; 4.

Diffuse-interface phase-field models are among the most general approaches for considering such microstructure scenarios with multiple interacting forces at mesoscopic scale 5; 6; 7. In a diffuse-interface model, the boundary between two grains or phases is not a sharp surface. Instead, a continuous order parameter changes smoothly from its value in one grain or phase to its value in the other. This change takes place over a finite width, the interface thickness. The interfacial energy and the boundary motion are computed from spatial derivatives of this smooth profile. These derivatives are accurate only when the computational grid places several points across the interface thickness. The interface thickness therefore often sets the grid spacing, and hence the computational cost. The size of the microstructural features of interest is often much larger. Phase-field models encode interfacial thermodynamics in continuous order parameters. They couple naturally to conserved and mechanical fields 8; 9; 5; 10; 11. Relevant applications include multiphase formulations 12 and grain growth in two and three dimensions 13; 14. They also include recrystallisation and chemically or elastically coupled phase evolution 15; 16. Quantitative calculations must resolve a finite interface thickness in phase-field model frameworks. In addition, polycrystalline models have to evolve by tracking multiple (grain-specific) order parameters. This renders three-dimensional and/or many-grain calculations computationally very costly and conceptually demanding.
