Grid-based sharp-interface methods offer a different balance. They divide the specimen into computational cells. Each cell receives a discrete label, such as “grain 17” or the “aluminium-rich phase”. Simple local transition rules can then move a boundary by changing a cell’s label. This representation is computationally economical. It can also produce complex collective microstructure evolution. The rules must, however, be designed carefully. The reason is that a pixelated boundary does not directly provide a curvature or a unique normal direction. Cellular automata are a widely used example in recrystallisation modelling 17; 18; 19. Their neighborhood rules are conceptually simple. They can, however, make curvature, anisotropy and thermodynamic calibration difficult to control, and they can introduce grid dependence. This renders proper time-step scaling challenging. It also makes it difficult to consider configurational and scalar driving forces at the same time. Level-set methods instead represent a boundary as the zero contour of a continuous, distance-like field. They provide accurate sharp-interface motion and kinetic evolution for grain growth and recrystallisation 20; 21. Threshold dynamics alternates convolution and relabelling to reproduce mean-curvature flow 22; 23. These methods avoid resolving a physical diffuse layer. Additional machinery is, however, needed when several phases, thermodynamic driving forces and cell-wise mechanical fields interact.

We develop Gaussian-projected kinetics (GPK) to combine the strengths of both approaches. GPK keeps the compact state of a grid-based label method. It adds the smooth geometry and the explicit material laws that are familiar from continuum models. The central idea is to separate what the microstructure is from how its boundary geometry is measured. Integer labels preserve grain or phase identity from one timestep to the next. A temporary Gaussian projection, computed separately for each label, converts the stepped boundary into a smooth measurement field. A sub-cell fraction records where the sharp boundary lies inside an interfacial cell. This fraction does not depend on the Gaussian width. Interchangeable material modules then provide the mobility, the free-energy difference and the interfacial energy. The projection therefore tackles the numerical capillarity problem. It supplies a stable local interface normal and curvature. It does not replace the constitutive model, and it does not prescribe how far the boundary moves. This is an important difference from Gaussian threshold dynamics. There, convolution and thresholding together define the curvature-flow timestep. In GPK, convolution only measures geometry, and a separate physical kinetic law determines the displacement. Figure 1 summarises this distinction and exemplifies a complete modelling cycle.

The study addresses three questions. First, can a common data structure hold grain and phase identity, optional material fields and temporary interface geometry, with one strictly defined role for each? In particular, the identity labels and material fields should be the only information carried from one timestep to the next. The temporary geometry field should only measure the boundary shape. It should never change a label or a material field by itself. Second, can one kinetic law and one Gaussian geometry measurement be stated with unambiguous signs, units and resolution limits? Third, can different material processes use the same geometry and update engine in both two and three dimensions? The evaluation therefore tests the complete modelling framework. It does not test the Gaussian function or the curvature formula in isolation.

papers.title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering
papers.abstract: Defect states directly influence not only functional properties, but also oxynitride formation during ammonolysis. Along with structural stability and charge balance, these defects can cause non-uniform nitrogen incorporation. To address this, the recently proposed Fermi Level Engineering concept provides a powerful alternative of rationalising oxynitride synthesis. By using the electron chemical potential, i.e., the Fermi level, as a unique descriptor, this approach can predict, understand, and manipulate defect formation enthalpies and charge transition levels, subsequently allowing to incorporate defect-property correlations to the concept. This work combines theoretical modelling and experimental characterisation of barium titanium oxynitrides to explain an intrinsic, self-limiting nitridation process. Progressive nitrogen incorporation causes a Fermi level downward shift, leaving further nitrogen substitution on oxygen sites energetically unfavourable, up to 0.03 N per unit formula. We demonstrate that A-site cation substitution in Eu$_{1-x}$Ba$_x$TiO$_3$- and Eu$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$TiO$_3$-derived oxynitrides can be applied to control compensation of the additional negative charge from N$^{3-}$ and keep the Fermi level high. The Eu$^{2+/3+}$ redox couple enables substitution of oxygen by nitrogen through pinning of the Fermi level at the europium charge transition level, at $\sim$ 2.9 eV above the VBM. This allows for higher nitrogen uptake of up to 0.65 per formula unit (taken from hot gas extraction) through a more controlled process. Further incorporation is then limited by an intra-Ti(O,N)$_6$ octahedra distortion due to internal bond-angle variance. These findings demonstrate that Fermi Level Engineering provides a pathway to predict and overcome intrinsic synthetic and thermodynamic limitations in oxynitride synthesis.

papers.title: Non-Interfering Asymmetric AdamW Updates for Constrained Exploration of Equifinality in Hybrid Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid models let neural networks supply the unresolved parameters of a process-based simulator, and are fitted to observations that constrain aggregate fluxes and storages but not the internal partitioning that produces them. Such a fit is equifinal: configurations indistinguishable in the observed aggregates can disagree substantially about the unobserved internals, and therefore about the mechanism they attribute to the same data. We study evapotranspiration, whose total flux is observed while its split into transpiration and evaporation is not. A model ensemble built from random seeds alone spans only a narrow band of the partitionings the data admit. We produce the spread deliberately, training members under auxiliary repulsion on transpiration, subject to the fit to observations not degrading. Non-interference is usually arranged by making the auxiliary gradient orthogonal to the main one, but under AdamW the applied step is a preconditioned momentum direction, so orthogonality between raw gradients no longer implies it. We introduce Non-interfering Asymmetric Network Optimization (NANO), an update whose first-order effect on the main loss is exactly that of the main objective alone, whose auxiliary step is bounded, and which concentrates repulsion in the coordinates the main gradient leaves idle.

papers.title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. papers.title: Safeguarding Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Connected and Automated Vehicles with Recursively Feasible Control Barrier Functions
papers.abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) shows promise in coordinating connected and automated vehicles but offers no safety guarantee. Although Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) can add this guarantee, their optimization problem can become infeasible in practice due to control bounds. Moreover, they often overapproximate vehicle and road geometry, which makes them conservative. This paper proposes the Backup-Horizon CBF (BH-CBF), which evaluates safety along a horizon until all vehicles stop. BH-CBF is recursively feasible under control bounds, and it considers the exact vehicle and road geometry. Based on BH-CBF, we derive a fully decentralized safety filter that only needs a single broadcast of vehicle states and routes per step and stays real-time in dense traffic. We use BH-CBF to safeguard a MARL policy over its life cycle: as a reward during pre-training, as a run-time filter at deployment, and as a filter in the training loop that keeps fine-tuning on unseen maps collision-free. In simulations on real-world maps of a roundabout and an intersection, BH-CBF avoids all collisions of unsafe MARL policies and keeps its safety guarantee at every step. Existing filters either collide, lose the guarantee, or fall back to full braking far more often. In recorded roundabout traffic with 1264 human-driven vehicles over 115 km, our safeguarded policies shorten the median travel time by 14% compared with the human drivers, without any collision.

papers.intro:
Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policies have become a promising approach to coordinating Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) in interactive traffic such as merges, lane changes, intersections, and roundabouts [1, 2, 3, 4]. Such policies are fast at run time and scale with the number of vehicles, and they can learn cooperative behavior from interaction instead of relying on hand-designed coordination rules [1]. However, a learned policy offers no safety guarantee since it is trained to maximize a reward that scores its behavior. Collision penalties reduce collisions but do not exclude them, and the behavior of the policy degrades in scenarios that differ from training, such as unseen road layouts [5] or the transfer from simulation to real vehicles [6]. Therefore, safety-critical deployment requires a safeguard for the learned policy that does not depend on how well the policy generalizes.

Safeguards for learned policies can be classified by how they modify the action proposed by the policy [7], which we call the nominal action. Action masking restricts the action space to verified actions, action replacement substitutes a verified action, as in shields [8], and action projection moves the action to the closest safe one. We focus on action projection, which keeps interventions small. Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety filters are among the most prominent projection methods, where a Quadratic Program (QP) modifies the nominal action minimally so that a barrier condition holds [7]. The barrier condition bounds how fast a safety margin (e.g., the distance to the nearest vehicle) may shrink in the next step. It thereby keeps the system in a safe set of states at all future times, i.e., it renders the safe set forward invariant [9, 10]. Since CBF filters work with any nominal planner, they suit learned policies [11]. Learned graph CBFs even scale to more than a thousand agents, although their learned barriers are not verified [12]. For CAVs, MARL policies have been safeguarded by replacing unsafe merging actions with those of a priority-based supervisor [2] and by testing discrete lane-change actions for the feasibility of a CBF-QP [3]. However, two shortcomings of existing CBF filters limit their use for CAVs in dense urban traffic.

Lane-keeping CBFs bound the lateral offset of a reference point from the lane center [9, 14] or shrink the admissible lateral offsets and yaw angles of a rectangle on a straight lane to an inscribed ellipse [15]. Such approximations remove the lateral space a rectangular vehicle has in a narrow lane, which makes the filter conservative, lowers throughput, or even causes deadlocks. Optimization inside the filter can compute exact distances between convex shapes, but these methods solve one centralized QP over all robots [16] or address a single robot [17]. Moreover, the distance is zero for overlapping shapes, so it gives no direction to recover from a collision. The largest gap along the edge normals of two polygons is a closed-form lower bound of their signed distance that is negative when they overlap [18]. However, its smoothed version is proven to be a conservative continuous-time CBF only for two single integrators with unbounded inputs [19].

Second, existing CBF filters lack recursive feasibility, i.e., the guarantee that the filter finds an admissible control that satisfies the barrier condition at every future step. This lack is the most consequential limitation for safeguarding MARL policies. A function whose nonnegative values define the safe set is only a candidate CBF. It is a valid CBF if such a control exists at every safe state, and only then does the filter remain feasible and keep the safe set forward invariant [20, 21]. Under control bounds, no general method yields a valid CBF, so candidate CBFs are often used in practice without this guarantee [22, 23]. This is because the barrier condition is myopic: it constrains only the next step, whether a continuous-time condition is enforced at the sampling instants [14, 15, 19] or a discrete-time condition is imposed on a one-step prediction [24]. Some constraints are affected by the control indirectly. For example, an acceleration command changes the distance between two vehicles only through their speeds. The High-Order CBF handles such constraints by chaining a set of class 𝒦\mathcal{K} functions [22], whereas the Truncated Taylor CBF (TTCBF) of our prior work imposes the condition on a truncated Taylor prediction with a single class 𝒦\mathcal{K} function [25, 26]. In dense traffic, vehicles approach each other quickly when merging or entering a roundabout and come close to each other or to a lane boundary. Then no control within control bounds satisfies the condition, the QP becomes infeasible, and the safety guarantee is lost. CBF-based merging of CAVs [27] and a CBF shield for MARL-based CAV planning [3] share this limitation: both guarantees assume that the QP is feasible at every step. Model predictive shielding [8, 30], gatekeeper [31], and fail-safe trajectories [32] use action replacement: they substitute the backup control for an unsafe nominal action, so an intervention can jump from the nominal action to full braking. Backup CBFs impose continuous-time conditions along the backup over a fixed horizon that must end in a known safe set [33, 34]. A related reach-avoid value has been approximated online by differential dynamic programming [38]. For CAVs, these backup-based filters either switch abruptly to the backup, require a fixed horizon ending in a synthesized terminal set, or are limited to one vehicle or to barriers without a guarantee.

papers.title: Equal Access, Unequal Gains? GitHub Copilot and Productivity Among Developers with Disabilities
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly used in software development and have been associated with benefits such as faster task completion and improved perceived productivity. However, whether these benefits extend across different developer populations remains unclear. This is especially relevant for developers with disabilities, whose work can already be impacted by accessibility barriers. Yet, evidence remains limited across a broader range of disability groups. This study investigates whether the wider availability of GitHub Copilot is associated with changes in productivity among GitHub users who self-identify as having a disability. Using publicly available profile and repository data, we curated a dataset of 199 developers across multiple disability groups and compared their activity before and after GitHub Copilot became freely available. We found that most disability groups showed a descriptive pattern of fewer commits but more code modified. In several disability groups, the distribution of developers across commit activity levels shifted toward both lower and higher level, leaving fewer developers at moderate level. However, we found no evidence that changes in commits or net lines modified differed across disability groups. These findings suggest that the wider availability of GitHub Copilot cannot be associated with a broad increase or decrease in observable development activity, while patterns of change varied across developers and disability groups.

papers.intro:
Generative AI tools have become increasingly integrated into software development workflows. Tools such as GitHub Copilot can assist developers with tasks such as generating code, explaining code, writing documentation, and finding solutions to programming problems. Previous research suggests that AI-assisted development tools can influence developer productivity by accelerating programming tasks and improving developers’ perceived productivity [1, 2, 3]. However, existing studies on the productivity effects of AI have largely focused on the general developer population, and less is known about whether these benefits extend to other developer groups.

In this paper, we investigate whether the wider availability of GitHub Copilot is associated with changes in the productivity of developers who publicly self-identify as having a disability on GitHub. Accordingly, we ask: how has the observable development activity of self-identified disabled GitHub developers changed following the wider availability of GitHub Copilot?. From an initial pool of over 3,000 users, we curated usage data pertaining 199 developers across multiple disability groups based on publicly available profile information. Because actual adoption cannot be determined from repository data alone, we first examine explicit references to Generative AI tools in commit messages to understand the visibility of AI use within our sample. We then compare commits, net lines modified, and pull request acceptance rates before and after GitHub Copilot became freely available to all GitHub users. Through this analysis, we examine both overall changes in development activity and whether patterns of change differ across disability groups. In the remaining of the paper we discuss background and related work (Section II), present the methodology we followed in our empirical study (Section III), report on the results (Section IV) and discuss their implications (Section V) and future work (Section VII).

papers.title: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games
papers.abstract: Colonel Blotto is a fundamental resource-allocation game in which two players divide their budgets across battlefields, and the higher allocation on each battlefield wins its value. The problem of computing an equilibrium efficiently has remained unresolved for its classical continuous version with arbitrary budgets and with values that may vary across battlefields but are the same for both players. We give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, and nearly linear in the input length for fixed $\varepsilon$. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, we also compute exact equilibria in linear time.

papers.intro:
Colonel Blotto is a fundamental model of competition with limited resources, dating back to Borel’s work in 1921 [8]. In the classical game, two players allocate their budgets of a divisible resource across several battlefields. Each player’s total allocation must not exceed its budget. The players may have different budgets, and values may vary across battlefields, but each battlefield has the same value for both players. On each battlefield, the higher allocation wins its value, and a tie splits that value equally. Each player seeks to maximize the total value it wins.

One approach to constructing Blotto equilibria starts from the General Lotto relaxation, in which the budget constraint holds only in expectation. Nash equilibria of General Lotto have been characterized [11]. To turn such an equilibrium into Blotto strategies, each player’s bid distributions on individual battlefields must be coupled into a joint distribution that respects its budget on every draw. [13] characterizes exactly when such couplings exist, shows that they yield a Blotto equilibrium, and gives an algorithm for computing and sampling an approximate equilibrium in this regime. Outside this regime, no pair of feasible strategies has these marginals, and an algorithm must find strategies with different marginals. Our approximation scheme removes this restriction.

papers.title: SN 2019qem: decades of extreme mass loss before the explosion of a luminous, long-lived Type IIn supernova
papers.abstract: We present the luminous, long-lived Type IIn SN 2019qem and use it to reconstruct how much mass its progenitor lost and when. We combine host-subtracted optical and mid-infrared photometry and 26 optical spectra from -22 to +699 d. We model the bolometric light curve with thin-shell CSM-interaction models in REDBACK, with the shock velocity constrained by the H$\alpha$ line widths, and compare them with an analytic interaction model. SN 2019qem rose in $\approx30$d to $M_I = -20.5$mag and a bolometric peak of $7.0\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and radiated $6.9\times10^{50}$ erg in the optical within 575 d, closely resembling luminous, strongly interacting SNe IIn such as SN 2010jl and SN 2015da. A Heii/Niii flash feature at -22 d and unresolved narrow Balmer lines reveal dense, slow CSM. From +78 to +445 d the H$\alpha$ wings are shaped by electron scattering, and the line stays blueshifted by 400-700 km s$^{-1}$, which points to an optically thick, asymmetric interaction region rather than to newly formed dust. In the preferred model, $\approx7 M_\odot$ of ejecta run into $\approx9 M_\odot$ of gas ejected $\approx2$ yr before explosion and then into a wind of $\approx0.6 M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ (for $v_w = 100$ km s$^{-1}$), sweeping up $\approx32 M_\odot$ by +544 d. The mid-infrared excess brightens for two years while the optical fades, tracing dust heated by the ongoing interaction. The host is a low-mass, star-forming galaxy, $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 9.19$, with a sub-solar metallicity at the explosion site. In its final decades the progenitor of SN 2019qem lost mass far faster than any steady stellar wind, ending with an eruption of $\approx9 M_\odot$ two years before core collapse, consistent with luminous-blue-variable-like eruptive mass loss. Taken at face value, the mass budget implies an initial progenitor mass of $\gtrsim40 M_\odot$.

papers.title: SBi3PCF: cosmology with Dark Energy Survey Year 3 cosmic shear
papers.abstract: We present the first cosmic shear data analysis of the integrated 3-point correlation function (i3PCF), a higher-order weak lensing statistic, and the first simulation-based inference (SBI) analysis of a three-point cosmic shear correlation function on survey data. Using SBi3PCF, our previously developed SBI framework for the i3PCF, we jointly constrain the $w$CDM parameter space with the cosmic shear 2-point correlation functions $\xi_\pm$ (2PCFs) and the i3PCFs $\zeta_\pm$ from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) weak lensing shape catalogue, from which we detect $\zeta_\pm$ with a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.8. Our forward model is built on the CosmoGridV1 N-body simulations and includes the survey mask, shape noise, intrinsic alignment, baryonic feedback, photometric redshift uncertainty and shear calibration bias. The analysis was carried out blind, with all choices frozen, and only unblinded once coverage tests, tests of the accuracy of the learned likelihoods, and internal consistency tests had been passed. For the joint $\xi_\pm$ + $\zeta_\pm$ analysis we obtain $\Omega_m = 0.272^{+0.038}_{-0.033}$, $S_8 = 0.784^{+0.024}_{-0.021}$ and $w_0 = -1.04^{+0.25}_{-0.19}$. Adding $\zeta_\pm$ improves the figure of merit in the $\Omega_m$-$S_8$-$w_0$ parameter space by a factor of $1.59$ over $\xi_\pm$ alone, as predicted by simulated i3PCF analyses. This gain comes from third-order information on angular scales $\geq 15'$ and aperture radii $\geq 50'$, a regime where baryonic effects are subdominant. The constraints are consistent with the other DES Y3 analyses of the same catalogue and with independent lensing analyses, and differ by at most $2.4\sigma$ from CMB and BAO data (Planck 2018 + BAO, in $\Omega_m$-$S_8$-$w_0$). This shows that $\zeta_\pm$ can be analysed on cosmological survey data with a fully simulation-based approach, an important step towards Stage-IV surveys.

papers.title: 6G ISAC Drone Detection: Signal Processing and Experimental Validation at FR1
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) enables mobile networks to detect passive targets such as drones at minimal additional cost. However, in ISAC, a small drone must be detected against strong ground clutter with the limited radio resources left by communications. In this paper, we propose two ISAC target detectors: a coherent detector, which combines all frames and beam dwells of a revisit, and a non-coherent detector, robust to inter-frame clock phase drift. The algorithms leverage per-dwell clutter whitening and the adaptive coherence estimator (ACE) detection statistic to improve performance. Both detectors estimate the range, radial velocity, and azimuth of targets in real time on a laptop graphics processing unit (GPU). Measurements with an FR1 ISAC proof-of-concept system based on a commercial base station show that the coherent detector outperforms the non-coherent one and recovers the full track.

papers.intro:
As the 6G (6G) of mobile communications draws closer to its expected release date, practical validation of its expected main use cases becomes increasingly necessary. This helps to ensure that the real-world deployment is effective within the constraints of commercial telecommunications hardware. One of the key use cases for 6G is ISAC (ISAC), which consists of using the mobile network infrastructure to perform sensing tasks, such as the detection and estimation of the spatial parameters of passive targets [1, 2]. The widespread deployment of mobile BS—initially intended exclusively for communications coverage—makes them the ideal option for providing widespread sensing capabilities at minimal cost [3].

Within the applications of ISAC, drone detection has been receiving substantial attention from the main mobile infrastructure providers, research institutions, and defense agencies [4, 5]. Keeping in mind that drones are being extensively used for warfare, effectively solving the drone detection problem is fundamental for securing critical airspace and, consequently, infrastructure [6, 7]. Common approaches for drone detection include dedicated radars, passive RF (RF) sensing, and acoustic and optical sensors [6], all of which require deploying dedicated sensing hardware.

ISAC drone detection inherently poses multiple challenges. First, sensing beam allocation requires a well-designed scheme for harmonious coexistence of sensing and communications. For example, TDD (TDD) solutions lead to aliasing in the Doppler domain[8], which needs to be addressed. Another relevant issue is the operating frequency band. Operating in FR2 (FR2) (24.25–71 GHz) has limited coverage per site [9], whereas FR1 (FR1) benefits from the existing macro-cell coverage. However, the limited bandwidth and wide beams in FR1 leave a small drone competing with strong ground clutter.

In this work, we propose two algorithms that address the problem of monostatic ISAC drone detection and parameter estimation. Both operate within the resource and beam allocation imposed by the communications system, using only the sensing symbols of a TDD frame. Our first and main approach leverages coherent combining, clutter whitening, and a modification of the ACE (ACE) [10], which has CFAR (CFAR) for properly whitened clutter. The other algorithm is a non-coherent estimator, robust to clock phase drift, which might be present in quasi-monostatic setups. The algorithms are conducive to implementation in a GPU (GPU), which allows them to operate in real time. We validate our methods with real-world measurement data from a quasi-monostatic FR1 PoC (PoC) setup and show that the coherent method consistently detects the drone and allows recovering its full track while simultaneously rejecting clutter.

papers.title: Tiny Galaxies, Mighty Nitrogen: Linking Chemical Anomalies to Compact Galaxies at High Redshift using JWST/JADES
papers.abstract: The origin of anomalous chemical enrichment in high-redshift galaxies discovered by JWST remains a key question in galaxy evolution. Enhanced nitrogen abundances have been identified in several galaxies at early cosmic times, but the physical conditions driving this enrichment, and their connection to galaxy morphology, remain unclear. We test whether morphologically compact galaxies at 4 < z < 7 show stronger chemical anomalies than extended systems. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopic data, we construct samples of compact and extended galaxies and analyse their rest-frame spectra. We stack the spectra of each population and measure key UV and optical emission lines. We detect nitrogen emission in the compact galaxy stack, including NIV], and [NII], while also detecting key carbon and oxygen lines. The detection of [OIII]{\lambda}4363 enables a direct-Te determination of the oxygen abundance. From these measurements, we infer chemical abundance ratios, including log(N/O) and log(C/O). We find that compact galaxies exhibit elevated log(N/O) (by ~ 0.7 dex) and log(C/O) (by ~ 0.5 dex) abundance ratios relative to extended systems. The abundance patterns of compact galaxy stacks are comparable to those of previously identified individual nitrogen-enhanced galaxies at high redshift and second-generation globular-cluster stars in the Milky Way. These results suggest a possible link between galaxy compactness and chemical enrichment pathways in the early Universe. Deeper JWST NIRSpec IFU observations of compact high-redshift galaxies will be crucial for determining the origin, spatial distribution, and evolutionary significance of these abundance patterns.

The early Universe consisted of pristine gas, composed of hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium, produced during the Big Bang nucleosynthesis (Hoyle and Tayler, 1964; Peebles, 1966; Wagoner et al., 1967; Cyburt et al., 2016). Small primordial density perturbations grew under gravity, leading to the formation of dark matter halos that provided the potential wells in which gas could collapse and the first stars and galaxies could form (Barkana and Loeb, 2011; Bromm and Yoshida, 2011; Klessen and Glover, 2023). As this gas cooled and condensed within these halos, the first generation of stars and galaxies were formed (Klessen and Glover, 2023). Stellar nucleosynthesis subsequently produced metals, elements heavier than helium, enriching the interstellar medium (ISM) and thus driving the chemical evolution of galaxies over cosmic time.

As this gas cooled and condensed within these halos, the first generation of stars and galaxies were formed (Klessen and Glover, 2023). Stellar nucleosynthesis subsequently produced metals, elements heavier than helium, enriching the interstellar medium (ISM) and thus driving the chemical evolution of galaxies over cosmic time.

The production and dispersal of metals provide fundamental insights into galaxy evolution by tracing star formation, stellar feedback, and black hole growth in the galaxy (Maiolino and Mannucci, 2019, see review by,). The metal content of galaxies, commonly referred to as metallicity, quantifies the abundance of elements heavier than helium relative to hydrogen. In this work, we focus on the gas-phase oxygen abundance, 12+log⁡(O/H)12+\log(\mathrm{O/H}), which we use as an observational proxy for gas-phase metallicity. Oxygen is particularly useful as it is one of the most abundant metals and its strong emission lines provide accessible and widely used diagnostics of the chemical state of ionised gas. The metals are synthesised in the stars and are expelled in the ISM through stellar winds and supernovae explosions, especially core collapse supernovae (CCSNe), which drive the metals out further. This enriches the surrounding gas with newly synthesized heavy elements (Izotov and Thuan, 1999; Berg et al., 2019; Kobayashi et al., 2020; Kobayashi and Taylor, 2023).

Consequently, metallicity is regulated by the interplay between star formation and inflow of pristine gas which can dilute the chemical content of the ISM (Kobayashi et al., 2020; Koeppen, 1994; Keres et al., 2005). Hence, these chemical abundances preserve a record of their past evolution (Davé et al., 2011; Lilly et al., 2013). Understanding the evolution of metallicity is therefore essential for constraining the processes that drive galaxy formation and evolution. Further studying the chemical abundances on spatially resolved scales provides a powerful means of probing the assembly of stellar populations and the distribution of metals across the ISM (Curti et al., 2020; Maiolino and Mannucci, 2019).

Among the known scaling relations in chemical abundances, one of the most widely studied is that between the gas phase oxygen abundance (O/H) and nitrogen-to-oxygen abundance ratio (hereafter N/O). Since oxygen and nitrogen are synthesized by stars on different timescales, the N/O ratio traces the yields of the dying stars across various masses, which helps us study the star formation histories of galaxies (Izotov et al., 2006; Vincenzo et al., 2016). Previous such studies have shown that N/O generally increases with gas-phase metallicity (O/H). This correlation has been observed between the O/H and N/O in the local H ii regions and in the ISM of star-forming (SF) galaxies (Vila-Costas and Edmunds, 1993; Zee et al., 1998; Pilyugin et al., 2012; Andrews and Martini, 2013; Berg et al., 2016; Berg et al., 2019; Berg et al., 2020; Belfiore et al., 2017; Nicholls et al., 2016; Hayden-Pawson et al., 2022).

Previous such studies have shown that N/O generally increases with gas-phase metallicity (O/H). This correlation has been observed between the O/H and N/O in the local H ii regions and in the ISM of star-forming (SF) galaxies (Vila-Costas and Edmunds, 1993; Zee et al., 1998; Pilyugin et al., 2012; Andrews and Martini, 2013; Berg et al., 2016; Berg et al., 2019; Berg et al., 2020; Belfiore et al., 2017; Nicholls et al., 2016; Hayden-Pawson et al., 2022).

In local galaxies, the nitrogen-to-oxygen abundance ratio exhibits little or no dependence on gas-phase oxygen abundance at low metallicities, 12+log⁡(O/H)≲8.012+\log(\mathrm{O/H})\lesssim 8.0, producing the well-known low-metallicity N/O plateau. This behaviour is generally attributed to the contribution of primary nitrogen, with massive stars providing a prompt source of primary N (Izotov and Thuan, 1999; Perez-Montero and Contini, 2009; Berg et al., 2019; Arellano-Córdova et al., 2025a; Scholte et al., 2026). Towards higher oxygen abundances, N/O increases with O/H as the contribution from low- and intermediate-mass stars, which can produce both primary and secondary nitrogen, becomes increasingly important. At the highest oxygen abundances, the N/O–O/H relation can become particularly steep. Chemical-evolution models have proposed several mechanisms for this behaviour, including differential metal loss through galactic winds, in which oxygen may be preferentially removed relative to nitrogen, although the relative importance of such processes remains model-dependent (Vila-Costas and Edmunds, 1993; Pilyugin et al., 2012; Vincenzo et al., 2016; Berg et al., 2020).

The change in the behavior of N/O with oxygen abundance is generally interpreted in terms of the different nucleosynthetic origins and metallicity dependencies of nitrogen production. Nitrogen is produced through primary and secondary channels, distinguished by the origin of the C and O nuclei that serve as seeds for the CNO cycle. In primary production, these nuclei are synthesized within the star itself, making the nitrogen yield relatively insensitive to the initial metallicity. In secondary production, the C and O nuclei are inherited from the material from which the star formed, causing the nitrogen yield to increase with initial metallicity (Meynet and Maeder, 2002; Vincenzo et al., 2016; Maiolino and Mannucci, 2019, e.g.). Both massive and low- to intermediate-mass stars can contribute to both channels. Massive stars can produce primary N through rotationally induced mixing, particularly at low metallicity, while AGB stars can produce primary N through dredge-up and hot-bottom burning as well as secondary N from pre-existing C and O. Massive stars provide relatively prompt nitrogen enrichment through stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, whereas low- and intermediate-mass stars contribute on longer timescales through their post-main-sequence evolution. Consequently, elevated N/O ratios are commonly observed in metal-rich local star-forming galaxies, while super-solar N/O at low metallicity is relatively uncommon, with notable exceptions such as Mrk 996 and NGC 5253 (Telles et al., 2014; James et al., 2009; Walsh and Roy, 1989, cf.).

papers.title: Up in smoke: carbon-destruction in the terrestrial planet-forming region of a young Class I disk
papers.abstract: Earth's surface and deep mantle are strongly depleted in carbon compared to the Sun. Sublimation of solid carbonaceous material in the inner midplanes of young disks could cause this depletion. We study such thermal processing in HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with a rich hydrocarbon spectrum. A companion paper has shown that it is recondensing refractory dust from a hot inner disk region, and that oxygen-bearing species are tracing a warm (300-500 K) molecular layer entrained in a disk-wind. In this work, we analyze the carbon species in the JWST spectrum of this source using local thermal equilibrium slab models. We detect warm (~400 K) HCN and C2H2 at the base of a disk wind, as well as colder (~40 K) C4H2, CH3, and CS in the outer disk or outflow cavity wall. Additionally, 13CCH2, CH4, and C6H2 are detected, while ALMA observations reveal C2H tracing the outflow cavity walls. We suggest that in a "refractory carbon destruction zone" in the inner disk, carbon-bearing species are released from the grains, possibly contributing to the observed carbon depletion of Earth. The disk wind then redistributes carbon carried by HCN and C2H2 from the inner disk to the colder outer disk, where UV-induced gas-phase reactions with C2H in the outflow cavity walls could produce the aliphatic carbon chains seen. This result implies that the Warm Carbon Chain Chemistry (WCCC, e.g. N. Sakai & S. Yamamoto 2013) might trace outflows rather than infall. The formation of aliphatic chains in the disk wind could promote the abundant aliphatic organics found in meteorites and asteroids.

Carbon is the basis of all life as we know it; the dry mass of the human body consists of over 50 % carbon [83]. However, the carbon abundance of the bulk silicate Earth (the entire Earth excluding the core) is depleted by four orders of magnitude compared to the Sun and the primordial dust in the interstellar medium (ISM) from which the Earth was born [11, 12].

There is no consensus yet on which mechanisms deplete carbon from the terrestrial planet-forming grains. Suggested mechanisms include photolysis and oxidation in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks [48, 3, 44, 81, e.g.], or chemical sputtering at the surface of grains [49, 15]. However, these mechanisms are insufficient to fully explain the depleted carbon content of Earth and small solar system bodies such as Ryugu [57]. [14] find that, although oxidation and photolysis alone is not sufficient to explain the observed carbon depletion of Earth, increased vertical mixing and thermal processing during accretion outbursts could be an important contribution.

papers.title: Outer pressure bumps beyond the dust disc: Missing Outer Rings in the exoALMA Sample: Physical Mechanisms Suppressing Dust Ring Formation Despite Strong Pressure Bumps
papers.abstract: The exoALMA survey has revealed candidate gas pressure bumps at radii beyond the observed millimetre continuum discs in several protoplanetary systems, raising the question of whether these regions could host undetected dust structures. We investigate this for nine of the exoALMA discs by reconstructing gas surface density profiles from midplane pressure gradient measurements derived from $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO ALMA Band 7 observations. We evolve the dust using DustPy across a grid of turbulence and fragmentation parameters ($\alpha \in \{10^{-4}, 10^{-3}\}$; $v_\mathrm{frag} \in \{1, 10\}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), followed by radiative transfer calculations with RADMC-3D to give predictions for the continuum emission. We find that the dominant outcome across the explored parameter space is efficient outer dust trapping, leading to prominent outer continuum rings that should be detectable at ALMA Band 7, in tension with the observations. The $^{13}$CO-based reconstructions almost universally produce detectable outer rings, whereas the $^{12}$CO-based reconstructions show more variation. We further test delayed formation of the outer pressure bump and enhanced outer-disc turbulence as possible suppression mechanisms of ring formation. Enhanced turbulence weakens the predicted outer continuum emission most effectively, although the efficiency of the mechanism depends on the system explored and on where the turbulence transition is placed. Delayed bump formation generally does not prevent rapid outer dust accumulation.

papers.intro:
High-resolution millimetre continuum observations with ALMA have shown that protoplanetary discs commonly have substructures in the form of rings, gaps, spirals and azimuthal asymmetries (Andrews et al., 2018; ALMA Partnership et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018; Long et al., 2018; Cieza et al., 2021; van der Marel et al., 2019; Jennings et al., 2022; Guerra-Alvarado et al., 2025; Bosschaart et al., 2026, e.g.).

High-resolution millimetre continuum observations with ALMA have shown that protoplanetary discs commonly have substructures in the form of rings, gaps, spirals and azimuthal asymmetries (Andrews et al., 2018; ALMA Partnership et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2018; Long et al., 2018; Cieza et al., 2021; van der Marel et al., 2019; Jennings et al., 2022; Guerra-Alvarado et al., 2025; Bosschaart et al., 2026, e.g.).

Early surveys of the brightest and most spatially extended discs, such as the DSHARP survey (Andrews et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018) demonstrated that these features are widespread. Similar structures were also identified across discs in Taurus and Ophiuchus star forming regions (Long et al., 2018; Cieza et al., 2021). Subsequent work has moved towards showing the high prevalence of substructures throughout the broader disc population: van der Marel et al. (2019) found that ring/gap systems span a wide range of stellar ages and luminosities, while parametric and non-parametric visibility fitting techniques demonstrated that substructures could be recovered at sub-beam resolution, including in systems with fainter and more compact emission (Long et al., 2019; Jennings et al., 2022, e.g.). More recently, Bosschaart et al. (2026) found that rings and gaps are a near-universal trait of extended discs (Rd​u​s​t>30R_{dust}>30 au) in nearby star-forming regions. However, this picture may not extend to the entire disc population; Guerra-Alvarado et al. (2025) found that two-thirds of the Lupus discs are compact (Rd​u​s​t<30R_{dust}<30 au) and look smooth at ∼\sim4 au resolution, suggesting that substructures could be more prominent primarily in the larger and more massive systems. The AGE-PRO large programme (Zhang et al., 2025), which targeted a representative sample spanning the disc lifetime in the Ophiuchus (≲1\lesssim 1\,Myr), Lupus (∼1−3\sim 1-3\,Myr) and Upper Scorpius region (∼2−6\sim 2-6\,Myr), provided some further insights. Visibility fitting of the continuum emission of the resolved discs revealed substructures in ∼\sim80 % in the Ophiuchus discs, providing support for early formation of substructures (Vioque et al., 2025), in agreement with the results from Hsieh et al. (2025) showing that dust substructures are already common in Class I discs. Substructures were similarly detected in the majority of well-resolved discs across the regions in the AGE-PRO sample; however, many of the compact discs (particularly in Lupus) are only marginally resolved, and some showed tentative visibility variations suggestive of unresolved structure (Vioque et al., 2025). Consistent with this, comparisons with dust evolution modelling suggest that the evolution of spectral index and continuum flux of the AGE-PRO sample are better reproduced by models with dust traps (Kurtovic et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026). This could imply that substructures are common even in compact discs but are hidden below current resolution limits. The nature and prevalence of substructures in the faint and compact discs are therefore still open questions.

These observations have motivated extensive efforts to link observed dust structures with underlying disc physics. Disc substructures are commonly interpreted as signatures of dust trapping at local gas pressure maxima, where the radial inward drift of solids is halted (Weidenschilling, 1977; Whipple, 1972, e.g.). These pressure maxima can arise through a diverse set of physical mechanisms, including gravitational interactions with planets embedded in the disc (Pinilla et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2015; Dipierro et al., 2015b), self-gravitating spiral arms (Dipierro et al., 2015a), and magnetohydrodynamic effects such as zonal flows and dead-zone edges (Johansen et al., 2009; Flock et al., 2015, e.g.) (see Bae et al. (2023) for a comprehensive review of proposed mechanisms). In such regions, particles accumulate and grow, producing the ring-like features seen in millimetre continuum emission. Theoretical and numerical studies have shown that these pressure perturbations can efficiently concentrate dust and create long-lived substructures (Pinilla et al., 2012; Dullemond et al., 2018; Stammler et al., 2019, e.g.). Observational support for dust trapping has emerged from ALMA observations, where gas kinematic perturbations and deviations from Keplerian rotation are found to be spatially associated with continuum rings and gaps, consistent with underlying pressure structure (Pinte et al., 2018; Teague et al., 2018; Rosotti et al., 2020; Izquierdo et al., 2023, e.g.).

These pressure maxima can arise through a diverse set of physical mechanisms, including gravitational interactions with planets embedded in the disc (Pinilla et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2015; Dipierro et al., 2015b), self-gravitating spiral arms (Dipierro et al., 2015a), and magnetohydrodynamic effects such as zonal flows and dead-zone edges (Johansen et al., 2009; Flock et al., 2015, e.g.) (see Bae et al. (2023) for a comprehensive review of proposed mechanisms). In such regions, particles accumulate and grow, producing the ring-like features seen in millimetre continuum emission. Theoretical and numerical studies have shown that these pressure perturbations can efficiently concentrate dust and create long-lived substructures (Pinilla et al., 2012; Dullemond et al., 2018; Stammler et al., 2019, e.g.). Observational support for dust trapping has emerged from ALMA observations, where gas kinematic perturbations and deviations from Keplerian rotation are found to be spatially associated with continuum rings and gaps, consistent with underlying pressure structure (Pinte et al., 2018; Teague et al., 2018; Rosotti et al., 2020; Izquierdo et al., 2023, e.g.).

Line-intensity maps of CO isotopologues are only an indirect probe of the midplane pressure structure, since the mapping from the gas column density to pressure is complicated by optical depth and thermal effects. Comparisons of the CO line emission and continuum substructures find that CO gaps tend to coincide with dust gaps but are often shallower and some deep dust gaps lack any clear CO counterpart (Zhang et al., 2021). However the statistical significance of any continuum and line emission substructure correlation has been questioned (Jiang et al., 2022).

A more direct tracer is therefore the gas kinematics: deviations of the rotation curve from Keplerian rotation reflect the radial pressure gradient in the disc midplane, and can reveal pressure perturbations even where the corresponding change in gas column density is weak or ambiguous. papers.title: The Galah survey and symbiotic stars. II. Discovery, validation, and intensive follow-up of 44 new systems accreting at the lowest detectable levels
papers.abstract: We report the discovery, validation, and characterization of 44 new symbiotic stars (SySts) accreting at the lowest detectable levels (Lacc =< 3 Lsun). Candidates were initially selected from the Galah survey among non-pulsating M-type red giants exhibiting Halpha excess. Between 2021 and 2025, these targets were subjected to intensive multi-wavelength campaigns, including ground-based, high-resolution Echelle spectroscopy over 544 nights, multi-epoch flickering searches down to 1 mmag, and UV/X-ray observations with the Swift satellite. Our high-resolution spectra allowed for a detailed investigation of Halpha flux and line-profile variability. Crucially, the radial velocities measured for the M-giant components yielded reliable spectroscopic orbits for 22 objects and preliminary orbits for an additional eight, corroborated by binary-induced modulations in ASAS-SN photometry. Measured accretion levels vary by factors of up to 20X, emphasizing the need for high-sensitivity, long-term monitoring. Swift X-ray data exclude neutron star companions in all targets, consistent with predominance of white-dwarf degenerates in known SySts. Combined with the 33 objects from Paper I, this sample of 77 new SySts significantly exceeds the number of previously known, accreting-only Galactic symbiotic stars, constituting the bulk of the low-accretion (LowAcc) variety discovered to date and representing >10 percent of all known SySts in the Galaxy. As SySts likely spend most of their lifetimes in LowAcc faint states, characterizing this population is essential for estimating the total Galactic SySt population and evaluating the role of SySts as Type Ia supernova progenitors or sources of UV excess in elliptical galaxies.

Symbiotic stars (SySts) are interacting binaries composed of a red giant (RG) and a degenerate companion (usually a white dwarf (WD), or very rarely a neutron star), typically orbiting with periods of a few years and separations of a few astronomical units. The companion accretes from the RG via wind interception or Roche-lobe overflow; so far, there is little evidence that magnetic fields play a significant role in this process, except perhaps in a few isolated cases (Sokoloski and Bildsten, 1999; Magdolen et al., 2023; Pichardo Marcano et al., 2026).

The classification criteria for SySts have widened over time. The original definition formulated by Allen (1984) tended to isolate SySts undergoing nuclear burning at the surface of a white dwarf (Sokoloski et al., 2001; Sokoloski et al., 2016; Mikołajewska, 2003; Munari, 2019; Merc, 2025, e.g.,). Later, Belczyński et al. (2000) relaxed these constraints to include systems that are not burning but are accreting onto a WD at a high rate. The discovery that some SySts contain a neutron star (NS) instead of a WD (Masetti et al., 2007, e.g.,)—along with the recognition of SU Lyn as the prototype of a large, previously unsuspected population of SySts accreting on WDs at (very) low rates (Mukai et al., 2016)—has shaped the modern definition; i.e., any binary where a WD or an NS accretes enough material from an RG companion such that the interaction is detectable at some wavelength is considered a SySt.

The traditional view (Kenyon, 1986, e.g.,) implicitly assumed a steady-state evolution for the different types of SySts; thus, a burning system was thought to keep burning for its entire symbiotic lifetime. This posed the problem of refueling the burning shell, which was circumvented by assuming that—regardless of radiation pressure or stellar winds—accretion onto the WD proceeds unabated, matching precisely the rate at which fuel is consumed. In a more modern approach (Munari, 2019, as discussed by), SySts are seen to alternate between burning phases and accreting-only states; longer intervals are spent accreting material onto the surface of the WD, which is subsequently ignited once the conditions for nuclear burning are reached. When the shell fuel is exhausted, burning ceases and accretion resumes to prepare for a new cycle.

papers.title: Beyond just a torus? Re-contextualising the AGN type paradigm using data-driven host galaxy quenching histories
papers.abstract: The orientation of a dusty torus within a unified model explains the presence (Type-1) or absence (Type-2) of broad emission lines in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) spectra. This orientation-based unified model, however, fails to explain differences in host galaxy properties, such as star formation rates, of Type-1 and Type-2 AGNs. Star-formation histories (SFHs) can shed light on the connection between AGN type and host galaxy properties, but are challenging to extract from Type-1 AGN that outshine their host galaxies. We use mean-field independent component analysis (MFICA) spectrum decomposition to extract the stellar populations of $\sim$3000 optically selected Type-1 and Type-2 AGN host galaxies from the seventh data release (DR7) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), matched in redshift ($0.16 \leq z \leq 0.4$) and AGN luminosity ($6.5<\log_{10} [L_{[OIII]}/L_\odot] <9.5$). Using MFICA, we find that only $\sim$10 per cent of AGN host galaxies have recently ($\lesssim1$\,Gyr) and rapidly quenched star formation following a starburst, with Type-2 AGN host galaxies having done so at most 100\,Myrs more recently than Type-1 AGN host galaxies. For most ($\sim$90 per cent) AGN hosts with normal recent star formation histories, Type-2 AGNs are associated with slightly younger stellar populations than Type-1 AGNs. The younger stellar populations of Type-2 AGN hosts can be explained by a link between dusty torus covering factors and stellar populations, by host-galaxy obscuration of AGN, or by an evolution in AGN type without major bursts or rapid quenching of star formation.

AGNs, however, are not observationally homogeneous, and instead represent a family of objects with distinct observational properties, such as the presence or absence of broad-emission lines (Lawrence, 1991).

The orientation-based unified model of AGNs asserts that the presence or absence of broad-emission lines arises from different line of sight orientations of an equatorial dusty torus that surrounds the black-body accretion disk/flow characterising all AGNs (Antonucci, 1993; Urry and Padovani, 1995). According to this orientation model, we would observe a “Type-2” AGN when our line of sight is intercepted by the dusty torus, which blocks emission from rapidly moving clouds near the SMBH (the Broad-Line Region, BLR), leaving only narrow emission from more distant clouds visible (Schmitt et al., 2003; Husemann et al., 2014, the Narrow Line Region, NLR, spanning 10s of pc to kpc scales,). If our line of sight is not intercepted by the dusty torus, we observe the broad line region and, therefore, a “Type-1” AGN.

If orientation combined with nuclear obscuration explains the difference between Type-1 and Type-2 AGNs entirely, then their host galaxies should be identical. On the contrary, several studies have reported differences in the host galaxy stellar masses (Zou et al., 2019), dust contents (Maiolino and Rieke, 1995; Buchner and Bauer, 2017, e.g.,), environments (Villarroel and Korn, 2014), morphologies (Li et al., 2024) and halo masses (Jiang et al., 2016; Powell et al., 2018). In particular, some studies have found that Type-2 (or obscured) AGN host galaxies have higher star-formation rates (SFRs) than Type-1 (or unobscured) AGN host galaxies (Kim et al., 2006; Lacy et al., 2007; Zakamska et al., 2008; Silverman et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009; Hiner et al., 2009; Page et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2015; Zakamska et al., 2016; Villarroel et al., 2017; Zhuang and Ho, 2020; Andonie et al., 2022).

To understand what differences in SFR imply for the AGN type dichotomy, we need to distinguish between the multitude of quenching and star-formation histories (SFHs) that AGN host galaxies could follow to attain the same SFR differences. Accurate measurements of galaxy SFHs require fitting stellar population models to rest-frame optical spectra (see, e.g., Walcher et al., 2011; Conroy, 2013, for reviews). Measuring the SFHs of the host galaxies of luminous, unobscured Type-1 AGNs, however, is additionally challenging due to AGN light contaminating starlight. Several spectral decomposition codes have been developed to address this challenge and separate host galaxy and central engine light in AGN spectra (e.g., pyqsofit, Guo et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2024, badass, Sexton et al. 2021, qsfit, Calderone et al. 2017, q3deblend, Husemann et al. 2013, and many other such codes).

In Krishna et al. (2025, hereafter K25 ), we introduced a data-driven decomposition technique based on Mean-Field Independent Component Analysis (Højen-Sørensen et al., 2002, MFICA,) that simultaneously decomposes AGN spectra and characterises the recent (≲1\lesssim 1 Gyr) SFHs of their host galaxies. Some post-starburst galaxies may originate from disruptive events, such as galaxy mergers (Pawlik et al., 2018; Sazonova et al., 2021; Verrico et al., 2023; Ellison et al., 2024), which may be capable of triggering dust-obscured AGN activity (Treister et al., 2010; Ricci et al., 2017; Weston et al., 2017; Blecha et al., 2018, e.g.,). papers.title: XMM-Newton and NuSTAR quasi-simultaneous follow-up of the very high energy flare of PKS~1725+123 in August 2025
papers.abstract: We report the results of the spectral timing analysis of the quasi-simultaneous X-ray follow-up with XMM-Newton ($50\,\rm ks$) and NuSTAR ($180\,\rm ks$) of the very high energy flare of the blazar PKS 1725+123 ($z=0.586$) in August of 2025. The X-ray monitoring started $\sim3$ days after the announcement of the VHE flare by LST-1, MAGIC and H.E.S.S. and lasted for almost 5 days. The high sensitivity of XMM-Newton reveals two spectral components, a soft ($\Gamma_{\rm X}>2$) and a hard ($\Gamma_{\rm X}<2$) power law. While the soft component dominates at $E<2\,\rm keV$, the hard component dominates at $E>2\,\rm keV$, likely marking the transition between the synchrotron and the high-energy emission, the "valley" of this blazar's spectral energy distribution. Within the XMM-Newton pointing ($\sim14$ hours) we witness the shift of the synchrotron component out of the X-ray band. In the following $\sim 4$ days, NuSTAR further reveals the brightening by a factor of 1.5 of the hard component, following the shift of the high-energy part of the SED into the X-ray band. Overall, within a week (observed frame) of the VHE flare, PKS 1725+123 went from temporarily being an intermediate synchrotron peaked blazar to transitioning back to its `normal' state of a low synchrotron peaked one. This is the first time that the evolution of a VHE flare from a blazar jet has been followed continuously in X-rays over such an extended period and our results highlight the importance of long-term quasi-simultaneous X-ray follow-up of VHE blazar flares.

In the extragalactic sky, their production is largely associated with accreting supermassive black holes in the centres of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) launching powerful relativistic jets (e.g. blazars, radio galaxies, and γ\gamma-ray narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies), as well as starburst galaxies and γ\gamma-ray bursts (Cherenkov Telescope Array Consortium et al., 2019). Blazars, AGN with jets aligned towards Earth (Angel and Stockman, 1980; Urry and Padovani, 1995), constitute about ∼40%\sim 40\% of the currently classified TeV emitters in the TeV catalog (Wakely and Horan, 2008). These sources are some the most powerful particle accelerators in the Universe and, notoriously, their emission is remarkably variable, showing orders of magnitude variability at all wavelengths (from radio to γ\gamma-rays) and timescales, from months to just a few hours (see, e.g., Raiteri, 2025, for a recent review).

Despite more than two decades of multi-wavelength observations, we do not have a single framework capable of providing a consistent description of blazar emission (see, e.g., Böttcher, 2019, for a review). Therefore, constraints on the particle distribution at these energies suffer from several modeling uncertainties. Additionally, follow-up multi-wavelength observations of these flares are often non-simultaneous, making the physical interpretation of flares and their evolution especially challenging.

papers.title: Selection instability and coefficient uncertainty in Cox modelling after Lasso selection
papers.abstract: After variable selection, uncertainty quantification often treats the selected model as fixed, although it may change under repeated sampling. We investigate whether this variability can be incorporated by repeating Cox-Lasso selection within a model-based bootstrap after unpenalised Cox refitting. We compare conventional post-selection Cox Wald intervals and a model-based bootstrap without re-selection, both of which keep the selected predictor set fixed, with two re-selection procedures: one retains the observed tuning-parameter value, whereas the other reapplies the cross-validation minimum (CV-min) tuning rule within each bootstrap sample. Against the data-generating coefficients, procedures holding the selected predictor set fixed frequently showed substantial undercoverage. Re-selection generally moved coverage closer to the nominal level, although performance varied across simulation regimes and coefficients. Sensitivity analyses evaluating coverage against the population Cox coefficients corresponding to each originally selected predictor set gave similar aggregate coverage for the primary interval comparison. In the NKI70 breast-cancer data, the four selected genes appeared together in only 0.6% of bootstrap samples under re-selection at the observed tuning-parameter value. These results suggest that selection instability can be an important component of post-selection coefficient uncertainty and that bootstrap re-selection can help incorporate this variability.

papers.intro:
After variable selection, the model used for inference is itself data dependent. In time-to-event analysis, Cox–Lasso selection can determine which predictors enter a subsequent unpenalised Cox model. One analysis strategy is to select predictors using the Cox–Lasso and then refit an unpenalised Cox model using only the selected predictors (Tibshirani, 1997; Schemet and Friedrich-Welz, 2026). We refer to this set of variables as the selected predictor set. This two-stage strategy is referred to here as post-Lasso refitting, by analogy with post-Lasso estimation in linear regression (Belloni and Chernozhukov, 2013). It is related to relaxed Lasso procedures, which allow the penalty to be reduced or removed after selection (Meinshausen, 2007). Conventional standard errors and bootstrap procedures that keep this predictor set fixed quantify refitting uncertainty without repeating the selection step. If another sample selects a different set, they do not represent the additional variability arising from that change. The inferential consequences of data-dependent model selection are well recognised: conventional confidence intervals need not retain their nominal coverage after model selection (Berk et al., 2013). One related way to account for model uncertainty is model averaging, which combines estimates across candidate models and has also been developed for Cox regression (Hjort and Claeskens, 2003; Hjort and Claeskens, 2006). Our approach addresses a different inferential question: it retains the coefficient estimate from the originally selected unpenalised Cox refit and uses bootstrap re-selection to assess uncertainty associated with the selection and refitting procedure, rather than constructing a model-averaged estimator. Bootstrap resampling has also been used to assess the stability of variable selection in Cox regression (Sauerbrei and Schumacher, 1992). However, describing selection stability does not itself establish the coverage properties of coefficient intervals. We therefore investigate how repeating Cox–Lasso selection within a model-based bootstrap affects empirical interval coverage and width.

We use the NKI70 breast-cancer data to illustrate this distinction. The data contain 144 patients, 48 observed events, and expression measurements for 70 genes that are used as candidate predictors. 10-fold cross-validation is used with the CV-min tuning rule, which selects λ^min\widehat{\lambda}_{\min}, the tuning-parameter value that minimises cross-validated partial-likelihood deviance. In the observed analysis, the Cox–Lasso selects four gene-expression predictors, labelled QSCN6L1, ZNF533, IGFBP5.1, and PRC1. In 500 model-based bootstrap samples in which Cox–Lasso selection is repeated at the observed tuning-parameter value λ^min\widehat{\lambda}_{\min}, this exact set reappears in 0.6% of the samples. The same observed tuning-parameter value λ^min\widehat{\lambda}_{\min} is used in every bootstrap sample, even though the selected predictor set can change. Stability also differs considerably between individual predictors. PRC1 is selected again in 78.4% of bootstrap samples, whereas QSCN6L1 is selected again in 48.6%. These frequencies describe the particular observed-data analysis and bootstrap design; the original selected set can also depend on the random cross-validation splits. They illustrate why stability of the complete selected set and re-selection frequency for an individual predictor are distinct quantities.

The selected Cox–Lasso model also depends on how the tuning parameter is chosen. In high-dimensional Cox regression, variable-selection properties have been shown to depend strongly on the value of the Lasso tuning parameter, motivating alternative rules for choosing this value (Ternès et al., 2016). This dependence is usually discussed in terms of the selected model itself, for example its sparsity or false-discovery properties. For post-selection inference, it raises a further question: whether variability introduced by tuning-parameter selection also propagates into coefficient uncertainty and confidence-interval coverage after refitting.

The inferential consequences are most apparent when selection is unstable. Reliable recovery of relevant predictors generally requires conditions on sparsity, signal strength, and predictor dependence that are difficult to assess in a single applied data set. When data perturbations change the selected set, intervals constructed as though the observed set had been prespecified may omit variation from the selection and refitting procedure. Different selected sets can also yield different coefficients for the same predictor. The implications for interval coverage therefore depend on both selection stability and the inferential target (Tibshirani et al., 2018; Schemet and Friedrich-Welz, 2026).

Several approaches address inference after variable selection from different perspectives. Bootstrap inference after model selection has a long history (Efron, 2014), and Garcia-Angulo and Claeskens (2025) recently developed bootstrap inference after model selection for likelihood-based models. In Cox regression, complementary approaches include selective inference for L1L_{1}-penalised likelihood models (Taylor and Tibshirani, 2018), conditional post-selection inference for interval-censored Cox data (Zhang et al., 2025), and debiased-Lasso procedures that target low-dimensional components of a larger Cox model (Xia et al., 2023). These approaches answer related but distinct inferential questions. Our focus is the selection and refitting procedure in which the Cox–Lasso selects predictors, an unpenalised Cox model is fitted using the selected predictors, and coefficient intervals are then reported.

papers.title: NP-Hardness and a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, with Applications to Dense Subgraphs
papers.abstract: Given intervals and points on a line, each point with a demand, and a budget $K$, Maximum Interval Multicover asks for at most $K$ intervals that satisfy as many points as possible, a point being satisfied if it lies in at least as many chosen intervals as its demand. One application is committee elections in which each candidate is approved by consecutive voters and voters have individual demands. Xu, Ran and Zhang introduced the problem and gave a $1/2$-approximation; the objective is not submodular when demands exceed one. Li, Tu, Zhang and Cao gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for the minimization counterpart, unweighted partial interval multicover, and asked for its complexity. We prove that both problems are NP-hard, even for intervals of equal length; as their optima are integers bounded by the input size, neither has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We then give a PTAS for Maximum Interval Multicover, also for arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing rewards for the coverage of each point. Building on a decomposition from Nonner's PTAS for Densest $k$-Subgraph on interval graphs, our scheme cuts the line into pieces at a small loss and solves every piece exactly. The key dynamic program handles intervals crossing a common point by choosing an interleaving of their left and right endpoints rather than sweeping along the line; it needs only two counters to track these intervals. The same algorithm yields PTASes on convex bipartite graphs for Bipartite Dense Subgraph, improving on the ratio $2/3$ of Backer and Keil for the subclass of bipartite permutation graphs, and on interval graphs for Maximum $k$-Vertex Cover and weighted clique counts.

Their hardness proof also applies to a weighted version of Densest kk-Subgraph. Their unweighted problem has the same decision version as MaxIMC: can at most KK intervals satisfy at least QQ points? papers.title: Evidence for a Dirac Spin Liquid in the Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet from High-Precision Neural-Network Quantum States
papers.abstract: The spin-1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet is a central model in the study of quantum spin liquids, yet its ground-state properties remain unresolved. We perform large-scale variational Monte-Carlo calculations using neural-network quantum states (NQSs) with kagome-geometry-aware message-passing convolution on two-dimensional tori containing up to 300 spins, and achieve exceptionally low variational energies for the kagome model. The spin and dimer structure factors show no evidence of magnetic or valence-bond long-range order. Moreover, the dominant symmetry-resolved spin and dimer correlations exhibit a common scaling behavior consistent with the emergent $SO(6)$ monopole multiplet of the Dirac spin liquid. Finally, the fidelity of the optimized NQSs with Gutzwiller-projected mean-field states increasingly favors the Dirac state over the competing $Z_{2}$ candidates as the system size grows. Together, these complementary results provide evidence for a $U(1)$ Dirac spin-liquid ground state in the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet.

papers.title: Physics-Based Plausibility Assessment of AI-Predicted Vehicle Parameters for Automotive Radar in Pre-Crash Scenarios
papers.abstract: Automotive radar is a key sensing modality for safety-critical vehicle functions due to its robustness under adverse weather and lighting conditions. Recent advances in AI-based radar perception enable the direct estimation of object parameters from a single radar measurement cycle. However, the internal decision process of data-driven models is typically not explicitly linked to the underlying radar sensing physics. Consequently, object estimates may achieve high statistical accuracy while remaining physically inconsistent with the measured radar signature, particularly in previously unseen scenarios. Such inconsistencies are especially critical for heading estimation, as they directly affect trajectory prediction and collision assessment in pre-crash scenarios. This paper presents a physics-based consistency assessment framework for validating AI-derived vehicle hypotheses in automotive radar perception. The proposed approach generates an expected radar signature from AI-estimated object parameters using a physics-based reference model that incorporates occlusion-dependent edge visibility, aspect- and angle-dependent RCS modeling, and characteristic wheel-induced MD signatures. The expected signature is compared with the observed radar point cloud using a Wasserstein-distance-based consistency metric computed from three complementary features: the spatial distribution of detections along object edges, the local detection count, and the radar reflection intensity. In this way, physically implausible object hypotheses can be identified and corrected independently of the underlying neural network architecture and without model retraining or architectural modifications. The proposed consistency module is integrated as a cascaded post-processing stage for vehicle heading estimation.

papers.intro:
The ongoing integration of driver assistance and automated driving functions is expected to contribute to an increasingly heterogeneous traffic environment. As a result, vehicles with different levels of automation will operate alongside manually driven vehicles and other traffic participants, leading to more complex interaction patterns and dynamic traffic situations [1]. Consequently, vehicle safety systems increasingly depend on a reliable perception of surrounding traffic participants and their motion patterns. This is particularly important for traffic safety and pre-crash applications, which impose stringent end-to-end latency requirements while requiring highly dependable prediction and decision-making capabilities [2, 3, 4]. Errors in perception can propagate to downstream prediction and planning modules, ultimately degrading the safety performance of the overall driving systems [5] and can compromise collision assessment and the activation of pre-crash occupant restraint systems [6]

Among the sensing modalities used in automotive applications, radar has gained prominence due to its robustness in adverse weather and lighting conditions and its ability to provide direct measurements of object distance and relative radial velocity [7, 8, 9]. In particular, radar measurements can contain distinctive md signatures that capture object-specific motion patterns and provide additional information beyond object-related parameters such as position, velocity, orientation, and spatial extent [10, 11]. Among these parameters, the heading angle is particularly important, as it describes the object’s orientation and forms part of the vehicle state representations used for state estimation and trajectory planning [12, 13]. An erroneous heading estimate can adversely affect subsequent trajectory prediction and collision assessment algorithms, thereby impairing the performance of downstream pre-crash vehicle safety systems [14, 15]. Consequently, automated driving functions rely on continuously available and reliable object information, making accurate object state estimation safety-critical [16].

One major challenge is the substantial variability and complexity of real-world traffic scenarios, including rare and previously unseen situations, which cannot be exhaustively captured during development and validation [21]. Even with comprehensive training data, previously unseen variations in sensing conditions, environmental conditions, and traffic scenarios may arise during deployment, potentially degrading model performance in ways not captured by offline evaluation metrics [22, 23]. This issue is particularly relevant for radar sensing, where measurements are generated through electromagnetic wave propagation and are influenced by a variety of physical effects, including multipath propagation [24], target-dependent reflection behavior [25], coherent interference effects [26], partial occlusions, and overlapping object responses. As a result, the measured radar response of the same target may vary considerably with small changes in aspect angle, target distance, and other influencing factors, posing challenges for robust radar perception [7, 27]. This motivates an additional assessment of whether ai-estimated object parameters, particularly the heading angle, are physically consistent with the radar response generated by the corresponding object.
