papers.title: From Navier-Stokes to Measure-Valued Euler-Brinkman Equations: Homogenization in the Inviscid Limit
papers.abstract: We study the behaviour of the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations with vanishing viscosity and a no-slip condition in a periodically perforated domain. The behaviour depends on the particle size and the viscosity of the fluid. We prove convergence to a measure-valued solution, provided that the local Reynolds number is small, in the subcritical and critical regime. In the first case, the limit solves the Euler equations, whereas in the second case it solves the Euler-Brinkman equations. This extends the results of https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6544/acfe56 for less regular limit functions. In particular, we also prove existence of measure-valued solutions to the Euler-Brinkman equations, along with weak-strong uniqueness.
papers.intro:
Mixtures of fluids with many small particles, called suspensions, appear in a lot in nature and industrial applications – be it in the form of blood, dust storms or air-fuel injections in engines. Since tracking every particle is not feasible, one wants to find and study an effective model for these mixtures (as has been done in for example [1, 3, 10, 13, 11, 17]). Moreover, many of the physically interesting fluids have low viscosity, so it also interesting so study the homogenization setting together with a vanishing viscosity coefficient. In this work, we will only consider stationary particles with a no-slip boundary condition.

Mixtures of fluids with many small particles, called suspensions, appear in a lot in nature and industrial applications – be it in the form of blood, dust storms or air-fuel injections in engines. Since tracking every particle is not feasible, one wants to find and study an effective model for these mixtures (as has been done in for example [1, 3, 10, 13, 11, 17]). Moreover, many of the physically interesting fluids have low viscosity, so it also interesting so study the homogenization setting together with a vanishing viscosity coefficient. In this work, we will only consider stationary particles with a no-slip boundary condition.

Some mathematical results dealing with such a combined homogenization and inviscid limit are [13, 14, 12], where the problem is studied in a periodic geometry and the particle size is of the same order as the inter-particle distance, resulting in Darcy-type equations. Results dealing with smaller particles are [8, 6, 5]: in [8], the subcritical 22-dimensional regime is studied, in [6], all corresponding three regimes in the 33-dimensional case are analyzed leading to the Euler, the Euler-Brinkman and Darcy’s law in the subcritical, critical and supercritical case, respectively. In [5], the results of [6] are extended to random particle configurations in (parts of) the critical and subcritical regime. The results [8, 6, 5] are restricted to the cases where the limit function uu is sufficiently smooth (which is not necessary if the viscosity does not vanish, like in [1, 3, 10]). However, in light of the recent blow-up results for the Euler equations, smooth solutions can only be expected to exist for small times, even with smooth initial data. In this work, we extend the results of [6] with less assumptions on the regularity of uu, where we of course have to relax the notion of solution to the Euler(-Brinkman) equations. Namely, we prove that without assuming additional regularity of the limiting velocity field, up to a subsequence, the solutions converge to a measure-valued solution of the Euler–Brinkman equations. In particular, this provides existence for measure-valued solutions to the Euler-Brinkman system arising from a microscopic fluid model.

In [5], the results of [6] are extended to random particle configurations in (parts of) the critical and subcritical regime. The results [8, 6, 5] are restricted to the cases where the limit function uu is sufficiently smooth (which is not necessary if the viscosity does not vanish, like in [1, 3, 10]). However, in light of the recent blow-up results for the Euler equations, smooth solutions can only be expected to exist for small times, even with smooth initial data. Namely, we prove that without assuming additional regularity of the limiting velocity field, up to a subsequence, the solutions converge to a measure-valued solution of the Euler–Brinkman equations. In particular, this provides existence for measure-valued solutions to the Euler-Brinkman system arising from a microscopic fluid model.

Requiring less regularity of the limit function is a natural question since the regime of low viscosity is generally characterized by turbulent flow (that is, flow with little regularity). Understanding the regularity of fluids, even with initially smooth data, is in itself a very interesting question and has attracted much research. To this end, various notions of weaker solutions to the Euler equations have been introduced - for example the dissipative solutions already by Lions in the 90s [9], and since then more general measure-valued solutions, dissipative weak solutions (confusingly, these are not the same as the ones from Lions) or energy-variational solutions. All of these concept have the property of global existence and weak-strong uniqueness. In fact, for the Euler equations, the latter three concepts have been shown to be equivalent, see [2] (and the dissipative solutions of Lions are a special case of them). Since we want to study vanishing viscosity limits, we have decided to work with measure-valued solutions, where existence is usually shown by considering a vanishing viscosity sequence of the Navier-Stokes equations (see [18, 4, 2] and references therein for further reading on this topic). This article is structured as follows: below, we first introduce the mathematical setting and state our main results. Then, we recall in Section 2 important results for Young measures and measure-valued solutions to the Euler equations, as well as introducing measure-valued solutions to the Euler-Brinkman equations. In Section 3, we recall some preliminary results from [6] which we will use in Section 4 to prove our main results.

papers.title: TTSonic: A Unified Framework for Composable and Controllable Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems can synthesize natural and expressive speech, yet a practical speech foundation model must go beyond naturalness to offer stable quality, precise controllability, and a broad set of composable capabilities within a unified framework. We present TTSonic, a unified speech generation model that supports zero-shot TTS, voice cloning, prosody cloning, instruction following, voice conversion, and cloning from noisy reference speech. Rather than relying on separate task-specific models, TTSonic accommodates diverse conditioning signals, including text, natural language instructions, reference speech, and text-described timbre, within the same model framework. Specifically, we develop a semantic--acoustic disentangled speech tokenizer through ASR-supervised semantic learning and reconstruction-guided generative refinement. Serving as the representational foundation of our unified framework, the tokenizer enables the Text-to-Semantic autoregressive model to focus on semantic and prosodic planning, while the acoustic flow-matching model specializes in high-quality speech rendering under diverse acoustic and timbre conditions. Building on this framework, we incorporate CoT-guided instruction-following planning and Text2Timbre voice design to support controllable speech generation. Experiments across zero-shot synthesis, multilingual and cross-lingual TTS, instruction following, voice design, voice conversion, and noisy-reference cloning demonstrate the competitive performance and broad applicability of TTSonic.

papers.intro:

papers.title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

Scaling has become the dominant paradigm of modern artificial intelligence (Kaplan et al., 2020). However, scaling model size incurs a fundamental trade-off: increased capability at the cost of higher computational latency and degrading real-time responsiveness. While higher latency may be tolerable in static or text-based applications, it presents a critical failure mode in robotics. Physical robotics requires tight perception-action loops to handle real-time contact dynamics and sudden environmental shifts, such as grasping falling objects or absorbing unexpected bumps.

However, scaling model size incurs a fundamental trade-off: increased capability at the cost of higher computational latency and degrading real-time responsiveness. While higher latency may be tolerable in static or text-based applications, it presents a critical failure mode in robotics. Physical robotics requires tight perception-action loops to handle real-time contact dynamics and sudden environmental shifts, such as grasping falling objects or absorbing unexpected bumps.

Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) (Brohan et al., 2022; Zitkovich et al., 2023) models fall victim to this bottleneck, creating a persistent tension between model capability, computational overhead, and closed-loop reactivity. Consequently, scaling the vision-language backbone improves high-level reasoning at the expense of motor agility, yielding a system that is semantically rich but physically lag-bound and depends on open-loop deployment. To resolve this friction, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policies (ARP). As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), ARP breaks the reactivity-capability trade-off, enabling the seamless integration of significantly larger foundational models into robot pipelines without significantly compromising dynamic reactivity or real-time performance.

Making robot policies asynchronous, however, introduces several new challenges. The fast action expert must continuously act on a compact semantic memory produced by a slower VLM, while the robot state evolves during both VLM and action expert inference. This creates two sources of mismatch: the semantic memory may be stale relative to the current observation, and newly predicted actions may arrive after execution has already progressed. Performing the two loops asynchronously can therefore lead to outdated conditioning, delayed actions, and discontinuities across replanning cycles. ARP addresses these challenges by compressing rich VLM activations into fixed-width asynchronous memory, explicitly conditioning the action expert on semantic staleness and execution delay, and training with temporally mismatched memories and action-prefix conditioning to support smooth continuous replanning.

papers.title: Multi-modal Laplace-based sampling
papers.abstract: We study the multi-modal Laplace approximation, given by a weighted Gaussian mixture centred at the local minima of the negative log-density, for sampling from probability measures that concentrate around finitely many modes as an inverse-temperature parameter $n$ grows. Such distributions occur in Bayesian inference in the small noise or large data regime. We derive explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on the Hellinger distance between the multi-modal Laplace approximation and the concentrating posterior. The bound decays like $n^{-1/2}$ with $n$ and the constants depend only polynomially on the dimension $d$. Moreover, we analyse the Laplace mixture as a proposal distribution for self-normalised importance sampling and independent Metropolis--Hastings (IMH) targeting concentration multimodal distributions. We derive asymptotic results, as $n\to\infty$, on the effective sample size in case of importance sampling as well as on the average acceptance probability, lag-one autocorrelation, and spectral gap in case of IMH. Numerical experiments illustrate and verify our theoretical findings.

papers.intro:
The extraction of information from complex, multi-modal distributions that are specified only implicitly through evaluations of their densities is a long-standing problem in applied sciences. A promising approach is approximate sampling, that is, generating realizations from a probability measure that is ‘sufficiently close’ to the target distribution. This methodology is frequently used in computational statistics, machine learning, and statistical physics, where the desired distribution often depends on an inverse-temperature parameter. As the inverse temperature increases, intuitively, the distribution becomes increasingly concentrated. While this concentration can make it possible to identify a particularly high probability area, it also poses significant challenges for sampling and can substantially reduce the efficiency of the sampling scheme. We propose a multi-modal Laplace mixture approximation that can serve as a proxy for the target distribution and under suitable assumptions remains capable to capture the asymptotic behavior when the ‘concentration’ increases.

papers.title: Correctness Firewalls for Synthesized Database Components
papers.abstract: For the first time in history, high-performance code is cheap. Today's coding agents can generate bespoke, instance-optimized data systems with excellent performance, and such agents will continue to improve as LLMs advance. But a purely agentic approach, even when validated with strong testing techniques, does not automatically inherit the correctness guarantees our community has spent decades building. We propose a middle ground between hand-crafted and agent-crafted systems: correctness firewalls, lightweight design patterns under which a synthesized component can affect a system's performance but never its results. Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. Drawing on these case studies, we outline a research agenda for how data management systems can exploit coding agents without giving up their hard-won correctness guarantees, from protecting synthesized code to measuring the cost of correctness.

papers.title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
papers.abstract: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

papers.title: Automated consolidation of dispersed DSO data resources into a consistent digital twin of the distribution grid
papers.abstract: The energy transition causes a growing number of distributed flexible energy resources in the low voltage grid. To utilize that flexibility, automation and control algorithms are needed, which typically are developed in theoretical research. We build a cyberphysical algorithm test bed to bridge the gap between theoretical research and practical application in cooperation with a local DSO in Walenstadt, Switzerland. To obtain suitable monitoring and data analysis capabilities from their existing data landscape, we propose tool-independent data harmonization measures in preparation for a digital twin of the grid. For data extraction from high-security network zones we developed a secure pipeline that implements a logical data diode ensuring one-way traffic only. Furthermore, we established a test community of voluntary prosumer households, whose flexible assets were made accessible through a common backend, giving us actuation capabilities. The presented publish-subscribe architecture is not only suitable to integrate various data sources into a central data collection, but also to manage access privileges of different stakeholders. This could support unbundling of an organization's data flows and the implementation of data space concepts.

Complementary to this top-down approach, we identify the steps and technologies required to achieve the same goal starting from a DSO’s day-to-day operation and legacy software systems in use in a bottom-up manner. Therefore existing assets and systems are integrated into the proposed framework with minimal overhead while laying the foundation for a wide range of research opportunities. Like many electricity utilities, our project partner manages their grid related data in use-case-specific software tools and documents, that are optimized for day-to-day operation rather than research and analysis. Data from different sources must be linked, transformed into machine-readable and preferably open formats, and kept up to date automatically. Besides data harmonization, real-time monitoring and command transfer are essential to utilize flexible assets in closed-loop control schemes.

papers.title: 2D Navier-Stokes with viscosity-dependent Navier slip: strong convergence for unbounded initial velocity
papers.abstract: For the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with Navier friction on a smooth, bounded, simply connected domain, we establish strong vorticity convergence along a subsequence in the vanishing viscosity limit for initial vorticity in $L^p$ with $p>1$. The friction coefficients may grow as viscosity vanishes under an explicit growth restriction depending on $p$, which includes regimes of vanishing slip length. The main challenge, even for viscosity-independent friction, is to control the vorticity generated at the boundary. We split the vorticity into contributions from the initial data and the boundary. By combining renormalization and estimates for the normal velocity near the boundary, we show that the boundary contribution vanishes in the inviscid limit. As a consequence, the limiting Euler solutions conserve kinetic energy.

papers.title: The Hot Neptune Initiative (HONEI): IV. TOI-4129 b, an Adolescent Neptune in the Ridge
papers.abstract: Recent exoplanet demographics studies have uncovered the Neptune ridge: an overdensity of intermediate-size planets at orbital periods between 3--6~d. The origin of this pile-up remains unclear, but it could be a consequence of high-eccentricity migration (HEM). Here, we confirm TOI-4129\,b, a planet that may help to reveal the origin of the Neptune ridge. Using radial velocities from HARPS-N and transit photometry from TESS and four ground-based telescopes, we found that TOI-4129\,b has a relatively low density ($R_p = 5.7 \pm 0.2\, R_\oplus$, $M_p = 26\pm 6 \,M_\oplus$, $\rho_p = 0.8 \pm 0.2 ~\textrm{g}~\textrm{cm}^{-3}$) and orbits a $V = 12.9$ K dwarf star every 3.27~d, placing it at the inner edge of the Neptune ridge. We detect the stellar rotation period at 12.7~d in the photometry, implying a fairly young gyrochronal age of $1.20^{+0.16}_{-0.30}~$Gyr for the system. With a Transmission Spectroscopy Metric of $112\pm 30$, this adolescent Neptune is a good target for atmospheric observations with \textit{JWST} and \textit{Ariel}, and we also find that it is amenable to future constraints on the (three-dimensional) stellar obliquity. TOI-4129\,b will therefore be an important testing ground for the idea that planets in the Neptune ridge underwent HEM to arrive at their current locations.

In Section II, we describe the TESS observations that revealed the initial transit signals and the accompanying photometric, spectroscopic, and imaging observations that aided in confirming the planet. In Section III, we present the joint fit of RV and transit data using jaxoplanet. We continue to discuss the implications of the planet’s density, age, and prospects for future atmospheric and obliquity constraints in Section IV. We conclude with a brief overview of our findings in Section V.

papers.title: Self-governed access control in open robot swarms using a blockchain-based DAO
papers.abstract: Robot swarms harness simple, local interactions among many individually limited robots to produce complex, coordinated collective behavior, making them valuable across domains from agriculture to disaster response. We envision the next frontier for such swarms as open swarms, in which robots join or leave the swarm dynamically at runtime. The ability to dynamically adjust swarm size has been shown to be beneficial, for instance by reducing inconsistencies and network partitioning, especially under sparse connectivity or in complex environments, ultimately improving task performance. For practical deployment, however, open swarms requires governance, particularly protection against Byzantine behavior (i.e., faulty or malicious robots), since allowing robots to join freely also makes the swarm easier to infiltrate. Blockchain technology has recently been incorporated into robot swarms, offering secure, decentralized coordination and improved resilience, though largely in closed settings with a fixed, predetermined membership. In this work, we extend these benefits to open swarms by introducing robot swarms governed by a blockchain-based decentralized autonomous organization (DAO), in which the swarm regulates itself using autonomous rules encoded in smart contracts. We outline several DAO-based governance mechanisms for robot swarms, depending on the needs of the application, and present a proof-of-concept implementation of a simple DAO that regulates swarm membership and prevents Byzantine infiltration. Our simulation results and real-robot validations show that DAO-governed access control and robot removal can maintain proper swarm functioning while keeping the number of Byzantine robots within acceptable limits.

papers.intro:
Robot swarms are decentralized systems, typically composed of a large number of autonomous robots that coordinate to perform tasks [22, 24, 34], achieving outcomes that no single robot could accomplish alone. Within such systems, robots exchange information and task-critical data with one another. These local interactions, both among robots and with their environment, give rise to self-organized collective behavior. Swarm robotics systems have been shown to hold potential across a wide range of domains, including agriculture [4, 5], environmental monitoring [84, 41], construction [92, 6], and disaster response operations [86, 73]. The decentralized nature of robot swarms facilitates parallel task execution and ensures scalability across swarm sizes, while also providing fault tolerance against individual failures. Realizing these benefits, however, depends on effective coordination among robots, each of which must act on consistent information and pursue shared goals across the swarm. To date, such coordination has largely been achieved within swarms deployed and owned by a single entity, in which membership is fixed and known in advance. As robotics technology matures and its use across real-world applications continues to gain traction, we envision open swarms as the new paradigm for robot swarms, i.e., multi-robot teams in which robots join and leave dynamically at runtime.

Realizing these benefits, however, depends on effective coordination among robots, each of which must act on consistent information and pursue shared goals across the swarm. To date, such coordination has largely been achieved within swarms deployed and owned by a single entity, in which membership is fixed and known in advance. As robotics technology matures and its use across real-world applications continues to gain traction, we envision open swarms as the new paradigm for robot swarms, i.e., multi-robot teams in which robots join and leave dynamically at runtime.

The dynamic regulation of swarm size in open swarms brings forth several advantages. When task demand increases, additional robots can be recruited to scale up resources, and when robots become redundant, they can be removed from the swarm or relocated elsewhere to maintain resource efficiency, providing performance benefits over static deployments [31]. Looking ahead, the increasing accessibility of the technology is likely to further drive the deployment of autonomous robots by companies and private users alike, for widespread tasks such as environmental monitoring, waste management, pest control, surveillance, and mapping. As such deployments become more widespread, robots belonging to various stakeholders will increasingly need to operate within shared physical spaces [25, 94], giving rise to the need for robot swarms that evolve dynamically rather than being operated as a fixed, closed system. Dynamic membership, however, introduces a governance challenge. Due to the decentralized nature of robot swarms, no single entity exists to make decisions such as regulating swarm membership, assigning roles, managing hierarchical relationships among robots, upgrading protocols, or allocating resources in an open swarm setting. Among these governance needs, regulating swarm membership, that is, establishing who may join, remain in, or be removed from the swarm, is especially important. As there are no inherent mechanisms to verify their trustworthiness before admission, allowing robots to join freely in open swarms increases the risk of infiltration by Byzantine robots (that is faulty or malicious robots whose behavior deviates from their intended specification), turning this governance gap directly into a risk to task execution. This gap also leads to security concerns, as open membership can expose robotic systems to Sybil attacks, in which an adversary creates multiple identities to amplify its influence.

Several studies have highlighted need for security in swarm robotics [39, 37, 43]; yet, as is often the case with emerging technologies, security has largely been treated as an afterthought, and research in this area remains in its infancy. Most studies either consider closed swarms, which restrict participation to a predefined set of identities, or assume non-malicious interactions. In the real-world, open swarms require secure mechanisms to govern membership.

Most studies either consider closed swarms, which restrict participation to a predefined set of identities, or assume non-malicious interactions. In the real-world, open swarms require secure mechanisms to govern membership.

Research on securing robot swarms has primarily focused on collective decision-making, especially the best-of-nn problem, in which a swarm must reach a consensus on the most suitable of nn options [88, 87, 70]. In the best-of-nn problem, Byzantine behavior, arising from malicious agents or communication manipulation, can lead to consensus deadlocks (analogous to denial-of-service in computing security) or cause the swarm to converge on suboptimal options (known as the wrong addressing problem, since the swarm is led to incorrect choices) [54, 7, 100]. Prior research has proposed defenses such as neighborhood filtering and probabilistic trust models to assess received information based on its consistency with a robot’s own data [101, 99, 71, 17, 58, 68, 83]. Other approaches protect the confidentiality and integrity of inter-robot data exchanges while preventing the disclosure of the details of the mission performed by the robot swarm [14, 66]. However, these works primarily focus on limiting the impact of Byzantine behavior. More recently, blockchain-based approaches have shown promise for actively identifying and mitigating Byzantine robots [77, 103, 57, 89]. Blockchain enables tamper-proof algorithms to be executed in a decentralized manner through smart contracts (see Section Methods, Blockchain fundamentals), supporting not only the control and coordination of swarm behavior but also the active identification and removal of Byzantine robots. However, these implementations assume closed settings in which the total number of robots, and therefore the number of Byzantine robots to be neutralized, is fixed and known a priori, preventing scalability. Recent work has shown that runtime scalability achieved by forming open swarms can effectively regulate latency in blockchain-enabled robot swarms [102], but this scalability gives rise to a related security concern, since once the swarm is open, the risk of Byzantine infiltration becomes a threat. Similarly, prior work on open membership in general multi-robot systems does not resolve this risk, remaining vulnerable to Sybil attacks or often relying on a centralized authority to vet newly joined members [11, 105], an assumption that defeats the vision of a truly open, decentralized swarm. Robot swarms therefore demand a fundamentally different approach, one that can detect and remove Byzantine robots without relying on any centralized control, even as membership changes at runtime.

papers.title: A Neuroprosthetic SoC Featuring Rapid Local Sensory Feedback with On-Chip Unsupervised Multi-Class Spike Sorting
papers.abstract: This letter presents a 65 nm neuroprosthetic system-on-chip (SoC) featuring a rapid feedback pathway from motor recording to sensory stimulation. To enable low-latency sensory mapping modulated by individual-neuron firing rates, the SoC integrates a mixed-signal unsupervised spike-sorting module with stimulation-artifact rejection, a programmable sliding-window firing-rate calculator, and a closed-loop controller for adapting stimulation parameters. The spike-sorting module combines event-driven analog feature extraction with Manhattan-distance-based digital clustering while consuming 1.6 $\mu$W/channel. On the Quiroga Difficult-1 benchmark, it achieves 94.58% three-class accuracy, with only a 0.4% reduction when stimulation artifacts are introduced at 20% of the spike count. The closed-loop controller supports polynomial and logarithmic mapping functions and incorporates Mitchell's approximation for power saving. The SoC is fully characterized on the bench and in vivo.

papers.intro:
Tens of millions worldwide have motor impairments caused by limb loss, paralysis, or neurodegenerative disease [1]. Neuroprostheses translate neural recordings into commands for assistive devices, enabling intention-driven control. Advances in electrode resolution and recording electronics provide large volumes of data for motor decoders, but gains from additional channels are limited by steep learning curves and inadequate feedback. Conventional prostheses rely solely on visual feedback, while sensor-driven stimulation adds artificial touch for dexterous manipulation but remains limited by signal-chain latency and trial-and-error learning. Rapid local feedback between the motor and sensory cortices provides a promising alternative approach [2], in which sensory feedback inferred directly from motor signals modulates sensory stimulation, thereby reducing latency and simplifying learning. Animal studies using optogenetic stimulation show that rapid feedback can accelerate motor target acquisition [3]. Given the limited clinical translatability of optogenetics, electrical stimulation offers an alternative but requires reliable artifact rejection.

papers.title: Ermakov--Based embeddings as a parameter-free layer for physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Evolution equations with time-dependent coefficients force a neural solver to spend capacity on a scale that the equation already determines. We show that a single classical object, the Ermakov-Pinney scale function $\rho$, can be written into the input layer of a physics-informed neural network as a parameter-free embedding. One construction covers three problem families through the two signs of the Pinney constant $c$: linear diffusion ($c=-1$, $\omega\equiv0$), diffusion in a time-dependent confining trap ($c=-1$, $\omega\neq0$), and the quantum oscillator with time-dependent frequency ($c=+1$). An exact moment identity gives $\rho$ in closed form from the initial data alone, so no auxiliary network or knowledge of the solution is needed. Our central finding is comparative: each family requires a different component of the construction and has a different honest control. In family I, the diffusive-time reparametrisation alone reproduces most of the gain, so that family is a poor test of the idea and shows why an ablation is mandatory. In family II no time reparametrisation exists, the control degrades accuracy, and the amplitude prefactor becomes essential (40.8x). In family III the adiabatic approximation also fails, and the quadratic phase factor is what matters (5.7x). The method does not help when the reduced solution does not converge to a fixed point: its extrapolation advantage then disappears. The reduction itself is the classical scaling-variable change of the self-similar-asymptotics literature; what is new is the moment identity that makes it architectural for time-dependent coefficients, and the comparative anatomy above.

papers.title: On the Primacy Bias in RLVR Training
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models. However, it still remains unclear whether RLVR can extend reasoning capabilities beyond what is already encoded in the base model. In this paper, we study this question through the lens of primacy bias: the tendency of models to over-rely on already-learned representations, disproportionately improving performance on problems they already handle well while underexploring harder ones that require departing from those representations. Through our controlled experiments and large-scale analysis, we show that RLVR training on mixed data tends to further sharpen performance on easier problems while yielding only marginal gains on harder ones. We find that although hard problems lead to modest gains overall, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model's reasoning capabilities and pushing the representations. However, prolonged training on these hard problems may also hurt and lead to forgetting on easy problems. These findings help to better understand some of the prior conflicting observations about RLVR, specifically, why on (OOD) domains where the base model performs poorly, improvements on hard problems can expand reasoning; while on well-trained domains, forgetting can reduce performance and mask genuine gains obtained from hard problems.

Large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned for reasoning have recently achieved remarkable gains on complex reasoning benchmarks. A key driver is Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) [10, 20], which iteratively optimizes LLMs using simple, verifiable rewards, thereby incentivizing complex reasoning behaviors such as backtracking and self-verification within the reasoning traces of these models.

A key driver is Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) [10, 20], which iteratively optimizes LLMs using simple, verifiable rewards, thereby incentivizing complex reasoning behaviors such as backtracking and self-verification within the reasoning traces of these models.

Despite this progress, the answer to the question “does RLVR expand toward new reasoning capabilities?” still remains under debate. Some studies have suggested that RL fine-tuning only improves sample efficiency on problems already solvable within the base model, rather than enabling it to solve new problems [41, 23, 36]. On the other hand, some other works [31, 22, 35, 40] have provided evidence that RL-trained models can still induce novel reasoning strategies on out-of-distribution (OOD) domains. These works, however, suggest that the relationship between the base model and the evaluated task—specifically the extent to which the base model can already solve the task problems—may play an important role in explaining whether RLVR leads to reasoning expansion or sharpening.

In this paper, we seek a principled explanation for these seemingly contradictory outcomes through the lens of primacy bias—the tendency to overfit to initial experiences (i.e., the pre-trained knowledge) that can damage the rest of the learning process [17, 2]. This bias not only limits exploration but also impairs the learnability of on-policy data during RL training. It arises because the model becomes increasingly rigid and remains confined near its pre-trained initialization, rather than allowing meaningful adaptation of its internal representations towards new downstream tasks—a behavior commonly referred to as the lazy training regime [24, 8, 24]. To study this hypothesis, we first investigate primacy bias in RLVR using experiments that fully control both pre-training and post-training pipeline (Section 4). We compare coverage dynamics during RL fine-tuning induced by pre-training against random initialization. Our results show that primacy bias leads to coverage shrinkage, regardless of the fine-tuning distribution. Furthermore, we observe that this primacy bias induces sparser parameter updates during training which hinders the network’s ability to learn rare or more challenging problems (i.e., those that the pre-trained or base model struggles to handle). These observations suggest that the RLVR model mostly operates in the lazy regime [8, 15], staying close to its pre-trained initialization and requiring prolonged training to meaningfully adapt to harder examples [27, 18, 24].

Our results show that RLVR-trained models could often be well approximated by the linearization around their pre-trained base model, while exhibiting minimal feature drift. This result suggests that RLVR in this more general setting also operates in the lazy regime, providing a possible explanation for the sparse parameter updates observed during RLVR training, as reported in [26]. We believe that these findings place RLVR within a theoretically tractable regime, which can provide a foundation for more principled, scalable, and analyzable studies of learning dynamics in reasoning post-training [27, 18, 6].

Motivated by our findings, we identify an unlearnable phenomenon that emerges from the interaction between primacy bias and the lazy training regime in RLVR-based LLM training (Section 6). To study this, we first perform fine-tuning across a mixture of easy and hard reasoning problems and observe that mixed training disproportionately improves rewards on easy examples while limiting learning on harder ones. Our results show that although hard problems lead to only modest overall gains during training, they are actually the ones that help most in expanding the model’s reasoning capabilities. At the same time, focused training on hard problems introduces a subtle trade-off that must be carefully taken into account. We find that prolonged training on these difficult examples can also hurt and lead to catastrophic forgetting on the easier problems, likely due to substantial deviations from the initial base model representations. This explains why, as observed in [22], prolonged RLVR training can expand the reasoning boundary in less familiar or out-of-distribution domains, where the pre-trained model initially struggles. In such settings, extended training enables the model to gradually escape the lazy regime and meaningfully adapt to the new target tasks [18, 35, 40], ultimately leading to broader reasoning coverage. In contrast, in domains where the pre-trained model already performs well—such as mathematical or code reasoning, particularly on easier problems—prolonged training may provide limited benefit and can even lead to adverse effects such as coverage shrinkage or catastrophic forgetting. In these cases, the gains obtained from adapting to harder examples may be outweighed by degradation on the easier ones due to substantial deviations from the base model representations and the effects of catastrophic forgetting.

We find that prolonged training on these difficult examples can also hurt and lead to catastrophic forgetting on the easier problems, likely due to substantial deviations from the initial base model representations. This explains why, as observed in [22], prolonged RLVR training can expand the reasoning boundary in less familiar or out-of-distribution domains, where the pre-trained model initially struggles. In such settings, extended training enables the model to gradually escape the lazy regime and meaningfully adapt to the new target tasks [18, 35, 40], ultimately leading to broader reasoning coverage. In contrast, in domains where the pre-trained model already performs well—such as mathematical or code reasoning, particularly on easier problems—prolonged training may provide limited benefit and can even lead to adverse effects such as coverage shrinkage or catastrophic forgetting. In these cases, the gains obtained from adapting to harder examples may be outweighed by degradation on the easier ones due to substantial deviations from the base model representations and the effects of catastrophic forgetting.

We hope that our study provides a clearer understanding of the conflicting observations surrounding RLVR post-training and motivates more principled approaches for studying and controlling the trade-off between adaptation and forgetting.

papers.title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
papers.abstract: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

papers.intro:
Recently, there has been a growing interest in scaling frontier language models to different AI R&D processes (Huang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026). From optimizing a set of hyperparameters to post-training small language models, agents are becoming more autonomous, and more capable of tackling complex and lengthy tasks (Karpathy, 2026; Rank et al., 2026). As these agents shift towards longer horizon tasks, they increasingly accumulate insights, strategies, and practical experience. In real-world research, scientists often carry lessons from one project to the next, whether by reusing code or reapplying a specific post-training algorithm for example. We ask the question of whether experience acquired from one problem can benefit subsequent ones. Answering this requires understanding whether agents can retain knowledge across tasks and use it to adapt more effectively to new ones, bridging continual learning and meta-learning (Zhao et al., 2024; Asawa et al., 2026; Shu et al., 2026). We study this setting without updating model weights, in which case experience is transferred only through the state accumulated during execution.

We study this setting without updating model weights, in which case experience is transferred only through the state accumulated during execution.

Existing evaluations treat each R&D problem in isolation by resetting the agent from scratch before each new task. Although autoresearch-style loops allow agents to use feedback to optimize solutions iteratively, the acquired experience is discarded once the task is finished. Consequently, these evaluations cannot assess if lessons about experimental design, modeling choices, or execution failures can be applied to related tasks and improve future research. While resetting prevents irrelevant or misleading experience from carrying over, it may also force agents to rediscover useful practices or repeat avoidable mistakes. However, retaining experience is not necessarily beneficial (Shu et al., 2026). Experience becomes useful only to the extent the tasks share transferable structure, such as common data-generating factors, modeling principles, or experimental approaches. Thus, whether autonomous research agents can identify and adapt such transferable experience to new tasks remains largely unevaluated. Figure 1 summarizes the paired evaluation pipeline.

papers.title: Korringa factor in Dirac-nodal-line systems
papers.abstract: The Korringa factor $K(\alpha)$ in the nuclear magnetic resonance studies is a widely used measure of electron-correlation effects in metals and is conventionally interpreted using the non-correlated value $K(\alpha)$ = 1. In Dirac-fermion systems, however, the non-correlated reference value depends on the electronic density of states (DOS) and differs from that of conventional metals. Here, we theoretically investigate the non-correlated Korringa factor $K^*(\alpha)$ in a Dirac nodal-line (DNL) system with finite nodal-line dispersion using a DOS-based approach. We show that $K^*(\alpha)$ exhibits an intrinsic temperature dependence, continuously evolving from the Dirac-fermion value of 1.71 at high temperatures to the metallic value of 1 at low temperatures. The crossover temperature is found to be proportional to the nodal-line dispersion width, identified as the characteristic energy scale governing the non-correlated Korringa factor in DNL systems. We further demonstrate that Landau quantization generates singular DOS structures that strongly enhance $K^*(\alpha)$, producing pronounced peaks even in the absence of electron correlations. In addition, $K^*(\alpha)$ exhibits two distinct types of magnetic oscillations arising from intra-level and inter-level contributions. The latter originates from the overlap of singular points belonging to positive and negative quantum-number Landau subbands at the Fermi level and represents a unique consequence of the finite energy dispersion of a DNL. These results provide a quantitative reference for interpreting NMR experiments in DNL materials and for identifying genuine correlation effects beyond DOS-induced contributions.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Evidence for Multiple Field-Induced Phases in an Anisotropic Kagome Antiferromagnet
papers.abstract: Kagome antiferromagnets are predicted to host exotic field-induced phases, yet experimental identification of their thermodynamic signatures remains challenging. Here we combine specific heat ($C$) and ultrasound measurements up to 36 T and down to 0.5 K to map the $H-T$ phase diagram of the anisotropic kagome magnet Y$_3$Cu$_9$(OH)$_{19}$Cl$_8$. We show that the suppression of long-range antiferromagnetic order with field at $\sim 15$ T approximately coincides with the onset of the unconventional $1/6$ (or $1/9$) magnetization plateau previously observed in this system. The attenuation (and sound velocity) then intriguingly increases down to 0.5 K just at $\mu_0H = 15$ T, and $C/T$ becomes temperature independent. Moreover, our measurements are consistent with the opening of a spin gap $\Delta_0\simeq3.5\pm 0.3$ K within the plateau and reveal a further compressible (ungapped) phase beyond the plateau phase, unveiling a rich sequence of field-induced phases in this quantum magnet.

papers.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na$_3$PS$_4$
papers.abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described by mobile cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder enhances transport remains unresolved at the mesoscale, inaccessible to ensemble-averaged probes. We use Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy to measure nanoscale structural dynamics of a single ball-milled Na$_3$PS$_4$ particle. We find that the cubic phase behaves as a strain glass: a frustrated configuration of three degenerate tetragonal variants with short-range order. Its domain-wall motion is stress-driven, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing as residual milling stress is depleted. Rearrangements follow scale-free avalanche statistics, matching ferroelastic martensites but without external driving. The tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics occur on timescales comparable to estimated ionic diffusion across the particle, indicating the host structure cannot be assumed static on transport-relevant timescales.

papers.title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
papers.abstract: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.

A common approach updates the virtual DT representations and uses them to guide operational decisions in the physical system, such as resource allocation in edge networks [2, 7]. However, updating the DT itself requires communication and computational resources. Transmitting large volumes of sensing data to the DT server can cause substantial communication overhead and processing delays [5, 8]. The resulting synchronization delays may cause the DT to rely on outdated information, reducing its usefulness in real-time applications. Moreover, depending on the application, updating the DT may require only a subset of the sensing data or information extracted from it [9, 10, 5, 8].

papers.title: Base change between canonical basis and path basis
papers.abstract: Almost 30 years ago Littelmann conjectured that there is a unitriangular base change between the dual canonical basis and the path vector basis for all symmetrizable Kac-Moody Lie algebras. In this paper we give a positive answer to the conjecture for the case of classical Lie algebras and type $G_2$, when the path model is given by standard Young tableaux.

papers.intro:
Almost 30 years ago, Littelmann [14] conjectured that there is a unitriangular base change between the dual canonical basis and the path vector basis for all symmetrizable Kac-Moody Lie algebras. However, little progress has been made since then. This is primarily for two reasons: First, the path vector basis is incompatible with the crystal structure of the canonical basis. This can be seen from the fact that the path basis is not perfect in the sense of Baumann, Kamnitzer and Knutson [1] (the definition of perfect by Berenstein and Kazhdan [3] is identical up to normalization). Second, the canonical basis is incompatible with the Frobenius splitting in general [2, 18]. However, the definition of the path vectors makes use of the Frobenius splitting. Thus, to prove the conjecture a new perspective is required.

papers.title: The Evolution Strategies Paradox: Better Models from Worse Perturbations
papers.abstract: How is it possible for perturbation-based methods like Evolution Strategies (ES) to optimize billion-parameter large language models (LLMs)? Classical search methods are highly dependent on finding good candidates within generated populations. However, when using ES to fine-tune LLMs, a phenomenon can occur where all offspring models consistently perform worse than the parent model, yet during training, the parent model consistently improves. This paradox occurs across models, tasks, and even modalities. This paper characterizes the paradox, then examines how the local reward landscape and properties of the ES estimator contribute to it: in high-dimensional spaces, exploration leads to worse performance, yet still highlights good directions; aggregating those directions then allows for making local improvements. The result can be seen as a new optimization paradigm where a principled interaction of noise and curvature produces the paradox as a byproduct of effective optimization. These findings provide guidance for taking advantage of perturbation-based methods in LLM fine-tuning and in high-dimensional optimization in general.

Optimization using population-based search, i.e. evolutionary computation, relies on generating and selecting high-quality candidates. Genetic algorithms optimize by discovering beneficial recombinations and mutations along with selection of candidates with higher fitness (Goldberg, 1989). Particle swarm optimization pressures particles to search for better positions while maintaining the previously best found positions (Eberhart & Kennedy, 1995). The original evolution strategies (ES) compared a single parent to a single offspring and selected the better solution (Rechenberg, 1965). In each of these methods, the generation of higher-fitness candidate solutions is crucial to the optimization process.

The original evolution strategies (ES) compared a single parent to a single offspring and selected the better solution (Rechenberg, 1965). In each of these methods, the generation of higher-fitness candidate solutions is crucial to the optimization process.

For ES specifically, this story has changed over time. With the introduction of natural evolution strategies (Wierstra et al., 2011, NES,), which updates the parent model using a weighted sum of all generated candidates, ES was shown to potentially behave as a gradient approximator instead of working through the selection of candidates with an improved fitness. NES was a precursor to implementation of ES on large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) problems such as Atari (Salimans et al., 2017) that then inspired theoretical analysis that found that ES with isotropic Gaussian noise is a gradient estimate: with high enough population sizes (ranging from thousands to hundreds of thousands), correlation between the ES update direction and network gradient stays consistent while ES performance on a per-iteration basis would match that of backpropagation (Zhang et al., 2017). This along with further work concluded that ES operated as a gradient estimator that naturally favors robustness (Lehman et al., 2018).

papers.title: Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes
papers.abstract:
Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) enables drones to observe forest canopies by warping and averaging multiple displaced views at a common depth. However, occlusion is suppressed rather than eliminated, causing poorly observed regions to appear occupied and leading to systematic biomass overestimation. The Deep Forest project cannot distinguish reconstruction artifacts from real vegetation because its training data relies on measured reflectance points, excluding empty space and preventing the network from learning explicit occupancy boundaries.
  This thesis addresses the problem by modifying training labels rather than the imaging process. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal-stack generation and as 550 depth-clipped slabs derived from scene geometry to provide occupancy labels, explicitly representing void space as a negative class. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural forest stands containing 80-200 trees across three species. A pretrained Pix2Pix model translates rendered RGB images into a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces aligned focal stacks of 550 planes across three channels.
  Four architectures were evaluated on a held-out scene. The plain 2D U-Net achieved an IoU of 0.6290, outperforming the volumetric 3D U-Net (0.5707). Established reconstruction methods performed substantially worse: COLMAP achieved 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959, both after their respective optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture achieved the highest IoU of 0.6514 without dilation or per-scene calibration. These results highlight the limitations of conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Lakehouse: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Managing Enterprise Knowledge Graphs at Scale
papers.abstract: Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse through metadata, indexes, and caching. Enterprise knowledge graphs (KGs) offer an alternative approach to such integration for the purposes of data analysis, but handling them at scale must address the Three Vs of big data: volume, velocity, and variety. Contextualized KGs (CKGs) meet part of that challenge by enriching facts with contextual information, yet many applications require only a context-specific subset of that knowledge. We propose the Knowledge Graph Lakehouse (KG Lakehouse), a cloud-native microservice architecture that adapts the data lakehouse paradigm for management of CKGs at scale. The KG Lakehouse indexes incoming source documents along configurable context dimensions and stores these documents in a data lake, from which application-specific CKGs are constructed on demand instead of maintaining a single, monolithic KG. We realize the proposed architecture as a proof of concept, with independently deployable services built from established cloud technology; context dimensions and format-specific document handling enter as configuration, leaving the architecture independent of the application domain. We evaluate the implemented system in experiments on a distributed cluster deployment.

papers.intro:
Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse (see [37] for an overview). A data warehouse stores structured data that is clean and consistent [62, p. 63], optimized for recurring analytical tasks, with analytical results typically summarized in reports or dashboards [62, p. 625]. A data lake retains raw or minimally processed data to support flexible exploratory analysis and future analytical use cases [62, p. 624]. Although flexible, the data lake’s schema-on-read approach requires complex cleaning and transformation before analysis [62, p. 625], increasing processing overhead and complicating data management for large datasets. The data lakehouse [14] combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse by leveraging metadata, indexes, and caching to support complex data analysis while providing storage efficiency and query flexibility.

Enterprise knowledge graphs have been proposed as an alternative approach to integrating heterogeneous data sources; see [55] for one such proposal. A knowledge graph (KG) comprises facts about real-world entities and their relationships. KGs have been described as “large networks of entities, their semantic types, properties, and relationships” [41], “a set of interconnected typed entities and their attributes“ [35, p. 1] with possibly arbitrary relationships [49]. Apart from the instance-level facts, or assertional knowledge (ABox) [49], a KG also often comprises terminological or ontological knowledge (TBox) representing “the vocabulary used in the knowledge graph” [35, p. 2] and enabling ontological reasoning over the facts [19]. Unlike open KGs, an enterprise KG is “typically internal to a company and applied for commercial use-cases” [38, p. 71:4], containing relevant knowledge for an organization [19]. Due to their versatility, enterprise KGs “are a natural data model for data integration” [55, p. 10]. By combining assertional and ontological knowledge, enterprise KGs capture both data and their semantics, making it easier for data consumers to discover actionable knowledge [55].

By combining assertional and ontological knowledge, enterprise KGs capture both data and their semantics, making it easier for data consumers to discover actionable knowledge [55].

Effective deployment of enterprise KGs relies on a KG management system (KGMS), which not only provides ontological reasoning capabilities but also supports large-scale data management and analytical tasks [19]. The knowledge represented in enterprise KGs expands and evolves over time, incorporating information from various structured and unstructured sources and existing at multiple levels of granularity and abstraction [48]. Data sources continuously provide large volumes of heterogeneous information, often at high velocity, that must be integrated into the enterprise KG. The KGMS must therefore be able to handle the Three Vs of big data [43]: volume, velocity, and variety.

At the conceptual level, contextualized KGs [56, 21] provide a model for managing heterogeneous and evolving knowledge by enriching facts with contextual information. In a contextualized KG (CKG), facts are typically organized into subgraphs, each corresponding to a distinct context. To represent CKGs, the Knowledge Graph OLAP (KG-OLAP) model [53] employs a multidimensional context model with hierarchically organized dimensions. The dimensions capture different contextual characteristics, e.g., geographic scope, temporal applicability, and topic. The hierarchical organization of the dimensions supports the representation of contexts at different levels of granularity (e.g., sector and country for geographic scope, and day and month for temporal applicability). Dedicated operations, adapted to KGs from traditional online analytical processing (OLAP), enable the navigation and combination of contexts as well as the transformation of the graph structure as required for specific analytical tasks.

At the architectural level, a cloud-native microservice architecture provides the modularity, elasticity, and scalability required to manage CKGs at scale. Different services can be independently developed, deployed, and horizontally scaled according to workload requirements. New services can be introduced to integrate additional data sources without affecting existing components. A microservice architecture may further leverage the contextual partitioning of knowledge in CKGs to enable parallel processing of independent contexts for improved performance.

Even with CKGs and a cloud-native microservice architecture, maintaining a single, monolithic enterprise KG at scale remains challenging and introduces overhead that many applications do not require. A KG typically covers a variety of topics rather than focusing exclusively on a single aspect of the real world [49]. For specific tasks, however, only a subset of the knowledge represented in an enterprise KG may be relevant, since “most people do not care about all entities that exist in the world, but rather a small fraction or subset that is personally relevant to them” [48, p. 43]. For example, in air traffic management, which serves as a motivating use case and setting of the running example throughout this paper, a KG may represent knowledge about the air traffic network, including infrastructure, airspace, operational events, weather conditions, and flight plans [54]. A pilot preparing for a flight from Munich to Vienna only requires knowledge of weather conditions and operational events, such as airspace closures and operational restrictions of navigation aids, that are relevant to the airspace sectors along the planned route on the day of the flight, rather than knowledge about the entire European air traffic network [52]. An air traffic controller, on the other hand, requires the same contextual knowledge, together with the flight plans as well as positions of aircraft operating in the supervised airspace sector and its adjacent sectors during a specific period of responsibility. Hence, maintaining a single, monolithic KG is both impractical and unnecessary for many applications, which instead require only context-specific subsets of the available knowledge.

papers.title: Asymptotic preserving IMEX Active Flux schemes for a hyperbolic approximation of the Korteweg-de Vries equation
papers.abstract: We present a theoretical and numerical analysis of novel IMEX Active Flux schemes for a hyperbolic approximation of the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. For this approximation, it is important that the numerical schemes recover the limit equations (asymptotic preserving) and retain their order of accuracy in the limit (asymptotically accurate). Using formal asymptotic analysis and numerical experiments, we show that an Active Flux spatial discretisation (closely related to the standard semi-discrete Active Flux scheme), combined with an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta scheme, is asymptotic preserving but not asymptotically accurate. We therefore propose alternative spatial discretisations that differ in the update equations of the point values. First, we derive a scheme by rescaling and eliminating terms in the upwind matrices. Second, we develop a second-order scheme by using central discretisation for the terms treated implicitly in time and present two modifications of it to third-order. Finally, we formulate a scheme with predefined upwind directions that are not chosen based on characteristics. We show that the alternative schemes are not only asymptotic preserving but also asymptotically accurate, and compare their accuracy, stability, and energy conservation numerically.

One can approximate high-order PDEs with a first-order hyperbolic system. This process is called hyperbolisation or hyperbolic relaxation. Hyperbolisation can serve multiple purposes, among them the easy implementation into existing codes and imposition of boundary conditions. In certain cases it can be used to remove numerical stiffness. Moreover, high-order PDEs allow for infinite propagation speed, which might be considered a violation of causality and is not the case for first order hyperbolic systems [32]. The hyperbolisations offer an approach to Riemann problems for PDEs that do not a priori admit discontinuous solutions. A substantial amount of research has been dedicated to hyperbolisation. For example, in recent years, hyperbolic approximations of the Navier-Stokes-Korteweg system [17], the conduit equation [29], the Serre-Green-Naghdi model [10], and a class of dispersive and diffusive-dispersive equations [9] have been presented and analysed. The latter class includes the KdV equation.

papers.title: Learned Smartphone ISP on Mobile GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
papers.abstract: With the increasing importance of mobile camera quality in modern smartphones, growing attention has been directed toward computational photography and advanced image signal processing (ISP) algorithms aimed at enhancing various perceptual attributes of captured images. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can reconstruct RGB photos from RAW Bayer camera data while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale Fujifilm UltraISP dataset consisting of RAW-RGB image pairs captured with the Sony IMX586 Quad Bayer mobile sensor and a professional 102MP medium format FujiFilm GFX100 camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct high-quality 5MP RGB image from raw data on both platforms under 100 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

papers.intro:
A primary driver of performance improvements in smartphone cameras can be attributed to sophisticated image processing algorithms, including those for noise suppression, accurate color reproduction, and high dynamic range (HDR) imaging. While individual stages of the traditional image signal processing (ISP) pipeline can be replaced by dedicated deep learning models to enhance reconstruction quality, a more comprehensive paradigm involves substituting the entire RAW-to-RGB pipeline with a unified neural network that implicitly learns all intermediate processing steps. Such an approach enables direct utilization of the richer 10–16 bit information contained in the original, unprocessed RAW Bayer data, thereby potentially leading to improved image restoration performance. In [54], the authors first introduced this approach by constructing the Zurich RAW-to-RGB dataset comprised of paired RAW and RGB images captured using both a mobile camera sensor and a high-end DSLR camera. This dataset was subsequently used to train a deep neural network for end-to-end image reconstruction. The experimental results demonstrated the strong potential of this method in comparison to the commercial hand-crafted ISP of the Huawei P20 smartphone. Even better results were achieved by the models proposed in the follow-up challenges and papers using the same dataset [52, 15, 78, 58, 46]. A further advancement in deep learning–based ISP development was presented in [42, 29], where the authors introduced a more advanced Fujifilm UltraISP dataset for the considered task along with mobile-efficient CNN architectures capable of processing high-resolution images directly on smartphones. In this competition, we use the same dataset and propose the participants to design even more efficient learned ISP models that can run on recent smartphone GPUs.

Designing deep learning models that run efficiently on mobile devices — especially across different AI accelerators like NPUs — is a complex challenge. It demands careful analysis of hardware constraints such as limited operator support, restricted memory capacity and bandwidth, reduced accuracy for quantized models and specific driver behavior of NPUs. Even when certain layers or operations are technically supported, they may be executed inefficiently due to constraints related to NPU hardware architecture or its driver implementation, and thus create performance bottlenecks during inference. A striking example here would be the Google Tensor NPU present in all recent Google Pixel smartphones that, despite having quite high theoretical peak performance, is unable to efficiently accelerate the vast majority of even simplistic CNN-based models [39]. As a result, achieving low latency and energy efficiency often requires partial or complete redesigns of model architectures. For a more detailed discussion of these challenges and the performance of modern mobile AI accelerators we refer to [47, 44]. Overall, all these limitations require various adaptations of the standard deep learning models for their efficient deployment on mobile NPUs, including conventional optimizations like 16-bit / 8-bit [12, 57, 56, 93, 67, 73, 8, 77, 79, 68] and low-bit [10, 83, 5, 55, 70, 97, 6, 60, 16, 7, 65] quantization, network pruning and compression [12, 66, 69, 74, 59, 20, 96, 89, 61, 85], NPU-specific adaptations, platform-aware neural architecture search [21, 80, 87, 84, 72, 14, 95, 88, 13, 94], etc.

In this Mobile AI Challenge, the participants were proposed to develop efficient deep learning models that can reconstruct 5MP RGB image from RAW Bayer data while running on smartphone GPUs. For this, the participating teams were provided with the Fujifilm UltraISP dataset [42] consisting of thousands paired photos captured with a normal mobile camera sensor and a professional 102MP medium-format FujiFilm GFX100 camera. The runtime of the models was evaluated on mobile GPUs present in the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and the Dimensity 9500 chipsets. Each submission was evaluated based on both image fidelity and runtime efficiency, thus balancing reconstruction quality with model efficiency. All solutions developed during this challenge are fully compatible with the LiteRT [75] (former TensorFlow Lite) framework, enabling deployment on a variety of Linux and Android-based IoT platforms, smartphones, and edge devices.

papers.title: RGB Photo Enhancement with Deep Learning on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
papers.abstract: On-device RGB photo enhancement is a popular task that is needed for quality improvement of photos captured with mobile devices as well as for retouching of images acquired through other sources. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose participants to design fast solutions that can perform comprehensive enhancement of RGB photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale DPED dataset consisting of RGB image pairs captured with an old iPhone 3GS smartphone and a professional Canon 70D DSLR camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to enhance Full HD resolution RGB images on both platforms under 300 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

papers.intro:
Image restoration and enhancement are fundamental problems in computer vision that aim to improve various aspects of image quality, including denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, color correction, contrast enhancement, dynamic range reconstruction and artifact removal. These research areas have attracted significant attention from the computer vision and graphics communities in recent years due to their broad practical relevance and inherent technical challenges. With the rapid growth of mobile photography, enhancing images captured by compact mobile camera sensors has become an active area of research, driving the development of advanced image enhancement techniques for smartphones and other resource-constrained devices. Tackling this problem as an end-to-end photo enhancement task was first proposed in [23, 24], where the authors presented a deep learning model for mapping low-quality smartphone photos to superior-quality images obtained with a high-end DSLR camera. The collected DPED dataset was later used in a number of subsequent challenges [48, 51] and works [79, 66, 13, 20, 19, 63] that proposed numerous performant solutions for this problem. In this competition, we use the same dataset and propose the participants to design even more efficient RGB image enhancement models that can run on recent smartphone GPUs.
