papers.title: The Devil is in the Context: Nine Dimensions of Prompt Injection Attacks
papers.abstract:
Prompt injection is usually discussed and evaluated as a single, homogeneous type of attack. However, vulnerabilities reported in real-world systems show that prompt injections vary widely. Moreover, the same instruction can be a prompt injection in one context and a legitimate request in another, depending on the user's intent and the system's policies. Ignoring this variation leaves gaps in how defenses are evaluated, and can give a false sense of security against real-world attacks.
  We identify nine dimensions along which prompt injection attacks differ. Together, they form a taxonomy that describes the injected instruction itself, its relation to the user's task, and how it manifests in the target system. Each dimension affects which defenses can detect or prevent an attack.
  We first use the taxonomy to characterize six real-world prompt injection vulnerabilities, showing how much these attacks differ. We then apply it to nine prompt injection benchmarks and find that most cover only a small region of this space. Combining benchmarks helps, but 13% of pairwise category combinations remain untested, mostly among the less commonly represented categories. Finally, we show that the taxonomy supports automated annotation of benchmarks and targeted generation of new test cases to fill these gaps.
  The taxonomy is also useful beyond benchmarks. Defense authors can use it to state which types of prompt injection they evaluated against, and system operators can use it to identify which attacks apply to their system and choose defenses to match.

papers.intro:
Indirect prompt injection is widely considered to be the foremost security threat to AI agents [1]. In prompt injection, an attacker “injects” instructions into the context of a user’s agent, e.g. by inserting them in a document or a webpage that the agent visits [2]. This enables the attacker to affect the agent’s control flow, with consequences such as unwanted actions, exfiltration of the user’s data, or even account takeover. Numerous prompt injection detections and mitigations have been proposed [3, 4, 5], and multiple benchmarks have been defined to evaluate these defenses [6, 7, 8].

However, defenses and benchmarks alike treat prompt injection as a single, homogeneous threat. This has concrete consequences. First, robustness claims are not comparable. A defense that reports a low attack success rate on one benchmark may have been tested on only a narrow slice of the attack space, and the aggregate number says little about attacks with different properties. Second, benchmark size is mistaken for coverage. Thousands of samples may exercise only a handful of distinct attack properties, leaving whole classes of attacks untested. Third, application developers cannot match defenses to their threat model. An email assistant that reads messages from untrusted senders and keeps long-term memory faces very different injections than a single-turn document summarizer.

If a user asks an agent to summarize the document, their expectation is for the sentence to be treated as part of the content to report, rather than an instruction. Second, whether an attack succeeds also depends on properties of the system and of the injection itself. For instance: 1) The trust label of the source matters: an email containing “Please get back to me with the IPO details” may be a legitimate request or a prompt injection, depending on whether it was sent by a colleague or by someone else. Information-flow defenses [10, 3] can limit what untrusted sources are able to cause, but some cases, such as insider threats or mislabeled sources, still require a prompt injection classifier to exercise judgment. 2) The visibility and interpretability of the injected instruction affect whether a user, and more importantly a prompt injection classifier, can detect it [7]. 3) Whether the attack is meant to be one-off, or to persist in the agent’s memory and affect its future responses [11]. In this paper, we characterize prompt injection instances by introducing a taxonomy with nine dimensions. Unlike previous categorizations that focus solely on the injected instruction (e.g., [12]), the unit of classification in our taxonomy is the injected instruction in the context of (i) the user’s intended task and (ii) the affected system (including the agentic harness), as illustrated in Figure 1. The inclusion of the user’s intentions into the taxonomy enables capturing aspects such as the alignment of the injected instructions to the user’s task and topic. Complementarily, by looking at the affected system our taxonomy can encompass any trust labels, intended effects of the attack (e.g., if it persists in memory or it causes tool calls), as well as whether the injections are visible and interpretable by the user. Each dimension captures a distinct property whose variation changes what a defense must observe, where it can intervene, or which assumptions it relies on.

papers.title: Approximating Distributions on Vertex Degrees in Random Hypergraphs via Stein's Method
papers.abstract: Complex data are increasingly represented as hypergraphs. We establish bounds for approximating joint vertex-degree distributions by independent multivariate Poisson and correlated normal distributions in hypergraph models with independent hyperedges. We discuss the approximation of the distribution under different density regimes which are further supported by simulation studies.

papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Multi-Criteria Network Design Problems
papers.abstract:
Min-max multi-criteria optimization asks for a single feasible solution minimizing the maximum of its costs under $\ell$ nonnegative cost functions, a formulation that captures both fairness across groups and robustness across scenarios. It has proved hard to approximate even for basic problems: for robust shortest paths, polylogarithmic approximations are known only in quasi-polynomial time. For network design, the best known guarantee is an $\ell$-approximation, which is tight for the natural LP relaxation.
  We show that exponentially better and nearly optimal guarantees are achievable for two fundamental network design problems. For multi-criteria connectivity augmentation (MC-CAP), which asks to increase the edge connectivity of a given undirected graph by one, we give a randomized polynomial-time $O(\log \ell)$-approximation algorithm. Applying our augmentation procedure iteratively and analyzing its randomized choices jointly across iterations yields an $O(\log k \log \ell)$-approximation for the multi-criteria $k$-edge-connected spanning subgraph (MC-$k$-ECSS) problem, for every $k \geq 2$. We complement these algorithms with a nearly matching lower bound: for every fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, MC-CAP admits no polynomial-time $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} \ell)$-approximation, even when the underlying graph is a star, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}\bigl(n^{\log^{O(1)}n}\bigr)$. The same hardness extends to the MC-$k$-ECSS problem.

papers.title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
papers.abstract: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.

papers.title: Weakly viscous nonlocal wave equations: forward theory, Lebesgue Runge approximation, and inverse problems
papers.abstract: We study forward and inverse problems for weakly viscous nonlocal wave equations with elastic term $(-\Delta)^s u$ and dissipative term $(-\Delta)^r\partial_tu$, where $0\leq r<s$. For time-dependent potentials in suitable $L^\infty(0,T;L^p(\Omega))$ classes, we establish finite energy well-posedness, strong continuity in time, and an energy identity by parabolic regularization and time-regularization arguments. Under explicit nonlocality and nonresonance assumptions on the fractional orders, we prove Runge approximation in $L^2(0,T;\widetilde H^r(\Omega))$ and hence in $L^2(\Omega\times(0,T))$. As an application, partial exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements uniquely determine the potential in all three exponent regimes of the Runge theorem, including integer elastic orders with noninteger dissipative orders. The recovery argument combines equality of solutions with the same exterior input, unique continuation or the entanglement principle, and a single Lebesgue-space Runge approximation. It applies to the full admissible potential class, without spatial boundedness, sign, or smallness assumptions.

The recovery of an interior coefficient from exterior measurements is a central question in inverse problems for nonlocal equations. For fractional wave equations, the interaction between nonlocality and time evolution makes it possible to probe the interior by prescribing data on an arbitrarily chosen open subset of the exterior. When dissipation is also nonlocal, the measurement contains contributions from both the displacement and its time derivative. papers.title: Space--time Runge approximation for weakly viscous nonlocal waves and identification of coefficients
papers.abstract: We study very weak solutions and Runge approximation for weakly viscous nonlocal wave equations with elastic term $(-\Delta)^su$ and dissipative term $(-\Delta)^r\partial_tu$, where $0\leq r<s$. For time-dependent potentials satisfying a smallness condition, we establish a transposition theory for sources in the dual of the natural space--time energy space. Under explicit nonlocality and nonresonance assumptions, we prove Runge approximation in $L^2(0,T;\widetilde H^s(\Omega))$ and in $L^2(0,T;\widetilde H^s(\Omega)) \cap H^1_0(0,T;\widetilde H^r(\Omega))$. As an application, partial exterior Dirichlet-to-Neumann measurements uniquely determine a bounded, nonnegative, time-dependent coefficient in the nonlinear velocity damping term $q|\partial_tu|^{p-2}\partial_tu$ for $0<r<s$ and $2<p\leq 2+4r/n$. The proof establishes the small-amplitude response by energy estimates, weighted $L^p$ monotonicity convergence, and a linear Green identity, then applies adjoint Runge approximation followed by a forward velocity approximation in $L^2$. No smallness or positive lower bound is imposed on the nonlinear damping coefficient.

The purpose of this article is to establish such a space–time approximation property for weakly viscous nonlocal waves and to apply it to the recovery of a nonlinear damping coefficient.

papers.title: Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics
papers.abstract:
System prompt is a critical intellectual property of large language model (LLM) services. To analyze its leakage, prompt extraction attacks have been extensively studied. However, we validate that existing attacks substantially degrade on recent LLM services, whose complexity has evolved in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. Specifically, (1) system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc., and (2) only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent's actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed.
  In this paper, we address the above increased complexity by proposing Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which (1) decomposes the prompt extraction into a hierarchical reconstruction process with a pre-defined structural prompt template, and (2) iteratively updates the adversarial query with guidance of feedback-template differences to observe diverse outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of attack optimization to early stop or reset it for a good trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency.
  We also find that existing evaluation metrics for prompt fidelity can be misleading because they do not account for structural information. Therefore, we rely on global textual similarity and prioritize structural keywords. Moreover, we introduce a system-level metric, adversarial utility, to measure the help of prompt extraction for real-world downstream attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent superiority of ExtraHerO, with average improvements of 12.5\% (fidelity), 2.3\% (functionality), and 6.0\% (adversarial utility) on chatbots, and 12.2\%, 34.3\%, and 30.5\% on agents.

papers.intro:
The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized the landscape of artificial intelligence services, enabling highly specialized applications through the use of system prompts [26, 20, 34, 3, 42]. System prompts constitute a key intellectual property of LLM-based services. They define a service’s unique value through textual information that outlines sophisticated information, such as operational logic, strategic task instructions, and safety guardrails [18]. However, this concentration of value has rendered the system prompt a primary target for adversarial reverse-engineering, also known as extract attacks [20, 49, 36, 41, 5, 39]. Such system prompt attacks can replicate sophisticated service functionalities, including the internal security architecture [27], at near-zero cost, leading to considerable asset loss.

Such system prompt attacks can replicate sophisticated service functionalities, including the internal security architecture [27], at near-zero cost, leading to considerable asset loss.

To understand the risk, prompt extraction attacks have evolved from manual heuristics to automated algorithms. Early methods rely on manual prompt engineering to exploit empirical flaws [20, 10, 5]. These range from direct requests (e.g., “Repeat your instructions”) to indirect manipulation like “Now translate” or “Ignore previous instructions.” To bypass safety filters that block direct leakage, recent attacks use backward prediction. Specifically, output2prompt [49] reconstructs the system prompt by analyzing the model’s responses to fixed inputs. PRSA [41] improves this by categorizing LLM services and matching the style, tone, and wording of the target. T-GPS [36] further exploits text-based gradients to optimize the recovered prompt, making it functionally closer to the original.

However, we argue that all existing attacks have been limited to overly simplistic threat models. As illustrated in Figure 1, with the rapid evolution of recent LLMs and their powered agents, the complexity of extraction has increased in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. First, system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc. This modern design paradigm, as exemplified by emerging prompt programming frameworks [12, 46, 23], treats instructions not as static text but as modular configurations to regulate complex model behaviors and ensure stable task delivery in production environments. This makes the extraction based on direct requests or linearly iterative optimization insufficient. Second, only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent’s actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed by the (normal or malicious) user. From a functional standpoint, production agents encapsulate raw textual reasoning into discrete operational actions to streamline user experience (UX) [43, 48, 38, 52, 47, 25, 2]. This architectural design naturally imposes constraints on the adversary’s ability to extract the internal logic from the post-processed output information [13].

Specifically, for the system prompt, we synthesize system prompts with diverse function components and collect in-the-wild ones (with possible defenses) across five increasing complexity levels. For the output constraints, we post-process the output information to hide partial information from the adversary. In addition to the attack method, we also note that existing evaluation metrics may lead to misleading or insufficient results. For example, since token-level similarity used for measuring the prompt fidelity does not consider structural information, extracting non-functional stop words, such as “please” and “You are”, unexpectedly inflates the scores.

Specifically, we propose Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which addresses the increased complexity in both the prompt and output: (1) ExtraHerO decomposes the extraction task into a multi-stage recovery process by utilizing a pre-defined structural template. This ensures that execution-critical components, e.g., tool schemas and multi-step logic, are reconstructed with high structural fidelity. (2) ExtraHerO iteratively updates the adversarial query guided by the text gradient between the current template and the observed feedback. This allows the adversary to extract internal logic from sparse, post-processed outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of each optimization step to trigger early stops or resets, maintaining a good trade-off between effectiveness and query efficiency.

papers.title: Bayesian Cluster-Adjusted Standardised Mean Differences: A Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Reporting standardised mean differences of continuous psychometric measures is omnipresent in psychology. In a randomised controlled trial with a multilevel structure, one can define a cluster-adjusted version of these quantities naturally taking into account heterogeneous residual variances and accounting for the multilevel structure. In this article, we carefully define the underlying location-scale distributional mixed-effects models and derive cluster-adjusted standardised mean differences using partial pooling. Estimating these quantities is best handled using Bayesian statistics, and we perform an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study to test the performance of these metrics under different simulation configurations. We conclude that in order to measure the a-priori heterogeneous treatment effect across clusters in practically relevant scenarios, it is enough to consider random effects only on the location model and not on the scale model. Even under artificial severe heteroscedasticity, this reduced model performs well both in terms of parameter bias and predictive accuracy. The resulting cluster-adjusted standardised mean difference is an average value across clusters, where the heterogeneity is summarised via its standard deviation.

papers.title: Intra-unit-cell Josephson scanning tunneling spectroscopy of the cuprate Bi$_{1.2}$Pb$_{0.8}$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$
papers.abstract: The predominantly $d_{x^2-y^2}$-wave pairing symmetry of cuprate superconductors is well established, yet its microscopic manifestation in local Cooper-pair tunneling remains less explored. Here, we investigate Bi$_{1.2}$Pb$_{0.8}$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$, using Josephson scanning tunneling spectroscopy with a conventional $s$-wave superconducting Pb tip. We observe a zero-bias conductance enhancement whose approximately quadratic dependence on junction conductance is consistent with phase-diffusive Josephson tunneling. Atomic-resolution conductance maps and site-resolved spectra reveal a pronounced intra-unit-cell modulation, with enhanced Josephson response near oxygen sites and strong suppression near copper sites and along diagonal directions. Microscopic calculations incorporating the bilayer electronic structure and realistic Wannier-based tunneling matrix elements reproduce the observed spatial pattern through interference between pairing contributions of opposite signs. Our results reveal how the sign-changing $d$-wave superconducting order parameter manifests itself in atomic-scale Josephson tunneling, providing complementary evidence for unconventional pairing symmetry in cuprates.

papers.title: Observation of Scaling of Higher-Order Flow in a Unitary Fermi Gas
papers.abstract: Collective flow emerging from spatially anisotropic many-body systems is a fundamental manifestation of strongly interacting quantum matter, from ultracold quantum gases to the quark-gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Yet how collective flow emerges across different spatial harmonics and how dissipation modifies its evolution remain largely unexplored. Here we investigate the nonequilibrium expansion of a unitary Fermi gas initially confined in nearly homogeneous potentials with engineered angular deformations. By suddenly releasing the confinement, we resolve anisotropic flow harmonics up to the seventh order. Remarkably, after normalization and rescaling by the characteristic expansion timescale, the different harmonics and system sizes exhibit a universal early-time evolution. At longer times, this universality breaks down and we observe an approximately quadratic dependence of the harmonic attenuation on harmonic order, consistent with viscous acoustic scaling. Furthermore, temperature-dependent measurements reveal the role of shear viscosity in the dissipative evolution of higher-order flow. Our results open a new route to exploring the interplay between universal hydrodynamic expansion and dissipative transport, connecting collective dynamics in ultracold quantum gases with anisotropic flow in strongly interacting nuclear matter.

papers.title: Matchings under One-Sided Preferences with Soft Quotas
papers.abstract: Assigning applicants to posts in the presence of applicant preferences and quotas associated with posts is extensively investigated. For a post, a lower quota guarantees, and an upper quota limits the number of applicants assigned to it. Typically, quotas are assumed to be fixed, which need not be the case in practice. We address this by introducing a soft quota setting, in which every post is associated with two values - lower target and upper target - which together denote a range for the intended number of applicants in any assignment. Unlike the fixed quota setting, we allow the number of applicants assigned to a post to fall outside the range. This leads to assignments with deviation. Here, we study the problem of computing an assignment that has two orthogonal optimization objectives - minimizing the deviation (maximum or total) with respect to soft quotas and ensuring optimality with respect to preferences of applicants (rank-maximality or fairness). The order in which these objectives are considered, the different possibilities to optimize deviation combined with the well-studied notions of optimality with respect to preferences open up a range of optimization problems of practical importance. We present efficient algorithms based on flow networks to solve these optimization problems. We also consider a generalization of the soft quota setting, where every deviation is associated with a cost. We show extensions of our algorithms for solving the problems in this setting.

Every applicant ranks all the posts in its neighbourhood, and this ranking can involve ties between the posts. We assume that there are no gaps in the preference list of an applicant. In many practical applications, quotas need not be as rigid as assumed in the fixed quota setting, and relaxing lower quotas and augmenting upper quotas have been considered in the literature. Lower quotas have been extensively investigated in the two-sided preference list setting called the Hospital Residents problem [27, 29, 30, 23, 37, 40, 39, 24]. Here, the lower quota of a hospital denotes the minimum number of residents (doctors) needed for the smooth functioning of the hospital. As mentioned earlier, in the presence of lower quotas, a feasible matching may not always exist. Therefore, relaxing these lower quotas has been considered as a solution. For instance, instead of hospitals closing down due to the lack of a minimum number of doctors, they may simply reduce their service levels, as described in the work of Goko et al. [27]. Similarly, in the context of school choice, capacity planning to augment the number of available seats has recently been considered in multiple works [1, 12, 13]. Motivated by such applications, we relax the fixed quota assumption by proposing and studying a soft quota setting for the assignment problem in the one-sided preferences model.

papers.title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
papers.intro:
Humans navigate unfamiliar cities with little effort. Given a destination, a person consults a web map and follows its turn-by-turn directions, such as continuing along a sidewalk, turning onto a crosswalk or taking the stairs. Neither a metric goal nor precise position is required. The map indicates the next manoeuvre and its approximate location, while vision resolves where the crosswalk begins and when a turn has been completed. Since web maps provide such directions for nearly every place where people walk, a robot that follows them in the same manner could be deployed in any city given only a destination and without a prior mapping run, enabling applications such as last-mile delivery, urban inspection and guidance of visually impaired people.

Existing learned navigation methods fall short of this goal over long routes. Point-goal methods [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] receive the route as a sequence of GNSS waypoints, and their performance is therefore bounded by the accuracy of the position estimate. In cities, GNSS errors of several metres are common [6], enough to place a waypoint on the road or on the opposite side of the street, and over routes of several hundred metres such errors inevitably lead to failures. Waypoints also carry no notion of the social norms, such as staying on the sidewalk and crossing at crosswalks, so a policy that reaches every waypoint may still violate them and pose a safety risk in urban traffic.

Recent models bring vision-language navigation to real robots [10, 11, 12, 13], but they are typically demonstrated on single instructions over short distances. Recent models bring vision-language navigation to real robots [10, 11, 12, 13], but they are typically demonstrated on single instructions over short distances. We find that these models are brittle even at the level of a single atomic instruction (Section V-D), which makes it infeasible to follow a kilometre-long route by chaining such instructions.

In this work, we simplify the problem. Web-map directions already decompose a route into a sequence of atomic instructions, each describing a single manoeuvre such as “cross the road” that can be grounded in the camera image. Long-range navigation thus separates into deciding which atomic instruction applies at the current moment and executing that instruction reliably. The first problem requires the map and contextual reasoning but only a coarse position, since GNSS is needed only to identify the current step of the route rather than the exact position of the robot. The second problem requires only the camera and a short observation history. Language is a suitable interface between the two levels, since it is what web maps produce and what vision-language models (VLMs) reason in. Based on this observation, we propose WayTrace, a map-to-language-to-trace hierarchy (). An off-the-shelf orchestrator VLM reads the web-map directions, a satellite map of the surroundings and the recent camera images, and issues the next atomic command. An onboard trace predictor draws the path for this command in image space, and a reinforcement learning (RL) policy tracks the path lifted to 3D.

We evaluate WayTrace on ten long-range missions in a simulated Zurich old town and in real-world deployments. With perfect GNSS, WayTrace completes 83 % of the missions. It achieves the highest success rate at every level of GNSS error, and its success rate decreases gradually to 63 % with a drifting GNSS error of 7 m RMS, whereas that of point-goal baselines drops below 25 % and they leave the crosswalk or the sidewalk about ten times as often. Vision-language baselines complete at most 7 % of the missions, even with language commands from a tuned oracle. In the real world, WayTrace completed three missions of up to 426 m through a busy city centre fully autonomously, and a 1.37 km mission along rural trails and through a university campus with two short operator interventions. We will release the simulation environment, the long-range navigation benchmark, the trace prediction benchmarks, the dataset, the models and the code.

papers.title: From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals. These proposals can make assignments: who should act, what must be done, how much one should spend and by when. However, if the assignments change when the same opinions are processed again, publishing a single proposal can hide alternatives that participants never get to see. We examined this issue in four LLM mediators (three open-weight and one commercial) using opinions from DeliberationBank and Polis. For each task, a mediator drafted a proposal from thirty opinions five times, varying either the random seed or the order of the opinions. In 17% of five-run sets from the open-weight mediators and 20% from the commercial one, some runs contained assignments while others did not. Reordering the opinions changed the assignments almost as often as replacing them with opinions from different citizens. Three human annotators confirmed that the detected differences between runs were real, although the LLM judge overstated how often they occurred. Substantial variation remained under four safeguards: temperature zero, a commercial mediator, draft selection, and draft merging. The mediator's objective also shaped representation: prompts seeking agreement covered minority positions much less often than prompts asking to describe differences. A single proposal can therefore obscure choices in both the assignments it proposes and the views it excludes. We propose audits that make alternative assignments visible and disclose the objective behind each proposal.
papers.intro:
Participatory budgeting, citizen assemblies, and online consultations give citizens a direct say in public decisions [1, 2, 3]. Platforms such as Polis, vTaiwan and Decidim now involve thousands of people at once [4, 5, 6]. The difficult step has therefore moved from collecting input to making sense of it. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to perform this step. They write consensus statements that groups prefer over those by human mediators [7, 8], summarize Polis conversations [9], draft policy guidelines from collective dialogues [10], and analyze responses to national consultations [11]. Other systems, such as CIME and the Habermas Machine, use AI to support structured group deliberation and synthesize diverse perspectives through iterative feedback and voting [8, 12]. Existing evaluations have examined factors such as efficiency, alignment with human analysts, and acceptance of AI-generated outputs by participants [11, 7]. However, two additional aspects deserve attention: variability in proposals generated from the same opinions, and the influence of mediation objectives on which views are represented. As these systems move from summarizing views to drafting proposals, the assignment of responsibilities may become part of the decision-making process [13], which makes the design of mediation essential for democratic participation [14, 15, 16].

Existing evaluations examine whether participants endorse a statement and whether it represents their views [8, 17, 18]. A further question concerns the alternatives that a single output leaves unseen. In Fig. 2, the same model received the same thirty opinions in two different orders at temperature zero. The first output recommends policies without explicit assignment of responsibilities to a particular party. The second calls on every state to spend at least $10,000 per student by 2025. If an organizer publishes only one run, readers cannot see that changing the input order produces a different assignment of responsibilities. We call this a silent choice: a procedural factor that carries no information about citizens’ views changes the assignments in a proposal, while the published output leaves the alternative undisclosed.

A proposal that names who must act, what must be done, how much and by when is the part of mediation that decision-makers can adopt, and it is where pluralism and human agency are most directly affected [19, 20]. Organizers decide whether the mediator should look for agreement among citizens or set out where they differ. papers.title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

Existing methods provide several forms of multi-objective steering. Unlike standard fine-tuning objectives, expected hypervolume cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward. A candidate’s value depends on the objective-space regions covered by the other samples, so its reward must adapt to the current sampling distribution (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Perez Jensen et al., 2026). This identity gives the reward a clear interpretation and makes it tractable to estimate directly from model samples. papers.title: Beyond Anonymous Order Flow: Wallet Identity as a Feature for Short-Horizon Return Prediction
papers.abstract: Conventional public order-book data summarize trading without identifying the accounts behind it. Hyperliquid's Level-4 record also exposes persistent pseudonymous wallet addresses. We reconstruct full-depth books from consensus-ordered messages and evaluate wallet identity as a feature for short-horizon return prediction. The July 1-27, 2026 record covers 17.1 billion messages, 14.3 million aggressive orders by 147,113 wallets, and $84.3 billion in taker notional across ten markets. In the three model markets, notional-weighted ten-second markout rankings persist across adjacent ten-day windows (Spearman rho = 0.52); covariate-adjusted validation markouts reach 3.11 basis points in the top ventile. On a 100-millisecond grid, eleven features describing previously scored top-decile wallets raise one-second out-of-sample R2 from 10.88% to 12.

papers.intro:
Short-horizon return prediction from limit-order-book data is a supervised learning problem with established predictors: signed order flow, depth imbalance, recent returns, realized volatility, and the quoted spread (Cont et al., 2014; Sirignano and Cont, 2019; Kolm et al., 2023). These aggregate variables summarize what the market is doing. Persistent account identifiers also allow a model to condition on whose activity it observes. Adverse-selection models motivate this distinction: counterparties differ in the price movements following their trades (Bagehot, 1971; Kyle, 1985; Glosten and Milgrom, 1985). Conventional public exchange feeds usually do not expose account histories, whereas wallet-attributed decentralized feeds can.

Because the canonical models leave the counterparty unidentified, adverse selection has been inferred from anonymous data: spread decompositions (Glosten and Harris, 1988), permanent price impact (Hasbrouck, 1991), and the structurally estimated probability of informed trading (Easley et al., 1996). These measures can fail exactly when identification matters most (Collin-Dufresne and Fos, 2015). Where identifiers have been observable they matter: anonymity changes liquidity (Foucault et al., 2007; Meling, 2021), visible identifiers are learned from (Linnainmaa and Saar, 2012), account-level records show performance and information to be persistent trader attributes (Kirilenko et al., 2017; Baron et al., 2019), and a leaked client identity is worth trading against (Barbon et al., 2019). These traditional account-level studies generally rely on identifiers visible to a broker, regulator, or researcher rather than to all users of a public feed. Crypto microstructure has studied arbitrage and market quality (Makarov and Schoar, 2020), the strategic games public blockchains enable (Daian et al., 2020), perpetual futures (He et al., 2024), and wallet-tagged insider activity (Félez-Viñas et al., 2022); on Hyperliquid’s Level-4 record specifically, Albers et al. (2026a) introduce the data, Albers et al. (2026b) show that rejected orders predict returns, and Barone and Lillo (2026) that disclosed execution intentions lower trading costs, while Zhang et al. (2026) recover trader types by clustering NASDAQ order events. Optimal quoting conditions on inventory and adverse selection (Avellaneda and Stoikov, 2008) and, inside dealers, on client identity (Cartea et al., 2026), whereas anonymous forecasting models cannot construct wallet histories at all (Cont et al., 2014; Sirignano and Cont, 2019; Kolm et al., 2023). We shift the unit of analysis to the persistent wallet and measure its incremental forecasting content directly.

papers.title: Steerable Single-step Retrosynthesis with Electron-pushing Discrete Flow Matching and Feynman-Kac Steering
papers.abstract: Expert chemists perform retrosynthetic analysis in a strategic manner, where each reaction in a route is employed with a specific purpose, combined with mechanistic reasoning represented as electron-pushing arrows to visualize how bonds are formed or broken via electron redistribution. Yet contemporary single-step retrosynthesis models exhibit neither of these properties: their learned reaction distribution is fixed to that of the training data, and reactions are predicted via de-novo generation of the precursors or molecular graph edits, omitting the electron redistribution that governs the chemical transformations. We introduce Verso MAELLE, the first electron-pushing-based single-step retrosynthetic model, representing disconnections as continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) comprised of edits in the electron space, and is trainable using a discrete flow matching formulation. Being a generative model, Verso MAELLE is optionally steerable at inference time through the Feynman-Kac (FK) framework, using rewards that promote certain types of disconnections. We show that besides in-distribution learning, Verso MAELLE can be steered toward cyclization reactions which are scaffold-constructive but underrepresented in the training corpus, via a ring-breaking reward. As a proof of concept, we show how the electron-pushing reasoning, learned from patented data, combined with a domino incentivizing reward, could steer Verso MAELLE toward creative and strategic disconnections, demonstrated on the key domino sequence that was used to synthesize Punctaporonin U, a complex natural product of the sesquiterpene family.

papers.intro:
One of the challenges in experimental validation of in-silico generated materials and drugs is their synthesizability [1, 2]. Decomposing a complex organic molecule into readily available precursors is one of the most challenging and intellectually demanding tasks in chemistry [3], being simultaneously a science as well as an art. Corey formalized this endeavour into what is now known as retrosynthesis [4, 5]. Efforts in automating retrosynthesis into Computer-Aided Synthesis Planning (CASP) began more than 50 years ago [6, 7], when Corey and Wipke started with hard-coded reaction rules. Modern, data-driven CASP approaches [8, 9] involve combining a search algorithm [10, 11, 12] with a single-step policy trained on a reaction corpus [13, 14, 15].

While this approach works well on simple and small molecules, recent work by Armstrong et al. [16] has shown that complex targets such as natural products require a paradigm that goes beyond exhaustive tree search, incorporating strategic planning, where each reaction has a different purpose at different stages of the synthesis: strategic disconnections often involve breaking the central scaffold of the molecules, while supporting reactions focus on manipulating functional groups [17]. However, single-step policy models are fixed to the reaction distribution they are trained on. Moreover, the training data is often derived from patents [18], which are biased toward routine reactions while scaffold-constructive ones such as cyclizations are underrepresented [19]. Therefore, a mechanism to steer the single-step policy models at inference time is needed to adapt to diverse strategic requirements of synthesis planning.

The second facet of strategic retrosynthesis among synthetic chemists is the practice of reaction reasoning by drawing arrow-pushing diagrams (also known as electron-pushing or curved-arrow diagrams) [5, 20]. The arrows describe a symbolic, directional transfer of electrons from a source to a sink. The direction of the arrow cannot be drawn arbitrarily: electrons have to flow from an electron-rich donor, called a nucleophile, to an electron-deficient acceptor, called an electrophile. The pattern of nucleophile and electrophile serves as the basis of organic synthesis and generalizes across diverse reaction types. Reasoning about reactions through electron flow also tightly connects to another facet of strategic retrosynthesis that is employed by expert chemists: planning a reaction at the synthon level before completing the functional groups [5, 21]. Synthons are an abstract representation of the precursors, formed by a broad disconnection strategy, where hypothetical charges are placed on atoms to be later completed with compatible functional groups.

papers.title: VidUEU-Agent: A Data-Curation Agent for Multimodal Understanding, Editing, and Unified Tasks
papers.abstract: The advancement of multimodal learning is heavily constrained by the scarcity and high annotation cost of high-quality instruction data. While raw videos offer an abundant and dynamic source of visual knowledge, transforming them into precise instruction data remains highly challenging. To bridge this gap, we present VidUEU-Agent, an automated pipeline that synthesizes instruction data from raw videos for multimodal understanding, editing, and unified tasks. VidUEU-Agent follows a four-stage pipeline: it performs global perception to filter low-quality shots, mines keyframes and multimodal signals, constructs metadata and routes the metadata to synthesize instruction samples. More importantly, our agent framework can autonomously iterate the data distribution based on downstream training results, thereby optimizing data quality, balance, and training effectiveness. Scaling this pipeline, we construct VidUEU-100K, a large-scale dataset of 100K training samples spanning multiple domains and tasks, providing a robust foundation for developing comprehensive multimodal capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning baseline models on VidUEU-100K yields significant and consistent performance gains across diverse representative benchmarks, validating the effectiveness of our proposed agent framework and dataset.

papers.title: OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
papers.abstract: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

papers.intro:
Industrial recommender systems are typically organized as cascades that retrieve candidates and refine them with increasingly accurate pointwise scoring models [10]. The scoring stages of these cascades have benefited from scaling. Architectures such as HSTU, Wukong, and OneTrans consistently translate additional data and computation into improved ranking accuracy [52, 53, 56]. Slate generation, however, has not followed the same trajectory. The slate ultimately exposed to users is still assembled by an expert-engineered system, built around hand-crafted rules and specialized components for tasks such as scattering, quota allocation, de-duplication, fatigue control, and commercial boosting. These are combined with a shallow model that scores candidates under a strict latency budget and with manually tuned fusion weights. Slate generation is a combinatorial problem, and only a small part of the search space is reachable under this design. Extra computation at serving time is therefore spent on a more exhaustive search over this restricted space, and expanding the space requires additional rules and components. Slate quality thus improves with expert knowledge and engineering effort rather than with data and computation.

We instead formulate slate generation as a learning problem. A reward model is trained on logged user feedback to evaluate complete slates, so the objectives that shape a slate are learned from data rather than encoded by hand. A single general policy is then optimized against this reward to generate slates from the candidate pool, and the search space is no longer restricted by hand-crafted rules but covers all feasible slates over the candidates. The reward model is used only during training, and its capacity is therefore limited by offline resources rather than by the serving budget. With a larger reward model and a deeper policy, additional data and computation now translate into better slates, exactly the scaling behavior that the expert-engineered system lacks. What changes is the role of the rules rather than their presence. Hard constraints are enforced during decoding, and soft preferences are incorporated into the reward. Figure 1 contrasts the rule-based expert system with the learning-based policy.

We instantiate the unified reranking and mix-ranking formulation in a large-scale industrial recommendation system for e-commerce. Candidates—product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards—are supplied by distinct upstream business channels and compete for positions within a single exposure slate under multiple objectives and business constraints. Recent advances provide the necessary mechanisms. Reinforcement-learning post-training demonstrates that autoregressive policies can be optimized directly against sequence-level rewards [33, 41]. Generative recommendation systems similarly cast retrieval and ranking as sequential generation [39, 52, 11], and reported studies show performance gains with model scale and training compute [52, 11]. Instantiating the formulation in production, however, introduces three challenges. First, unlike language generation over a fixed vocabulary, slate generation selects from a request-specific pool of pre-scored candidates. Second, reward is defined over the complete slate rather than individual items. An item’s utility depends jointly on its position, neighboring items, and the slate’s composition across content types. Slate-level feedback is therefore non-decomposable into independent item-level supervision. Third, every generated slate must satisfy production business constraints, whereas unconstrained autoregressive generation provides no such guarantees. These challenges lead to the central question of this work: can a single learned policy, optimized offline against slate-level rewards, replace the expert-engineered system that assembles the slate today?

OneTrans-GSR (Generative Slate Ranking) answers this question in production. The system models slate generation as autoregressive decoding over the per-request candidates. A single decoder receives them from the upstream fine-ranker and emits the exposure slate directly, so no separate rule-based assembly engine, specialized components, or downstream reranking remain on the serving path. The decoder is the only model served at this stage. The training signal, in turn, comes from a slate-level reward model that scores complete slates rather than summing independent item scores. The decoder and the reward model are both built from OneTrans blocks [56] and use the fine-ranking score as a candidate feature. OneTrans thus serves as a shared backbone across fine ranking, reward modeling, and slate generation. Deployed at full traffic, OneTrans-GSR paves the way for gradually integrating fine ranking into slate generation.

We train the decoder in two stages. The decoder is first pretrained on long user-behavior sequences with a next-token prediction loss, and then post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL) against the reward model. For the post-training stage we propose Geometric-Mean Reward Policy Optimization (GMR-PO), a method for multi-objective policy optimization. GMR-PO aggregates the reward model’s scores for multiple objectives into a scalar reward. The scalar reward and the reward for business preferences are standardized independently, and the resulting advantages are combined to optimize the policy. Soft business preferences thus serve as training signals, while advertiser value and hard business constraints are controlled during decoding.

papers.title: Modeling runaway electron mitigation via passively driven plasma instabilities in a high-current tokamak
papers.abstract: A critical challenge for tokamak-based fusion power plants is the formation of high-current, relativistic runaway electron (RE) beams during abrupt confinement loss events called disruptions. RE beams may significantly damage machine components if left unmitigated, jeopardizing the operational and economic viability of fusion power plants. We present the first self-consistent extended magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) computational study of RE mitigation with a passively driven RE mitigation coil (REMC) in a high-current tokamak. RE generation and transport are coupled with REMC-driven MHD activity in a 3D simulation that models the thermal and current quench phases of a mid-plane disruption, together with the vertical displacement and final termination of the plasma and RE beam on SPARC -- a high-field, high-current tokamak designed to achieve a fusion gain Q > 1. We demonstrate that REMC-driven magnetic stochasticity can reduce the RE current by over an order-of-magnitude when compared to unmitigated disruptions. The final termination is mediated via a post-thermal-quench "cold" vertical displacement of the plasma, which, together with magnetic stochasticity, increases RE losses via scrape-off once the plasma contacts the first wall. These results demonstrate a viable mechanism for RE mitigation using passively driven plasma instabilities on high-current tokamaks.

papers.title: Recognizing Label-Connected Graphs
papers.abstract:
In classical gossiping, each participant initially knows a distinct piece of information. Whenever two participants call each other, they exchange everything they know. We study Gossiping: given an undirected multigraph whose vertices represent participants and whose edges represent available calls, decide whether the calls can be ordered so that every participant learns all information, using each edge at most once. Equivalently, can one time label per edge make the graph temporally connected by strict temporal paths? This recognition problem is NP-complete; we study its parameterized complexity.
  After linear-time preprocessing, we give an exact $O(3^{n/3}n^3)$-time algorithm and a deterministic $2^{O(tw)}n$-time algorithm, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $tw$ is the treewidth of the underlying simple graph. We introduce a Tree Contraction Rule that extends the treewidth algorithm to single-exponential algorithms for parameters that may remain small on dense graphs, such as tree-independence number and clique-width, without requiring a decomposition as input. For the excess $\delta=m-(2n-4)$ over the minimum number of calls, where $m$ is the number of edges, we give a randomized $2^{O(\delta)}n^3$-time algorithm with one-sided error. Its main subroutine solves Rooted Independent Cycle: finding a cycle through four prescribed vertices whose edges are independent in a represented linear matroid. We solve this problem deterministically in $2^{O(r)}m$ arithmetic operations over the finite field representing the matroid, where $r$ is its rank. Gossiping is polynomial-time solvable at maximum degree four, counting parallel edges, but NP-complete on planar simple graphs of maximum degree five. The treewidth algorithm yields a $2^{O(\sqrt n)}$-time algorithm on planar graphs.

In a peer-to-peer exchange, two participants can share both their own information and everything they have learned from earlier exchanges. When the available pairwise exchanges are fixed, their order determines how far information can spread. We ask whether these exchanges can be scheduled so that every participant receives all information, without introducing additional exchanges.

The classical gossiping problem captures this question in a particularly clean form. Each participant initially knows a distinct piece of information, and whenever two participants call each other, they exchange everything they currently know. If every pair may communicate, 2​n−42n-4 calls are necessary and sufficient for n≥4n\geq 4 participants [5, 35]. We instead prescribe the available calls by an undirected multigraph: vertices represent participants, and each edge represents one call between its endpoints. The task is to decide whether these calls can be ordered so that all information reaches every participant. Thus the difficulty lies not in selecting sufficiently many calls, but in coordinating a fixed and possibly highly constrained set of calls.

papers.title: Ly$\alpha$ in Compact Broad-Line Emitters, Including Little Red Dots, Is More Closely Linked to the Host Galaxy than to the Broad-Line Nucleus
papers.abstract: JWST has found many faint broad-line AGN at $z>4$, but it is unclear whether the Ly$\alpha$ we see from them comes from the accreting black hole or from its host galaxy. The answer matters for how these sources are interpreted and for how many ionizing photons they release. We use deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the DIVER program to measure Ly$\alpha$ in 12 compact broad-line emitters (CBEs) at $z=4.2$--5.5 in GOODS-N. CBEs include little red dots (LRDs), little blue dots, and other broad-line AGN. Six are detected in Ly$\alpha$. Every source shows a broad-line region, yet Ly$\alpha$ does not follow it: the sources with the strongest H$\alpha$ relative to the UV include weak detections and nondetections, and every detected Ly$\alpha$ line (FWHM $\approx300$--1000~km~s$^{-1}$) is narrower than broad H$\alpha$ (1100--3300~km~s$^{-1}$). Instead, Ly$\alpha$ appears to track the host galaxy. We model the AGN-subtracted host with a dust-attenuated SED fit. Including the upper limits, the observed Ly$\alpha$ follows the Ly$\alpha$ production in this host model more closely than it follows H$\alpha$/UV, in both equivalent width and luminosity. Every detection exceeds its host-model value by a factor of 1.5--18, leaving room for a nuclear contribution. The black hole is visible in these sources, but the Ly$\alpha$ we observe is more closely tied to its host. The median effective Ly$\alpha$ escape fraction of the detections is only 0.09, which suggests that ionizing escape from CBEs is typically modest and varies widely.

papers.intro:
JWST has revealed a large population of faint broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGN) at z>4z>4 [72, 52, 102, 60, 61, e.g.,]. Most are identified through broad Hα\alpha emission from dense gas moving at thousands of km s-1 near an accreting black hole. Many are also X-ray weak and show little variability, which keeps their physical nature under debate [101, 68, 56, 34]. A prominent subset, the little red dots (LRDs), pairs compact red rest-optical continua with blue rest-UV emission. LRDs have been studied through their identification, sizes, number densities, and dust emission [6, 81, 99, 65, 27, 29], black-hole and host masses [51, 49, 42], rest-UV and rest-optical spectra [1, 84, 24, 98], low-redshift analogs [10, 85, 62, 63], and possible origins and descendants [43, 78, 103]. If these AGN are common and their ionizing photons escape efficiently, they could contribute substantially to the ionizing background during reionization. Whether their Lyα\alpha and Lyman-continuum (LyC) photons escape depends on gas beyond the visible broad-line region (BLR).

Lyα\alpha traces high-redshift galaxies and the ionization state of the intergalactic medium [70, 19, 93, 22, 37, IGM; e.g.,]. Lyα\alpha and LyC photons may escape through the same low-column-density, low-attenuation channels, and observations and simulations find a broad connection between their escape fractions [59, 7, 21]. The observed Lyα\alpha also depends on transfer through neutral gas, dust, the circumgalactic medium (CGM), and the IGM [8, 20, e.g.,], so it is a useful but indirect probe of LyC escape [80, 39, for reviews, see]. In the Case B limit, the intrinsic Lyα\alpha/Hα\alpha ratio is fixed to first order [79], although optically thick or density-bounded gas can move it away from Case B [88, 74]. Because JWST measures both Hα\alpha and Lyα\alpha in AGN at z>4z>4, broad-line AGN offer a direct test of whether strong nuclear recombination emission comes with strong observed Lyα\alpha. A type-1 view shows the BLR along one sightline, but Lyα\alpha photons scatter through gas from nuclear to intergalactic scales and need not escape along the same path.

Recent JWST observations show that the two can differ. LRDs and other broad-line sources can have strong broad Balmer emission but weak, narrow, or spatially extended Lyα\alpha [96, 44], and broad Lyα\alpha is uncommon even when broad Hα\alpha is clearly present [53]. Some LRDs may still have a BLR contribution: a stacked medium-resolution spectrum shows a broad Lyα\alpha wing that matches broad Hα\alpha [32]. Compact blue broad-line sources, or little blue dots [67, LBDs;], show higher Lyα\alpha visibility, possibly through lower gas columns [69]. LRD selections still differ between studies, which use different color cuts or continuum-slope criteria [33, 55, 54, 2, 36, 102], and spectroscopic LRD samples are heterogeneous [25, 82]. To avoid depending on a particular LRD definition, we refer to LRDs, LBDs, and other broad-line AGN collectively as compact broad-line emitters (CBEs). This umbrella term spans the full range of continuum colors and is broader than the blue CBE selection of S. Mascia et al. [69]; we select our sample on broad Hα\alpha alone.

papers.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly advise backers on which crowdfunding campaigns to support. LLMs have known race and gender problems, and it is unsettled whether they reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance. We ask when, and through which decision process, LLM assistants use founders' gender and ethnicity. In a pre-specified choice-based conjoint experiment, seven LLMs chose among five synthetic campaigns with independently randomized quality signals and founder names, under three backer personas and a persona-free control (40,248 responses). By default, founder names barely matter: under budget-conscious and delivery-focused personas, gender and Black-name effects are statistically equivalent to zero. When the backer wants to support underrepresented creators, the models favor Black-signaled (+8.1 percentage points; positive in all seven models) and female-signaled (+5.1) founders. They do so most strongly among near-tied campaigns and for the founder who alone carries the signal, and they almost never name gender or ethnicity in their reasons. The results fit an agency account of algorithmic discrimination: an aligned assistant takes its demographic preferences from its user rather than from its training data.

papers.intro:
Founders’ race and gender shape who receives entrepreneurial finance: venture investors favor pitches by men (Brooks et al., 2014; Kanze et al., 2018), and reward-crowdfunding backers fund African American men less often and value their products less (Younkin and Kuppuswamy, 2018; Younkin and Kuppuswamy, 2019), yet fund women more often (Greenberg and Mollick, 2017; Gafni et al., 2021). Backers and platforms increasingly ask LLM assistants which project to support, letting the assistant allocate attention and capital across founders (Metaxa et al., 2021; Aggarwal et al., 2024). LLMs have well-documented race and gender problems: they learn stereotypes from human text that persist covertly even in models that appear unbiased (Hofmann et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025), and the post-training that suppresses them (Raj et al., 2024) sometimes overshoots into favoring the groups that human evaluators penalize (Tamkin et al., 2023; Gaebler et al., 2024).

Backers and platforms increasingly ask LLM assistants which project to support, letting the assistant allocate attention and capital across founders (Metaxa et al., 2021; Aggarwal et al., 2024). Whether LLM gatekeepers reproduce, erase, or reverse the discrimination documented in entrepreneurial finance is therefore open, and the evidence is divided. LLMs reproduce racial penalties in mortgage underwriting (Bowen et al., 2025) and fund-manager allocations (Wang and Gu, 2026), show no gender bias in portfolio advice (Fieberg et al., 2025), and practice “symbolic compliance” when evaluating founders’ pitches (Botelho and Wang, 2026). Research on LLMs in venture finance has mostly studied the model as an advisor or screener (Fieberg et al., 2026; Vismara et al., 2026), not as the party that decides which founder receives capital.

Research on LLMs in venture finance has mostly studied the model as an advisor or screener (Fieberg et al., 2026; Vismara et al., 2026), not as the party that decides which founder receives capital.

The divided evidence points to a mismatch between theory and practice. Theories of discrimination locate preferences and beliefs in the evaluator (Becker, 1957; Phelps, 1972), and LLM audits likewise treat the model as an evaluator with fixed dispositions. An assistant, however, acts for a user, and post-training teaches it to pursue that user’s stated goals (Ouyang et al., 2022). Whose preferences then govern how it treats founders: those absorbed in training, or those of the user it serves? Single-prompt audits cannot tell. We therefore ask: When, and through which decision process, do LLM assistants use founders’ gender and ethnicity in recommending which crowdfunding campaign to back, and do their recommendations reproduce, erase, or reverse the demographic patterns documented among human backers?

We answer with an algorithm audit (Sandvig et al., 2014) built on a randomized choice-based conjoint experiment (Hainmueller et al., 2014) that varies the backer’s goal, and contribute to three literatures: to theories of discrimination in entrepreneurial finance, by showing that with an AI evaluator the preference for treating groups differently comes from the principal; to the debate on bias in LLMs, by identifying the principal’s goal as the boundary condition between the mirror and alignment accounts; and to research on AI in venture finance, by showing that an AI allocator uses demographics as an undisclosed tie-breaker.

papers.title: A Side Condition Principle With Applications
papers.abstract: We introduce a combinatorial principle $\textsf{SC}(\kappa)$, for any regular cardinal $\kappa \ge \omega_2$, which asserts the existence of a family $\mathcal{Y} \subseteq [H(\kappa)]^\omega$ of elementary substructures of $H(\kappa)$ which is closed under finite intersections and satisfies that for stationarily many $N \in \mathcal{Y}$, if $M \in \mathcal{Y}$ and $M \cap \omega_1 < N \cap \omega_1$, then $M \cap N \cap \kappa \in N$. We explore the idea of defining forcings with side conditions consisting of finite subsets of such a family $\mathcal{Y}$. If $\textsf{SC}(\omega_2)$ holds, then there exists a thin stationary subset of $[\omega_2]^\omega$, and consequently $\textsf{SC}(\omega_2)$ is independent of ZFC. Assuming that $\mu$ is a Mahlo cardinal, the L\'{e}vy collapse $\mathrm{Col}(\omega,<\mu)$ forces that $\textsf{SC}(\kappa)$ holds for all regular cardinals $\kappa \ge \omega_2$. Local instances of $\textsf{SC}$ can be forced using matrices of models or derived as consequences of square principles. We apply the principle $\textsf{SC}$ to define two kinds of forcings: a streamlined version of a strongly proper collapse, and a forcing which is strongly proper on a stationary set and adds arbitrarily many Baumgartner clubs. Finally, we prove two consistency results using forcings derived from $\textsf{SC}$ related to Aronszajn trees, the guessing model principle, strong failures of club guessing, and the higher dominating number.

papers.intro:
The purpose of this article is to introduce a new tool in side condition forcing which is based on a background combinatorial principle. We review some history of side conditions in forcing and explain the motivation for our suggested approach. The method of forcing with models as side conditions originated in work of Todorčević [39], who incorporated finite ∈\in-chains of countable elementary substructures into forcing conditions to ensure that the forcings are proper. Such conditions split into a working part, which approximates the main object to be added by the forcing, and a finite ∈\in-chain of models on the side, with requirements on how the working part and the models are related. Subsequent developments in the side condition method have focused on presenting lists of requirements for how the models appearing in a side condition are related to each other. Sometimes these requirements are generated in order to achieve a specific forcing effect, and other times they are presented as the basis for a general framework intended for a variety of applications. papers.title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling
papers.abstract: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

papers.intro:
Over four years, video generation has passed through several distinct regimes. In 2023, general-purpose video creation remained largely aspirational. In 2024, early systems produced compelling demonstrations, but with limited reliability and control. By 2025, leading models could generate production-usable shots and creative assets. By 2026, frontier systems had begun to produce usable short-form audiovisual sequences that coordinate multiple shots, persistent subjects, performance, camera language, dialogue, music, and sound. The unit by which progress is judged has expanded from the frame to the clip, then to the shot, and now to the complete sequence.

This expansion changes the technical problem. Quality at the frame or clip level can often be assessed locally, whereas usefulness at the sequence level is compositional: constraints interact, errors accumulate over time, and decisions in one shot affect the interpretation of the next. The system must infer a latent creative specification from heterogeneous inputs, express it as conditions the generator can execute, and evaluate the result at the same semantic granularity. Multimodal understanding has evolved accordingly, from coarse text–video correspondence to dense spatiotemporal description, reference grounding, creative planning, and multidimensional judgment, and it has helped make synthesis controllable and usable.

High aggregate scores in visual question answering (VQA) do not imply reliable understanding of camera language, left–right relations, composition, lighting, shot boundaries, identity binding, or dense temporal change. These capabilities are weakly represented in standard supervision, yet they determine whether a generated result is controllable and editable; evaluation research has shifted in the same direction, from superficial realism toward controllability, commonsense, and physical faithfulness [69, 1]. For video generation, the question is therefore not whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) is broadly capable, but which semantics reach the generator, through what representation, and with what evidence of downstream benefit.

An observed generation failure is not, by itself, a diagnosis. This perspective leads to four claims: • The bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. Improvements in visual fidelity do not automatically yield correct actions, camera language, reference binding, or narrative continuity. Generation-oriented understanding is an independent axis of progress. • Data efficiency depends on description density. A diffusion transformer (DiT) is trained on far fewer samples than a language model, and both training throughput and the supply of usable video preclude closing this gap through scaling. Each training video must therefore carry as much supervision as possible, which makes the density of textual description per unit of video duration the central measure of data efficiency.
