A small fraction of ULXs may instead be intermediate-mass BHs (Mezcua et al., 2015; Mezcua, 2017), young supernova remnants (SNRs), beamed sources or mis-identified background quasars. In fact, the launching of massive, fast outflows is one of the hallmarks of super-critical accretion. While in SNRs all the energy is injected at the initial moment of the stellar collapse, in ULX bubbles the kinetic power is supplied gradually by winds and/or jets (with Pkin≳1039P_{\rm{kin}}\gtrsim 10^{39} erg s-1) over the duration of the super-critical accretion phase, which can last for up to several times 10510^{5} yr. papers.title: Small-data physics-informed ML model for magnetic exchange based on chemical composition and structure
papers.abstract: In this paper we propose an ensemble model based on a swarm of dense neural networks, able to predict Heisenberg exchange interactions within less than 1% error. The model uses the inputs of the ab-initio Schr\"odinger equation, i.e. the compound structure and chemical composition. In this first work, we trained the model on a few compounds of the hexagonal manganite family and were able to infer, with similar accuracy, the J values for other compounds of the same family at randomly chosen geometries, thus showing that we accurately learned the effect of the chemical composition and structure on effective magnetic integrals J.

Strongly correlated quantum materials, such as transition-metal oxides and ff-electron systems, display remarkable electronic and magnetic properties (superconductivity, magnetism, topological order) that arise from the complex interplay of electron–electron interactions, spin–orbit coupling and lattice effects.

Strongly correlated quantum materials, such as transition-metal oxides and ff-electron systems, display remarkable electronic and magnetic properties (superconductivity, magnetism, topological order) that arise from the complex interplay of electron–electron interactions, spin–orbit coupling and lattice effects.

The consequence of these interplay is that these properties cannot be described by conventional single-particle theories. The standard approach is to build an effective many-body low-energy Hamiltonian (for instance an Heisenberg [21] or Hubbard [23] model) that captures the relevant physics. These simplified models give access to ground states, phase diagrams and low-energy excitations, either through standard condensed-matter methods (exact diagonalization, Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) [34], Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS) [10], Monte Carlo, etc.) or, more recently, deep-learning approaches [9, 8].

The associated effective interactions, such as the UU and tt of a Hubbard’s Hamiltonian or the magnetic exchange integrals, JJ, of the Heisenberg one, are intrinsically dependent on both the atomic structure and the chemical composition of the compounds. As a consequence they provide insight to the composition-structure-properties relationship. Accurate and fast methods to obtain these effective interactions for given compounds and geometries are thus of importance, not only for the understanding of the physical properties and their grounding in the structure and chemistry of the materials, but also for computational material design.

Even if Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods are often used to evaluate the effective interactions, they lack accuracy and reliability due to their intrinsic difficulty to describe strong electronic correlation. To reach those goals one thus has to rely on post-Hartree-Fock multi-reference (MR) wave-function methods. Ab-initio methods, whether of MR-wave-function type or DFT, are however computationally demanding and rapidly become prohibitive, for instance when associated with material design algorithms. This is a typical case where artificial intelligence models can provide new avenues. papers.title: H 0557$-$385: A Candidate Missing Link Between Radio-Quiet Seyferts and Young Radio Galaxies
papers.abstract: The Seyfert 1 galaxy H 0557$-$385 (z = 0.034) has long been classified as radio-quiet on the basis of its radio-to-optical flux ratio, yet its radio properties are physically inconsistent with this designation. We present a broadband ($0.076 - 258.8$ GHz) radio spectral analysis combining new Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) observations with archival Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) data. The spectrum requires a two-component model: a compact, self-absorbed component with a stratified gigahertz-peaked (GPS)/high-frequency-peaked (HFP) spectral shape (turnover at $9.4^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ GHz), superposed on an extended, optically thin power-law lobe ($\alpha_{\rm pl} = -0.78$) that dominates below ~1.6 GHz. The derived parameters $-$ a source size of ~15 pc, an equipartition magnetic field of 2.8 mG, a synchrotron age of $\lesssim1.8\times10^{3}$ yr, and a time-averaged jet power of ${\sim}5\times10^{41}$ $-$ $5\times10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ $-$ are characteristic of compact steep-spectrum and GPS young radio galaxies, not of canonical radio-quiet AGN. The two-component structure admits two interpretations that the present data cannot distinguish: the extended emission may be the growing lobe of a genuinely young, expanding radio galaxy, or relic plasma from an earlier episode of a transient or recurrent jet. Under either, H 0557$-$385 is better understood as an intermediate object: optically a Seyfert, but with the radio-physical properties of a newly ignited or recently re-triggered radio galaxy. It is therefore a candidate missing link between radio-quiet AGN and large-scale radio galaxies. Distinguishing these scenarios will require high-resolution imaging and multi-epoch monitoring

papers.intro:
The classification of active galactic nuclei (AGN) into radio-loud and radio-quiet categories has shaped our understanding of AGN physics for over half a century (Kellermann et al., 1989; Sikora et al., 2007, e.g.,). Radio-loud AGN are characterised by large-scale, relativistic jets that can extend to megaparsec scales, depositing enormous amounts of energy into the surrounding intergalactic medium and regulating the co-evolution of black holes and their host galaxies (McNamara and Nulsen, 2007; Fabian, 2012; Morganti, 2017). Radio-quiet AGN, by contrast, are thought to lack such prominent outflows; their radio emission is typically attributed to star formation, coronal activity, or weak, sub-relativistic winds (Laor and Behar, 2008; Panessa et al., 2019, e.g.,). This binary framework has provided a useful organisational structure, but its underlying classification has important limitations because it relies on radio-to-optical flux ratios measured at a single frequency—a metric that is sensitive to orientation, variability, host-galaxy contamination, and spectral shape (Kellermann et al., 1989; Kellermann et al., 2016; Falcke et al., 1996; Padovani et al., 2017). In its classical form, an AGN is deemed radio-loud if the ratio of its 5 GHz to BB-band (4400 Å) flux densities exceeds R=S5​GHz/S4400​Å>10R=S_{\rm 5\,GHz}/S_{4400\,\text{\AA}}>10, and radio-quiet otherwise (Kellermann et al., 1989).

Compact steep-spectrum (CSS), gigahertz-peaked spectrum (GPS), and high-frequency peaked (HFP) sources offer a useful counterpoint to the RL/RQ dichotomy. These young radio galaxies form a size sequence that is inversely related to their turnover frequency: HFP sources are the most compact (typically ≲0.1\lesssim 0.1 kpc, with turnovers above ∼5{\sim}5 GHz), GPS sources are somewhat larger (≲1\lesssim 1 kpc, turnovers near 1 GHz), and CSS sources are the most extended (up to ∼20{\sim}20 kpc, with turnovers at a few hundred MHz). Their radio spectra are characterised by a spectral turnover caused by synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) or free-free absorption (FFA) within the compact emitting region (O’Dea, 1998; Orienti and Dallacasa, 2014; Callingham et al., 2017, e.g.,). The evolutionary sequence HFP →\rightarrow GPS →\rightarrow CSS →\rightarrow large-scale radio galaxy is well established for powerful, radio-loud systems (O’Dea, 1998; Orienti, 2016), yet the boundary between these young radio galaxies and the broader AGN population is not as clear-cut as once assumed. In particular, several objects with optical or X-ray properties that would classify them as Seyferts or low-luminosity AGN have been found to harbour GPS/CSS-like radio spectra, parsec-scale compact radio emission, and synchrotron ages of 10410^{4}–10610^{6} yr (Giroletti and Panessa, 2009; Doi et al., 2013; Doi et al., 2016; Congiu et al., 2017; Inoue and Doi, 2018, e.g.,).

A key limitation of the conventional RL/RQ classification is that it does not account for the possibility of young, newly ignited radio activity in sources that would otherwise be labelled radio-quiet. Indeed, proper motions of mildly relativistic jets have now been measured via VLBI in systems such as Mrk 110 (Wang et al., 2025), Mrk 335 (Yao et al., 2021), and KISSR 872 (Kharb et al., 2024), and the growing consensus is that the RL/RQ boundary is better understood as a continuum shaped by black hole spin, accretion rate, magnetic field topology, and evolutionary stage (Blandford and Znajek, 1977; Sikora et al., 2007; Merloni et al., 2003; Tchekhovskoy et al., 2010), rather than a sharp physical divide. We note, however, that the detection of mildly relativistic ejecta is not by itself proof of a genuinely young radio source: episodic or recurrent nuclear activity can produce compact, relativistic outflows in an AGN that is not in the early stages of an HFP →\rightarrow GPS →\rightarrow CSS evolutionary track. Distinguishing genuine youth from transient activity requires additional evidence, such as a measured expansion rate or a steadily evolving turnover.

papers.title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
papers.abstract:
Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $\lambda$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6\lambda-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$.
  We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18\lambda-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $\lambda$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.

papers.intro:
Physical implementations of cryptographic algorithms leak information about their internal state through side channels such as running time, power consumption, and electromagnetic radiation. This has motivated a large body of work on leakage-resilient cryptography, which extends the traditional black-box security model to account for side-channel leakage and designs schemes that provably withstand it [DBLP:conf/crypto/IshaiSW03, DBLP:conf/tcc/MicaliR04, DBLP:conf/focs/DziembowskiP08, DBLP:conf/tcc/AkaviaGV09, DBLP:conf/eurocrypt/Pietrzak09, DBLP:conf/crypto/NaorS09, DBLP:conf/crypto/AlwenDW09, DBLP:conf/eurocrypt/FaustRRTV10, DBLP:conf/focs/DodisHLW10, DBLP:conf/focs/BrakerskiKKV10, DBLP:conf/crypto/GoldwasserR10, DBLP:conf/eurocrypt/DucDF14, DBLP:books/acm/19/KalaiR19]. The central goal of leakage-resilient cryptography is to compute arbitrary programs securely in the presence of side-channel leakage. This goal is formalized by leakage-resilient circuit compilers [DBLP:conf/crypto/IshaiSW03, DBLP:conf/eurocrypt/FaustRRTV10], which transform any program, modeled as a Boolean or arithmetic circuit, into a protected circuit that is secure against leakage. Security means that the leakage is useless to the adversary: anything it learns from the leakage together with the input/output behavior of the protected circuit could also be learned from the input/output behavior alone.

The standard remedy is to refresh the encoding periodically, replacing (ℓ,r)(\ell,r) by a new encoding (ℓ′,r′)(\ell^{\prime},r^{\prime}) of the same secret, so that leakage in different periods concerns different shares [DBLP:conf/asiacrypt/DziembowskiF11, DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1209-4820]. The difficulty is that a refresh must remain secure under composition: the new shares must be correlated with the old ones to encode the same secret, yet the refresh itself leaks, and the adversary may exploit this leakage to combine information from different periods.

papers.title: Joint Channel Scanning and Geometry-Aware Codebook Design for Movable Antenna Arrays
papers.abstract: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems rely on spatial degrees of freedom, but fixed antenna geometries cannot adapt to propagation environments. Movable antenna (MA) systems address this by adapting antenna positions to the channel. In discrete MA architectures, active antennas are selected from candidate positions, requiring channel state information (CSI) at those positions. With limited radio-frequency (RF) chains, CSI is acquired through successive pilot rounds, or antenna scanning, whose overhead can offset reconfiguration gains. This paper studies discrete MA geometry optimization when only a fraction of candidate positions is scanned. We show that a geometry-aware (GA) steering-vector codebook, constructed from the actual antenna coordinates, reconstructs channels more accurately than a conventional discrete Fourier transform (DFT) codebook when the optimized array departs from a uniform grid. We then show that the scanning fraction required to approach full-scan sum-rate performance depends on the CSI acquisition method: least-squares (LS) estimation degrades sharply under sparse scanning, while codebook-based acquisition remains robust. We also propose an adaptive scanning procedure that probes candidates in batches and stops automatically using the acquired pilots, avoiding a preset scanning budget. Finally, we quantify sum-rate losses as users move from their initial positions and evaluate recovery through re-scanning and geometry re-selection, relative to fixed-aperture operation with outdated or fresh CSI. Numerical results show that adaptive scanning achieves about 99.5% of the full-scan sum rate while scanning only 11% of candidate positions.

papers.intro:
The rapid evolution of wireless applications, including extended reality, ultra-high-definition multimedia, and massive machine-type communications, is driving the demand for higher spectral efficiency, reliable communication, and enhanced connectivity in future wireless systems, including 6G. Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology exploits the spatial degrees of freedom provided by multiple antennas to improve spectral efficiency and communication reliability [1]. In principle, the MIMO technology can evolve by increasing the number of antennas and deploying more base stations (BSs), but this might not be financially sustainable. This raises the question of whether one can achieve better performance with a fixed number of antennas and a fixed BS grid [2]. Conventional MIMO arrays have a given number of antennas at fixed antenna positions, limiting their ability to adapt their spatial configuration to changing propagation conditions and user locations [3]. Although digital beamforming can adjust the signals’ amplitudes and phases to shape the effective beam pattern, it cannot change the physical antenna positions or directly reconfigure the channel by moving the antennas. Consequently, the spatial configuration of a fixed array may not be optimal for a given propagation environment or user distribution [4].

Although digital beamforming can adjust the signals’ amplitudes and phases to shape the effective beam pattern, it cannot change the physical antenna positions or directly reconfigure the channel by moving the antennas. Consequently, the spatial configuration of a fixed array may not be optimal for a given propagation environment or user distribution [4].

Movable antenna (MA) systems have recently emerged as a promising solution to the above challenges. By design, MA-enabled systems feature an additional spatial degree of freedom, as the antenna positions can be adapted to the propagation environment [5, 6]. This allows the channel itself to be reshaped, rather than merely accommodated: (i) channel gain can be improved by moving antennas away from deep fades, which enhances received signal strength and diversity; (ii) channel rank and conditioning can be improved by increasing the number of effective spatial modes and reducing the singular value spread (i.e., the condition number) of the channel matrix, which increases spatial multiplexing gain; and (iii) array response can be reshaped to improve beamforming, e.g., by steering nulls toward interferers and suppressing sidelobes[7, 8, 9, 10]. Closely related fluid antenna systems (FAS) exploit reconfigurability through position or port selection [11, 12, 13]. MA formulations fall into two main categories. In the continuous model, each antenna can occupy any position within a given region [14, 15]. In the discrete model, the region is divided into a finite set of candidate locations, to which the available RF chains are moved or activated [16, 17]. In both cases, the search space grows rapidly with the aperture size, and for large apertures the number of candidate antenna positions can reach the hundreds.

In both cases, the search space grows rapidly with the aperture size, and for large apertures the number of candidate antenna positions can reach the hundreds.

Selecting active antenna positions from a discrete candidate set dynamically is a form of antenna selection [18, 19]. Although an exhaustive search over all possible antenna location subsets is generally computationally prohibitive (e.g., placing 16 antennas from 64 candidate locations already yields hundreds of trillions of possible configurations), even low-complexity selection algorithms require channel state information (CSI) to identify promising antenna configurations. Acquiring this CSI is challenging because the number of RF chains equals the number of active antennas, which is much smaller than the number of candidate positions. We refer to measuring the channel between the users and an antenna placed (or switched) at a given candidate position as scanning that position, and to repeating this over the candidate set as antenna scanning. Unlike conventional channel estimation, which estimates the channel of the fixed, active antennas, antenna scanning determines which antenna positions are worth activating. Its overhead grows with the number of candidates, which can diminish the practical benefits of MA reconfigurability.

Importantly, however, the availability of a large candidate set does not necessarily imply that every candidate location must be scanned at each point in time to obtain good antenna-selection performance. If a carefully chosen subset of locations provides sufficient information to identify a high-performing antenna configuration, partial scanning could substantially reduce acquisition overhead while retaining most of the achievable sum rate. Existing MA and antenna-selection works typically assume that full CSI of the candidate set is available, which leaves open a fundamental question: How much of the candidate region must be scanned to approach full-scan performance, and how does the required scanning effort depend on the CSI acquisition method and the spatial distribution of the scanned locations?

The effectiveness of partial scanning depends on how the measurements collected at the probed locations are used to characterize the channel across the candidate region. Conventional estimators obtain channel information directly at the scanned positions and require no assumption on the channel structure beyond its statistics (e.g., least-squares (LS)). In contrast, codebook-based acquisition represents the channel using a set of steering vectors [20, 21], whereas compressed-sensing approaches recover the unobserved channel components by exploiting the spatial sparsity of the channel, i.e., the small number of dominant propagation paths [22, 23, 24]. However, the standard DFT codebook, designed for a uniformly spaced array [25, Ch. 7], may not accurately represent the spatial response of an optimized, irregular MA geometry. A geometry-aware (GA) codebook constructed from the antenna coordinates can address this mismatch. These differences motivate evaluating not only the number of scanned locations but also how the scanning fraction interacts with the channel estimation approach.

papers.title: On Photon Propagation in Strong Magnetic Fields: Time Delays from Pulsars
papers.abstract: We study photon dispersion in the presence of a strong external magnetic field for propagation both perpendicular and parallel to the field, considering (i) the magnetized QED vacuum and (ii) a magnetized electron-positron medium at finite density (nonzero chemical potential). The analysis is performed in one-loop QED at finite temperature and density, and we extract polarization-dependent dispersion relations and phase velocities from the eigenmodes of the photon polarization operator. Using these phase velocities, we estimate propagation-induced time delays for photons emitted from neutron stars in the strong-field regime, adopting a simplified magnetosphere model with a toroidal magnetic field geometry and a radially varying chemical potential profile in the degenerate limit. We compare the predicted delays with observational timing constraints and discuss how strong-field QED and plasma corrections can generate measurable departures from the light cone, with potential signatures relevant for magnetars and modern polarimetric and timing observations. It should be noted that the time-delay estimates derived here are based on the phase velocity and serve as indicative order-of-magnitude predictions.

papers.intro:
Maxwell’s theory predicts that electromagnetic waves propagate in vacuum at the universal speed cc. Quantum electrodynamics (QED), however, implies that the vacuum is polarizable: virtual electron-positron fluctuations couple to external fields and modify the propagation of photons [1, 2]. In the presence of sufficiently intense background fields, these radiative corrections promote classical electrodynamics to an effective nonlinear theory, enabling phenomena such as vacuum birefringence, photon splitting, and field-induced pair creation [3, 4, 5].

In the presence of sufficiently intense background fields, these radiative corrections promote classical electrodynamics to an effective nonlinear theory, enabling phenomena such as vacuum birefringence, photon splitting, and field-induced pair creation [3, 4, 5].

Our calculations for the magnetized medium present at least three aspects to be highlighted. The first concerns an improved treatment of the one-loop corrections to the polarization operator, refining previous results for the dispersion relations and phase velocity of photons propagating in a magnetized medium in the degenerate limit (zero temperature and nonzero chemical potential). In particular, for perpendicular propagation, the eigenvalues have been computed for the first time. In contrast, for parallel propagation, they have been obtained without relying on some of the simplifying assumptions adopted in earlier work [23]. The resulting eigenvalues are analyzed in two limiting regimes: the long-wavelength approximation and the infrared limit. The second contribution establishes the connection between the one-loop calculation and the effective-action formalism. papers.title: iMED: A Multi-Endoscope Dataset for Surgical 3D Perception
papers.abstract: We introduce iMED, the first synchronized multi-endoscope dataset for robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS), designed to address a fundamental limitation in surgical vision benchmarking: the absence of independent held-out viewpoints. Existing surgical datasets capture single-trajectory sequences from a single endoscope, making it impossible to distinguish geometric generalization from photometric interpolation along a narrow forward-facing path. iMED provides 340 sequences ~170K synchronized timepoints with 4 views per timepoint) recorded simultaneously from two independent stereo endoscopes across ex vivo, postmortem, and live surgical settings, spanning 14 specimens with diverse anatomical regions and motion regimes. The dataset includes calibrated camera intrinsics, ArUco-based frame-wise pose estimates with uncertainty quantification, instrument segmentation masks, and rich clinical metadata. Using a train-on-one-endoscope, test-on-another evaluation protocol, we benchmark 23 state-of-the-art methods across rigid and deformable novel view synthesis, pose estimation, feature matching, and monocular depth estimation. Our experiments show that methods relying primarily on photometric supervision degrade substantially under this held-out-endoscope setting, while methods with explicit geometric regularization are more robust across views in our benchmark. Notably, large-scale foundation models transfer surprisingly well to surgical imagery, often outperforming domain-specific models, suggesting pitfalls in current fine-tuning protocols. iMED establishes a new evaluation protocol for geometric generalization in surgical vision.

papers.intro:
Non-rigid scenes with constrained camera motion are among the most challenging regimes for image-based 3D perception tasks (i.e. pose estimation, feature matching, optical flow, depth estimation, and novel view synthesis (NVS)). Although challenging, such conditions often arise in real-world robotic applications like digital human modeling of clothed bodies [7], submarine exploration [10], and robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) [54]. Among these, RAMIS represents an extreme regime. Cameras operate inside the body under severe viewpoint constraints, typically following narrow, forward-facing trajectories through deformable tissue with strong specularities and transient phenomena (smoke, bleeding, topology changes). These conditions compress multiple failure modes for 3D perception methods, making RAMIS an informative stress test for visual geometry in real-world robotic systems.

Computer vision benchmarks have historically advanced 3D perception through standardized evaluation protocols [20]. In rigid environments, datasets capturing scenes from many surrounding viewpoints with known camera poses enabled progress in multi-view reconstruction and mapping [1, 31, 12, 75]. Dynamic-scene benchmarks later extended these ideas to time-varying NVS and reconstruction [51, 45, 46, 28], typically relying on wide-baseline or 360∘/180∘ capture where cameras observe scenes from diverse directions. Surgical vision datasets have enabled progress in reconstruction, camera tracking, and tool analysis [3, 54, 23, 22]. Unlike the surrounding-view capture in general benchmarks, endoscopic cameras follow narrow forward-facing paths through tissue, producing sequences with significant image overlap and limited viewpoint diversity.

In NVS and 3D scene representation, models are typically evaluated using images at held-out camera poses and reporting metrics such as PSNR and SSIM against held-out views [5, 56, 24, 73, 30]. These metrics quantify photometric fidelity and have become standard quantitative benchmarks. However, they are proxies for reconstruction quality rather than direct measures of geometric consistency: high PSNR/SSIM can reflect local interpolation between nearby viewpoints, without uniquely determining whether the model has learned the underlying 3D structure [68]. This limitation is amplified when train and test poses lie along the same forward-facing trajectory, where test views are typically sampled from nearby frames in time so differ only slightly in view. A complementary evaluation is to test generalization under larger viewpoint shifts. In classic multi-camera dynamic-scene benchmarks, this protocol is well established: models are trained on a subset of cameras and evaluated on held-out cameras [28, 8, 34].

papers.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
papers.abstract: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.

papers.intro:
Geospatial decision-making during disasters often requires executing complex, multi-source workflows rather than retrieving a single fact or generating an isolated map. This challenge is especially pronounced for policymakers and emergency-response teams in the Global South, where access to technical expertise, computational resources, and integrated geospatial infrastructure can be limited (Chen et al., 2021a; Villagran de Leon, 2023). Answering an operational question may involve identifying the correct disaster extent, retrieving relevant infrastructure and road networks, selecting satellite imagery from appropriate pre- and post-event periods, performing spatial and raster operations, and producing reusable outputs such as maps, tables, GeoJSON layers, or GeoTIFFs. For example, determining whether hospitals near a flood remain potentially accessible requires combining hazard boundaries, healthcare facilities, and transportation networks while preserving valid spatial reference and distance calculations. Although GIS experts can manage these dependencies explicitly, natural-language systems must coordinate them automatically. A failure at any step such as selecting the wrong spatial extent, time window, or coordinate system can produce a plausible but operationally incorrect result.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic systems that can autonomously plan, invoke tools, and adapt to intermediate observations (Wang et al., 2024b; Xi et al., 2025). While such systems have shown strong performance on text-centric multi-step tasks, applying them to geospatial analytics introduces three key challenges. (i) Domain complexity: geospatial reasoning requires specialized knowledge of spatial databases and coordinate systems, satellite imagery and spectral information, map-derived data, and raster analysis. (ii) Data heterogeneity: operational pipelines combine vector layers, multi-band raster imagery, tabular summaries, and temporal products, each requiring distinct tools, formats, and validation procedures. (iii) Scale and context: geospatial artifacts can be large; GeoJSON layers may contain thousands of features, while raster products can reach gigabytes. Passing complete intermediate results through LLM context windows is therefore impractical, even though downstream correctness depends on preserving metadata such as coordinate reference systems, band names, acquisition timestamps, and spatial bounds.

General-purpose coding agents provide a promising execution framework for addressing these challenges. By decomposing tasks, generating and executing code, inspecting outputs, and revising plans based on intermediate observations, they offer a natural foundation for geospatial decision support. A straightforward approach is therefore to equip such an agent with geospatial libraries, spatial databases, map APIs, and satellite imagery catalogs, and ask it to solve geospatial workflows end-to-end. However, disaster-response workflows introduce failure modes that are not captured by successful code execution alone. An answer may appear fluent and its code may execute successfully, while the underlying analysis remains incorrect because the agent selected the wrong disaster footprint, used an inappropriate spatial boundary, searched imagery outside the relevant event window, computed distances in an invalid CRS, or relied on an intermediate artifact that was planned but never produced.

A key feature of GeoFaham is artifact-aware collaboration. Agents do not pass large coordinate arrays, raster data, or complete imagery payloads through the LLM context. Instead, full outputs are persisted in a working memory called the Response Store, while the Orchestrator exchanges compact response identifiers and typed metadata. Agents reason over schemas, summaries, spatial bounds, temporal ranges, and band metadata, while deterministic geospatial engines operate on the full artifacts. This design reduces context overhead, reduces the risk of critical spatial and temporal metadata loss, and keeps downstream computation grounded in the full artifacts.

Existing geospatial benchmarks evaluate remote-sensing tool use and geoprocessing workflows (Shabbir et al., 2025; Kao et al., 2025; Krechetova and Kochedykov, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a), but do not fully capture cross-source w9orkflows that require coordination across heterogeneous geospatial data, intermediate artifact handling, and recovery from spatial or temporal execution failures. We therefore introduce GeoFaham-Bench for evaluating multi-step geospatial disaster workflows. GeoFaham-Bench contains 40 natural-language tasks grounded in 17 real-world disaster records spanning fires, floods, hurricanes, cyclones, earthquakes, and tornadoes. Each task captures an operational workflow relevant to GIS analysts, humanitarian workers, or government decision-makers. The tasks require integration across disaster databases, OpenStreetMap features (OpenStreetMap contributors, 2025), satellite imagery catalogs, and raster products, together with operations such as spatial joins, aggregation, ranking, and artifact generation. Because multiple valid execution traces may satisfy the same task, GeoFaham-Bench uses a non-rigid evaluation protocol that checks spatial, temporal, methodological, and output-level invariants rather than enforcing an exact execution trace.

papers.title: Effect of molybdenum content on phase transformations during continuous heating of metastable {\beta} Ti-Mo alloys
papers.abstract: Three metastable $\beta$ titanium alloys with different molybdenum contents, Ti-12Mo, Ti-15Mo and Ti-18Mo (wt.%), were investigated to determine the influence of $\beta$-phase stability on phase transformations during continuous heating. Electrical resistance measurement, dilatometry and differential scanning calorimetry were performed during linear heating at 5 {\deg}C/min up to 750 {\deg}C. The in-situ experiments were complemented by electron microscopy observations of specimens heated to selected temperatures and subsequently water-quenched. All alloys exhibited a sequence involving partial dissolution of athermal $\omega$ phase, stabilization and growth of isothermal $\omega$ phase, subsequent $\omega$ dissolution and precipitation of $\alpha$ phase. Increasing molybdenum content progressively suppressed $\omega$ phase evolution and subsequent $\alpha$ precipitation and narrowed the temperature interval associated with $\omega$-related transformations. The excellent agreement between electrical resistance measurements, DSC, dilatometry and electron microscopy enabled a consistent description of phase evolution during heating and demonstrated the benefits of combining complementary experimental techniques for investigation of complex transformation pathways in metastable $\beta$ titanium alloys.

papers.title: Local Visibility Roadmaps in Continous Multi-agent Path Finding
papers.abstract: We address the problem of smooth continuous multi-agent path finding (SC-MAPF), where agents move in a continuous environment along smooth curves in continuous time. The paths for individual agents are searched in local visibility roadmaps that consider obstacles and other agents. A new algorithm is proposed in this work, which combines the previous algorithm CE-CBS for high-level search with any-angle path finding for local single-agent planning, where agents are to avoid obstacles, both static and other agents. The new algorithm is tested and compared to CE-CBS, the algorithm building individual paths using RRT$^*$, and SMT-CCBS algorithm, an algorithm for MAPF$_R$. Experimental results show various advantages of the new algorithm over CE-CBS and SMT-CCBS in comparable settings.

Some recent work such as [1] and [26] has focused on MAPF with a continuous time but discrete environment. A collision between a pair of agents is resolved in the time domain by making one of the agents participating in the collision to wait. In contrast to this, we address not only continuous time but also a continuous environment so that agents have a chance to change their trajectory to avoid the collision. We present a new model combining the previous continuous environment conflict-based search [6] and visibility roadmaps, in which we construct an individual visibility roadmap for each agent according to its constraints (derived from previous collisions) and static obstacles. The paths found on these roadmaps are then smoothed by B-spline curves [13] to obtain trajectories that can be followed by real robots more easily.

papers.title: Rate-dependent gradient flows of integral currents via varicurrents
papers.abstract: Motivated by the analysis of recent models of dislocation motion in crystalline materials, this work introduces space-time varicurrents, a form of Young measures over integral currents, to describe their evolutions with rate-dependent dissipation potentials. This addresses the problem that rate-dependent versions of the (rate-independent) space-time variation suffer from a lack of lower semicontinuity with respect to the natural weak topology. This causes a dynamical relaxation to occur by means of infinitely fine oscillations. Varicurrents retain a description of this ``microstructure'' (in space-time) and, based on this theory, we are able to establish the existence of solutions to a rate-dependent gradient flow. This is in contrast to the classical formulation using integral currents, which does not have a solution in general.

papers.intro:
In crystalline materials, plastic deformation is predominantly driven by the motion of dislocation lines, which are one-dimensional topological defects within the crystal lattice [10, 3]. Recently, the work [9] formalized this within a large-strain mesoscopic model for dislocation-driven plasticity, starting from first principles. A central idea in that work is to geometrically express dislocation motion through so-called “slip trajectories”, that is, the trajectory of a dislocation line traced out in space-time. To express this in a mathematically rigorous way, [17] introduced the theory of space-time integral currents (we remark that some of these ideas were also developed independently in [12]). Using this framework, it is possible to establish the existence of energetic solutions for elasto-plastic evolutions driven by (discrete) dislocation motion in the rate-independent regime, as carried out in [18].

The works [17, 18] are limited to the rate-independent regime, where the dissipation of dislocation motion does not depend on the speed of movement (equivalently, the dissipation potential is 11-homogeneous). However, dislocation motion is usually rate-dependent [8], so the work [18] must be seen as a slow loading limit of the underlying physical model.

A fundamental issue in the rate-dependent regime is that the dissipation potential lacks weak lower semicontinuity in the topology of space-time currents. This geometric degeneracy echoes the phenomenon observed already in [14, 13] regarding the geometry of spaces of plane curves, and also the examples in [12]. Specifically, a sequence of currents can undergo microscopic oscillations or cancellations to distribute its movement over a larger volume at a lower velocity, thereby artificially decreasing its superlinear cost (as we will illustrate in Examples 1.2 and 1.3, respectively). When passing to the weak limit of increasingly fast oscillations, the limit current straightens and so “forgets” the microstructure. Consequently, the dissipation evaluated on the limit curve jumps up relative to the limit of the dissipation of the approximating motions, violating the standard requirement of weak lower semicontinuity.

With the necessary lower semicontinuity secured, we formulate a solution concept for a prototypical setup of rate-dependent dislocation evolutions using the so-called Energy-Dissipation Inequality (EDI). This is a robust framework extensively developed for metric gradient flows and doubly-nonlinear evolutions [2], notably by Mielke, Rossi, and Savaré [15]. To construct these solutions, we employ the Weighted Energy-Dissipation (WED) principle, introduced for gradient flows by Mielke and Stefanelli [16]. It should be noted that a similar approach had already been used in the context of mean curvature by Ilmanen [11]. Our specific approach is heavily inspired by the extension of the WED principle to metric spaces by Rossi, Savaré, Segatti, and Stefanelli [19]. As our space-time varicurrents are inherently global-in-time, they are natural objects for the global-in-time nature of the WED scheme. This alignment allows us to pass to the limit in a sequence of global variational problems, establishing the energy-dissipation inequality and thus obtaining EDI solutions.

papers.title: Non-local approximations for the Schr\"odinger operator with a general point interaction via the non-relativistic limit
papers.abstract: We consider the one-dimensional Dirac operator $D_{A,c}$ with a general, not necessarily self-adjoint, point interaction at the origin, whose strength is described by an arbitrary complex $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ and suitably rescaled by the speed of light $c$, together with its non-local approximations $D_{A,c}^{\epsilon}$ obtained by replacing the Dirac distribution by a rank-one projection onto a scaled function $v_\epsilon$. It is known that $D_{A,c}^\epsilon \to D_{A,c}$ as $\epsilon\to 0+$ and that $D_{A,c}-c^2/2$ converges, as $c\to+\infty$, to the Schr\"odinger operator $H_A$ with the general point interaction, both in the norm resolvent sense. We prove that the first convergence is uniform with respect to $c$ in a neighbourhood of $+\infty$, and we provide explicit rates of convergence. Combining this with an explicit computation of the non-relativistic limit of $D_{A,c}^\epsilon$ for fixed $\epsilon$, we show that the two limits can be interchanged and that the corresponding double limit exists. As a by-product we obtain a family of non-local, rank-two approximations $H_A^\epsilon$ of $H_A$ that converge to $H_A$ in the norm resolvent sense. Contrary to the relativistic setting, the coupling constants of $H_A^\epsilon$ are renormalized; we give an explicit formula for this renormalization.

papers.title: Localisations of rings of weak global dimension at most one
papers.abstract: We characterise the commutative rings of weak global dimension at most one whose derived categories can be stratified by the Balmer-Favi support theory. For such rings, this yields a bijective correspondence between the class of localising subcategories of the derived category, and the subsets of the Zariski spectrum. For a large class of rings of weak global dimension at most one including all valuation domains, this occurs if and only if the ring is locally strongly discrete, if and only if the Telescope conjecture holds, and if and only if the module category has Gabriel dimension. However, we also give an example of a valuation domain where all these conditions fail, and yet the residue fields generate its derived category and we can classify all the localising subcategories of $D(R)$. Additionally, in the same example, we show that the Balchin-Stevenson smashing support cannot stratify $D(R)$ either.

papers.title: On the van der Corput property for cubes
papers.abstract: We prove a power-saving form of the van der Corput property for cubes. As a consequence, we obtain a power-saving bound $|A|\ll_\varepsilon N^{59/60+\varepsilon}$ for sets $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with no nonzero cube differences.

papers.title: De-lensing cosmic birefringence with joint reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstruction of anisotropic cosmic birefringence from the CMB is limited by lensing $B$-mode sample variance and partially degenerate with the lensing curl. We study the joint reconstruction of lensing (gradient and curl) and birefringence at the maximum-a-posteriori point, whose spectra are near-optimal statistics. We predict the joint response and noise analytically, validate them on simulations, and show unbiased inference of its amplitude. Errors will shrink $5$-fold relative to quadratic estimators at SPT-3G+ depths, promising much tighter constraints on parity-violating new physics, owing to the removal of the lensing $B$-polarization sample variance.

papers.title: Sharp decay of the spherical averages of the Fourier transform of open sets
papers.abstract: For a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, the spherical average $E_\Omega(R)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}|\widehat{\mathbb{1}_\Omega}(R\omega)|^2d\omega$ is never $O(R^{-a})$ with $a>d+1$, and for smooth boundaries it is $O(R^{-d-1})$, as it is for the ball, whether or not the boundary is curved. In 2003, Brandolini, Hofmann and Iosevich extended this to every convex domain and to every domain with $C^{1,\frac{1}{2}}$ boundary, and this regularity condition has not been improved since. How much regularity does the decay $R^{-d-1}$ require? We show that among H\"older classes the answer is $C^{1,\frac{1}{4}}$. Every bounded domain with $C^{1,\frac{1}{4}}$ boundary satisfies $E_\Omega(R)\leq C_\Omega R^{-d-1}$, while for every $0<s<\frac{1}{4}$ any smooth domain can be altered near a single boundary point to produce a $C^{1,s}$ domain for which this bound fails along a sequence of radii. More generally, when the boundary has fractional Sobolev regularity $W^{1+s,p}$, we determine the optimal decay exponent under a Dini condition on the normal, and in a large range of $s$ and $p$ without it. The upper bounds follow from $L^2$ estimates for nondegenerate oscillatory integral operators whose phases are distances between points of two graphs with Dini or fractional Sobolev gradients, and hence barely better than $C^1$. These are far too rough for the integrations by parts techniques from the smooth theory. We replace derivatives by finite differences adapted to the phase, a device that we expect to be useful in a variety of related problems.

papers.title: Dataset Recommendation for Heterogeneous and Dynamic Scholarly Graphs via Multimodal Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Researchers struggle to find relevant datasets amid the growing volume of data across repositories and scholarly publications. Manual dataset retrieval is time-consuming and often fails to identify valuable resources that are not easily discoverable through direct links or popularity metrics. Dataset recommendation, which aims to identify datasets relevant to a paper, author, or query, has become essential for improving dataset discoverability and reuse. However, this task remains challenging because Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) are large-scale, heterogeneous, dynamic, and incomplete. Although openly available SKGs organize scientific knowledge by linking scholarly outcomes, they often lack meaningful connections between datasets, leaving them isolated and underutilized. These graphs contain millions of evolving relations but still suffer from missing or inaccurate metadata, duplicate records, and weak dataset integration. This work presents the Multimodal Scholarly Attention Network (MM-SAN), a heterogeneous multimodal graph representation learning method for recommending datasets relevant to research publications within real-world SKGs. MM-SAN combines topology-aware and text-based embeddings, enabling effective recommendations even when textual metadata is limited or absent. It operates in transductive, semi-inductive, and fully inductive settings, adapting to evolving SKGs without requiring retraining. Experiments show that MM-SAN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, providing a robust and scalable solution for dataset recommendation.

In this paper, we tackle the task of dataset recommendation, where the goal is to recommend datasets that are relevant to a given research publication. We propose MM-SAN (MM-SAN), a multimodal heterogeneous graph representation method for dataset recommendation, accommodating heterogeneous, sparse, and incomplete real-world SKG. MM-SAN integrates topology-based and text-based embeddings, exploiting a multimodal learning design, making it effective even when textual features are absent or of low quality. MM-SAN works in transductive and inductive scenarios and is effective whether complete or incomplete textual metadata are available. For evaluation, we rely on subsets of OAG, the backbone of the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC, https://eosc.eu/), which is open-access, frequently updated, and contains scientific datasets. We address three research questions: RQ1 (Robustness).: To what extent can MM-SAN provide effective dataset recommendations in the presence of the topological sparsity typical of real-world SKG, characterized by limited connectivity between publication and dataset nodes? RQ2 (Flexibility).: To what extent can MM-SAN guarantee effective recommendation performance across transductive, semi-inductive, and fully inductive settings, consequently adapting to new, previously unseen nodes without requiring the model to be retrained? RQ3 (Versatility).: To what extent can MM-SAN preserve effective recommendation performance under progressively reduced textual metadata availability by leveraging graph topology to compensate for missing semantic information? Regarding the first question, we examine how well MM-SAN performs in the presence of sparse and incomplete graphs, which are typical in real-world SKG scenarios. The second research question focuses on inductiveness, defined as the model’s ability to adapt to an evolving graph without requiring full retraining. In other words, the model is trained on an initial version of the graph and evaluated on an updated version containing new nodes and edges not used for training. Hence, we present for the first time a method that is able to generalize across different learning scenarios, i.e., transductive, inductive, and semi-inductive settings. Lastly, the third question focuses on whether the method can effectively exploit graph structure to mitigate the impact of missing or limited textual metadata.

papers.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
papers.abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

Social interactions involving multiple people are common in everyday life. As social robots become increasingly integrated into society, they need to interact effectively in multi-party or group settings (Nigro et al., 2025; Sebo et al., 2020). Robots typically communicate in these settings through speech, gestures, or body movements that everyone present can observe. Although this overt communication can support transparency and mutual understanding, it may be unsuitable when information is intended for only an individual, particularly when that information is privacy-sensitive (Nilgar et al., 2024; Nilgar et al., 2025; Dietrich et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2022; Zand et al., 2025). For example, a healthcare robot may need to coordinate with a patient, healthcare provider, or caregiver without unnecessarily exposing patient information to others who are present (Jayaraman et al., 2024). This creates a need for an interaction channel that can direct task-relevant information to a person and receive a response while limiting how readily co-present others can access or interpret the exchange.

papers.title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
papers.abstract: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

During the second phase, the robot delivered two scripted critical feedback messages concerning the participant’s pronunciation and handwriting. The messages were independent of participants’ actual performance, allowing the feedback content to remain constant across conditions. In the context-invariant condition, the robot delivered the critical feedback aloud despite the bystander’s presence. In the context-adaptive condition, the robot scanned for and detected the bystander, turned its body and display away from them, provided the participant with a spoken attention cue, and then presented the same feedback messages silently on its display (Figure 1). Thus, the conditions differed in whether the robot adapted the modality and presentation of its feedback to the changed social context, while the feedback content itself remained constant.

papers.title: Mass-Metallicity Relation of the Fossil Disk in Six Nearby Galaxies using JWST RGB Stars
papers.abstract: We here present the first ever mass-metallicity relation (MZR) of fossil disk populations using the resolved stellar populations in the James Webb Space Telescope Near-Infrared Camera (JWST/NIRCam) images of six nearby galaxies. Both the mass and metallicity were determined using the Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars, employing methods that have been well established to study the halo populations of nearby galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope images. Specifically, we obtained the mass and metallicity by comparing the color, magnitude and number density near the tip of the RGB (TRGB) stars in the F115W$-$F200W vs F200W color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) with that of the PARSEC isochrones of 4 and 13~Gyr. The RGB metallicities of the disks of nearby galaxies closely match those found in galaxies at redshifts $z>8$, with the metallicity range following a power-law relation with the fossil disk mass. The power-law index of the fossil disk MZR, $\gamma\approx0.26$, compares well with the typical value found in MZRs obtained using gas metallicities across redshifts. Through this work, we illustrate the utility of JWST/NIRCam images for obtaining the mass and metallicity of the fossil disks of nearby galaxies at precisions that were not possible earlier, which opens up a new method to carry out the near-field cosmological studies.

papers.intro:
The mass-metallicity relation (MZR), which is the correlation between a galaxy’s stellar mass and metallicity [49, 42], is one of the most fundamental scaling relations in galaxy evolution [47, and references therein], where galaxies with larger stellar mass have higher metallicities. This relation is sculpted by the interplay between gas-accretion, star formation and feedback-driven outflows [22, 41, 26, 73, 37, 67, 72].

At z=0z=0, this relation is particularly well established through surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey [75, SDSS;]. With the advent of efficient spectrographs at near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths, the MZR has been extended well beyond z=0z=0 [23, 46, 39, e.g.]. Studies indicate that its overall functional form remains broadly similar with cosmic time, while its normalization evolves. Most strikingly, recent James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) spectroscopy has pushed metallicity measurements out to z≈8z\approx 8 and beyond, probing the MZR at the earliest observable epochs of galaxy formation. However, these high-redshift anchor points carry large uncertainties as they are generally derived from strong optical emission lines and spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling. Given the intrinsic faintness and complexity of high-redshift galaxies, the observational uncertainties that get carried forward into mass and metallicity estimates are quite significant.

An alternative to high-redshift observation for studying early epochs of galaxy evolution is to study the fossil resolved stellar populations of nearby galaxies where the observational uncertainties are minimal. Nearby galaxies host old stellar populations that trace the current disk which was probably formed during the early epochs of galaxy assembly, analogous to a young disk at high redshift. Although the morphology and mass of the fossil disk could have changed [54, e.g.], the chemical properties are still preserved. This local, resolved approach is in the tradition of near-field cosmology, in which the present-day fossil record of nearby galaxies is used to constrain conditions and processes at earlier cosmic times.

One of the key tools enabling such studies is the relationship between red giant branch (RGB) star color and metallicity. The tip of the red giant branch (TRGB), the sharp luminosity-function discontinuity marking the onset of the helium flash in stars with initial masses ≲\lesssim 2 M⊙ and ages >> 4 Gyr, has long served as a standard candle for distance measurement [40, 35, 59, 34, 50, 6, 21, 70, 1]. Its color and magnitude also depend systematically on metallicity, a relation grounded in stellar evolution theory [65, 66] and calibrated empirically using the Galactic globular clusters [9]. Since then, the TRGB color-metallicity relation has been used to derive metallicities in nearby galaxies where the RGBs can be identified in resolved stellar populations using the ground-based observations in the Magellanic Clouds [43] and M31/33 [44] and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations of nearby dwarf and irregular galaxies [8, 69, 17], firmly establishing the RGB/TRGB color as a robust metallicity tracer beyond its original distance-measurement role.

In Section 2, we briefly describe the galaxy sample utilized in this work, along with the JWST data. papers.title: A Practical Causal Framework for Autonomous Mobile Robots: From Simulation to Real-World Human Environments
papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.

papers.intro:
Deploying autonomous mobile robots in human-populated environments (e.g., warehouses, hospitals, airports, malls) requires safe and efficient interaction with humans. Understanding how robot actions causally affect their surroundings enables better action selection, motivating methods that reason about causal relationships in the environment and human-robot interactions. Accordingly, the robotics community has increasingly embraced causal approaches in various fields Hellström (2021), including robot manipulation Lee et al. (2021); Cannizzaro et al. (2025); Castri et al. (2024c), explainable robotics and HRI Diehl and Ramirez-Amaro (2022); Love et al. (2024), spatial interactions Castri et al. (2024b), planning Cannizzaro and Kunze (2023), and robot understanding Edström et al. (2023). However, transitioning these algorithmic frameworks from theoretical formulation to real-world deployment remains a challenge. Even in purely robotic scenarios, this process is hindered by the need for extensive and time-consuming data collection Zhao et al. (2020). This difficulty is amplified in human-populated settings, where long-term data collection is often impractical.

However, transitioning these algorithmic frameworks from theoretical formulation to real-world deployment remains a challenge. Even in purely robotic scenarios, this process is hindered by the need for extensive and time-consuming data collection Zhao et al. (2020). This difficulty is amplified in human-populated settings, where long-term data collection is often impractical.

Despite these constraints, users typically expect robots to be immediately functional. To meet this operational demand, a robust strategy must leverage simulation for extensive data collection and subsequent causal discovery, while enabling rapid adaptation to real-world dynamics. This necessitates a modular, end-to-end causal inference framework—spanning from raw sensor data acquisition and structure learning directly to online reasoning. Crucially, such a framework must be capable of efficient sim-to-real transfer, retaining the high-level logic learnt in simulation while seamlessly updating its parameters to the physical environment.

Crucially, such a framework must be capable of efficient sim-to-real transfer, retaining the high-level logic learnt in simulation while seamlessly updating its parameters to the physical environment.

Prior work Castri et al. (2026) laid the groundwork for our approach with a modular, causality-enhanced decision-making framework supporting both causal discovery and reasoning. However, the authors evaluated task execution efficiency and human safety only in simulation, leaving real-world deployment and validation unaddressed. This paper bridges the gap between simulated and real applications by proposing an improved framework with a data-efficient adaptation process that tunes the initial simulation-learnt causal model to work equally well on a physical mobile robot in human environments (Fig. 1). We validate this approach in two real-world scenarios – a poster session and a social event – proving that the causal framework operates as expected onboard of a robot for solving challenging navigation tasks, outperforming a non-causal alternative while maintaining low inference time. Our main contributions include: • A new data-efficient sim-to-real transfer that exploits structural causal invariance to adapt the framework via rapid parameter update on limited real-world data. • The first real-world deployment and validation of an end-to-end causality-based framework applied to robot navigation tasks in human environments, made publicly available11 1 https://lcastri.github.io/causal-sim2real/ for reproducibility and future applications. • An experimental evaluation across challenging simulated and real-world group encounters, focusing on task success, operational safety and inference time.

papers.title: Balance laws with measure valued source for commuting dynamics
papers.abstract: In this paper we consider balance laws with measure-valued sources modeling commuters traveling along a road from residential to workplace locations. We introduce a notion of $(m_I, m_F)$-entropy solution, prove a compactness result for this class, and establish existence of solutions with prescribed spatial marginals for the sources representing the lodging and workplace distributions. Moreover, adopting a Lagrangian viewpoint, we describe commuting strategies as measures on Lipschitz curves with assigned entry and exit times, compatible with a given transport plan. Using the compactness result and a semi-discrete micro-macro scheme with source, based on the celebrated Follow-the-Leader model, we prove existence of admissible commuting strategies. Finally we prove the existence of optimal solutions for classical traffic cost functionals.

papers.title: Eddy currents and error fields in the toroidally segmented shell configuration aka Armadillo
papers.abstract: A stream function formulation for the calculation of the eddy current distribution in a toroidally segmented conducting shell (Armadillo) is presented and verified. The governing Poisson-like equation is solved spectrally via a Discrete Sine Transform, which enforces the zero-current boundary condition at each gap exactly by construction, and the related radial magnetic field at the plasma surface is obtained by Biot-Savart integration. The toroidal eddy current flows in the same direction on every sector with a cosine-like poloidal distribution, while the poloidal return current, required by current continuity, peaks near each gap and reverses sign between adjacent sectors. The scaling of both components with the number of gaps is governed by the competition between the poloidal geometric scale of the shell and the toroidal segmentation scale. The transition between the two regimes is set by the aspect ratio of the device, around eight gaps for an RFX-mod2-like geometry, as predicted by the analytical wall time model of the Armadillo configuration. At the gap, the poloidal return current produces a radial field of opposite sign to the value far from the gap; the resulting non-axisymmetric error field peaks near this transition and becomes negligible for highly segmented shells. These results provide a first characterisation of the eddy currents and error fields of the Armadillo configuration, needed for future resistive wall mode and tearing mode stability analyses.

papers.title: Long-time behaviour and bifurcation analysis of a non-reciprocal two-species aggregation-diffusion system on the torus
papers.abstract: A two-species aggregation-diffusion system on the one-dimensional torus with antisymmetric cross-interactions modeling pursuit-evasion dynamics is studied. The self-interaction strength is used as a bifurcation parameter, and the linear stability of the homogeneous state is characterized by Fourier analysis. It is shown that non-reciprocal coupling enlarges the stability region. In a symmetric diffusion setting, exponential convergence to the homogeneous state is established for sufficiently weak self-interactions by means of an entropy argument, with a decay condition independent of the cross-interaction strength. Under suitable nondegeneracy and spectral assumptions, the first loss of stability is shown to occur through a Hopf bifurcation associated with a single spatial Fourier mode. A branch of time-periodic patterns is thereby obtained, along which the two species oscillate with a fixed phase difference. An explicit formula for the cubic Hopf coefficient is derived, and an essential dependence of the direction and stability of the bifurcating branch on the second spatial harmonic is identified. In the case of matching diffusion coefficients and interaction kernels, sufficiently strong non-reciprocity is shown to transform a subcritical stationary instability of the corresponding reciprocal system into a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with stable periodic solutions. An exchange-of-stability result is proved, and the theory is illustrated for Kuramoto, two-mode cosine, and top-hat interaction kernels.

papers.title: Nonintegrability theorem on perturbed integrable Hamiltonian dynamical systems with two independent resonances
papers.abstract: In this paper we establish a new theorem for nonintegrability of a perturbed, autonomous, two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian dynamical system with two independent resonances, based on a criterion which utilizes the well-known theorem of Poincar\'e and a Lie-series symplectic transformation. We also make certain assumptions and suggestions as to when the theorem holds and when it does not.

papers.title: iGC: Antibody Optimization via Reinforcement Learning over a Learned Somatic Hypermutation Prior
papers.abstract:
Antibody affinity maturation is a natural optimization process in which B cells acquire mutations through somatic hypermutation (SHM), undergo selection for improved antigen binding, and iteratively evolve toward higher affinity. Computationally modeling this process requires capturing both biologically plausible mutations and antigen-specific selection. However, existing mutation models do not directly optimize binding, while affinity optimization often neglects realistic mutation trajectories.
  We introduce iGC (in silico Germinal Centers), a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) framework for antigen-specific antibody optimization. Stage 1 learns an SHM mutation prior from parent-child pairs in B-cell lineage trees and adapts it to a target affinity-maturation dataset. Stage 2 initializes an RL policy from this prior and optimizes antigen binding with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization toward the frozen prior. To prevent reward exploitation, including repetitive high-reward substitutions and structurally tolerated framework mutations, we introduce a Reward-Tax Meta-Gradient objective. RewardNet smooths the affinity landscape, while TaxNet penalizes reward overexploitation, jointly defining a learned meta-reward for policy optimization.
  We evaluate iGC on mutation prediction, SHM consistency, affinity optimization, and mutation diversity. The mutation prior more than doubles the strongest baseline in mutation-site prediction. Following RL optimization, iGC maintains SHM sequence structure. It also achieves a strong exploration-exploitation balance, yielding competitive reward-diversity products across candidate-selection cutoffs. These results demonstrate that iGC integrates biologically plausible mutation generation with antigen-specific affinity selection, providing an in silico framework for iterative antibody affinity maturation.

papers.intro:
The immune system naturally optimizes antibody sequence repertoires through the process of affinity maturation in specialized anatomical structures called germinal centers (Victora and Nussenzweig, 2012). In B cells, somatic hypermutation (SHM) of the antibody-encoding Ig locus introduces mutations concentrated in Complementarity-Determining Regions (CDRs), specifically diversifying antigen binding. Competition for antigen drives selective expansion of high-affinity binders while eliminating sequences that compromise protein structure or exhibit autoimmune cross-reactivity. This can be formally represented as a sequential decision process: a unique antibody sequence represents a state, binding improvement supplies the reward, and each selected mutation alters the epistatic context for subsequent decisions. Iterative cycles of diversification and selection thus function as a natural optimization loop, yielding B cells that express potent, physiologically optimized antibodies (Figure 1a).

Computational antibody design typically models only one half of this loop. B-cell-receptor repertoire and antibody language models learn statistical patterns of SHM and natural sequence evolution but do not directly optimize binding to a specified antigen (Ruffolo et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2024). Conversely, antigen-specific affinity-optimization methods search directly for stronger binders but do not explicitly model the sequential, biologically regularized mutation trajectories that produce them (Shan et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2022; Tagasovska et al., 2025). Such optimization can move toward sequences that score well for binding yet lie far from mutation paths naturally accessible to the body, bypassing physiological constraints that preserve structural integrity and prevent off-target polyreactivity. Existing approaches also generally optimize individual variants rather than learning how to make successive, context-dependent mutation decisions across the full mutation–selection process.

A frozen copy of the adapted SHM prior remains a KL-regularization anchor throughout Stage 2, allowing affinity-driven optimization without unconstrained drift from repertoire-plausible mutation behavior.
