papers.title: Conformer diversity over quantity in COSMO-RS-based LLE predictions
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of phase equilibria is essential for chemical process design, particularly in systems characterized by complex intermolecular interactions. This work investigates the influence of conformer selection and sigma-profile characteristics on COSMO-RS predictions of liquid-liquid equilibria (LLE), using the tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol (THFA)-methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK)-water system as a case study. Calculations were performed at the TZVP and TZVPD-FINE levels of theory. While TZVP failed to capture the experimentally observed phase behavior, TZVPD-FINE provided substantially improved predictions. The differences are attributed to the relative importance assigned to less-polar conformers and more-polar conformers capable of hydrogen bonding. Although the TZVPD-FINE calculations reproduced the main experimental trends, the predicted organic-phase composition showed a mean percentage deviation of 5.27%, slightly exceeding the adopted 5% agreement threshold. Investigations using individual conformers demonstrated that predictions can be strongly influenced by conformer selection and that representative conformer ensembles are necessary for reliable results. Further analysis showed that diversity in sigma profiles is more important for predictive accuracy than the total number of conformers. These findings emphasize the importance of carefully selecting conformers when applying COSMO-RS to liquid-liquid equilibria involving phases of contrasting polarity.

papers.title: A Wolf-Rayet nebula in its disruption phase: high-resolution radio observations of PCG 11
papers.abstract: (abridged abstract) Wolf-Rayet stars have high mass-loss rates and fast stellar winds. Their interaction with circumstellar material from previous evolutionary phases can produce complex nebular morphologies. Hydrodynamic instabilities can fragment wind-swept material, producing condensations, filaments, and gaps that alter the confinement of stellar wind and ionizing radiation. The role of fragmentation in the late evolution and dispersal of WR nebulae remains poorly constrained. PCG 11, with its fragmented morphology and regular scalloped rim, offers an opportunity to investigate these processes. We aim to characterize the structure of PCG 11 and investigate its ring-like morphology and scalloped rim. We constrain its three-dimensional geometry and determine whether the optical fragmentation pattern is also traced by ionized gas. We obtained high-resolution radio continuum images with MeerKAT at 2.6 and 3.1 GHz and ATCA at 5.5 and 9.0 GHz. The radio emission reveals a hollow, equatorially enhanced structure viewed close to its symmetry axis. The images resolve the rim into condensations, low-brightness gaps, and finger-like protrusions. We quantify the fragmentation scale and relate it to the nebular geometry. We also detect an unresolved source coincident with WR 75ab, whose rising radio spectrum is consistent with thermal wind emission. The nebula processes only a small fraction of the stellar ionizing radiation, indicating substantial photon leakage. PCG 11 captures a poorly observed stage in massive-star bubble evolution: the swept-up shell has developed a coherent instability pattern and become fragmented and porous, while remaining dynamically coupled to the stellar wind. It provides a clear view of how fragmentation and erosion reshape the circumstellar environment during a transitional evolutionary phase.

papers.intro:
Massive stars profoundly shape their environment through strong stellar winds and ionizing radiation. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars represent a particularly powerful wind phase in their evolution, with wind velocities of v∞∼1000v_{\infty}\sim 1000–3000 km​s−1\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}and high mass-loss rates (Crowther, 2007). Such fast winds can sweep up the slower, denser material shed during the previous evolutionary stages, carving shells and bubbles (Chu, 1981; Toalá and Arthur, 2011, e.g.), whose morphology retains information on the previous mass-loss history and also influence how the mechanical energy of the current wind is transferred to the surrounding medium. During the evolution of the swept up shell, hydrodynamical instabilities can fragment it, changing the confinement of the shocked wind and the coupling of mechanical energy to the surrounding gas (Garcia-Segura et al., 1996; Dwarkadas, 2022; Dwarkadas, 2023, e.g.). Numerical models show that the fraction of the stellar mechanical energy retained by the circumstellar gas can be substantially lower than predicted by simple energy-conserving bubble models (Freyer et al., 2006; Dwarkadas, 2023).

Such fast winds can sweep up the slower, denser material shed during the previous evolutionary stages, carving shells and bubbles (Chu, 1981; Toalá and Arthur, 2011, e.g.), whose morphology retains information on the previous mass-loss history and also influence how the mechanical energy of the current wind is transferred to the surrounding medium. During the evolution of the swept up shell, hydrodynamical instabilities can fragment it, changing the confinement of the shocked wind and the coupling of mechanical energy to the surrounding gas (Garcia-Segura et al., 1996; Dwarkadas, 2022; Dwarkadas, 2023, e.g.). Numerical models show that the fraction of the stellar mechanical energy retained by the circumstellar gas can be substantially lower than predicted by simple energy-conserving bubble models (Freyer et al., 2006; Dwarkadas, 2023).

When and how a swept-up shell fragments is therefore an important aspect of understanding how massive-star winds transfer energy and momentum to their surroundings. Although the formation of wind-blown bubbles around massive stars has been extensively investigated both theoretically and observationally (Weaver et al., 1977; Toalá et al., 2015, e.g.), much less is known about shell fragmentation and dispersion, that is a short-lived process difficult to identify observationally.

Although the formation of wind-blown bubbles around massive stars has been extensively investigated both theoretically and observationally (Weaver et al., 1977; Toalá et al., 2015, e.g.), much less is known about shell fragmentation and dispersion, that is a short-lived process difficult to identify observationally.

How efficiently stellar winds transfer mechanical energy to the surrounding gas is also relevant on the larger scales of young stellar clusters and associations, where the combined winds of massive stars constitute an important source of mechanical feedback during the early evolution of the cluster. The powerful winds of WR stars can make a significant contribution during this phase, although in crowded environments the effects of individual stars are difficult to disentangle, Westerlund 1 is an example of combined effect of WR winds (Umana et al. in prep). More isolated WR nebulae provide a simpler view of the wind-shell interaction. Radio continuum observations are particularly valuable in this respect, as they trace the ionized gas independently of dust extinction and, at high angular resolution, resolve the structure of the swept-up shell. They can also detect the thermal emission from the stellar wind itself, thus probing both the current mass loss and the material with which the wind interacts. The combination of sensitivity, angular resolution, and broad spatial-scale coverage offered by modern radio interferometers is revolutionizing the study of evolved stars, allowing for fast snapshots that reveal numerous circumstellar structures at once (Umana et al. in prep, Buemi et al. in prep, and Bordiu et al., 2025). MeerKAT currently provides these capabilities up to S-band frequencies, while higher-frequency observations can be obtained with facilities such as the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA). The advent of SKA-Mid will bring high-sensitivity, broad spatial-scale imaging capabilities to frequencies up to 15.4 GHz, opening new possibilities for spatially resolved studies of the interaction between massive-star winds and their circumstellar nebulae (Buemi et al., 2026). In this context, the Wolf-Rayet star WR 75ab and the associated nebula PCG 11 provide an interesting case study in which the structure of a WR nebula and its interaction with the central star can be investigated in detail.

PCG 11 (PHR 1633−-4928) was discovered by Cohen et al. (2005) during the follow-up of the Macquarie/AAO/Strasbourg Hα\alpha (MASH) survey, initially as a candidate planetary nebula. Optical spectroscopy revealed a Population I central star of type WN7h (van der Hucht, 2006, WR 75ab;) at a distance of 4.1±0.44.1\pm 0.4 kpc, surrounded by a nearly circular Hα\alpha ring of radius 36′′36^{\prime\prime}. (2005). The optical nebula shows an unusual scalloped rim and a central region largely devoid of Hα\alpha emission. papers.title: Solutions of the space-fractional heat equation with polynomial growth: Liouville theorems and Schauder estimates
papers.abstract: With the aim of extending to parabolic equations the framework developed by the first three authors in [Dipierro, Savin, and Valdinoci, Rev. Mat. Iberoam. (2019)], we introduce a notion of (viscosity) solutions for the space-fractional heat equation modulo $k$. In turn, we are able to define $s$-caloric functions with polynomial growth at infinity, showing also related Schauder estimates, a Liouville-type result, and a stability property with respect to the $L^\infty_{\rm{loc}}$-convergence.

papers.title: DenseTwins: Dense Modality Decoupling for Multimodal Self-Supervision
papers.abstract: Multimodal perception is central to many computer vision applications, including robotics and autonomous driving, where different sensing modalities provide complementary cues. Self-supervised learning offers a scalable solution for exploiting large amounts of unlabeled multimodal data. However, existing methods either neglect modality-specific information by enforcing feature-space alignment between modalities or learn only global representations without preserving spatial structure. We propose DenseTwins, a multimodal self-supervised framework that learns dense representations by explicitly decoupling the dense feature space into shared and modality-specific components. The proposed approach combines dense cross-modal correspondences with redundancy-reduction objectives, enabling the model to capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues within a structured dense embedding space. DenseTwins jointly optimizes an intra-modal objective across augmented views and a cross-modal objective that aligns shared features while decorrelating modality-specific information. We evaluate DenseTwins across multiple multimodal benchmarks and sensing setups, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive performance across multimodal self-supervised baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/DenseTwins.

Many real-world perception systems rely on multiple sensing modalities, such as RGB cameras, depth sensors, LiDAR, event cameras, or thermal imagery [7]. These modalities provide complementary information about the same scene, and their joint exploitation is crucial in perception applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and video understanding [5, 27]. Unfortunately, collecting large-scale annotated multimodal datasets is expensive and often impractical. Self-supervised learning (SSL) provides a natural alternative, enabling learning latent representations directly from unlabeled data [41].

Many real-world perception systems rely on multiple sensing modalities, such as RGB cameras, depth sensors, LiDAR, event cameras, or thermal imagery [7]. These modalities provide complementary information about the same scene, and their joint exploitation is crucial in perception applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and video understanding [5, 27]. Unfortunately, collecting large-scale annotated multimodal datasets is expensive and often impractical. Self-supervised learning (SSL) provides a natural alternative, enabling learning latent representations directly from unlabeled data [41].

SSL has been widely studied in single-modal settings [10, 37, 6]. A common approach to extend SSL to multiple modalities is to project inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space and align their representations. The most prominent example is CLIP [26], which demonstrates that contrastive learning can effectively align images and text in the latent space. Alignment can also be achieved through redundancy-reduction objectives [37, 6], which avoid representation collapse by decorrelating feature dimensions. However, in multimodal perception, different sensors provide only partially overlapping information: while some semantic content is shared across modalities, other cues are inherently modality-specific (e.g., texture in RGB, discontinuities in depth images, thermal signatures, or event dynamics). Therefore, an effective multimodal representation should preserve both the shared and the modality-specific information [33].

A common approach to extend SSL to multiple modalities is to project inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space and align their representations. The most prominent example is CLIP [26], which demonstrates that contrastive learning can effectively align images and text in the latent space. Alignment can also be achieved through redundancy-reduction objectives [37, 6], which avoid representation collapse by decorrelating feature dimensions. However, in multimodal perception, different sensors provide only partially overlapping information: while some semantic content is shared across modalities, other cues are inherently modality-specific (e.g., texture in RGB, discontinuities in depth images, thermal signatures, or event dynamics). Therefore, an effective multimodal representation should preserve both the shared and the modality-specific information [33].

This motivates modality decoupling, where the embedding space is explicitly separated into shared and modality-specific components. To the best of our knowledge, DeCUR [33] is the only multimodal SSL method that explicitly performs decoupling. However, it operates on global representations of the input modalities, discarding spatial structure and limiting the applicability to downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection, which are particularly relevant in multimodal perception. On the other hand, dense approaches that learn pixel-level representations have been studied mainly in the single-modal setting, e.g., DenseCL [32].

However, it operates on global representations of the input modalities, discarding spatial structure and limiting the applicability to downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection, which are particularly relevant in multimodal perception. On the other hand, dense approaches that learn pixel-level representations have been studied mainly in the single-modal setting, e.g., DenseCL [32].

In this work, we propose DenseTwins (Figure 1), the first SSL framework explicitly performing decoupling in a dense latent space, preserving the spatial structure while retaining both shared and modality-specific information. Two modality-specific encoders extract dense feature maps from the input modalities, which are then projected into a structured embedding space. Part of the embedding space captures information shared across modalities (the shared subspace), while the remaining dimensions preserve modality-specific cues (the modality-specific subspace). This decomposition allows the model to learn spatially consistent multimodal features while retaining complementary information from each sensing modality. Our experiments demonstrate that resulting representations are particularly well-suited for dense perception tasks, while remaining general-purpose representations transferable to global downstream tasks.

Our experiments demonstrate that resulting representations are particularly well-suited for dense perception tasks, while remaining general-purpose representations transferable to global downstream tasks.

DenseTwins builds on three established principles: redundancy reduction from Barlow Twins [37], hence its name, modality decoupling [33], and dense correspondence learning [32], combining them within a unified multimodal SSL framework. Distinctive design choices that are key for DenseTwins include: (i) designing a structured dense embedding space that separates shared and modality-specific components spatially, (ii) establishing patch-level cross-modal correspondences within the shared subspace, and (iii) combining dense intra-modal and cross-modal training losses coherently. Specifically, we first establish dense correspondences across modalities to identify semantically related spatial locations. We then align the shared information while decorrelating the modality-specific content. This design enables the model to learn spatial multimodal representations that capture both shared semantics and modality-specific cues. Since correspondences are estimated directly in feature space, DenseTwins only requires paired observations of the same scene, and can be applied to arbitrary spatially organized modality pairs without modality-specific design choices.

papers.title: Metric Facility Location under Batched Random Order
papers.abstract:
We study online metric facility location in the batched random-order model. An adversary partitions $n$ clients into $B$ nonempty batches, which arrive in uniformly random order. Each batch is revealed in full, and its clients must be connected to open facilities before the next batch arrives. Openings and assignments are irrevocable, and the objective is to minimize the total opening and connection cost. For both uniform and nonuniform opening costs, we prove that the tight competitive ratio is \[
  \Theta\!\left(\min\left\{\log(B+1),
  \sqrt{\log(n-B+2)}\right\}\right). \] Thus, the ratio is constant both when there is a single batch and when every batch is a singleton, but intermediate numbers of batches can require a $\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ ratio. Our algorithms build on Meyerson's algorithm (2001) and do not need to know $n$ nor $B$. A key algorithmic novelty is that we process the clients in a batch one by one in uniform random order (hence neglecting the global properties of the batch). We present a novel analysis of this algorithm that hinges on the random order of the batches, as well as of the clients within each batch. We also provide a matching competitive ratio lower bound already for uniform costs, and even when the entire metric is known in advance.

papers.title: An Agentic Framework for Quality-Aware and Scenario-Adaptive Image Compression
papers.abstract: Despite decades of progress, image codecs remain difficult to adapt to diverse real-world compression scenarios for two main reasons. First, most image codecs are optimized for a specific objective and require substantial redevelopment when the compression goal changes. Second, they typically assume clean inputs, whereas sensor-captured images often contain degradations that alter rate-quality behavior. To address these challenges, we propose Practical Image Coding Agents (PICA), a multi-agent framework that adapts existing codecs to diverse user requirements and potentially degraded inputs. PICA consists of four collaborative agents: a Perception agent that interprets user intent and analyzes image content, an Improvement agent that jointly considers bitrate and reconstruction quality to guide pre-coding restoration, a Coding agent that refines quality-control settings from global to regional levels, and an After-coding improvement agent that addresses residual degradations and compression-induced artifacts through restoration guided solely by image quality. To enable codec-agnostic regional adaptation, we introduce Agentic ROI Coding (AROIC), which treats the codec as a black box and allows the agent to automatically schedule, execute, evaluate, and reflect ROI coding plans without architectural modifications or codec-specific retraining. We integrate these four agents with a Scenario-Guided Quality-Rate (SGQR) evaluation strategy to enable more effective scenario-adaptive compression across heterogeneous codecs. Comprehensive experiments on clean, noisy, and blurred images across standard, perceptual, and machine-vision compression scenarios demonstrate that PICA consistently enhances the compression performance of both the conventional H.266/VVC codec and the neural Cheng2020 codec, outperforming competing compression methods on the Kodak, CLIC2020, and HEVC datasets.

papers.intro:
Image compression is a fundamental problem in signal processing, as the rapidly growing volume and resolution of visual data impose substantial costs on storage, transmission bandwidth, and communication latency. This has been extensively studied for more than three decades, leading to mature hand-engineered image coding standards such as JPEG [1]. Such traditional codecs remain widely used in practical image storage and communication systems. More recent standards, such as H.266/VVC [2], also support high-efficiency image compression through intra-frame coding. With rapid advances in deep learning, neural image compression (NIC) methods have achieved substantial progress by jointly optimizing nonlinear transforms and entropy models under end-to-end rate–distortion (RD) objectives [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Representative methods such as Cheng2020 [11] have demonstrated RD performance competitive with or superior to those traditional codecs on the standard compression benchmarks.

Representative methods such as Cheng2020 [11] have demonstrated RD performance competitive with or superior to those traditional codecs on the standard compression benchmarks.

Despite this tremendous success, most widely deployed codecs are designed primarily for generic pixel-fidelity reconstruction, with their RD performance conventionally optimized and evaluated using distortion metrics such as PSNR, a compression scenario referred to as standard compression. However, modern visual-data ecosystems increasingly involve heterogeneous consumers and objectives with distinct compression intents. For example, some compressed images are primarily expected to preserve visual realism and semantic fidelity for human observers [12, 13, 7, 14], a compression scenario referred to as perceptual compression. Meanwhile, an increasing proportion of visual data is consumed by downstream machine-learning systems, where compression should preserve task-relevant information and downstream accuracy [15, 16, 17], a compression scenario referred to as machine-vision compression. Unfortunately, prior studies [7, 14, 16, 17] have shown that commonly used standard codecs can become suboptimal in these specialized compression scenarios.

Developing dedicated codecs for these specialized scenarios provides an intuitive solution. With the flexibility of NIC, several scenario-specific methods have therefore been proposed. For example, machine-vision compression approaches [16, 17] introduce task-aware compression modules to produce latent representations that preserve information relevant to downstream vision tasks. Meanwhile, perceptual NIC methods [13, 7] combine powerful generative models with human-perception-oriented objectives, such as LPIPS [18], to reconstruct visually plausible content. Though these specialized designs achieve substantial improvements in their respective scenarios, they are typically tightly coupled with extensive scenario-specific modules and objectives, thereby requiring considerable architectural redesign and substantial re-optimization when the compression intent changes. Consequently, they exhibit limited generalizability across diverse compression scenarios. This limitation motivates our first research question (RQ): RQ1: Can existing widely-used codecs be rapidly adapted to diverse compression scenarios without architectural redesign or substantial re-optimization?

Beyond their limited generalizability across compression scenarios, most existing codecs are developed under the assumption of clean input images. In practice, however, acquired images may exhibit degradations (e.g., noise) due to limitations of imaging sensors, such as those in smartphone cameras. These degradations not only compromise visual quality but also introduce undesirable signal variations that may increase the number of bits required for compression [19, 20]. To address this issue, recent studies have jointly optimized restoration and compression or introduced restoration-aware compression modules [19, 21, 20, 22, 23, 24, 25]. However, these approaches still rely on dedicated components and degradation-specific optimization. Moreover, they generally assume that the degradation type and restoration objective are known in advance, rather than autonomously determining whether restoration is necessary and how it should be coordinated before and after coding. It motivates our second RQ: RQ2: Can an existing widely used codec autonomously detect image degradations and adaptively coordinate pre-coding and post-coding restoration without substantial re-development?

PICA consists of four collaborative agents: a Perception Agent, an Improvement Agent, a Coding Agent, and an After-Coding Improvement Agent. Specifically, the Perception Agent interprets the user-specified compression intent while analyzing the input image, including its visual content, quality condition, and regions of interest, thereby providing structured guidance for subsequent agents.

To address RQ1, we introduce a Coding Agent with a global-to-regional coding quality refinement scheme. Guided by the compression intent summarized by the Perception Agent, it first performs Global Quality Control (QC) Search, applying estimated QC to the target codec and iteratively refining them based on the measured bitrate and reconstruction quality until the user-specified requirements are satisfied. Starting from this feasible global operating point, we further refine the coding quality of individual regions, motivated by prior studies showing that different compression scenarios assign different importance to image regions. For example, machine-vision compression often requires stronger preservation of task-relevant objects than background regions [17, 16]. However, most existing methods [26] rely on codec-specific ROI coding mechanisms, requiring the underlying codec to be explicitly designed or trained with dedicated ROI functionality and thus limiting their generalizability to heterogeneous codecs without native ROI support.

papers.title: Large time dynamics for non-autonomous weakly damped KdV-Burgers equations on the real line
papers.abstract: The large time dynamics of the weakly damped non-autonomous Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers equation \begin{equation*} u_t + u_{xxx}+ uu_x + \lambda u - \mu u_{xx} = g(x,t) \end{equation*} in the phase space $L^2(\mathbb R)$ is investigated. Due to the low regularity of the initial data, the framework of Bourgain spaces is employed. We first obtain the existence of a unique pullback attractor $\{\mathcal A_\mu(t)\}_{t\in\mathbb R}$ in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ for each $\mu \ge 0$. Then we show an optimal asymptotic smoothing effect of the equation, namely the pullback attractor is compact in $H^3(\mathbb R)$. These results are proved by using an energy equation method, splitting solutions into parts with low and high frequencies and exploiting a dispersive regularization. Furthermore, the attractors are shown to be upper semicontinuous as $\mu \to 0$ and have finite fractal dimensions in $H^1(\mathbb R)$.

The KdV-Burgers equation has been derived as an asymptotic model for the propagation of weakly nonlinear dispersive long waves in certain physical situations when dissipative and damping effects occur, such as waves in an elastic tube, ion-sound waves damped by ion-neutron collisions, waves in a tube filled with viscous fluid, flow of a fluid containing gas bubbles, turbulence, or crystal lattice theory (see e.g. [Joh70, Joh72, OS70, SG69]) and as a model for propagation of tsunamis (see [Dut07]). The well-posedness of homogeneous KdV-Burger equations, i.e. with g≡0g\equiv 0, has been thoroughly studied (see e.g. [MV11, MV13, CDKR14] and references therein). The large time dynamics of KdV-Burgers in the phase spaces H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) or H2​(ℝ)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}) have also been extensively investigated, see e.g. [Dlo11, DS10] for the autonomous case and [AB12] for the non-autonomous case. Concerning the phase space L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) and autonomous external force g≡g⁡(x)g\equiv g(x), the existence, regularity and finite fractal dimension of a global attractor are obtained in [BY98], [GW17] and [GC20], respectively. It is also worth mentioning the related works with low regular initial data such as [Goy22, McC23]. In practice, the external force is likely to be time dependent, i.e. g≡g⁡(t,x)g\equiv g(t,x), leading to the non-autonomous equation (1.1). The long-time behavior of solutions this equation in phase space L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) has not been studied, and this serves as a motivation for the current paper.

In practice, the external force is likely to be time dependent, i.e. g≡g⁡(t,x)g\equiv g(t,x), leading to the non-autonomous equation (1.1). The first objective of this paper is to study the existence and regularity of a pullback attractor in for the non-autonomous process associated to problem (1.1). papers.title: Counterexamples to the Happy Edge Conjecture in Plane Spanning Trees
papers.abstract:
We study the problem of reconfiguring plane, straight-line spanning trees on point sets in the plane. A flip is a reconfiguration step in which one edge of a tree is replaced with another, yielding again a plane spanning tree. For a given point set $P$, the flip graph has a vertex for each plane spanning tree on $P$, and an edge between any two trees that differ by a single flip.
  The folklore happy edge conjecture suggests that any edge shared by both the initial and the target tree (a happy edge) is never flipped in a shortest flip sequence. This conjecture was computationally verified for up to 10 points in convex position.
  In this paper, we disprove this conjecture both on general point sets and on point sets in convex position by providing two counterexamples on $16$ and $30$ points, respectively. The counterexample for point sets in general position also holds for compatible flips, while the happy edge property holds for compatible flips in convex point sets as shown by Aichholzer, Dorfer, and Vogtenhuber [GD 2025].
papers.intro:
Reconfiguration problems ask whether one feasible state of a system can be transformed into another through a sequence of allowed moves. A classical example concerns the reconfiguration of triangulations of a convex point set. In this context, a flip replaces the common diagonal of two adjacent triangles with the other diagonal of the convex quadrilateral they form. The resulting flip graph, whose vertices are triangulations and whose edges correspond to flips, is the 11-skeleton of the associahedron. These triangulations are in bijection with binary trees [28], and each flip corresponds exactly to a rotation in the associated tree. Consequently, the minimum number of flips needed to transform any triangulation into any other equals the number of rotations needed to transform their corresponding binary trees. This provides an algorithmic motivation for studying shortest flip sequences: rotations are basic operations of binary trees, and having a fast method to compute shortest distances would immediately improve the efficiency of algorithms that are based on those data structures.

In other words, the happy edge conjecture postulates that any two plane spanning trees on a point set admit a shortest flip sequence that preserves every edge common to the initial and target trees. This conjecture has been a subject of significant interest for multiple decades, with several works providing improved bounds on the flip graph diameter by giving constructive arguments that satisfy this property [1, 11, 14]. These constructions provided evidence that shortest sequences might also have this structure. Recent work has further attempted to strengthen the original conjecture and obtain additional structural properties. The parking edge conjecture [1] intuitively states that shortest flip sequences on points in convex position use only edges in the union of trees and on their convex hull. papers.title: Anomaly Detection on Resource-Constrained Devices with Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection at the edge requires the deployment of models that achieve competitive performance, while minimizing computational cost and memory footprint. In this article, we investigate the suitability of the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS), an unsupervised time-series anomaly detection method, for resource-constrained devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. Specifically, we replace random reservoir connectivity (MDRS-Rand) with a circular shift (MDRS-Circ) and show that the anomaly score for an entire time series can be computed from the final reservoir state alone. Furthermore, we show that exploiting the reservoir's temporal memory enables more efficient input preprocessing, further reducing computational cost. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods, and deploy their inference kernels on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller to assess latency, estimate energy consumption, and measure memory footprint. Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the autoencoder meet the benchmark's performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and smaller models. With optimized preprocessing, MDRS achieves an ROC AUC of 0.869, a model size of 24 KB, an estimated energy consumption of 24 uJ per inference, and a latency of 0.32 ms, corresponding to a 75.9x speedup over the autoencoder with standard preprocessing.
papers.intro:
IoT and resource-constrained devices are increasingly used to perform tasks at the edge. Many of such tasks fall into the category of anomaly detection applied to time-series [1]. For example, networking intrusion detection systems require methods that analyze incoming packets and infer whether they compose an ongoing cybersecurity attack. Another example is the analysis of environmental conditions (e.g., video or audio signals) to monitor processes and identify suspicious deviations from the normal conditions. To achieve the near real-time performance necessary for carrying out these tasks successfully, computations need to be performed locally. Offloading them to the cloud is often not viable, as the communication overhead is non-negligible. However, given the limited computational capabilities of resource-constrained devices, it is crucial to develop computationally-efficient methods.

Offloading them to the cloud is often not viable, as the communication overhead is non-negligible. However, given the limited computational capabilities of resource-constrained devices, it is crucial to develop computationally-efficient methods.

Tiny machine learning (tinyML) [2] has emerged as an area specifically targeting these settings, enabling the deployment of ML models on resource-constrained devices with limited memory, storage, and computational capabilities. To stimulate the development of methods for tinyML, the MLPerf Tiny benchmark [3] provides a standardized framework for evaluating such models, including an anomaly detection task based on acoustic machine-condition monitoring. By defining target detection performance and measuring computational efficiency, the benchmark supports the evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy and deployment cost.

To stimulate the development of methods for tinyML, the MLPerf Tiny benchmark [3] provides a standardized framework for evaluating such models, including an anomaly detection task based on acoustic machine-condition monitoring. By defining target detection performance and measuring computational efficiency, the benchmark supports the evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy and deployment cost.

Reservoir computing is a family of randomized recurrent neural networks promising for tinyML [4]. In reservoir computing, most network weights are initialized randomly and remain fixed, and only the output weights are trained [5]. This architecture drastically reduces training cost compared to fully-trainable neural networks, making reservoir computing particularly suitable for resource-constrained deployment. Building on this foundation, Tamura et al. recently proposed the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS) [6], an unsupervised anomaly detection method that detects point-wise anomalies by measuring the deviation of reservoir states from an estimated distribution of normal conditions. Unlike previous reconstruction- or prediction-based reservoir computing methods, MDRS produces temporally stable anomaly scores and avoids the need for supervised training of the output weights, making it a promising candidate for unsupervised anomaly detection on resource-constrained devices.

Building on this foundation, Tamura et al. recently proposed the Mahalanobis Distance of Reservoir States (MDRS) [6], an unsupervised anomaly detection method that detects point-wise anomalies by measuring the deviation of reservoir states from an estimated distribution of normal conditions. Unlike previous reconstruction- or prediction-based reservoir computing methods, MDRS produces temporally stable anomaly scores and avoids the need for supervised training of the output weights, making it a promising candidate for unsupervised anomaly detection on resource-constrained devices.

In this article, we investigate the suitability of MDRS for anomaly detection on resource-constrained IoT devices and propose two optimizations to reduce its computational requirements. First, we replace the random reservoir connectivity with a circular shift operation [7, 8], eliminating the need for a dense recurrent matrix multiplication. Second, we introduce an end-only score that computes the Mahalanobis distance only for the final reservoir state rather than at every time step. We evaluate the MDRS variants on the MLPerf Tiny anomaly detection benchmark against the reference autoencoder and other anomaly detection methods (Section III) in terms of detection performance, computational cost, and memory footprint (Section V). Among the evaluated methods, only MDRS and the reference autoencoder meet the MLPerf Tiny performance target, with MDRS requiring fewer operations and a smaller model. Moreover, since the reservoir integrates its input over time, MDRS can process single frames without the temporal stacking required by the autoencoder to meet the performance target, allowing further reductions in computational cost. When deployed on a NUCLEO-F401RE microcontroller (Section VI), MDRS achieves 6.9×\times lower latency and estimated energy consumption than the autoencoder with identical inputs. With optimized preprocessing, these improvements reach 75.9×75.9\times while meeting the MLPerf Tiny performance target with a model size of 24 KB.

papers.title: DualClusterNet: Personalized Pattern-Space Composition for Next-POI Recommendation
papers.abstract: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation supports personalized place discovery on location-based Web platforms. Mobility routines can recur across users while being realized at different places and adapted to individual preferences. We present DualClusterNet, a causal sequential recommender that composes two population-shared prototype dictionaries. At each observed prefix, soft routers retrieve pattern and spatial mixtures; a factorized multiplicative interaction couples them, feature-wise affine modulation adapts the shared representation, and a separate user-conditioned branch with an additive--projective gate retains individual variation. The prediction head combines this representation with a learned first-order transition term and ranks the complete training POI vocabulary. We evaluate on NYC and TKY using a training-only vocabulary and an original-final-target protocol that neither bridges unknown POIs nor substitutes earlier targets. The available single-seed results show competitive full-candidate ranking, while controlled analyses support the contribution of the compositional and personalized branches. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DualClusterNet-F4EE/.

papers.intro:
Location-based Web platforms connect online place discovery with users’ physical activities. Their ranking systems must select useful destinations from a city-wide catalog while accounting for the order, timing, and geography of past visits. Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation formalizes one part of this problem: given an observed check-in history, rank the concrete POI that the user will visit next (Luo et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022). This work addresses the Search, Recommendation, and Retrieval-Augmented AI setting through a specific Web recommendation challenge: reusing behavioral regularities across users whose spatial contexts and individual preferences differ. The prediction concerns the immediate next place, not a route, a new-to-the-user destination, or a POI conditional on a supplied future timestamp.

A useful distinction is between a routine and its realization. Consider an illustrative routine such as visiting a workplace, obtaining a meal, and then stopping at a shop. Two users may exhibit a similar ordering of activities without sharing a single POI. Conversely, the same neighborhood may host different routines at different times, and two users in the same neighborhood need not prefer the same restaurant. A model should therefore have a way to reuse population-level regularities, condition them on where a trajectory is unfolding, and retain user-specific variation. The example motivates an inductive bias; it does not presume that latent clusters are already validated semantic labels such as “commuting” or “shopping.”

Existing methods provide complementary ingredients. Recurrent and attention-based models encode temporal and spatial dependencies (Liu et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2021). Long- and short-term preference methods distinguish persistent tastes from recent behavior (Wu et al., 2022). papers.title: Co-Decompositions and FO Model Checking
papers.abstract:
Tree decompositions describe large graphs as gluings of smaller component parts. Here we study their categorical duals, tree co-decompositions, which construct large graphs via fibered products of small constituent parts. Co-decompositions are compressed representations of graphs or relational structures: the decomposed object can be exponentially larger than the space required to specify the co-decomposition.
  Our main contribution is an algorithmic meta-theorem for first order logic: given only a co-decomposition of a $\sigma$-structure $G$ with $b$ bags, each of size at most $w$ and an FO sentence $\phi$, there is an algorithm which, without ever constructing or inspecting $G$, operates on the co-decomposition and determines whether $G \models \phi$ in time $f_\sigma(w,|\varphi|)\cdot b$. We pair this algorithm with structural results on tree co-width, including its relationship to tree-width and a separation from twin-width. Furthermore, we characterize bounded path co-width using a graph grammar. In contrast to our logical meta-theorem, we prove that $(s,t)$-Path becomes NP-hard on co-decomposition inputs. These results demonstrate how categorical constructions can enable efficient computation on exponentially compressed structures.

Whether mathematical concepts are discovered or invented, the path by which we arrive at them is not always the best route to understanding. We came to tree co-decompositions by dualizing a categorical generalization of tree-width [22], where the topological viewpoint is replaced by a more algebraic one.Yet the notion of a co-decomposition extends beyond graphs and tree-shapes: co-decompositions of vector spaces are precisely cellular sheaves, which play a growing role in applied topology [29, 51, 75]. In this introduction, however, we choose a more natural way, at least in hindsight, and which hints at potential applications of our algorithms: the use of coordinates to organize distinct concerns in scientific modeling [65, 9].

Suppose Letícia, an epidemiologist, is trying to understand the spread of a new disease; let’s call it X. She knows that various factors influence its spread: infection dynamics, host population movement patterns, population demographics, other diseases, etc. She would prefer to model each of these aspects independently, making it is easier to reason about, communicate, and explain her findings. She sets up a disease spread model, a model to account for ageing, a model to record movement from one city to another, and a model for a separate disease, Y, which is known to interact with X. Of course, what Letícia is really after is a combined model which is appropriately stratified, in the sense that she can combine states across the various models: for instance, she might want a part corresponding to those individuals who live in São Paulo, are elderly, are exposed to X, and have recently recovered from Y. This sort of situation arises in practice, and several mathematical frameworks have been developed for this purpose [65, 8, 9]. Some of these use fibered products, also known as pullbacks, to negotiate the relationships between the constituent models so that they may be assembled into a much larger model of the process Letícia actually cares about [65, 9]. A co-decomposition is precisely such a “recipe” for assembling large models as fibered products of smaller pieces.

In practice, Letícia might cope with this intractability by describing the individual models as small combinatorial structures, which interact through what we call adhesions. We state this formally for graphs, but there is an analogous definition for arbitrary relational structures.

papers.title: Rings in which every semiprime left ideal is an intersection of prime left ideals
papers.abstract:
We study rings over which every semiprime submodule of every module is an intersection of prime submodules. This holds if semiprime two-sided ideals satisfy ACC, if principal two-sided ideals are finitely generated as left ideals, or if the ring is PI. Over Jacobson PI rings, every finitely generated module is Jacobson: its prime submodules are intersections of maximal submodules. For affine PI algebras this extends the Amitsur-Procesi theorem to modules.
  In every ring with involution, real two-sided ideals are intersections of real prime two-sided ideals. The same holds for real submodules of modules over PI rings and hereditary Noetherian prime rings, but can fail for real left ideals in Noetherian domains. Formally real affine PI algebras need not be real Jacobson: their real prime two-sided ideals need not be intersections of real primitive ideals. We give a sufficient positivity criterion. Over real Jacobson PI rings, finitely generated modules are real Jacobson: their real prime submodules are intersections of real maximal submodules.
  Over finitely generated free associative algebras, every finitely generated semiprime submodule of a finite free module is a finite intersection of finitely generated prime submodules and an intersection of maximal submodules of finite codimension. Semiprime hulls of finitely generated submodules are finitely generated. Evaluation at finite-dimensional irreducible representations and nonzero vector tuples gives a Hilbert Nullstellensatz over arbitrary fields. For free algebras with involution, the corresponding real results are known over the real or complex numbers when the involution permutes the generators. We extend real prime decomposition to arbitrary fields and involutions, and give new algebraic proofs of the real Nullstellensatz and finite generation of real radicals, without the GNS construction or Groebner bases.

papers.title: The Price of List Replicability: Tight Bounds for Bias Estimation
papers.abstract:
We study the sample complexity of list replicable algorithms for estimating the biases of $d$ coins. An algorithm is $(k,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable if for every bias vector $\mathbf{p}\in[0,1]^d$, there is a set of outputs $L_{\mathbf{p}}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ of at most $k$ elements such that every $\mathbf{y}\in L_{\mathbf{p}}$ satisfies $\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}\rVert_\infty\leq\varepsilon$, and the algorithm output is in $L_{\mathbf{p}}$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. Prior work gave a $(d+1,\varepsilon,\delta)$-list replicable algorithm with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{d^3}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, but no nontrivial sample complexity lower bound was known.
  We establish the first non-trivial sample complexity lower bound for this problem and give an improved algorithm that matches it up to polylogarithmic factors. Together, these results determine the optimal sample complexity for list size $d+1$ to be $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$, showing that the quadratic dependence on dimension is inherent up to polylogarithmic factors. More generally, for every $k\in[d+1,2^d]$, we establish matching upper and lower bounds of $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log k}\right)$ on the total sample complexity.

Typically, learning algorithms observe samples from an unknown distribution and produce an output. In general, such algorithms are not replicable: two different runs of the algorithm observe two different samples (though drawn from the same distribution), resulting in potentially different outputs. Motivated by this, various notions of replicable learning have been introduced in the recent literature. In particular, the work of [23] formalized a notion of replicability called ρ{\rho}-replicability, and the works of [10] and [5] introduced the notion of list replicability. Since then, the notion of replicable learning has received considerable attention and has been studied in various contexts such as PAC learning, Reinforcement learning, multi-armed bandits, etc. [21, 3, 4, 13, 9, 12, 22, 11, 1]. A basic problem studied in this area is dd-CoinBiasEstimationProblem: given sample access to dd coins with unknown biases, estimate every bias to within additive error ε\varepsilon. The dd-coin bias estimation problem is a basic instance of high-dimensional mean estimation over Bernoulli product distributions and captures central challenges in designing replicable algorithms and understanding their limitations.

papers.title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures
papers.abstract:
A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible.
  We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time.
  We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

A hypergraph H=(V,E)H=(V,E) is a representation of a set system, where each hyperedge e∈Ee\in E is an arbitrary subset of the vertex set VV. While set systems are studied extensively throughout combinatorics, there is an increasing trend in network science and data mining towards thinking of data in terms of hypergraphs [61, 62, 9, 18] (the recent survey [34] has hundreds of papers on this topic). By allowing for arbitrary hyperedge sizes, we can represent interactions beyond pairs. Many instances of real-world graphs are actually hypergraphs, where hyperedges are replaced by cliques. For example, while a coauthor network is represented as a graph, the raw data is a hypergraph. The vertex set consists of researchers and a hyperedge corresponds to the authors of a publication. Hypergraphs are a faithful model of the original data and practitioners suggest they should be analyzed directly. There are numerous software packages developed to process hypergraphs [58, 53, 40].

papers.title: Unstable Stokes waves in constant vorticity flows of finite depth
papers.abstract: We study the spectral instability of small-amplitude Stokes waves in finite-depth flows with constant vorticity. A center-manifold reduction and the periodic Evans function give two explicit indices, one for long-wave instability near the origin and the other for an order-two resonance away from the origin. We prove instability when the low-frequency index is positive or the high-frequency index is nonzero, and obtain the leading expansions of the unstable spectral points. At low frequency, first- and second-order monodromy coefficients determine the leading figure-eight curve. At high frequency, we prove that the resonance exists uniquely and derive a limiting ellipse. An algebraic identity expresses the high-frequency index as a positive factor times the square of a real coupling coefficient. Thus every parameter pair with nonzero coupling gives high-frequency instability. The explicit formulas also permit a comparison of the two criteria in the parameter plane.

papers.intro:
We study the spectral instability of small periodic gravity waves in water of finite depth with constant vorticity. The fluid is incompressible and inviscid, and the motion is two dimensional. We consider perturbations with the same constant vorticity as the underlying flow. Our purpose is to determine how unstable spectrum arises near the origin and at a nonzero resonance, and to calculate the corresponding instability criteria in terms of the vorticity and wave number.

Periodic traveling water waves are commonly called Stokes waves, following the work of Stokes [29]. Their existence at small amplitude was proved by Nekrasov [27], Levi-Civita [22], and Struik [30] in the irrotational setting. For rotational flows, we refer to [10, 32, 11] and the references therein.

For irrotational gravity waves, the formal calculations of [1, 33, 34] predict a change of modulational stability at the dimensionless depth 1.3627827​…1.3627827\ldots in the zero-amplitude limit. Berti, Maspero, and Ventura [3, 4] described the local spectrum in deep and finite depth, including its closed figure-eight shape in the unstable regime. The same authors treated the degenerate case at the critical depth in [5].

papers.title: Unstable Stokes waves in constant vorticity flows of infinite depth
papers.abstract: We study the spectral stability of small-amplitude Stokes waves with constant vorticity in infinite depth. We describe the spectrum near the origin and near the first nonzero double eigenvalue. For nonzero vorticity $\omega<2\sqrt{g/3}$, where $g$ is the gravitational constant, the eigenvalues near the origin form a figure eight, whereas for $\omega>2\sqrt{g/3}$ the local spectrum remains purely imaginary. Away from the origin, the interaction of two Fourier modes whose indices differ by two produces an unstable isola when $\omega>-\sqrt{g/6}$, $\omega\ne0$, and the resonant wave numbers are noninteger. This curve is a real analytic oval with an explicit leading ellipse and maximal growth of quadratic order in the amplitude. We also prove instability at the integer resonances needed to cover the remaining vorticities. Together with the classical irrotational result, these two mechanisms show that sufficiently small nonzero Stokes waves are spectrally unstable for every fixed constant vorticity. The proof uses finite-dimensional spectral reductions of the full Euler linearization. Near the origin, the finite-dimensional linearized operator has a one-sided limit as the Floquet exponent vanishes, which differs from the periodic linearization. We use the Kato transformation to construct a three-dimensional reduction with biorthogonal bases and use all three eigenvectors of the reference operator to calculate the Benjamin--Feir coefficient. At the nonzero collision, a real two-dimensional reduction and an explicit second-order calculation determine the unstable curve.

papers.intro:
We consider two-dimensional gravity water waves of infinite depth with constant vorticity. The waves are periodic in the horizontal direction and travel at a constant speed. Our purpose is to determine how the background shear affects the spectral stability of a small-amplitude Stokes wave. We study longitudinal perturbations, which depend on the direction of propagation and preserve the prescribed constant vorticity.

We consider two-dimensional gravity water waves of infinite depth with constant vorticity. The waves are periodic in the horizontal direction and travel at a constant speed. Our purpose is to determine how the background shear affects the spectral stability of a small-amplitude Stokes wave. We study longitudinal perturbations, which depend on the direction of propagation and preserve the prescribed constant vorticity.

There are two relevant parts of the spectrum. Eigenvalues close to the origin describe the Benjamin–Feir, or modulational, instability. They form a figure eight when the wave is unstable to long-wave perturbations. Other instabilities arise from collisions at nonzero imaginary eigenvalues. The unstable branches produced by these collisions form small closed curves, usually called isolas. We describe the low-frequency spectrum and the first such isola. Their parameter ranges overlap, and together they imply spectral instability for every fixed constant vorticity and sufficiently small nonzero amplitude.

The modulational instability of irrotational Stokes waves was discovered by Benjamin and Feir [4]. Related modulation criteria were obtained by Lighthill [29] and Zakharov [36]. The full Euler problem requires more than an envelope approximation: one must locate the eigenvalues of the linearized water-wave equations and control the error terms on the scale where the instability occurs. Bridges and Mielke [13] proved the Benjamin–Feir instability in finite depth by spatial dynamics and a center-manifold reduction. Nguyen and Strauss [31] proved spectral modulational instability in deep water by a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction and obtained the unstable branches near the origin. Hur and Yang [24] developed a periodic Evans-function method and obtained instability results both near and away from the origin in finite depth. The shape of the unstable spectrum was determined by Berti, Maspero and Ventura [9]. They reduced the four-dimensional spectral space at the origin to two 2×22\times 2 blocks and proved that the unstable pair traces a complete figure eight. Their argument uses a symplectic Kato transformation and the Hamiltonian and reversible structure of the linearized equations. They subsequently treated finite depth in [10, 11]. These results describe the local spectral geometry of irrotational gravity waves.

papers.title: Post-Inference Model Chaining: A Problem Statement and a Model-based Bootstrap for Training End-to-End Digital Twins
papers.abstract: End-to-end digital twins can be constructed by fitting separate stage models and connecting them after inference. We investigate the Frequentist prediction properties of a commonly used Monte Carlo simulation scheme that forwards complete predictive draws through such a chain when measured stage outputs contain independent normal errors, but the latent stage means are deterministic. Analytical two-stage examples show persistent asymptotic interval and coverage inflation and, with quadratic propagation, mean bias dependent on the parameters to be estimated. Simulations of four- and eight-stage linear-quadratic univariate chains with 7, 15 or 30 training runs demonstrate pronounced input-dependent distortions. A diagnostic using error-free latent training predictors shows that the effect is mainly not attributable to errors in variables, but to the MCSim approach even showing underestimation of coverage. We propose a model-based bootstrap: an initial chain forwards fitted means, bootstrap chains are refitted on fixed-center bootstrap data while forwarding their mean prediction, and a target-stage future error enters a studentized prediction root. Across the investigated scenarios, relative mean bias is substantially reduced, and coverage is closer to the nominal 90%. At sample size 30, the eight-stage bootstrap has mean width ratios of 1.16-1.42 relative to the known-parameter normal reference, compared with 4.11-4.97 for observed-to-observed MCSim. These results support improved endpoint prediction in the tested setting. Further investigations of the bootstrap scheme in the supplement for a bivariate 6-stage process show similar satisfactory results.

papers.title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
papers.abstract: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

Pedagogical drawing textbooks decompose image creation into a small set of basic primitives, e.g., edges, contours, proportions, and light-and-shade, from which complex scenes can be composed [46, 9]. A related principle appears in visual neuroscience, where neurons in early visual cortex respond to low-level features such as oriented edges [22, 23], which are present in any visual input, whether a natural photograph or a medical scan.

A similar pattern motivates transfer learning in computer vision. Initialising from ImageNet (IN) [6] is the standard approach in supervised medical imaging. Early works on convolutional models find that transfer benefits are modest, mostly faster convergence and reuse of low-level (generic) features [53, 25]. Mustafa et al. Interestingly, transformers rely on feature reuse more than convolutional networks. State-of-the-art diffusion generative models fall into two broad paradigms: pixel diffusion and latent diffusion. Pixel diffusion applies the denoiser directly to pixels. Latent diffusion pairs a tokeniser with a denoiser that operates in its latent space. In latent diffusion, natural-image priors can be transferred through the tokeniser, the denoiser, or both. In the medical domain, natural-image tokenisers have been reused, and a few works fine-tune pretrained text-to-image denoisers [3, 70]. Yet denoiser transfer remains uncommon [52, 21, 16, 36, 66] and is treated as an implementation detail rather than a studied phenomenon. Whether natural-image denoiser transfer is beneficial for medical image generation, and which aspects of the pretrained model account for any observed benefit, remain open questions.

papers.title: Latin hypercube sampling to reduce the variance in Monte Carlo integration: a practical guide and an application to gravitational-wave astronomy
papers.abstract: In applied statistics, likelihoods involving high-dimensional integrals are often approximated via Monte Carlo summation. Controlling the resulting numerical variance is crucial for reliable inference. We provide a practical introduction to Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) and its extension based on orthogonal arrays (OA-LHS) as strategies to reduce this variance by stratifying the sampling distribution. LHS asymptotically removes variance contributions from individual coordinates, while strength-2 OA-LHS also removes those from pairwise interactions, yielding orders-of-magnitude improvements over plain Monte Carlo estimators for suitable integrands. As a case study, we investigate their application to the selection function entering hierarchical inference of gravitational-wave populations. At approximately one million injections, we find only a marginal reduction in variance, with low statistical significance. Nevertheless, the computational cost of constructing these designs is negligible relative to evaluating gravitational-wave injections, making even marginal gains worth considering for future applications. This practical introduction to LHS and OA-LHS offers a starting point for other applications in physics and astronomy involving computationally expensive Monte Carlo calculations.

Monte Carlo summation is a powerful technique for approximating high-dimensional integrals, often scaling more favorably than conventional grid-based quadrature (Caflisch, 1998). Such integrals arise naturally in hierarchical Bayesian inference, where likelihoods involve marginalization over parameters at lower levels of the hierarchy. Evaluating these integrals with Monte Carlo sums introduces numerical noise into the likelihood estimate, which can hinder sampler convergence or bias inference. Estimating and controlling this uncertainty is therefore crucial to prevent numerical fluctuations from obscuring the posterior structure.

Whenever computationally feasible, the variance of Monte Carlo estimators can be reduced simply by increasing the number of samples. Less trivially, the sampling strategy can be optimized to reduce the variance at a fixed sample size. This is the domain of simulation design (Garud et al., 2017; Pronzato and Müller, 2012), which is concerned with optimizing the placement of sample points within a given parameter space. In this context, Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) is a popular space-filling strategy for drawing randomized multidimensional samples with uniform stratification in each one-dimensional marginal (Eglajs and Audze, 1977; McKay et al., 1979; Helton and Davis, 2003). Generalizations such as orthogonal-array Latin hypercube sampling (OA-LHS) extend this stratification to higher-dimensional marginals (Owen, 1992b; Tang, 1993). Crucially, under appropriate regularity conditions, the asymptotic variance of an LHS-based Monte Carlo estimator is mathematically guaranteed to be no greater than that of a standard Monte Carlo estimator (Stein, 1987; Owen, 1992a).

In GW astronomy, hierarchical Bayesian statistics is used to estimate the population properties of merging black holes and neutron stars. The resulting population likelihood combines single-event likelihoods with a population model and includes a normalization term that accounts for selection effects (Mandel et al., 2019; Vitale et al., 2022). Of these, NobsN_{\rm obs} integrals arise from marginalizing over the parameters of each individual source, while the additional integral captures the detection efficiency and thus encodes our model of the detectors. This latter integral enters the denominator of the likelihood raised to the NobsN_{\rm obs}-th power, amplifying the impact of numerical uncertainty.

In GW population fits, approximating integrals with Monte Carlo sums is particularly convenient because it allows existing data products to be reused efficiently: single-event posterior samples obtained with convenient but unphysical priors and sensitivity injections. A substantial body of literature has been devoted to quantifying the variance these approximations introduce into the GW population likelihood (Farr, 2019; Essick and Farr, 2022; Talbot and Golomb, 2023; Mancarella and Gerosa, 2025; Heinzel and Vitale, 2025; Wolfe et al., 2026). While this is often referred to, at least colloquially, as a “data-dependent prior,” it in fact corresponds to modifying the likelihood, invalidating the assumptions used to derive the likelihood itself. At present, this is the only workable solution.

papers.title: Real-to-Integer Reduction for All-Pairs Shortest Paths
papers.abstract:
Efficient graph algorithms often use techniques that are specific to integer-valued inputs and do not work for real-valued versions of the problems. Is it a limitation of current techniques, or are the real-valued variants inherently harder? One way to study this question is through real-to-integer reductions. We give (randomized, combinatorial) subcubic real-to-integer reductions for two central graph problems in fine-grained complexity: All-Pairs Shortest Paths and Exact Triangle. That is, we show that if the integer variants of these problems can be solved in truly subcubic time, then the real variants can also be solved in truly subcubic time.
  Our work extends and combines techniques from three previous works: (1) our real-to-integer reduction for the 3SUM problem (Fischer, Polak, Schmidt, FOCS 2026), which itself combines the Frank--Tardos theorem from optimization with Freiman's theorem from additive combinatorics; (2) universe reduction for APSP (Fischer, STOC 2026), which we generalize to reals and use to reduce the doubling of the set of edge weights; and (3) the ``Fredman's trick meets dominance product'' technique (Chan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, STOC 2023), which is needed to adapt the prior real-to-integer framework from equality constraints to inequalities.
  As a corollary, our reduction combined with Yuval's fast Integer APSP algorithm in the real RAM model with multiplication (IPL 1976) shows that the Real APSP Hypothesis is false in this model, which also follows from the very recent breakthrough by Alman and Vassilevska Williams using a very different approach.

papers.title: A remark on singular solutions of semilinear elliptic equations in two dimensions
papers.abstract: We study positive radial singular solutions of $-\Delta u=f(u)$ in two space dimensions. Fujishima, Ioku, Ruf, and Terraneo constructed such solutions under asymptotic assumptions on $f$ and an additional convergence-rate condition, denoted by $(f_3)$. We prove their local existence result, with the same approximate solution and remainder estimate, under the original assumptions $(f_1)$ and $(f_2)$ alone. The proof combines a contraction on finite intervals with a nonlinear energy estimate uniform in the terminal point and requires only $C^2$ regularity of $f$ near infinity. We also obtain derivative asymptotics and, under additional global assumptions, a singular Dirichlet solution which solves the equation distributionally across the origin. An analytic oscillatory example satisfies our hypotheses but violates both $(f_3)$ and the derivative assumptions of Kikuchi and Kumagai. For every fixed finite iterate of the exponential of order at least two, we verify the hypotheses and quantify the remainder; condition $(f_3)$ fails for all iterates of order at least three.

papers.title: A sharp Mittag-Leffler bound for series with separated exponents
papers.abstract: Let $\eta\geq 0$ and $\delta>0$, and let $(r_j)_{j\geq 0}$ be a sequence of real numbers satisfying $\eta \leq r_0 < r_1 < r_2 < \cdots$ and $r_{j+1}-r_j \geq \delta$ for every $j\geq 0$. We prove that, for $\delta\leq 1$ and every $x>0$, \[ \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{x^{r_j}}{\G(1+r_j)} \leq \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{x^{\eta+j\delta}}{\G(1+\eta+j\delta)} = x^\eta E_{\delta,1+\eta}(x^\delta), \] where $E_{\delta,1+\eta}$ denotes the two-parameter Mittag-Leffler function. Moreover, equality holds for some $x>0$ if and only if $r_j = \eta + j\delta$ for every $j$. The proof combines a finite compression argument for unimodal functions with a shift inequality for the Mittag-Leffler function. The upper bound $\delta \leq 1$ is sharp, since counterexamples exist for every $1 < \delta < 2$.

papers.title: Identifying the determinants of soccer coach turnover by competing risks models: a case study on Italian League Serie A
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the determinants of head coach turnover in the Italian Serie A over the period 2010-2019 by explicitly accounting for multiple exit mechanisms within a competing risks framework. Four mutually exclusive exit types are considered: end of contract, mutual consent, resignation, and sacking. To identify robust predictors of turnover, we combine classical cause-specific Cox models with a variable selection procedure based on forward selection, LASSO regression, and Random Survival Forests. The results show that performance-related variables are the primary drivers of coach turnover, while personal characteristics play a limited role once performance is controlled for. Short-term performance indicators, such as points per match until turnover, strongly influence the risk of dismissal. Conversely, cumulative poor performance substantially increases dismissal risk: a higher proportion of losses over a coach's tenure raises the hazard of sacking by more than four times. Season timing also plays a crucial role, as sackings and mutual-consent terminations are significantly more likely to occur during the season, whereas contract expirations concentrate at the end of the season. Overall, the findings highlight that clubs differentiate between short-term performance shocks and longer-term performance trajectories when deciding how and when to replace a head coach. By distinguishing among exit mechanisms and adopting a conservative variable selection strategy, the study provides a robust and nuanced assessment of managerial turnover dynamics in the most important Italian professional football league.

papers.title: TuneBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Power System Dynamic Model Calibration
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents can automate complex engineering workflows by interacting with tools, interpreting feedback, and making iterative decisions. This paper introduces TuneBench, a benchmark for evaluating Agentic AI in power system dynamic model calibration, where controller parameters are adjusted to reproduce target dynamic responses. The benchmark reflects a common Transmission System Operator (TSO) practice, in which equivalent models used for Dynamic Security Assessment (DSA) are calibrated against measurements from grid-code compliance tests when proprietary models are unavailable. Two cases of increasing complexity are considered: the governor and Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) of a synchronous generator and the control system of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), both tuned against active-power and voltage step tests within a budget of 15 simulations. LLM-based agents are compared with random search and Genetic Algorithm (GA) baselines over 10 independent runs. Only the most advanced models, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6, accurately reproduce all target trajectories, with median R2 above 0.995 in every test and tracking errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than the baselines. The agent logs show that these agents autonomously extract dynamic performance indices, such as settling time and damping, and relate them to specific control parameters, decomposing the tuning problem into physically interpretable sub-problems. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/Power-Agent/PowerAgentBench/tree/main/benchmarks/dynamic/level3.
