papers.intro:
In recent years, Transmission System Operators (TSOs) have increasingly integrated Dynamic Security Assessment (DSA) into Energy Management Systems (EMSs) to complement steady-state contingency analysis with time-domain simulations [1]. While power flow analysis assesses the feasibility of post-contingency operating conditions, dynamic simulations capture the transient evolution of key variables, including frequency, voltage, and active and reactive power. The growing penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) further increases the importance of modeling fast control dynamics [2]. Although electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations provide greater detail, their computational requirements limit their application to large-scale operational studies. Consequently, DSA predominantly relies on phasor-domain (RMS) simulations, balancing accuracy and computational efficiency [3]. The reliability of these analyses depends strongly on the accuracy of the underlying dynamic models [4]. Since proprietary models and control parameters are not always disclosed to TSOs, equivalent models often need to be developed and calibrated using measurements from grid-code compliance and commissioning tests, including active-power, reactive-power, and voltage-control tests. Model parameters are then iteratively adjusted to minimize the mismatch between simulated and measured trajectories, either manually or through optimization techniques such as genetic algorithms [5] and Kalman filtering [6]. Despite existing calibration approaches, this process still relies heavily on experienced engineers to identify relevant parameters, interpret their effects, and refine the model.

Recent advances in Agentic AI have enabled language models to execute code, interact with external tools, and adapt their decisions based on feedback, making them promising for multi-step power engineering workflows. Previous studies have investigated LLMs for electricity-market bidding [7], unit commitment and dispatch [8], optimal power flow [9, 10], and grid control [11], alongside broader power system applications [12, 13]. However, many approaches address individual tasks rather than complete engineering workflows. More recently, agentic frameworks have been developed for distribution grid analysis [14] and complex power system problems [15]. This growing interest is also reflected by the PowerAgent community [16] and its benchmarks, PowerAgentBench-SS [17] and PowerAgentBench-Dyn [18], targeting steady-state and dynamic studies, respectively. Similarly, RestoreBench addresses power flow non-convergence recovery [19].

This growing interest is also reflected by the PowerAgent community [16] and its benchmarks, PowerAgentBench-SS [17] and PowerAgentBench-Dyn [18], targeting steady-state and dynamic studies, respectively. Similarly, RestoreBench addresses power flow non-convergence recovery [19].

This paper introduces TuneBench, a benchmark for evaluating Agentic AI in power system dynamic model tuning. It assesses agents based on different LLMs in tasks requiring engineering knowledge, interpretation of dynamic responses, and iterative interaction with simulation tools. Unlike single-step approaches, agents must autonomously select and adjust model parameters based on simulation feedback. The main contributions of this paper are: • A general evaluation framework for agent-based dynamic studies, defining observations, actions, simulator feedback, constraints, and performance metrics. • A dynamic model tuning benchmark inspired by practical TSO workflows, requiring agents to identify relevant control parameters and calibrate models against reference dynamic responses. • A comparative evaluation of different LLM-based agents against random search and Genetic Algorithm (GA)-based optimization, considering tuning accuracy and computational requirements.

papers.title: Fault-tolerant shallow recurrent decoders for sparse sensing with missing sensor measurements
papers.abstract: Real-world sensing systems are inherently imperfect: sensors may fail, intermittently disconnect, operate with asynchronous sampling rates, and be subject to noise, leading to measurement streams that are irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneous. Nevertheless, sensing strategies for real-time state reconstruction typically assume synchronous and continuously active sensors, a constraint that substantially limits their applicability in operational environments. In this work, we introduce fault-tolerant sparse sensing strategies in the context of shallow recurrent decoders (SHRED) to enable high-dimensional state estimation from sparse, asynchronous, and missing sensor measurements. Specifically, we consider naive imputation strategies, fault-tolerant recurrent temporal encoders, and we introduce four different transformer-based masking mechanisms to make SHRED explicitly aware of sensor availability through the binary data-availability mask. Moreover, we further introduce a multi-step decoding training objective for SHRED, resulting in smoother latent trajectories and more robust predictions. Throughout a synthetic benchmark and three real-world problems in hydrodynamic and ocean modeling, we show that (i) transformer-based masking mechanisms outperform standard imputation techniques and fault-tolerant recurrent architectures, (ii) the multi-step decoding training objective enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness in the presence of heterogeneous missing-data patterns, while (iii) the computational efficiency of SHRED is preserved, with no additional inference-time overhead.

Many real-world dynamical systems evolve in high-dimensional state spaces that cannot be directly observed in their entirety [1, 26]. This challenge arises across a wide range of scientific and engineering applications, including fluid and solid mechanics, weather and climate modeling, plasma physics, and structural health monitoring. In these systems, sensors provide the primary interface between theory and reality, yet their deployment is inevitably limited by cost, reliability, physical inaccessibility, and operational constraints. However, being able to access local measurements is crucial to, e.g., inferring full state dynamics, designing feedback control strategies, or predicting quantities of interest.

Recovering the state of a dynamical system from partial observations enables downstream tasks such as monitoring, forecasting, anomaly detection, and control, while avoiding expensive and impractical full-field measurements. Traditional approaches to state reconstruction are grounded in linear algebra frameworks. The singular value decomposition (SVD) – also known as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) [35, 31, 6, 4] – provides an optimal low-rank approximation of high-dimensional state data through a linear projection onto a low-dimensional basis of spatial functions capturing most of the data variability. After computing the dominant POD modes from the training data, the coefficients of the low-rank representation can be estimated from a limited number of point measurements by solving a linear inverse problem, provided that the sensing matrix is well-conditioned [22, 49]. However, the requirement for a well-conditioned sensing matrix imposes constraints on both the number and placement of sensors, leading to an NP-hard optimization problem for identifying the optimal configuration [12, 29, 30] and potentially limiting its applicability in real-world settings [11, 36]. Moreover, the reconstruction accuracy of this method is bounded by the expressiveness of the POD modes used, so that fine-scales or nonlinear features of the field cannot be recovered entirely when only a few modes are retained.

The advent of scientific machine learning has introduced new data-driven methods for addressing limitations of traditional linear methods [23, 5, 40]. Neural networks and, in particular, shallow decoder networks (SDNs), leverage the universal approximation theorem of feedforward architectures [14] to learn an end-to-end nonlinear mapping from sensor measurements directly to the corresponding high-dimensional state [8, 42, 19, 34], without requiring an explicit basis representation as in POD-based methods. Similarly, the Senseiver [43] employs an attention-based architecture inspired by the Perceiver IO [28] to reconstruct spatio-temporal fields at arbitrary query locations from sparse observations. Once trained on a set of snapshots, these strategies can capture nonlinear spatial correlations in the data that are inaccessible to linear methods and have been shown to outperform linear POD-based architectures in field reconstruction, particularly in ill-posed settings, i.e., with few or poorly placed sensors. The temporal history of observations, naturally available whenever sensors operate continuously over time, is essential for capturing intrinsic dynamical features, such as temporal correlations between consecutive measurements.

The shallow recurrent decoder (SHRED) framework proposed by Williams et al. [51] addresses this limitation by combining a recurrent temporal encoder with a shallow spatial decoder. The encoder, which is typically modeled via recurrent neural networks such as, e.g., long short-term memory (LSTM) [25, 33] or gated recurrent unit (GRU) [10] networks, processes a sliding window of lagged sensor measurements, compressing their temporal history into a latent representation, which is subsequently mapped to the full field by a SDN. Thanks to the temporal history of sensor readings, SHRED achieves dramatically lower reconstruction errors than classical techniques, even with a very limited number of randomly placed sensors. Moreover, the SHRED framework has been extended to parametric systems [47, 46], demonstrating that the temporal history of a handful of sensors suffices to reconstruct and control high-dimensional fields across varying physical and geometrical parameters. papers.title: MiCaDe: Online LiDAR-Camera Miscalibration Change Detection for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Reliable multi-sensor perception in autonomous vehicles requires accurate calibration between cameras and LiDAR. However, calibration drift is often unavoidable in long-term deployments: vibrations, thermal effects, and minor mechanical shocks may alter the relative pose between sensors, leading to systematic errors in downstream fusion tasks. We propose MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online solution detecting when the extrinsic LiDAR-camera calibration parameters are no longer accurate by means of sequential change detection. MiCaDe requires no calibration targets, or modification of the perception stack, providing low false-alarm rates with negligible computational overhead. Our key insight is that 3D and 2D bounding boxes produced by standard object detectors should remain geometrically consistent under correct calibration. By matching cross-modal detections, we derive geometric consistency metrics that serve as sensitive indicators of extrinsic drift. These metrics are aggregated into fixed-size batches and scored against a reference distribution, producing a likelihood stream that is monitored by a Change Point Model (CPM). Crucially, the CPM accumulates statistical evidence over time, enabling detection of subtle drifts that would otherwise go unnoticed. Experiments on multiple long-sequence datasets and on a real-world dataset with physically induced miscalibration confirm reliable detection under diverse conditions. Code available at: https://github.com/CarloSgaravatti/MiCaDe.

Reliable perception in autonomous driving relies on accurate fusion between complementary sensors such as cameras and LiDARs, which in turn requires a precise extrinsic calibration. Unfortunately, minor shocks and gradual effects, such as vibrations or temperature changes, can cause calibration drifts that accumulate over time, degrading perception accuracy and compromising navigation safety.

Reliable perception in autonomous driving relies on accurate fusion between complementary sensors such as cameras and LiDARs, which in turn requires a precise extrinsic calibration. Unfortunately, minor shocks and gradual effects, such as vibrations or temperature changes, can cause calibration drifts that accumulate over time, degrading perception accuracy and compromising navigation safety.

Detecting when calibration becomes unreliable is therefore critical for long-term autonomous operation. Existing approaches typically formulate miscalibration detection as a frame-level classification problem. They first extract cross-modal cues, such as image edges, depth discontinuities, or learned multimodal features, and then train a classifier to decide whether the sensor pair is calibrated or not [4, 20]. While effective, these approaches present several limitations. First, they usually require dedicated training procedures and synthetic calibration perturbations. Second, they operate independently on each frame, making it difficult to distinguish transient detection noise from persistent calibration drift. Third, they often require specific neural networks, introducing additional computational overhead.

In this work, we introduce MiCaDe (Miscalibration Change Detection), an online monitoring framework for LiDAR-Camera extrinsic calibration. We formulate calibration monitoring as a sequential change-detection problem. Rather than learning whether a sensor pair is calibrated, we explicitly model the distribution of indicators derived from signals that are already available in modern off-the-shelf perception stacks, and monitor these over time. Specifically, we exploit the correspondence between 3D LiDAR detections and 2D image detections of the same object. Under correct calibration, the geometric relationship between these detections remains statistically stable over time. When the calibration drifts, we expect a systematic change in the consistency metrics, as illustrated in Figure 1. We therefore continuously monitor the stream of geometric consistency metrics and detect statistically significant deviations from their nominal behaviour. This approach offers several advantages: it requires no task-specific training, accumulates evidence over time to detect subtle relative displacements of the sensors that may be imperceptible in individual frames, and provides control over the nominal false-alarm rate through the Average Run Length (ARL0) parameter, though this control is only approximate when the monitored signal is not perfectly stationary, as we discuss in Section 5. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach that casts miscalibration detection as a sequential change-detection problem, rather than as per-frame supervised classification.

papers.title: Current control of spin-wave transport in YIG via the $\small\mathbf{VO}_{\mathbf{2}}$ insulator-to-metal transition
papers.abstract: Electrically reconfigurable spin-wave transport is central to realizing energy-efficient magnonic information technologies, yet existing current-driven approaches require current densities that undermine the fundamental dissipation advantage of spin-wave-based signal processing. Here, we demonstrate low-power electrical control of spin-wave propagation in a hybrid magnonic device comprising a low-damping yttrium iron garnet (YIG) film coupled to an adjacent vanadium dioxide ($\small\text{VO}_{2}$) stripe. Passing a small current through $\small\text{VO}_{2}$ triggers its insulator-to-metal transition (IMT), producing a sharp, reversible resistivity reduction exceeding three orders of magnitude. This abrupt phase transition locally modifies the spin-wave dispersion in YIG, reducing the group velocity and suppressing transmission by up to 40 dB near the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. Pulsed current excitation enables reconfiguration of spin-wave transport on a 10 ms timescale. Temperature-dependent measurements, corroborated by thermal modeling, decouple the respective contributions of current-induced heating of YIG and the IMT in $\small\text{VO}_{2}$, establishing the latter as the dominant control mechanism. Our results demonstrate that electrically induced phase transitions in correlated oxides constitute an energy-efficient strategy for dynamic spin-wave manipulation, providing a scalable route toward reconfigurable magnonic devices.

papers.title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
papers.abstract:
Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories.
  More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $\pi(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $\omega$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $\pi(A)$ is nowhere dense.
  In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $\omega$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

Reactive synthesis asks for an algorithm that, given a logical specification, constructs a program satisfying it for every input stream, or determines that no such program exists. It addresses a fundamental question in reactive-system design: how to ensure correctness of a program by construction.

Reactive synthesis asks for an algorithm that, given a logical specification, constructs a program satisfying it for every input stream, or determines that no such program exists. It addresses a fundamental question in reactive-system design: how to ensure correctness of a program by construction.

The problem was introduced by Church [Chu57, Chu63]. In its standard formulation, the input and output alphabets are finite, and the specification is given in monadic second-order logic over infinite words. The output program to be constructed is a finite-state transducer that reads one input symbol and produces one output symbol per round. Büchi and Landweber [BL69] proved decidability by viewing synthesis as an infinite game between the environment, which chooses inputs, and a controller, which chooses outputs. A winning strategy for the controller defines a program satisfying the specification. Shortly after, Rabin [Rab72] provided an alternative proof using tree automata, exploiting the tree structure naturally formed by the finite prefixes of a program’s possible executions.

Church’s synthesis problem has received sustained attention and has been extended in many directions [Tho08, BCJ18, Fij26]. An extension of particular relevance to distributed systems is synthesis under imperfect information, where a single process observes only part of the input [KV97, AVW03]. Pnueli and Rosner [PR90] posed the question for the distributed setting in which several processes, each observing only part of the input, must jointly realize a global specification. They proved that distributed synthesis is undecidable even for specifications in linear temporal logic [Pnu77] and an architecture consisting of just two processes, each receiving a different part of the input and unable to communicate with the other. By contrast, synthesis is decidable for pipeline architectures, in which processes can send messages only to their right neighbor along a line, and only the first process receives external input from the environment. The proof successively eliminates processes from the pipeline, using tree automata to reduce the problem to synthesis for a single process. Kupferman and Vardi [KV01] extended decidability to further architectures and Finkbeiner and Schewe [FS05] gave a complete characterization: the problem is decidable if and only if the architecture has no information fork. Distributed synthesis has also been studied for knowledge-based specifications [vdMW05]. A recurring condition behind decidability in synchronous distributed synthesis is hierarchical information: calling a process pp more informed than process qq if it can deduce the information of qq from its own, information is hierarchical if all processes can be linearly ordered with respect to informedness. Undecidability thus stems from processes holding incomparable information that they cannot reconcile: sharing information between processes is essential to solving the problem. This observation led Gastin, Sznajder, and Zeitoun [GSZ09] to consider specifications that refer only to external inputs and outputs, and not to the communication channels between processes: processes are then free to use these channels to share information, which made it possible to extend the class of decidable architectures.

Bérard, Bollig, Bouyer, Függer, and Sznajder [BBB+22] studied synthesis for two processes and an unstable communication between them, however, additionally assuming acknowledgments that make each round’s communication graph immediately known to both processes. They allowed messages to carry their complete causal histories, allowing for the synthesis of full information protocols that are not restricted to bounded messages. They proved that, for ω\omega-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if the number of consecutive rounds in which no message is delivered is uniformly bounded. The acknowledgment assumption changes the solvability of even basic tasks, though. For example, two processes can solve consensus in one round if at least one message is delivered and both processes know the communication graph. The decidability of synthesis without this assumption thus remained open.

papers.title: Self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation requires linear time
papers.abstract:
Synchronising the clocks of processes is a fundamental problem in distributed computing. We consider message-passing systems in which processes start in an arbitrary initial state (self-stabilisation) and up to $f$ processes may be non-transiently faulty. It is well known that synchronising clocks \emph{exactly} is at least as hard as consensus and requires $\Theta(f)$ time. In contrast, without self-stabilisation, clocks can be synchronised \emph{approximately} much faster, in time independent of the number of non-transient faults [Srikanth and Toueg, JACM 1987; Welch and Lynch, Inf. Comput. 1988].
  In this work, we show that deterministic self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks require $\Omega(f)$ time to stabilise. This gives the first non-trivial time lower bound for these tasks, whose time complexity has remained open for over two decades [Dolev and Welch, JACM 2004; Dolev, F\"ugger, Schmid and Lenzen, JACM 2014]. In particular, this answers the open question whether self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks are as hard as consensus or as easy as approximate agreement [Lenzen and Rybicki, JACM 2019].
  The results show that guaranteeing \emph{both} transient and non-transient fault-tolerance simultaneously is expensive even for approximate synchronisation tasks. The lower bounds hold in a very strong model: the faulty processes can only crash, the local clocks of processes have no clock drift, and the message delay is bounded and known to all processes. The proof is based on a combinatorial topological argument showing that no fast finite-state protocol can ensure that the clocks behave consistently across all executions. To our knowledge, this is the first use of topological arguments to prove time lower bounds in the self-stabilising setting.

papers.title: The Hyperclique Hypothesis is False
papers.abstract: The Hyperclique Hypothesis postulates that, for all constants $k > h \geq 3$, detecting a $k$-clique in an $h$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices requires time $n^{k-o(1)}$. This hypothesis is false: there is an algebraic algorithm that detects (and even counts) $k$-cliques in $h$-uniform hypergraphs in time $O(n^{(1-\epsilon_h)k})$. Via known reductions, this also refutes the recently proposed $k$-AP Hypothesis. As a consequence, many problems with conditional lower bounds based on these two hypotheses may admit faster algorithms after all. This result is almost entirely due to AI.

papers.intro:
The goal of fine-grained algorithm design and complexity theory is to pinpoint the best possible running time of every computational problem. On the one hand, this involves designing ever faster algorithms. On the other hand, it involves proving conditional lower bounds, that is, showing that a problem cannot be solved faster than currently known unless some established hardness hypothesis fails. Over the past fifteen years, this approach has developed into a major success story, connecting dozens of polynomial-time problems to a small set of canonical hardness assumptions; see, e.g., [47]. The reasoning behind this approach is not that we treat hypotheses as dogmas, but rather that they mark the current frontier of our algorithmic knowledge: if a problem cannot be solved faster without refuting some hypothesis, then one should first try to refute that hypothesis. In other words, the hypotheses show us where to concentrate our efforts.

papers.title: Must AI Spell It Out? Pragmatic Comprehension of Alerts in a Time-Critical Task
papers.abstract: Assistive systems typically tell users everything, often spending time and attention on what a user already knows, leaving less for what happens next. People, on the other hand, leave out what they expect the listener can supply. Can people use their prior knowledge to understand an incomplete message when the speaker is a machine though? We studied this pragmatic comprehension in a monitoring task controlling users' prior knowledge and the available time to detect critical situations. In a preregistered study (N=114), we compared a pragmatic planner that reasons over a model of the listener's knowledge to decide what to say, when, and how explicitly, with a baseline specifying problems fully in onset order. Participants resolved underspecified alerts almost as reliably as fully specified ones and sooner, detected more problems, and rated the pragmatic assistant helpful more often, with no increase in reported mental demand. Our findings show that people can recover what the system left implicit and that pragmatic communication can support effective assistance under the constraints of a changing world.

papers.intro:
Your assistive systems are built to tell you everything. Ask a navigation system about the way and it gives the same message no matter if you are a visitor or a local who has lived on that street for twenty years. That habit of completeness runs through even to assistive systems in high-risk or time-critical tasks. A surgeon needs decision-support mid-procedure (Ancker et al., 2017), a nurse tracks the alarms that cross an intensive-care ward (Gülşen and Arslan, 2025), an operator needs time-critical warnings about the systems they monitor (Khan and Neustaedter, 2019; Wu et al., 2025). In each case, systems give full information to their users as soon as a critical situation occurs (Joseph et al., 2021). This can be costly in time-critical and high-risk scenarios. Operators who spend limited time and attention on what they already know risk missing critical situations that come next (Lieder et al., 2026; Horvitz et al., 1999). An assistant’s overspecification without regard to their human partner then becomes expensive, and the resulting harm is well documented (Ancker et al., 2017; Gülşen and Arslan, 2025; Mongan and Kohli, 2020; Joseph et al., 2021).

People, by contrast, when communicating with one another, adapt messages to their partner constantly and, without effort, avoid overspecifying. Ask the way in a town you grew up in and your pragmatic friend will tell you “Left at the old cinema.”, where they would tell a visitor “Straight on through the traffic lights, then the left just after the mall’s petrol station.” They describe the same route, but reason about the listener’s knowledge to say only what they believe the listener cannot themselves supply (Grice, 1975; Hawkins et al., 2021). This is a rational and economical use of our limited attention (Lieder et al., 2026), and pragmatic speakers do it systematically (Piantadosi et al., 2012; Kanwal et al., 2017; Tourtouri et al., 2021). The Rational Speech Act (RSA) framework proposes a computational account of this behaviour. A speaker chooses an utterance by simulating how a listener with given prior beliefs will interpret it (Frank and Goodman, 2012; Goodman and Frank, 2016; Degen, 2023; Franke, 2011; Goodman and Stuhlmüller, 2013). Research shows that language models that incorporate this reasoning describe, refer and instruct more accurately (Monroe et al., 2017; Andreas and Klein, 2016; Fried et al., 2018). In contrast, consider generative systems, which, for all their competence, still systematically over-specify (Tang et al., 2024; Kapur et al., 2026) and produce misunderstandings more often than human speakers do (Tang et al., 2024).

However, whether people effectively interpret and cooperate with such a pragmatic system has not been tested.

It tracks what a user believes as the world changes and makes use of ambiguous, underspecified alerts wherever it judges the user can complete the reference, spending the time and resources saved on the next alert (Das et al., 2026). However, whether people effectively interpret and cooperate with such a pragmatic system has not been tested.

This is one instance of a broader argument that for effective cooperation with humans, systems ought to reason over a model of their human partner, and treat their user as an active partner, so that cooperation is designed in rather than hoped to emerge (Gmytrasiewicz and Durfee, 2001; Amershi et al., 2019; Collins et al., 2024; Miehling et al., 2024; Zhi-Xuan et al., 2024; Saad et al., 2025; Oulasvirta et al., 2022). However, this argument rests on an assumption that has drawn far less investigation than the machine side of it: that the user will, in return, reason over the system and complete what it leaves unspecified. Evidence in either direction is thin. While linguistics studies using pragmatic speakers in constrained settings showed promise (Andreas and Klein, 2016; Fried et al., 2018), studies with people suggest they might not even attempt the inference with a computer partner (Duran et al., 2011) at all. Despite rating ChatGPT as highly capable, people interpreted the same message less pragmatically when told that it came from ChatGPT rather than a person (Mayn et al., 2024). Crucially, none of the evidence was gathered under conditions that assistive alerting demands. In no study so far, was a human listener placed in a dynamic environment with a time-critical task to test if they could produce gains through pragmatic inference.

In this paper we aim to empirically establish whether people comprehend messages from an assistant that communicates pragmatically and whether such assistance helps in time-critical tasks. For this we introduce DroneWorld, a dynamic monitoring task inspired by earlier work (Das et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025). In a preregistered study, participants (N=114N=114) oversaw four drones on which problems turned critical in close succession, their task being to detect each as it arose. Two sources of information supported them: their prior knowledge and the assistant’s messages. A briefing before each scene covered most (high awareness) or few (low awareness) of the problems to come, so that each participant was in turn Alice and Bob of Fig. 1. Between participants, the assistant was either the pragmatic planner of Das et al. (2026), which varies the specificity of its spoken alerts by reasoning about the user’s prior knowledge, or a baseline announcing every problem in full, similar to typical alerting systems (Ancker et al., 2017; Joseph et al., 2021). The world advanced whether or not the assistant spoke or the participant acted.

papers.title: Catalan Hashing: Efficient Linear Probing for Variable-Length Items
papers.abstract:
A defining feature of the linear-probing hash table is its spatial locality: at load factor $1 - \varepsilon$, the hash table can be implemented so that each operation scans a single contiguous region of expected size $O(1/\varepsilon)$ (this is known as the \emph{scan cost}). This guarantee, however, relies on all items having unit size. In this paper, we ask whether it is possible to achieve a similar guarantee, but in a hash table that stores items of arbitrary lengths $|x| \ge 1$.
  The main result of the paper is a new hash table called \emph{Catalan hashing}, which supports amortized expected scan cost $O(|x|/\varepsilon)$ for positive queries, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ for negative queries, and $O(|x|\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{1+\delta}|x|)$ for insertions/deletions, for any constant $\delta > 0$. As a corollary, we obtain the same bounds in the cache-oblivious model, with a scan cost of $S$ translating to $1 + O(S/B)$ I/Os. Along the way, we introduce several high-level techniques that may be of independent interest; this includes a novel way of using erasure codes in order to perform write optimization within a hash table, and a connection to scheduling that allows us to place elements in a way which avoids clustering at high load factors.

First introduced in the 1950s [48, 35], the linear-probing hash table has stood for more than half a century as one of the simplest and most widely used hash table designs. In its most basic form, the hash table works as follows. Elements live in an array of some size mm, and each element xx hashes to a uniformly random position h⁡(x)h(x) in that array. To insert an item xx, we examine cells h⁡(x),h⁡(x)+1,h⁡(x)+2,…(modm)h(x),h(x)+1,h(x)+2,\ldots\pmod{m} until we find a free cell where we place the item; and, likewise, to query an item xx, we scan the cells h⁡(x),h⁡(x)+1,h⁡(x)+2,…(modm)h(x),h(x)+1,h(x)+2,\ldots\pmod{m} and until we either find xx, or until we encounter a free cell (meaning that xx is not present).

The basic idea is to store items non-contiguously, nesting smaller items inside larger ones. We then augment each cell of the table to store an O⁡(1)O(1)-bit tag indicating where items begin and end. The items are laid out in such a way that, whenever a smaller item xx overlaps a larger one yy, xx is contained entirely within yy. If one thinks of each tag as encoding either an open parenthesis (starting a new item) or a closing parenthesis (ending the current item), then the tags form a balanced-parentheses sequence (i.e., a Catalan sequence [53]), hence the name of the data structure.

papers.title: Surface chemistry as data for level-set simulation of etching and deposition
papers.abstract: Level-set simulators of etching and deposition move the surface with a velocity that depends on adsorbate coverages. These coverages are usually computed from balances solved and coded by hand for each chemistry, whereas voxel-based Monte Carlo profile simulators read the reaction mechanism as data. For the open-source level-set simulator ViennaPS, this work presents a surface model whose rate laws, Jacobian and velocity are derived from a reaction file and evaluated with ray-traced fluxes. Steady-state coverages are obtained with Newton's method and transient coverages with a conservative integrator. One compiled model is applied to eight chemistries for chemical vapour deposition, selective epitaxy, plasma etching, sputtering and atomic layer deposition. It reproduces a hand-written silicon etch model to seven significant digits at a single point and within the Monte Carlo noise in a masked trench. In a high-aspect-ratio cavity, alumina conformality is determined by a trimethylaluminium reaction probability within the measured range.

papers.intro:
Feature-scale process simulation predicts how the topography of a single device feature evolves during etching or deposition. The surface is commonly represented implicitly as the zero level set of a signed distance function that evolves under a Hamilton-Jacobi equation [1, 2]. The particle fluxes that reach the surface can be computed by Monte Carlo ray tracing, because at typical process pressures the mean free path is long compared with the feature size and transport inside the feature is therefore nearly ballistic [3]. The level-set method and Monte Carlo ray tracing are both available in open-source codes, among them ViennaPS [4], on which this work builds.

In a level-set simulator, the fluxes and the moving surface are connected by a surface model, which converts the incident fluxes at a surface point into the normal velocity vnv_{n} of the interface (Fig. 1a). In most chemistries, the velocity depends on the state of the surface, described by the fractional coverages θi\theta_{i} of the adsorbed species ii that take part in the reactions. Each coverage is determined by a balance between the reactions that create and consume the corresponding adsorbate. The velocity is then computed from the reactions that add or remove solid material.

Feature-scale simulators differ in how they treat the surface chemistry. In process emulation, the surface is moved by geometric operations whose parameters are calibrated against measured cross-sections, without a model of the chemistry. Voxel-based virtual fabrication emulates a complete process flow in this way at a small fraction of the cost of a physical simulation [7], and it is used in logic and memory development to predict structural variation and its effect on metrology [8, 9]. Geometric advection applies the same idea to level-set surfaces [10]. Because the parameters of an emulation describe shapes, a change in the chemistry requires a new calibration. Monte Carlo profile models start from the chemistry, given as a list of surface reactions with probabilities, and each simulated particle that strikes the surface undergoes one of these reactions. The Kushner group has developed this approach since the 1990s. Coupled to the reactor-scale fluxes of a hybrid plasma equipment model [11], its Monte Carlo feature-profile model predicted polysilicon etch profiles in an inductively coupled reactor [12]. Fluorocarbon mechanisms of the same form described silicon and SiO2 etching with polymer passivation [13, 14], and the method has since been applied to high-aspect-ratio SiO2 etching [15] and to the transients of quasi-atomic-layer etching [16].

In a Monte Carlo profile model, the list of reactions with their probabilities defines the update of the surface directly. When a particle strikes a cell, one of the reactions is selected and the cell is changed accordingly. A level-set surface moves with a velocity computed from a rate per unit area and time. This rate depends on the coverages, which have to be known at each surface point before the velocity can be evaluated. In level-set topography simulators, the coverage balance is usually solved analytically, and the closed form is implemented in code once for each chemistry. For the two coupled coverages of a silicon etch in fluorine and oxygen, the closed form is already a long expression [17, 5, 6], and its implementation in ViennaPS has separate cases for the limits in which one of the fluxes vanishes. Other hand-written models of such simulators are likewise derived for particular chemistries [18, 19]. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is usually described by purpose-written models as well. Models that combine a single Langmuir coverage and a prescribed growth per cycle with Knudsen diffusion reproduce the measured conformality in high-aspect-ratio structures with acceptable accuracy [20, 21].

Hand-written models work well for the chemistries they were written for, but they are difficult to extend to larger or different chemistries. Closed forms are available for two coupled species and rarely beyond, and chemistries with six or seven coverages are impractical to treat this way. The chemistry is also fixed when the simulator is compiled. Adding an intermediate, making a step reversible or changing the order of a rate law requires a developer of the simulator to derive and implement the balance again and to recompile the code (Fig. 1b).

In reactor-scale simulation, the corresponding problem was solved decades ago by treating the mechanism as data. Surface Chemkin introduced a formalism in which the heterogeneous reactions, site types and bulk phases are listed in an input file and the rate expressions are constructed from that file [22]. Detailed mechanisms for specific systems, such as the metal-organic chemical vapour deposition (MOCVD) of GaAs [23], fit this formalism, because they consist of gas-phase and surface reactions with rate parameters on distinct site types. The open-source code Cantera reads such mechanisms from input files in the same way [24]. The front-end process simulator FLOOPS separates the physical models from the grid and the numerics, and their parameters and model selections are set in scripts that users edit without recompiling the code [25]. Mechanisms in Chemkin form have also been coupled to feature-scale transport. Labun et al. transferred a tetraethoxysilane mechanism validated at reactor scale to a feature-scale profile simulation and compared the result with measured step coverage [26]. The autonomous optimization of a reduced SiO2 etching mechanism by Krüger et al. shows how strongly profile predictions depend on the reaction probabilities, yields, rate coefficients and threshold energies [27].

papers.title: Forget What Comes Next: LLM Unlearning via Statistical Independence
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, raising privacy and legal concerns that motivate machine unlearning. Yet poisoned training examples can remain statistically detectable after unlearning, which raises the question of whether current unlearning objectives remove what the model has memorized at all. In this work, we introduce PINT, a novel algorithm for machine unlearning that uses the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to reduce the statistical dependence between tokens to be forgotten and the internal representations used to predict them. We formally relate our HSIC-based objective to Exact Memorization through a computable upper bound, connecting the training objective directly to the model's ability to reproduce the forgotten tokens. In extensive experiments, we compare forgetting-utility trade-offs across eight settings with models up to 7B parameters and demonstrate scalability to 70B parameter models. Our evaluations cover unlearning Gaussian poisons, personal information, hazardous knowledge in biology and cybersecurity, and copyrighted books and news articles. PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average and is the only method to make Gaussian poisons undetectable while maintaining near-original model utility. Code is available at: https://github.com/shkabrii/PINT

papers.intro:
The tendency of large language models (LLMs) to memorize and reproduce fragments of their training data, including personally identifiable information and copyrighted text (Carlini et al., 2021; Carlini et al., 2022), poses significant privacy and legal concerns. With the right to be forgotten now formalized in major data protection frameworks across the EU, the US, and China (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016; California State Legislature, 2018; Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, 2021), there is a growing need for methods that can remove the influence of specific training examples without the prohibitive cost of retraining from scratch. A growing body of work on approximate machine unlearning has made empirical progress in this direction (Jang et al., 2023; Maini et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). Nevertheless, significant gaps remain: Pawelczyk et al. (2025) show that current methods may fail to unlearn poisoned examples injected during training, leaving them statistically detectable even after an unlearning attempt.

To understand how an LLM can forget a memorized sequence, we look at how it predicts each token from the preceding context. At each position in a sequence, an autoregressive LLM encodes the preceding context into a prefix representation. From this representation, the output head predicts the next token. Reproducing a memorized sequence requires that these prefix representations carry information about the tokens that follow. This relationship can be expressed in terms of statistical dependence. So, can we induce forgetting by minimizing this statistical dependence?

At each position in a sequence, an autoregressive LLM encodes the preceding context into a prefix representation. From this representation, the output head predicts the next token. Reproducing a memorized sequence requires that these prefix representations carry information about the tokens that follow. This relationship can be expressed in terms of statistical dependence. So, can we induce forgetting by minimizing this statistical dependence?

To answer this, we propose PINT (Prefix-representation Independence of the Next Token). On the data targeted for removal (the forget set), PINT minimizes the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) (Gretton et al., 2005) between prefix representations and their corresponding next tokens, capturing and penalizing complex, non-linear dependencies. To preserve utility, PINT constrains representations on a retain set to remain close to those of the original model (see Figure 2 for an overview). As illustrated in Figure 1, this approach is highly effective: across benchmarks for personal information, hazardous knowledge, copyrighted text and Gaussian poisons, PINT achieves the strongest forgetting-utility trade-off on average. It is also the only method that makes Gaussian poisons statistically undetectable (Pawelczyk et al., 2025) while retaining near-original utility.

papers.title: IDs That Mean Something: A Hands-On Tutorial on Semantic IDs for Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Traditional recommender systems rely on arbitrary integer IDs to identify items, which carry no semantic information and force models to learn representations from interaction data. While leveraging content information can partially mitigate cold-start, this paradigm inherently suffers from exploding embedding tables and scenario-specific architectures. Recent years have seen the emergence of semantic IDs, which encode semantic information directly into the item identity, reflecting content, hierarchy, and relationships. This framework addresses the above limitations by offering a principled way to encode large-scale semantic information into item identity, benefiting both generative and discriminative applications and unlocking more native unification across modalities, domains, and tasks. This tutorial traces the evolution from raw IDs to semantic IDs as a scalable means of information utilization, offering a comprehensive review of their development and applications across multi-modality, cold-start, and cross-domain recommendation. Hands-on exercises guide attendees through building and evaluating semantic IDs, training models, and exploring cross-domain transfer. We conclude by discussing open challenges, including dynamic semantic IDs and multi-stakeholder utility. All materials of the tutorial could be found at the official website https://semantic-id-tutorial.github.io.

papers.title: Formalizing PTX in Lean to Prove GPU Kernel Correctness
papers.abstract: We present an approach to mathematically formalizing PTX, an approach that allows modeling and reasoning about patterns common in GPU kernels for Deep Learning, including acquire-release, tensor cores, proxies, async operations, multi-kernel pipelines and data-dependent control flow. We implement it in Lean and use it to prove the correctness of simple implementations of a WGMMA GEMM kernel, FlashAttention, and a 3-kernel MoE pipeline.
papers.intro:
The correctness of GPU kernels is becoming increasingly critical in the age of AI. Furthermore, as more and more kernels are written by LLMs, it is desirable to reduce human review burden, letting them trust outputs without extensive manual review.

This approach lets LLMs write correctness proofs in a verifiable manner: only the mathematical specification of what the kernel should compute, the preconditions, our formalization and parsing of PTX in Lean and the Lean kernel, but not the LLM’s outputs, need to be trusted. Furthermore, it allows formalizing and checking human intuition for why a given kernel is correct.

papers.title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
papers.abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

papers.intro:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming part of how people write, code, learn and make decisions. It can improve immediate performance in a wide range of tasks, but it can also reduce performance at two levels. At the individual level, relying on AI may reduce the practice that maintains one’s capacity to work independently: AI assistance can help with a task yet reduce persistence and subsequent independent performance [1]. Whether assistance supports or harms learning also depends on how it engages the user [2, 3]. At the collective level, the value of AI-assisted work may decrease as more people rely on the same tools [4]. Their outputs become more similar, reducing the diversity of ideas and content [5, 6], much as navigation services that give the same advice to many drivers concentrate traffic on the same roads [7]. AI systems retrained on increasingly synthetic data can also progressively lose quality, a phenomenon known as model collapse [8, 9]. The adoption of AI is, moreover, a social process, as for any technology [10]. A software developer adopting a code assistant, a student solving exercises with a chatbot and an analyst drafting reports with a language model all observe how well these tools serve their peers, and may be encouraged to adopt them when others appear to benefit.

Models of social learning and evolutionary game theory provide a natural framework for such adoption dynamics [11, 12]. In conventional models, the payoff of a strategy depends on current strategies, but not on the history of the individual who plays it. AI adoption differs, as every individual carries an internal state, their skill, which evolves with their own behavioural history: using AI changes the skill of the user, and therefore the payoff of their future decisions. Coevolutionary games, in which strategies coevolve with individual attributes [13], come closest to this setting. We call the dependence of an agent’s skill, and hence of the payoff of their next choice, on their own history of actions individual memory. Two AI users can have the same behaviour at a given moment, while one, who has just adopted AI, retains the expertise of years of independent practice, and the other, who has relied on AI for a long time, has lost it. It is thus not memory in the sense of repeated games, in which strategies condition on past moves, but the impact that an agent’s past behaviour leaves on their own skill.

We derive the stationary skill distributions exactly, allowing us to determine how individual histories affect collective AI adoption and the conditions under which different adoption regimes coexist. papers.title: A Multidimensional Evaluation Framework for Artificial Intelligence-Based Ocean State Forecasts
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) based ocean state forecasts now approach or surpass those produced by operational ocean forecasting systems as measured by conventional pointwise metrics. However, these metrics may favor spatially smoothed forecasts and cannot determine whether forecast variables remain physically coherent. Forecast evaluation should therefore move beyond overall pointwise accuracy toward assessing forecast trustworthiness. We propose a multidimensional framework comprising overall pointwise accuracy, physical consistency, and distributional consistency. Overall pointwise accuracy summarizes forecast and reference agreement over all valid samples; physical consistency evaluates dynamical balances using model outputs alone; and distributional consistency evaluates distribution tails and multiscale spatial structures. Three AI models were deployed as representative testbeds in a unified operational environment. This comprehensive assessment shows that lower overall pointwise errors cannot preclude substantial dynamical imbalances and suppressed fine-scale variance. Conversely, higher pointwise errors may arise from spatial displacement of coherent structures rather than a poor representation of their amplitude. The results demonstrate that the evaluation of AI ocean forecasting models should be based on the multi-dimensional assessment of forecast trustworthiness, rather than solely relying on a single metric. The study provides a preliminary framework for AI model intercomparison, which is also informative for targeted model refinement and operational implementation.

papers.title: Extending the MM-AR Metamodeling Platform with Process Mining Capabilities
papers.abstract: Process mining derives process models from event data recorded by information systems, but its results are usually presented as two-dimensional visualizations that are separate from the environments in which enterprise models are created and maintained. Metamodeling platforms for extended reality (XR), such as MM-AR, allow users to define modeling languages and to display models in 2D and 3D, but they do not provide access to event data or mining algorithms so far. In this paper we therefore present a first proof-of-concept for showing how an XR-based metamodeling platform can be extended with process discovery capabilities without changes to the platform core through a separate Python service based on the open source PM4Py process mining library. We demonstrate the approach using three common discovery algorithms for obtaining Petri nets and BPMN models based on CSV or XES event logs. A technical evaluation using four public event logs shows that the element counts of the created model instances match those of the PM4Py models in all 16 configurations. The integration adds between about 8 and 53 seconds per run, and this overhead grows with the size of the discovered model rather than the size of the event log. Although the prototype does not yet use the third dimension to encode process information, it established the foundations for studying such approaches.

For enterprise modeling, such discovered models complement models elicited from stakeholders with models based on recorded behaviour. At the same time, platforms for conceptual modeling in extended reality (XR), such as MM-AR Muff et al. (2026), allow users to define modeling languages and interact with the resulting models in 2D and 3D. Previous approaches that bring process mining into virtual reality created dedicated clients for particular languages Wetzel and Koschmider (2022); Oberhauser (2022). However, the integration of process mining into an XR metamodeling platform that supports multiple modeling languages has so far not been accomplished.

(R1) Event log upload: users must be able to upload an event log, since metamodeling platforms have no notion of event data and thus no way to pass such data to an analysis. (R2) Mined models as model instances: discovery results must be transformed into model instances that conform to the platform’s meta2-model. (R3) Loose coupling of the process mining extension: as the platform is under continuous, independent development, a tightly coupled integration would be difficult to maintain. papers.title: The Critical Cauchy Boundary for Gibbs Partitions
papers.abstract: We study critical Gibbs partitions whose component law is in the domain of attraction of a spectrally positive stable law of index one. In the dense phase, we prove a local limit theorem for the number of components and functional limits for their sizes. We also describe convergent and divergent condensation regimes, and a phase transition at a boundary in which the dense and condensation contributions compete.

papers.intro:
Gibbs partitions are a general model of random partitions generated according to two weight sequences that bias the number and size of components. Alongside other general models [3, 4, 6] they enable a unified study of a wide range of combinatorial structures that decompose into smaller components, such as connected components of graphs, cycles of permutations and trees in forests. See [36, 8, 17, 43, 45]. In combinatorics, the term composition scheme is often used synonymously [19, 18, 5, 13].

We study critical Gibbs partitions whose component law belongs to the domain of attraction of a spectrally positive stable law of index one. Spectrally positive refers here to the fact that the associated Lévy process has no negative jumps. Our main interest concerns the number and the size of the components. papers.title: Ta-based S-I-S junctions for integrated superconducting Electronics
papers.abstract: In this work, we have presented S-I-S Josephson junctions with $\rm\alpha$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ barrier. We grew base and top ${\alpha}$-Ta electrodes using seed layer engineering, showing both Nb and ${\rm TaN}_x$ are viable seed layer choices, and particularly emphasize that at room temperature a re-seed layer is required to nucleate $\rm\alpha$-Ta for the top electrode. However, we note that the choice of seed layer can have subtle implications on the electrical tunneling behavior of the junctions. We used room-temperature probing of variable junction areas, combined with Ambegaokar-Baratoff physics, to characterize the wafer scale critical current densities. For 0.4 $\mu$m$^2$ junctions, we found junction spreads as low as 2.0% across the 20 x 20 mm chip relevant for device performance. The entire process was carried out using standard industry foundry processing using 150 mm wafer tooling, which is an important step towards proving that Ta-based junctions can be implemented at scale. We have successfully fabricated and tested junctions with $\rm\alpha$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ insulating tunnel barrier, demonstrating that this is a material platform which merits further investigation and studies for potential application in classical and quantum superconducting technologies.

papers.title: MDSKILL: Learning to Internalize Skill Memory through Multi-View Distillation for Efficient Dynamic Agent Self-Evolution
papers.abstract: Skill memories encode past experiences as textual prompts to improve reinforcement learning (RL) for self-evolving agents. Complementing RL, On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) provides dense, fine-grained supervision to internalize knowledge from skill-guided trajectories and accelerate policy learning. However, self-generated memories often contain noisy supervision and functionally entangled, redundant, or conflicting knowledge, making direct distillation difficult. Under limited training budgets, these issues can hinder knowledge internalization and even degrade performance. To address this problem, we propose MDSKILL, a multi-view distillation approach for skill memory internalization. MDSKILL organizes skill memories into three complementary functional views (state grounding, action planning, and execution control) and selects high-quality skills using dynamic metrics to construct view-specific and integrated reasoning branches. OPSD then transfers and consolidates complementary experiential knowledge across these branches into a shared policy, enabling efficient skill internalization and continuous agent self-evolution. We evaluate MDSKILL on three agent benchmarks against RL, skill-augmented, and self-distillation baselines that do not rely on stronger external teacher models. Without additional computational overhead, MDSKILL improves upon SOTA performance by up to 7.1% and 8.1% on ALFWorld and WebShop. Extensive ablations and evolution analyses further validate its effectiveness in knowledge internalization and policy improvement. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MDSKILL-CF53.

papers.intro:
Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated strong performance on multi-turn interactive tasks (Shao et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026). However, sparse and delayed rewards provide limited supervision for policy improvement. Skill memories offer a promising source of experiential knowledge: they summarize lessons from real interaction trajectories and guide subsequent decisions through textual prompts (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Although external skill memories improve task success, agent self-evolution requires internalizing their experiential knowledge into model parameters to retain and apply acquired capabilities without explicit memory retrieval. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) distills skill-view trajectories into the skill-free branch, providing dense supervision for skill internalization and policy learning (Zhao et al., 2026; He et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a). Combining OPSD with RL enables more effective agent self-evolution and greater performance gains (Lu et al., 2026a; Tu et al., 2026a).

OPSD uses high-quality reference responses to provide reliable teacher supervision (Zhao et al., 2026). In online agent self-evolution, however, the teacher branch relies on self-generated skill memories that may contain ineffective, harmful, or hallucinated strategies, potentially causing the skill-view branch to underperform its skill-free counterpart (Tu et al., 2026a). Our observational experiments further suggest that jointly applying skills with different decision functions entangles their roles, while redundancy and conflicts obscure their individual contributions. Consequently, direct distillation can propagate erroneous behaviors and provide inconsistent supervision for useful knowledge, hindering its internalization into model parameters.

papers.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

papers.intro:
Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) underlie many cellular processes, and the ability to design proteins that selectively engage a target has broad applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and synthetic biology (Zambaldi et al., 2024; Cho et al., 2025b). Computational protein design offers a powerful alternative by enabling binders to be tailored to specific targets and epitopes. Early physics-based approaches, such as Rosetta (Cao et al., 2022; Gainza et al., 2023), designed binders through scaffold docking and side-chain optimization. However, these methods typically have low experimental success rates and therefore require screening a large number of candidates (Bennett et al., 2023). Their reliance on docking predefined scaffolds onto rigid target structures can also produce geometric or chemical incompatibilities at the interface, resulting in suboptimal binding or making certain epitopes difficult to target.

However, these methods typically have low experimental success rates and therefore require screening a large number of candidates (Bennett et al., 2023). Their reliance on docking predefined scaffolds onto rigid target structures can also produce geometric or chemical incompatibilities at the interface, resulting in suboptimal binding or making certain epitopes difficult to target.

Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have transformed biomolecular modeling and design. AlphaFold2/3 (AF2/3) (Jumper et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Abramson et al., 2024), for example, demonstrated remarkable accuracy in predicting monomer and complex structures. AF-based filtering substantially improves binder-design success rates by identifying candidates predicted to form plausible complexes with their targets (Liu et al., 2026; Team et al., 2025). DL has also enabled the de novo generation of protein binders. A widely used pipeline combines RFdiffusion for backbone generation (Watson et al., 2023) with ProteinMPNN (Dauparas et al., 2022) for sequence design, achieving markedly higher experimental success rates. Nevertheless, it separates backbone generation from sequence design without explicitly modeling full atomic interactions, leaving AF filtering to bridge the gap between structural generation and functional interface design. Building on the success of AF-based filtering, another hallucination-based line, such as BindCraft (Pacesa et al., 2024), demonstrated that structure predictors can also serve as differentiable design engines. By backpropagating through AF2, they directly optimize binder sequences, producing high-affinity designs with substantially reduced experimental screening. This marked a shift from generate-then-filter pipelines toward prediction-guided optimization. However, direct gradient optimization can be myopic and exploit imperfections in the predictive model, motivating search-based approaches that combine gradient-guided proposals with a balanced exploration-exploitation trade-off.

In this paper, we formulate protein design as a combinatorial search problem, where nodes represent discrete sequences, edits define transitions between them, and structure predictors serve as verification oracles. Our central idea is to use gradient-based hallucination as a source of search directions, while using structural verification to decide which sequences to explore further. To this end, we introduce ProteoCraft, a tree-based search framework based on ESMFold2 (Candido et al., 2026). Specifically, gradients through the terminal diffusion step induce priors over residue substitutions, which guide a coarse-to-fine search from coordinated multi-site exploration to single-site refinement. Verification therefore becomes part of the search process rather than only a final filter. Each proposed sequence is independently evaluated by a complete ESMFold2 forward pass, allowing the search to combine gradient-informed mutation preferences with evidence accumulated from previously verified designs.

papers.title: ARLoop: Fully-Open Pre-trained Looped Transformers with Attention Residuals
papers.abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals, where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths (R = 1 to 5), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.

This provides an appealing alternative to conventional depth scaling: the same parameters can be reused for additional computation, and the number of recurrences provides an explicit axis along which training and inference compute can be varied. papers.title: Triboelectric nanogenerators across length scales: linking materials, multiscale modelling and applications
papers.abstract: Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency mechanical energy into electricity and enable self-powered sensing. Their performance depends on interactions among material properties, surface morphology, contact mechanics, charge generation and external circuits. This review examines these interactions across length scales to assess how material and interface descriptions support predictive device design. Polymeric, inorganic, composite and natural materials are discussed in relation to charge generation and retention, mechanical compliance, durability and application requirements. Modelling approaches span molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations, rough-surface contact mechanics, device-scale electrostatics and equivalent circuits. Their capabilities are assessed through the inputs they require, the quantities they predict and the experimental evidence used for validation. Particular attention is given to prescribed surface charge density, idealised geometries and nominal contact-area assumptions, which constrain predictions under realistic loading conditions. Applications are organised by macroscale, milliscale and microscale device dimensions to examine requirements for materials, architecture and integration. The review identifies evolving real contact area and contact-dependent charge generation and decay as critical links between interfacial behaviour and electrical output. A staged validation strategy is proposed for contact mechanics, electrostatics and circuit response, with independent testing beyond calibration conditions. These priorities guide the development of multiscale models and reliable TENG systems.

papers.intro:
Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) enable the harvesting of widely distributed mechanical energy to electrical output via contact electrification and electrostatic induction. They have gained unprecedented attention in recent times thanks to their wide material compatibility, simple architectures, low-frequency operation, mechanical adaptability, and high potential for self-powered sensing and energy harvesting in environments where typical power sources are difficult to use [221, 173]. With the development of the field, it has been recognised that a single design parameter cannot determine TENG performance; rather, the interplay among material chemistry, interfacial charge physics, device structure, and system-level integration is the key. Accordingly, the modern TENG-related literature can be categorised into three domains: the development of high-performance triboelectric materials, the improvement of analytical and numerical simulation tools, and the further extension of the application field from microscale sensors to large-area and macroscale energy systems [29, 196].

The output performance of TENGs is strongly influenced by the triboelectric characteristics of contact surfaces, dielectric properties, charge-trapping ability, surface roughness, flexibility, durability, and environmental stability. Therefore, the material portfolio for TENGs is rapidly expanding and includes fluorinated polymers, elastomers, engineering polymers, natural and biodegradable materials, inorganic functional constituents, and composites to enhance charge generation [229, 98, 36]. The optimisation of materials is not limited to open-circuit voltage or short-circuit current; it also extends to real-world applications such as flexible electronics, biocompatible systems, harsh environments, textiles, sustainable devices, etc. [36, 43]. Therefore, the material development for TENGs reflects a broader transition from proof-of-concept to more application-oriented and performance-engineered systems.

In addition, computational and theoretical modelling have become essential for understanding, predicting, and optimising TENG behaviour. These models have shown that the charge transfer, potential distribution, and output current are geometry-dependent, voltage-dependent, and charge-density-dependent [29, 196, 219, 153]. Modelling approaches are especially crucial for TENG operations because they encompass multiscales ranging from nanoscale charge transfer and interfacial states to microscale surface roughness and local field distributions, mesoscale device mechanics, and macroscale packaging and deployment. Existing modelling approaches have provided important insight into TENG behaviour. Analytical and equivalent-circuit models have been widely used to describe idealised contact-separation, sliding, single-electrode, and freestanding-layer TENGs [199, 40, 41]. Finite element simulations have further enabled the analysis of electric potential, electric field, capacitance, and charge distribution in more complex geometries [149, 160, 174, 120]. More recently, contact mechanics, rough-surface modelling, molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and circuit simulations have been introduced to investigate specific aspects of TENG operation. However, most existing models still rely on prescribed surface charge density, simplified contact assumptions, idealised geometries, or sequential coupling between mechanical and electrical fields. However, the literature addresses TENG materials, modelling methods, and applications separately, without considering them as interdependent components of a complete design framework [173, 221].

For instance, Zhang and Olin [221] comprehensively reviewed materials used in TENGs, highlighting their relationships to power density, stability, flexibility, and sustainability across various applications. Further, the theoretical background of TENGs was summarised by Zhang et al. [5] explored recent developments and future directions for TENGs in self-powered systems, including their operating modes, device architectures, and applications on autonomous platforms. Xu et al. [196] discussed the dynamics of TENGs, including the behaviour of springs, magnetic fields, structural movement, and optimisation of output under dynamic operating conditions. Han et al. This review discusses modelling approaches for TENGs across scales, from contact-electrification mechanisms to device-level material selection and design. It highlights the strengths and limitations of existing approaches and identifies promising routes towards predictive multiscale TENG applications. In a recent review, Li et al. Rajasekar and Sivakumar [143] discussed recent trends and prospects in advanced materials and emerging applications. Recently, Udofa et al.
