papers.title: P-SER: Physical Consistency-Constrained Scattering Expandable Representation for Class-Incremental HRRP Target Recognition
papers.abstract: High-resolution range profiles (HRRPs) provide compact radar target representations but exhibit strong aspect sensitivity, complicating class-incremental recognition when historical data are unavailable. Changes in viewing aspect shift scattering-peak locations and amplitudes, while reflector groups may produce responses resembling ships. Existing dynamic expansion methods can also incur substantial parameter and memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose P-SER, a Physical Consistency-Constrained Scattering Expandable Representation framework for exemplar-free class-incremental HRRP recognition. P-SER reconstructs dominant scattering points from complex-valued sum- and azimuth-difference-channel HRRPs and observation geometry. The reconstructed spatial structure, target extent, and energy distribution are used to derive class-level scattering prototypes and sample-level saliency priors, providing physically grounded constraints for feature learning and old-class knowledge retention. A primitive scatterer dictionary further characterizes local strong-scattering mechanisms and calibrates uncertain ship--reflector predictions at inference. Meanwhile, lightweight residual adapters are incrementally introduced into a shared HRRP backbone to learn new classes with limited model growth. Experiments on simulated and measured HRRP datasets show that P-SER delivers competitive recognition performance without retaining old-class exemplars, while maintaining physical consistency, interference robustness, knowledge retention, and model scalability.

papers.title: Polarimetric Scattering-Structure Contrastive Learning for Few-Shot HRRP Recognition
papers.abstract: Few-shot high-resolution range profile (HRRP) recognition is challenged by strong aspect-dependent variation and sparse novel-class support. We propose polarimetric scattering-structure contrastive learning (PSS-CL), which supplies an episodic HRRP encoder with a structured physical training view. Dominant local responses are represented by their soft affinities to canonical polarimetric mechanisms, normalized range locations, and energy contributions. A symmetric cross-view objective transfers this scattering structure to the learned HRRP representation, while episodic prototype learning supports novel-class inference without the physical branch. We conduct Random-aspect and Cross-aspect experiments on a six-class measured dataset. In Cross-aspect 1-, 3-, and 5-shot recognition, PSS-CL achieves 81.73%, 86.92%, and 90.98% mean class accuracy (MCA), respectively, outperforming the best competing results by 5.62%, 3.09%, and 3.56%.

papers.title: OpenBrain: An Auditable Generated-Label Release for Whole-Brain MRI Parcellation
papers.abstract: Automatic tools can now generate whole-brain MRI parcellations at cohort scale, but generated-label releases often provide little evidence about which cases are reliable enough to reuse. We introduce OpenBrain, a confidence-aware release of 35,838 provenance-verified OpenNeuro T1w cases from 607 source datasets. OpenBrain is organized as an auditable case-record release rather than a directory of standalone segmentation files: each record links a primary parcellation, two committee parcellations, source/license provenance, raw QC-7 measurements, percentile risks, a combined risk score R, and a confidence tier. QC-7 is a reference-free reliability panel over label geometry, image-label consistency, and committee disagreement, so users can filter, weight, audit, or re-threshold generated labels without rerunning inference. We evaluate this released evidence under a frozen protocol. Across external cohorts, lower QC-7 risk corresponds to higher generated-label quality; in fixed-budget training, lower-risk selections improve paired macro Dice over random selection by +3.2 to +3.7 percentage points. OpenBrain also exposes raw axes, committee outputs, provenance, and datasheet documentation, so confidence claims remain inspectable after download. It does not turn generated labels into manual annotations or clinical-grade segmentations. Its contribution is a large open generated-parcellation substrate, a reusable case-level risk-evidence layer, and an external validation protocol for release-time QC. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/lanqz7766/OpenBrain. Code: https://github.com/lanqz7766/openbrain.

papers.title: Rational points on loxodromic K3 surfaces and complex dynamics
papers.abstract: We establish an analogue of the Hilbert irreducibility theorem for all K3 surfaces over number fields that admit an automorphism of positive entropy. Our method draws ingredients from both algebraic geometry and complex dynamics.

papers.title: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior in LLM Agents?
papers.abstract:
LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to plan tasks, invoke tools, recover from errors, and complete workflows without modifying model parameters. Although these skills are typically developed to enhance benign tasks, they may also make an agent more capable of executing procedures for harmful purposes. We study this risk, which we call skill-induced behavioral misalignment: adding benign skills may cause an agent to execute external actions that violate safety requirements.
  We first conduct a systematic study to validate the existence of this phenomenon. It compares agents with and without benign skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks under matched requests. On average, skill augmentation improves benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points (pp), but also increases unsafe action rate (UAR) by 10.3 pp. The regression also occurs with skills curated by experts. A paired trajectory analysis shows that 24 of 50 newly unsafe trajectories fail to complete the harmful objective, revealing violations that task completion alone would miss.
  We further disclose multiple factors and scenarios that could exacerbate this risk. (1) Evolving skills with benign feedback can amplify unsafe execution; (2) This regression is more pronounced when retrieved skills are matched to task and contain procedural guidance; (3) Distilling benign experience into reusable skills yield higher UAR compared with their source trajectories. (4) A guard that checks proposed tool actions before execution reduces violations while retaining gains on benign tasks. All these findings confirm the significance of skill-induced behavioral misalignment, and the urgent need for new mitigation solutions.

papers.title: Do Retrieval Ranking Models Capture Event Order? A Study of Timeline-Constrained Retrieval
papers.abstract: Semantic retrieval models aim to match documents to a query's "meaning", yet it remains unclear whether they successfully encode temporal relations between events in their ranking mechanisms. We investigate this question by studying timeline-constrained document retrieval, where a query is an ordered sequence of natural-language event statements while a relevant document should match those events in a compatible temporal progression. We then test whether widely used dense retrievers and neural rerankers capture such constraints, and whether explicitly preserving temporal order improves ranking, using a controlled setting over a novel focused evaluation collection. Experiments show that state-of-the-art semantic retrievers and rerankers provide only limited improvements over lexical retrieval, suggesting that their semantic matching capabilities do not reliably capture temporal constraints. We then compare a timeline-aware method with both semantic matching and standard rerankers and find that it yields substantial improvements. This demonstrates that considering temporal order can provide a strong ranking signal in this setting, suggesting future research on improving temporal modeling in semantic retrievers.

papers.title: Reality and Perceptual Gaps in Expressive Swarm Robotics
papers.abstract: Moving robot swarms from simulation into the physical world can be difficult because small discrepancies in hardware, timing and communication can cascade across interacting robots and alter group behaviour. This challenge is known as the reality gap. When swarms operate in human environments, a second challenge emerges: a perceptual gap between what the swarm physically does and what human onlookers actually perceive. This study examines the same decentralised coordination code deployed across three robotic swarms-tabletop, aerial and human-scale mobile manipulators-during live artistic performances. We find that while the underlying algorithms executed reliably on all three platforms, physical embodiment drastically altered visible motion-distorting execution timescales by more than a factor of three and reshaping trajectory geometry. More importantly, audience surveys revealed that human interpretation does not mirror technical success: how observers attribute meaning (perceived purpose) and how they react emotionally (comfort versus threat) depend heavily on physical form. Meaning attribution and emotional responses did not vary together. Our results demonstrate that successfully transferring swarm software to physical hardware is insufficient for real-world deployment. Addressing the reality gap does not guarantee that the resulting collective motion will be readily interpreted by human observers. Swarms destined for human environments must be engineered not only for decentralised stability but also for the expressive physical dynamics through which humans interpret collective motion.

papers.title: Learning from Unlabeled Photographs for General Oral Image Analysis
papers.abstract: Oral photographs contain rich clinical information and hold significant potential for artificial intelligence applications; however, most models are trained for individual tasks and rely on costly expert annotations. We hypothesized that self-supervised training on unlabeled oral photographs could produce transferable visual representations for heterogeneous vision tasks. To test this hypothesis, we developed DOVE (Dental Optical Visual Encoder) by domain-adaptive self-supervised pretraining on approximately 530,000 unlabeled oral photographs collected from publicly accessible sources. DOVE was benchmarked against 3 established baselines across 5 classification datasets and 4 segmentation datasets, covering both frozen backbone evaluation and end-to-end finetuning. DOVE achieved the strongest overall performance, ranking best in few-shot transfer and label efficiency on most benchmarks. Under the 20-shot frozen-backbone protocol, DOVE outperformed the second best DINOv3 by 4.37 percentage points in mean macro-F1 across classification datasets and by 4.49 percentage points in mean macro-Dice across segmentation tasks. Under end-to-end finetuning, DOVE achieved at least 80% of the strongest full-data baseline's performance across most evaluation datasets using only 10% of the labeled training data. Qualitative retrieval and feature analyses further indicated better organization of image-level and spatial representations. These findings support DOVE as a generalizable and label-efficient backbone for oral vision research.

papers.title: Surface Nitrogen enrichment from the LMC to the Early Universe: the roles of rotation, overshooting and mass loss
papers.abstract: The strong nitrogen (N) features observed in high-redshift galaxies, such as GN-z11, with JWST point to an efficient source of N production in the early Universe. Very massive stars (VMSs) are promising candidates owing to their strong winds and large convective cores of CNO-processed material. Whether massive-star surfaces in general become N-enriched depends on the interplay of convective-boundary mixing (overshooting), rotation, and mass loss, which remains poorly constrained. Using a grid of MESA evolutionary models, we isolate the overshooting and rotation channels at $40$, $100$, and $200\,M_\odot$ and investigate how these channels bring N-rich material to the surface of massive and very massive stars as a function of initial mass and metallicity. We also construct a synthetic Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) population based on a larger initial mass grid ranging from $20-300\,M_\odot$ for comparison with the observed N-enriched fraction. VMS surface enrichment is remarkably robust across cosmic metallicity. At lower metallicities, wind stripping is weaker and the overshooting channel shuts off entirely, yet a modest amount of rotation of $\sim90\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ alone still enriches the surface. At higher metallicity, stronger winds dominate and uncover the core almost independently of the adopted mixing. The two channels operate through physically distinct mechanisms: overshooting enriches the surface only once winds strip the envelope down into the N-rich layers left by the receding core, giving an abrupt jump. Rotation, by contrast, mixes N outward continuously through the layers above the core, producing a gradual rise. Applied to the LMC, a population with modest rotation drawn from the observed velocity distribution and modest overshooting reproduces the observed N-enriched fraction without large core boundary mixing efficiencies otherwise required by non-rotating models.

papers.title: Recovering Hidden Wildlife--Vehicle Collisions from Existing Crash Data: A Cross-State Framework for Detection, Prevalence Estimation, and Under-Reporting Audits
papers.abstract:
Wildlife--vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large toll on U.S. highways, yet state crash databases often fail to record animal involvement, leaving agencies uncertain of the true missing count. This study evaluates whether existing crash records can identify individual WVCs and estimate overall unrecorded rates.
  We analyzed 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois (2007-2026). Each state's schema underwent a label-leakage screen to exclude explicit animal fields before harmonization into a shared vocabulary. Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state, interpreted using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated for prevalence estimation via Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood techniques across in-domain, cross-state, and synthetic reporting-gap scenarios.
  Detection performance depends heavily on record completeness rather than collision rarity. At ~4% prevalence, feature-rich Utah achieved an average precision of 0.88 versus 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and outperformed Iowa despite Iowa's 3x higher WVC rate. Within-state richness curves confirm feature depth drives accuracy. While classifiers ranked records accurately across states, probability calibration did not transfer directly. However, in-domain prevalence estimation recovered true collision rates within 0.001.
  This work shifts WVC analysis from spatial clustering to record-level detection and missing-data estimation using legacy datasets.
  Transportation agencies can retrospectively flag unrecorded WVCs, quantify total collision burden to support mitigation funding, and identify high-value reporting fields prior to revising crash-report manuals.

papers.title: Beyond the Federer paradox in tennis
papers.abstract: Roger Federer won about 80% of his professional matches with only 54% of the points. Hierarchical scoring amplifies small advantages on points into large advantages on matches, but also allows a player to win with fewer points than the opponent. Using Monte Carlo simulations and exact Markov chain calculations, we show that in tennis, badminton, volleyball and table tennis this amplification is set almost entirely by the number of points per match. We then let a player win ordinary points with probability p1 and crucial points, those closing a game, set or match, with probability p2. In every sport a narrow region of the (p1, p2) plane exists where a player wins most matches with fewer than half of the points, because crucial points carry more influence than their share of points. Of ATP matches played in 1991-2025, 4.7% were won with fewer points, 16% more than independent points predict (5% including the serve), a constant excess. Pressure performance measured in other seasons predicts match outcomes beyond the points won, and Fabio Fognini won 51% of his matches with 49% of the points, in what we call the Fognini paradox.

papers.title: The obstacle problem for fractional heat equations with memory
papers.abstract: We study the obstacle problem for the evolution equation $\partial_t^\alpha u+(-\Delta)^s u=0$ in the whole space $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $\partial_t^\alpha$ with $\alpha\in(0,1)$ is the Caputo derivative in time and $(-\Delta)^s$ with $s\in(0,1]$ is the fractional Laplacian in space ($s<1$) or the classical Laplacian ($s=1$). We prove that the problem has at most one bounded viscosity solution, and we obtain existence as the limit of an explicit monotone finite-difference scheme, which combines the L1 discretization of the Caputo derivative with powers of the discrete Laplacian. The scheme is also used to establish regularity estimates in space and time. We then study the large-time behaviour: solutions converge, along subsequences, to stationary solutions, and we identify the limit when the initial datum coincides with the obstacle (the minimal stationary solution) or has a limit $c_*$ at infinity. In the latter case the dimension plays a role, as a consequence of the recurrence of the underlying process: the limit is the unique stationary solution with limit $c_*$ at infinity if $d>2s$, and a constant (the maximum between $c_*$ and the supremum of the obstacle) if $d\le2s$. Numerical experiments in one dimension, based on an explicit stationary solution, illustrate the convergence of the scheme and the relaxation towards the stationary profile.

papers.title: The Hidden Markov Ising Model with Exogenous Covariates
papers.abstract: The Ising model, a type of Markov Random Field, from statistical physics has a long history of modeling spatial and network data as well as particle interactions. In this work, we consider inserting the Ising model into the framework of a Hidden Markov Model, a type of Bayesian Network, to model temporal state changes in a sequence of Ising observations. While this is entirely a discrete probability model, a main challenge is the fitting of such a probabilistic graphical model due to the exponential intractability of normalizing constants within the Ising model. To circumvent this problem, we consider the usage of maximum pseudolikelihood estimators that have a long history in Markov Random Fields. Validity of the pseudolikelihood Baum-Welch algorithm, model identifiability under likelihood, and consistency for large networks is also proved. The proposed Hidden Markov Ising Model is further extended to incorporate exogenous variables resulting in a hybrid hidden Markov autologistic model with graphical dependencies integrated into the model. This model is applied to a five year sequence of weekly gun violence events across the 3109 counties of the continental United States to identify state changes in gun violence activity from 2021 to 2025.

authors.name: Oscar Lopez
authors.institution: Centro de Investigaciones Energéticas, Medioambientales y Tecnológicas

papers.title: Global Existence for a Drift-Diffusion Model of Electrical Discharge in MEMS
papers.abstract: We study a coupled elliptic-parabolic system modelling electrical discharge in a micro-electro-mechanical (MEMS) capacitor: a Poisson equation for the electrostatic potential, coupled to drift-diffusion equations for the ion and electron densities with a Townsend ionization source whose rate per electron grows linearly in the electric field. Gimperlein, He and Lacey proved local well-posedness and left open whether the densities blow up in finite time. We first prove a continuation criterion in a weak norm: a finite-time singularity forces the space charge to be unbounded in H^1_D, the dual of the space of H^1 functions vanishing on the electrodes, so blow-up cannot be quasi-neutral. We then exclude it altogether when the two diffusivities coincide and the vacuum field is bounded: the weak solution is then global in time. To our knowledge this is the first global existence result without smallness assumptions for a drift-diffusion-Poisson model of gas discharge whose ionization rate is unbounded in the field. The proof uses the electrostatic energy and the number of carriers in place of the usual free energy: the ionization source cancels in the energy balance, the Joule heating is dissipative, and the two quantities close through a linear Gronwall inequality. Numerical experiments on a discharge in a micrometre gap, with the Townsend constants and the mobilities of air, provide evidence for the extension to unequal diffusivities and bear on the existence of a breakdown threshold.

papers.title: Collective animal motion: The case of midge swarms
papers.abstract: Among collective states of animal groups, midge swarms pose several puzzling questions. Their polarization order parameter is very small, and the insects interact only weakly with one another while remaining strongly bound to the swarm. In laboratory studies performed without external perturbations, the correlation length is small. By contrast, field studies reveal strong correlations, scale-free behavior, and power-law scaling of the correlation length, susceptibility, and correlation time. The dynamic correlation function exhibits data collapse only for short times when time is rescaled by the correlation time. Is there a theory that explains these disparate observations? We review several models proposed in the literature and extend our harmonically confined Vicsek model to anisotropic confinement. Within the extended criticality region of the phase diagram, numerical simulations predict elongated swarms and static critical exponents that lie between those of the two-dimensional and isotropic three-dimensional models. These values agree better with those measured in natural swarms. We also calculate probability density functions for both natural and laboratory swarms. Numerical simulations indicate that the laboratory distributions correspond to a different region of parameter space, although some open questions remain.

papers.title: On the Role of Geometry in Solving Variational Inequalities
papers.abstract:
The geometry of constraints in variational inequalities (VIs) plays a central role in applications ranging from resource allocation and equilibrium computation to constrained optimization. Yet, its effect on computational complexity has received surprisingly little attention beyond special cases. We examine this question when the constraint set is an $\ell_p$ ball. This family of problems encompasses two of the most extensively studied classes of problems in algorithmic game theory: symmetric bimatrix games for $p = 1$ and multi-player polymatrix games for $p = \infty$. Both of these problems are known to be PPAD-complete even for affine operators.
  We establish a comprehensive complexity landscape for VIs over $\ell_p$ balls across the full range $p\in[1,\infty]$. First, for any $p\neq 2$, we show that finding an inverse-polynomial approximate VI solution is PPAD-complete even for affine operators. In contrast, for $p=2$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for affine VIs, extending a classic result of Ye (1992) beyond symmetric operators. On the other hand, once the operator becomes quadratic, we establish PPAD-completeness even at inverse polynomial precision.
  From a technical standpoint, we develop a new toolkit for exploiting the geometry of the constraint set and the structure of the operator to characterize the complexity of equilibrium and optimization problems, which is of independent interest.

papers.title: CLARA: A Cognitively-Driven Clarification Framework for Grounding Ambiguous Requests
papers.abstract: Robotics and AI systems are increasingly deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) to follow high-level instructions, from routine household chores to more complex organizational tasks. Yet, broad directives like "clean the room" or "organize the desk" frequently omit crucial details about user preferences and specific arrangement of objects that influence the desired outcome. Without any further guidance, such models tend to overestimate their grasp of ambiguous instructions and frequently assume they have sufficient understanding despite missing important details. In this paper, we propose CLARA (Conversational cLArification for Robotic Arrangement), a cognitively-driven clarification framework that proactively elicits key information from users, in a similar fashion as humans' clarification seeking behavior. Through targeted questioning, CLARA refines ambiguous requests into structured, detailed instructions describing precisely how objects should be organized or rearranged, according to the user's preferences. These clarifications then guide a diffusion-based image generation pipeline, producing realistic visual renderings of the final, desired scene. This final rendering also serves as a visual confirmation of the system's understanding from the user. Experimental results and user studies demonstrate that CLARA leads to more accurate and consistent outcomes compared to another State-of-the-Art LVLM system, highlighting the importance of interactive clarification for bridging the gap between vague directives and fully grounded task specifications.

papers.title: Renormalisation of Hydrogen Partition Function and Saha Ionisation Equation
papers.abstract: An important physical quantity that is part of the Saha ionisation equation is the partition function of the neutral hydrogen atoms. An immense uncertainty is caused by the divergency of the neutral atom partition function arising due to the fast growing degeneracy factor of its excited n-state. We suggested a regularisation and renormalisation procedure for the partition function of the neutral hydrogen atoms. The renormalised partition function is well defined and allows to calculate the population of the energy levels and the ionisation state of the hydrogen plasma as a function of its temperature and pressure. In the low-temperature limit the behaviour of these functions smoothly transforms to the Saha equation, which is used in the description of the low-temperature plasma. At higher temperatures the renormalised ionisation equation describes the deviation from the Saha equation. The application of the renormalised ionisation equation to the solar core and atmosphere is considered.

papers.title: Radiative relativistic reconnection powering the hard-state emission of X-ray binaries: synchrotron-driven pair loading, MeV tail, and seed photons
papers.abstract: In the hard state, X-ray emission from black hole X-ray binaries is attributed to Comptonization in the corona, a highly magnetized region near the black hole. Relativistic magnetic reconnection drives bulk motions that can upscatter soft photons and reproduce the spectral peak at $\sim 100$ keV for parameters relevant to Cygnus X-1. However, the origin of the seed photons and of the MeV tail above the peak remains unclear. In 3D reconnection, so-called "free" particles escape the flux ropes and accelerate at the maximum rate set by the reconnection electric field. Their synchrotron emission extends to tens of MeV, which enables $\gamma \gamma$ pair production with the Compton-upscattered photons. We present 3D particle-in-cell simulations of relativistic reconnection in pair plasma, in which particles cool by inverse Compton (IC) scattering below the synchrotron self-absorption threshold and by synchrotron radiation above it. Of the incoming magnetic power, $\sim 40 \%$ is converted to IC radiation and $\gtrsim 10$-$20\%$ to synchrotron. Using analytical estimates and radiative calculations for Cygnus X-1, we model how the radiation from reconnection-accelerated particles is reprocessed in the corona. Pair production attenuates the synchrotron emission above $\sim 1$ MeV, and the escaping $\gamma$-rays form an MeV tail consistent with the observations, extending up to at least $\sim 10$ MeV. Most of the absorbed power goes into secondary pairs, whose Thomson optical depth can reach order unity. Their synchrotron emission, peaking at $\sim 0.1 \, \text{keV}$, can supply the seed photons for Comptonization. Our results support reconnection-based synchrotron self-Compton models of the hard-state emission in X-ray binaries.

papers.title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
papers.abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.

papers.title: Combination Theorems and the Farrell--Jones Conjecture for Graph Products of Pairs
papers.abstract:
We study the Farrell--Jones conjecture for graph products of pairs and for fundamental groups of polyhedral products. We introduce a pair-deletion decomposition and a local notion of FJ-admissibility, and prove a vertexwise combination theorem for graph products of pairs. The criterion applies, in particular, to ordinary graph products, free-factor pairs, suitable normal pairs, and classes controlled by acylindrical Bass--Serre actions.
  For polyhedral products, we combine these results with their description by relative graph products and graph products of pairs. We also obtain bounds and exact computations for amenable category, together with applications to simplicial volume and Borel rigidity of closed aspherical polyhedral-product manifolds.

papers.title: Linear Equivalence of Full Weight Spectrum Cyclic Orbit Codes
papers.abstract: We determine the linear-equivalence classes within the two families of full weight spectrum one-orbit cyclic subspace codes. This solves the second open problem posed by Castello, Polverino and Zullo [J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 212 (2025) 106005]. For the first family, the criterion is a fractional linear transformation over $\F_q$ followed by a power of $q$-Frobenius. For the second family, it is an affine transformation over $\F_{q^2}$ together with a power of $q$-Frobenius. We use polynomial spaces over finite fields, the linear-isometry theorem for cyclic orbit codes, and trace duality. The arguments include parameters belonging to proper subfields of the ambient field.

papers.title: Measure Before You Repair: An Explainable Agent for Blind Restoration of Multi-Artifact 3-D MRI
papers.abstract: A brain MRI scan can carry an unknown mix of artifacts, so restoration has to be blind, yet most deep-learning methods are built to correct one known artifact. We present Dx-Rx, an agent in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) measures suspected artifacts before it repairs them. To our knowledge, it is the first agent to restore whole 3-D MRI volumes, whereas earlier MRI agents restore 2-D slices. In a loop, it looks at slices of the 3-D volume, calls five diagnostic tools (noise, spike, ghosting, bias field, motion) and four restoration tools in any order it chooses, checks each repair, can return to any earlier version to change the order, and ends with a radiology-style report of its diagnostic reasons, the repairs it applied and their results. We simulated up to five artifacts on 148 whole 3-D T1-weighted volumes, at levels calibrated to radiologists' grades of real scans. An MLLM that only looked at the image, as earlier MRI agents do, removed at most 19.7 % of the artifact error. With the best of five MLLMs, Dx-Rx removed a mean 64.5 %, nearly matching the 64.6 % of the same tools given the ground-truth artifacts, which are never known for a clinical scan. With all five models, it made no volume worse and was on par with or better than an expert rule-based pipeline built from the same tools (62.3 %). Code and demo are public at https://itu-biai.github.io/measure-before-you-repair.

papers.title: How market volatility responds to a preceding price trend: a lag-resolved measurement in cryptocurrencies and equities
papers.abstract: We quantify the response of market volatility to a preceding price trend as a function of lag at minute resolution. The asymmetry of the response is investigated. The sample consists of trades in three of the largest cryptocurrencies on a single exchange and in three large US stocks and the S&P 500 exchange-traded fund between 2020 and 2026. For the cryptocurrencies the asymmetry is positive, matching the sign of the leverage effect. It follows the trend: it is greatest at the first measurable lag, 20 minutes, and weak at negative lags, where the trend follows the volatility. At those lags a scan over window lengths resolves a small component of opposite sign that has not yet been disentangled from what the statistic itself generates. For Bitcoin and Ether the asymmetry decays to one half by a lag of roughly an hour and a half. Decomposition under time reversal divides the asymmetry into a T-even part and a T-odd part. Only the latter carries an arrow of time. For Bitcoin and Ether the T-odd part is detected. At the first lag it is between 0.4 and 0.9 of the T-even part at windows of 10 and 20 minutes. At 20 minutes this is the ratio produced by a purely one-sided response in this statistic: at that window the response is consistent with being wholly one-sided in time. None of the equities exhibits a detectable T-odd part at 20 minutes in the straight-line fit over 2.5 trend scales. This fit is the shared instrument of comparison. The fund's return-variance correlation displays an arrow of time; the cryptocurrencies' asymmetry is independent of the shapes of the fits, and Bitcoin's and Ether's of their ranges. On simulated and shuffled data without coupling, the analysis yields zero with errors of the correct size. It also recovers the time scale of a one-sided response embedded in a simulated market.

papers.title: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking via Automated Adversarial Chain of Thoughts Discovery
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks by generating explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, but the safety implications of this intermediate reasoning surface remain underexplored. We demonstrate that the reasoning trace itself is a powerful attack vector. Safety alignment in large models is substantially less robust to malicious reasoning embedded in the context than to direct imperative prompts. We introduce BrainwashedLLM, a weak-to-strong adversarial framework that automates the discovery of reasoning-based jailbreaks. First, we use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm, with a multi-objective rule-based reward to fine-tune a small, white-box source model to generate adversarial reasoning traces. Crucially, the reward is computed entirely over the source's own reasoning trace. Second, we show that these traces transfer in a zero-shot manner. When traces are injected as input prefixes, they steer larger black-box LRMs to continue the adversarial reasoning and produce harmful outputs, without requiring prompt optimization, gradient access, or any form of output feedback from the target model. Across four state-of-the-art LRMs that span distinct architectures, BrainwashedLLM achieves ASR@5 between 0.74 and 0.98 across targets, within 16 points of query-based baselines, without querying the target during attack construction. To our knowledge, this is the first framework to use RL to directly optimize the CoT of LRMs as an attack surface without any target feedback, and the first to demonstrate zero-shot weak-to-strong transfer of reasoning traces. Our results suggest that exposed CoT is a vulnerability in LRMs and motivate architectural defenses that isolate the reasoning buffer. Warning: This paper contains potentially offensive and harmful text.

papers.title: HybridSpec: Throughput-Aware Speculative Decoding for Hybrid GDN-MoE Models
papers.abstract: In speculative decoding, parallel drafters such as DFlash make drafting cheap, so target verification dominates each round. A central choice is the verification length, the number of tokens that the target processes in each round. Verifying more draft tokens can accept more of them, but work after the first rejection is wasted. For hybrid target models that combine Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers, verification time grows much faster with this length than for dense models. In a single-request profile of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with DFlash, it grew by 71% from length 4 to 16, almost entirely in GDN and MoE layers, compared with 4%-6% for a dense Qwen3-4B target. Each GDN layer must update a recurrent state at every token and recover it at the end of the accepted prefix. The MoE cost depends on the experts that the tokens activate, which are known only once verification runs. We present HybridSpec, which selects the verification length on the GPU from draft-side acceptance estimates and measured target latency. Verification then runs this length plus one extra token up to the first MoE router, before any expert runs. There, a lightweight routing correction uses the observed expert assignments to decide whether to keep that token. The rest of verification runs only on the selected tokens. Block-parallel GDN kernels avoid storing a state after every token and reconstruct the accepted state of every GDN layer in one launch. In isolated benchmarks at verification lengths 4 to 16 with every draft token accepted, these kernels, including accepted-state reconstruction, are $1.54\times$-$4.04\times$ faster than the default kernels. With three GDN-MoE target models in single-request greedy decoding, HybridSpec is $1.75\times$-$1.88\times$ faster than autoregressive decoding and $1.30\times$-$1.33\times$ faster than DFlash.

papers.title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
papers.abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We present a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge model (VP-DDBM) for state-conditioned prediction of two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, the model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. Across two held-out thermal gradients, VP-DDBM produces lower long-horizon errors than deterministic U-Net and SI-ConvNeXt baselines in domain-mean phase, domain-mean Cu concentration, and leading-tip position. It also retains fine dendritic structure over long rollouts, whereas the deterministic U-Net progressively smooths the morphology. VP-DDBM predicts the phase and concentration evolution approximately $73\times$ faster than the phase-field solver, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

papers.title: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention
papers.abstract: Web systems infer user preferences from behavior, ratings, text, and LLM-generated profiles, yet explaining a proxy may reveal its measurement process rather than the preference of interest. We develop an audit framework distinguishing point identification, partial identification, and abstention relative to an explicit reference distribution. Under feature-dependent, arbitrarily signed proxy bias, a strict majority of uncontaminated proxy attributions lets the coordinatewise median recover latent-attribution support and direction and, with externally justified positive scales, magnitude. We prove this threshold sharp using response-valid indistinguishable worlds, characterize sharp minimax error and exact compatible-target sets under approximate cleanliness and scale uncertainty, and propagate clean-proxy attribution error. A frozen known-truth benchmark spans two response families, four proxy counts, all contamination counts, three bias strengths, and eleven methods, with a focal comparison confirmed on twenty unseen seeds. Under correct budgets, a direct attribution-tensor audit achieved 100% coverage, 95.40%-97.05% active-driver sign decisions, and no false signs. In a temporally separated Amazon study, median aggregation reduced comparator-relative conditional sign error for all four targets; six of eight prespecified target-metric contrasts had Bonferroni intervals excluding zero. A controlled real-covariate perturbation favored the median on the prespecified focal metric for all four targets. Compatible sets showed that the current proxy configuration rarely licensed strict-sign conclusions. Weak comparator calibration limits the Amazon evidence to fitted-surface alignment rather than latent-preference recovery.

papers.title: When Category Means Move: A Paired-Support Audit of Recommendation Logs with Random Insertions
papers.abstract: Content-category dashboards summarize production recommendation logs, although the serving policy selects the users, items, and contexts behind each mean. Using KuaiRand random-insertion impressions, we audit these summaries on the same 12,472 users and 5,486 videos in both logs. Standard means have absolute/centered mean absolute error (MAE) 0.1935/0.0491 and rank correlation 0.7833. User demeaning plus a random grand-mean anchor reduces absolute MAE by 80.0%, but centered MAE by only 21.0%, without reliably improving rank. A complete-support ledger allocates weighted squared error mainly to within-video residual (72.41%) and video mix (23.90%), with 3.65% from random support. In a frozen later test, early category calibration reaches MAE 0.0251 versus 0.0531 for scalar calibration; their direct difference is -0.0280 [-0.0296, -0.0172]. Decision evidence is cutoff-specific: the nominal top-10 regret change for row-weighted demeaning versus naive is -0.0062 [-0.0084, -0.0003], while top-5 and top-20 intervals include zero. The six-contrast family-wise top-10 interval [-0.0136, 0.0013] includes zero. An outcome-free disjoint randomized-reference split also leaves all six nominal contrasts covering zero. A known-truth stress test shows incomplete improvement under a mean-additive positive control and failure under item mix and weak overlap. All decompositions are descriptive and each result is conditional on its overlap cohort. KuaiRand intervals quantify user-cluster variation conditional on the realized catalog and calendar; we claim neither intrinsic category effects nor a universally valid correction.

papers.title: Low-Terahertz Channel Performance in Falling Wheat for Moisture Sensing
papers.abstract: Terahertz (THz) waves are highly sensitive to water and therefore offer a promising noncontact approach to wheat moisture sensing, but existing THz studies have been limited to static samples. This article investigates moisture sensing based on the performance of a THz channel in falling wheat, as encountered at grain intake. The channel power loss is measured at six frequencies from 120 to 320 GHz for three moisture contents and interpreted with a physics-based model that couples the double-Debye permittivity of water, Landau-Lifshitz-Looyenga mixing, and Lorenz-Mie extinction. The model reproduces the measured loss. Above the extinction maximum, the dielectric moisture response peaks where the wavelength approaches the kernel diameter, and that a two-frequency loss ratio removes the loading dependence. A channel-level analysis of QPSK and 16-QAM links shows that a 1 dB moisture-induced loss change alters the bit error rate (BER) by a factor of 3 to 30. THz communication channels at grain intake could therefore sense moisture as a byproduct of data transmission.

authors.name: Jiabiao Zhao
authors.institution: Beijing Research Institute of Mechanical and Electrical Technology

papers.title: Cross-Codec Robustness in Speech Watermarking
papers.abstract: Generative speech models synthesize audio that is difficult to distinguish from human recordings. Synthetic speech can be watermarked as a proactive disclosure method, but watermarking models remain vulnerable to resynthesis attacks using neural audio codecs. This article investigates speech watermarking robustness across neural codec and digital signal processing attacks, when specific neural codecs are used for channel augmentation during training. We also present a novel zero-bit watermarking system that uses Descript Audio Codec as the generator. Our results demonstrate that the choice of augmentation codec significantly influences robustness generalization. Experiments show that augmentation with low-bitrate, high-quality neural codecs-Mimi and SNAC-results in promising robustness against unseen neural codecs and traditional attacks with limited quality impact.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This work investigates the application of Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks to the binary classification of sleep-disordered breathing events in time-series data, aiming to distinguish between apneic and normal breathing episodes. A variational classical--quantum architecture is proposed and evaluated against classical Recurrent Neural Network models. Experiments were conducted on multiple real-world datasets with varying levels of complexity to assess the strengths and limitations of the quantum approach. In the comparative analysis, both classical and quantum models showed comparable performance. The quantum model achieved superior performance on the smallest dataset, while yielding slightly weaker results in the most complex setting. However, the quantum approach exhibited notable strengths, such as competitive performance despite a drastically reduced parameter count and low-qubit regime, as well as good generalization capabilities. These results suggest that, despite current hardware and algorithmic limitations, variational quantum recurrent models represent a promising alternative for time-series classification as Quantum Computing technologies continue to mature.

papers.title: Current-Future Rate Tradeoffs in ISAC Under Random Path Changes
papers.abstract: In mobile wireless links, motion changes path directions and visibility, and blockage can shift communication to a different propagation path. Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a base station (BS) to use echoes of data transmissions to monitor these changes and guide subsequent beam selection. Illuminating objects that govern future path availability may reduce the beamforming gain on the current communication route. Existing sensing-communication tradeoffs and dynamic beam-control frameworks do not directly quantify the future communication gain from this current-rate sacrifice. We quantify sensing value by the future-rate gain enabled by echo-adaptive beam selection. We derive explicit expressions for the future communication gain and the net gain after accounting for the current-rate loss. The analysis uses a coupled communication-echo channel with binary-state Markov motion over a finite burst informed by one processed echo. We show that monitoring is worthwhile when its future-rate gain exceeds the current loss, while more informative observations yield zero additional future rate if they cannot change any future optimal beam. We derive interpretable gain bounds exposing the roles of improved scene discrimination, motion memory and future beam-rate differences. Reciprocal-channel tests demonstrate positive net accumulated-rate gains from monitoring a moving blocker during reflected-path service, including continuous position uncertainty.

authors.name: Zhaofeng Liu
authors.institution: National Institute of Clean and Low-Carbon Energy

papers.title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
papers.abstract: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.

authors.name: Håkon Noren Myhr
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

papers.title: A Simulation-Driven Digital Workflow Integrating Bayesian Optimization for Early-Stage Process Design: A Methyl Acetate Production Case Study
papers.abstract: Methyl acetate production via direct carbonylation of dimethyl ether and carbon monoxide involves strong nonlinear interactions among reactor operation, recycle structure, and energy consumption, making conventional simulation-based optimization computationally demanding. In this work, a data-driven framework integrating steady-state process simulation, surrogate modeling, and Bayesian optimization was developed for process intensification. A dataset of 2730 steady-state simulations was generated using a Python-based automated process simulation workflow and a structured design of experiments across the operating domain. Surrogate models were trained to predict carbon conversion yield (C-yield) and cost of specific energy consumption (C-SEC), with neural network-based models showing the best predictive performance and robustness. These models were integrated into a multi-objective Bayesian optimization framework to identify optimal operating regions. Results indicate that high C-yield (up to ~95%) can be achieved with reduced energy cost through lower recycle flow rates and compression demand. Pareto analysis revealed a nonlinear trade-off between C-yield and C-SEC, where further improvements near the conversion limit require disproportionately higher energy input. Validation against rigorous simulations showed deviations below 3% for C-yield and 10% for C-SEC.

authors.name: Trung Thanh Nguyen
authors.institution: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City

papers.title: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics Reveals Grotthuss Transport in Concentrated Electrolytes
papers.abstract: Proton transfer is responsible for the anomalous high conductivity in acidic or basic aqueous solutions. Yet, the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the conductivity of concentrated aqueous solutions is unknown. In this work, we compute the transport properties of KOH(aq) systems with different concentrations, using Molecular Dynamics simulations with a Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIP), which includes proton transfer. We quantify the contribution of the proton transfer mechanism to the diffusivities of hydroxide ions and water molecules, and the ionic conductivity and transport numbers of the electrolytes. The contribution is substantial at lower concentrations, but diminishes at very high concentrations.

authors.name: Øystein Gullbrekken
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Sondre Kvalvåg Schnell
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Density-Aware Reward Scaling: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Reward-Proportional Sampling
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning objectives that maximize expected return can concentrate probability mass on a small subset of high-reward outcomes, limiting diversity when multiple distinct solutions are desirable. We introduce Density-Aware Reward Scaling (DARS), a simple reward-processing mechanism that promotes reward-proportional sampling in continuous outcome spaces while retaining standard policy-gradient training. DARS estimates the local density of outcomes within each on-policy rollout group and inversely scales rewards by this density. The method requires no learned density model, auxiliary objective, critic, or modification to the underlying policy-gradient objective. In a controlled multimodal navigation task, DARS-GRPO avoids the single-mode collapse exhibited by GRPO and closely recovers the target mode allocation. Applied to text-to-image prompt adaptation, DARS-GRPO consistently improves image and prompt diversity across datasets, Policy LMs, and reward settings while maintaining good semantic alignment. These results show that density-aware reward scaling provides a lightweight way to improve coverage of diverse high-reward outcomes within existing reinforcement-learning pipelines.

authors.name: Ria Shekhawat
authors.institution: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

papers.title: A Detailed Polarimetric Imaging Study of Type II Solar Radio Burst with the MWA: Detection of Linear Polarization
papers.abstract: Type II radio bursts, produced by magnetohydrodynamic shocks propagating through the solar corona and interplanetary medium, serve as powerful diagnostics of shock properties and ambient coronal magnetic fields. While circular polarization in type II bursts has been extensively studied, most investigations rely on dynamic spectra (DS), providing only spatially integrated measurements. DS obscures spatial variations of the polarization sign and magnitude, potentially causing cancellation effects and misrepresenting true polarization levels. We present a full-polarimetric imaging study of a metric type II burst observed with the Murchison Widefield Array at 78--133 MHz. Remarkably, we report the first detection of linear polarization in a metric type II burst, reaching a polarization fraction of $\sim12\%$ with significant spectro-temporal variability across observing bands. The spectro-temporal, spatial, and morphological properties found in this study establish linear polarization as a new diagnostic of large-scale coronal and interplanetary magnetic field structure through full-Stokes imaging of metric solar radio bursts -- challenging conventional paradigms predicting negligible linear polarization from coherent plasma emission processes.

papers.title: Descending Everest, Part II: Oracle Complexity of Minimizing a Sum of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions
papers.abstract: We study the minimization of the average of $n$ convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds $R$ on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and $\delta$ on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order $n(1+(L_1R)^{2/3}) +\sqrt{\frac{n(L_0+L_1^2\delta)R^2}{\varepsilon}+n(L_1R)^2}$. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.

authors.name: Alexander V. Gasnikov
authors.institution: Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology

papers.title: QPP-Aware MCX over Tactical Edge 3D Networks in Public-Safety Communications
papers.abstract: During disasters, public mobile networks may become unavailable, congested, or degraded, requiring deployable communication systems to support emergency operations. This article proposes a mission-critical communications system supporing Mission Critical Push-to-Talk (MCPTT), Mission Critical Video (MCVideo), and Mission Critical Data (MCData) over a private 5G standalone network with Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) connectivity. A context-aware Quality, Priority, and Pre-emption (QPP) mechanism is proposed to dynamically adapt network resource allocation according to the operational state of Mission Critical Services (MCX). Extensions to the Open5GS Policy Control Function (PCF) and Session Management Function (SMF) enable priority and pre-emption updates for existing flows without session re-establishment. The architecture supports tactical edge deployment of service and media functions while retaining centralized service control. Experimental evaluation considers three configurations: terrestrial backhaul with centralized media processing, satellite backhaul with centralized media processing, and satellite backhaul with edge media processing. Results show that tactical edge processing reduces communication delay and packet loss. Under satellite backhaul, edge processing reduced the 95th-percentile MCPTT audio transport delay by 60.03 ms and packet loss by 9.42 percentage points, while achieving a 95th-percentile MCPTT access time of 184.52 ms. These findings demonstrate the benefits of tactical edge media processing and provide an experimental foundation for context-aware priority mechanisms in public-safety networks integrating terrestrial and non-terrestrial components.

authors.name: Marco Araujo
authors.institution: Universidade Federal de Juiz de Fora

papers.title: Interstellar and intergalactic medium in the ultraviolet band
papers.abstract: This article presents an overview of key scientific challenges in the astrophysics and astrochemistry of the interstellar and intergalactic media. Addressing many of these challenges will become possible with the Russian space observatory Spektr-UF, which is currently being prepared for launch. The ultraviolet (UV) spectral range is critically important for studying the evolution of the Universe, as it contains fundamental absorption and emission lines of most chemical elements and the most important molecules. These lines make it possible to reliably determine the physical conditions and chemical composition of various astrophysical objects, as well as the characteristics of the processes occurring within them. The article examines the prospects for UV observations across a broad range of scientific problems, from investigating the epoch of helium reionization and the thermal history of the Universe to mapping ongoing star formation in galaxies. Dedicated sections address the study of the chemical evolution of galaxies at intermediate redshifts, the distribution of "hidden" baryons and metals, the small-scale structure of interstellar clouds, the physics of photodissociation regions and protoplanetary disks, and the modeling of UV emission from nebulae surrounding fast-moving pulsars. The high sensitivity and spectral resolution of the Spektr-UF instruments are expected to provide fundamentally new data across all these research areas, filling existing gaps in our understanding of the interstellar and intergalactic media.

authors.name: E. O. Vasiliev
authors.institution: P.N. Lebedev Physical Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences

papers.title: Effect of compensation on magnetic ordering in (Ga,Mn)As
papers.abstract: The real mechanism of ferromagnetism in III-V diluted magnetic semiconductors such as Ga$_{1-x}$Mn$_x$As is still debated. The experimental results point out the realization of appreciable ferromagnetism at filling of the impurity band close to one-half that can be expressed in terms of compensation degree. Based on our recent results on the existence of two competing mechanisms of pair indirect exchange (with ferro- and antiferro alignment of Mn $d$ shells), a theory of magnetic ordering in (Ga,Mn)As is presented. The molecular-field-like equation is derived in which the effective exchange constant contains all necessary information about material, including the Mn content, the compensation degree, the crystal coordination, and the parameters of two competing pair exchange interactions. The Curie temperature depends crucially on the compensation degree. Depending on Mn content and compensation degree, three possible magnetic phases (paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, and spin-glass-like) are predicted. However, the spin-glass-like phase in (Ga,Mn)As is apparently not realized due to the additional inevitable compensation caused by As antisites. The phase transition into the ferromagnetic state occurs not only with Mn content variation but through the change of the compensation degree as well. The new mechanism of photoferromagnetic effect is predicted and discussed in the context of possible clarification of the magnetic ordering mechanism. It is assumed that the main obstacle to a possible increase in the Curie temperature is the increasing contribution of the antiferromagnetic superexchange between the nearest-neighbor Mn's, rather than compensatory (electric or magnetic) effects from Mn interstitials, as was previously stated. The comparison of our predictions with available experimental data is presented.

papers.title: Quasiconformal distortion of the lower dimension and applications
papers.abstract: We study the distortion of the lower dimension and lower spectrum of sets under quasiconformal mappings. As an application, we verify weighted Hardy--Sobolev inequalities in Euclidean domains arising as quasiconformal images of domains with sufficiently regular boundaries. The regularity in question is phrased in terms of estimates for either the Assouad or the lower dimension of the complement. We also provide dilatation-dependent classification results for certain planar open sets.

papers.intro:
The theory of Hardy–Sobolev inequalities effectively demonstrates the close interplay between analytic inequalities and the geometry of domains. The topic is classical, originating in Hardy’s investigation of Hilbert’s inequality. Hardy stated the general integral inequality for p>1p>1 in 1920 [32] and published a proof of its sharp form on the half-line five years later [33]. We refer to [47] for a detailed account of the history behind Hardy’s inequality. The classical integral inequality is an LpL^{p} bound for the averaging operator on (0,∞)(0,\infty), which yields a weighted derivative estimate. More recent formulations of these inequalities involve control of weighted norms of functions by weighted norms of their gradients, where the weights in question involve distance to the boundary of the domain. The validity of such inequalities reflects quantitative geometric properties of the boundary of the underlying domain [49], but their significance extends beyond analysis and geometry, for instance to spectral theory and mathematical physics [21] or to the regularity theory of stable solutions to semilinear elliptic equations in high dimension [15, (1.1.4)]. In recent years, the theory has been developed in metric measure spaces, where often upper gradients and Poincaré inequalities provide the appropriate framework [46], [45], [39].

Quasiconformal and quasisymmetric mapping theory provides another setting in which analytic and geometric properties are closely related. It is a field with a rich history and connections to diverse areas, such as elliptic partial differential equations [5], nonlinear potential theory [35], and geometric group theory [51, 13]. We refer to the books of Väisälä [59] and Heinonen [36] for detailed expositions. The uniformization problem is a central question in quasiconformal mapping theory. Roughly speaking, it asks when a space can be transformed in a controlled way into a ‘canonical’ space with better geometric properties. The Euclidean unit interval, unit disk, and unit ball are examples of what is perceived as a canonical space. The Riemann Mapping Theorem is a signature result of this kind, but versions of this principle hold in higher Euclidean dimensions and metric spaces, the latter motivated by applications in geometric group theory and topology. A related question is to classify spaces, typically subsets of Euclidean spaces, up to quasiconformal equivalence in a quantitative way, via the dilation of the mappings in question. The celebrated paper of Gehring and Väisälä [29] made a gigantic contribution to this area, and these results have been further developed by many different authors throughout the years (see [20], [40], [11], [60] for a non-exhaustive list). We also refer to the surveys by Ntalampekos [54] and Bonk [14] for more information about the uniformization problem.

With an eye towards the behavior of Hardy inequalities under quasiconformal mappings (Theorem 1.3) and the quasiconformal classification problem for domains with cusps (Theorem 1.4), we establish quantitative dimension distortion estimates for quasiconformal maps. The broader program of quasiconformal dimension distortion has a long history of its own and dates back to the work of Gehring and Väisälä in the early 1970s [30, 31]. Its development is closely connected to the higher integrability of quasiconformal mappings [31]. Astala’s celebrated theorem [6] provides sharp conclusions for the Sobolev regularity of planar quasiconformal maps, and thereby yields sharp bounds for the distortion of Hausdorff dimension. Kaufman’s decisive contribution in [44] was the introduction of an appropriate stopping-time argument in this context, which enabled extension of such distortion results to other notions of dimension such as box-counting and packing dimension. Kaufman’s work inspired an avalanche of results by many different authors and the field remains very active. A partial and incomplete list of papers in this direction includes [22], [1], [37], [38], [17], [55], [18], [7], [8], [19], and [10]. A survey tracing the development of the subject from these early papers up to the most recent contributions can be found in [57].

Different notions of dimension capture different aspects of size and local scaling. A relatively new dimension notion, at least compared to the Hausdorff dimension, is that defined by Assouad in [2] (see also [3, 4]) which now bears his name. More recently, Fraser and Yu introduced the Assouad spectrum [23], a one-parameter family of dimensions naturally interpolating between the upper box dimension and the Assouad dimension. We refer to the book by Fraser [26] for a thorough introduction to the Assouad dimension and spectrum, along with applications of these notions to fractal geometry, probability, number theory, and functional analysis. In this paper we focus on the lower (Assouad) dimension, introduced by Larman [48], and the lower spectrum, introduced by Fraser and Yu [23], which are essentially the dual notions to the Assouad dimension and spectrum, respectively. Recent work on these dimensions includes quasi-Lipschitz invariance [16], regularity properties of measures [34], and the classification of attainable lower spectra [9]. One-parameter families such as the Assouad and lower spectra reside within the broader framework of dimension interpolants which has been heavily advocated by Falconer, Fraser, and their collaborators. A nice overview of the topic can be found in [25].

papers.title: Beyond Foundation Models: PFN Priors Improve Tabular Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.abstract: Synthetic priors have so far served one purpose: pretraining tabular foundation models. We ask whether the same priors can improve conventional tabular models, which are trained from scratch on each dataset. We propose PriorTune, a method that meta-tunes hyperparameter configurations on synthetic tasks alone. Offline, for a given model, we fit a pool of configurations on datasets sampled from a published PFN prior and greedily select the subset with the highest winrate over the random baseline. Online, a new dataset fits only the selected configurations, so the gain comes at no extra cost. Empirically, we observe that scaling both the number of configurations and synthetic datasets has an equal scaling effect on the performance of the final subset of configurations, which we also explain theoretically. On the full BeyondArena benchmark, LightGBM with TabPrep features with our configurations ranks above TabPFN-3 and RealMLP, while being much more efficient at inference. Overall, our results establish existing PFN priors as a scalable source of meta-training data for hyperparameter selection for non-foundational tabular models.

papers.title: Single-anchor Delta-learning with the cluster Gutzwiller approximation: predicting phase boundaries of strongly correlated bosons in optical lattices
papers.abstract: The cluster Gutzwiller method is widely used to study strongly correlated bosonic systems in optical lattices because it explicitly treats quantum fluctuations within a cluster. However, its computational cost grows exponentially with the cluster size, making large-cluster phase diagrams computationally expensive. To reduce this cost, we recently introduced Delta-learning into cluster Gutzwiller calculations and proposed multipoint regression Delta-learning (MPR-Delta), which learns the difference between small- and large-cluster results from four high-cost critical points of the target cluster and thereby predicts the complete target phase boundary. For sufficiently large target clusters, however, even computing one critical point on the phase boundary is already expensive, so obtaining four such points remains highly costly. A natural question then arises: can the complete target phase boundary be predicted with fewer high-cost critical points of the target cluster? To address this question, we propose single-anchor Delta-learning (SA-Delta), which requires only a single high-cost critical point of the target cluster to reconstruct the complete target phase boundary, thereby greatly reducing the computational cost. We test this framework on several classes of Bose-Hubbard models and find that, in the cases considered, it achieves lower reconstruction errors with fewer high-cost points than MPR-Delta. The combination of SA-Delta with the cluster Gutzwiller approximation thus provides an efficient framework for studying phase transitions of strongly correlated bosonic systems in complex optical lattices, and may be extended to more complex quantum many-body systems.

papers.title: Pseudo-Fredholm operators form a regularity on Hilbert spaces
papers.abstract: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. We prove that the class of pseudo-Fredholm operators on $H$ is a regularity in the sense of Kordula and M\"uller. We also prove that the classes of left and right generalized Drazin invertible operators are regularities on $H$. Consequently, the generalized Kato spectrum and the corresponding generalized Drazin spectra satisfy the spectral mapping theorem. We construct an operator $T$ on a separable complex Banach space such that $T^2$ is right generalized Drazin invertible whereas $T$ is not pseudo-Fredholm. In particular, the power axiom need not hold for pseudo-Fredholm operators on Banach spaces. Finally, we show that the accumulation sets of the approximate point and surjectivity spectra define regularities on Banach spaces, yielding another proof of the regularity of generalized Drazin invertible operators in $\B(X)$.

papers.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
papers.abstract: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: our review of leading journals finds that about 50% of articles state or imply LWD, versus 7% describing an imputation model. Assuming oracle regression with all required values observed consistently estimates the population average treatment effect, we ask when complete-case regression remains consistent. With constant effects, we offer two checks: whether covariates and the missing indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools valid within-covariate comparisons appropriately, potentially using inverse treatment-propensity weighting (IPW). For heterogeneous effects, assuming conditional effects carry over to the population, we reweight comparisons to the population covariate distribution. Simulations and empirical illustrations from American politics, comparative politics, and international relations demonstrate the framework's use and show why a missing-at-random (MAR) classification, although useful for assessing imputation, does not by itself establish whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the target population ATE. Thus, we recommend adding the missing indicator and its causes to causal models, then checking adjustment and weighting for LWD.

papers.title: CaliSplat: Sparse Gaussian Fitting and Calibrated Rate Allocation for Image Compression
papers.abstract: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and lightweight alternative for image representation, enabling fast deterministic decoding without a heavy neural synthesis network. However, existing per-image Gaussian codecs still require costly image-specific optimization to determine how limited Gaussian capacity should be distributed across heterogeneous regions. We introduce CaliSplat, an optimization-efficient Gaussian image codec that selectively explores candidate representations and globally allocates a constrained Gaussian budget. We exploit the closed-form reconstruction error of the single-Gaussian case as an inexpensive measure of local difficulty, fitting higher-capacity candidates only in regions where additional Gaussians are likely to be useful. To reduce selection errors caused by mismatched convergence rates across candidate sizes, a small set of longer-horizon fits is used to calibrate short-horizon distortion estimates before global budget-aware selection. The selected representation is then compressed into a bitstream. Across standard and large image datasets, CaliSplat achieves competitive or superior rate--distortion performance while reducing per-image fitting time by $3.0\times$--$15.7\times$ compared with representative Gaussian codecs. It further maintains high-throughput deterministic decoding at $175.9$--$478.2$~MP/s. These results demonstrate that content-adaptive Gaussian compression can substantially reduce per-image optimization cost while preserving strong reconstruction quality and efficient explicit decoding.

authors.name: Zhenbang Zhang
authors.institution: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
