papers.title: Interpretable Early Termination of Web Navigation Agents via Closed Sequential Pattern Mining
papers.abstract: Web navigation agents built on open-weight language models fail often and fail late, with most of the tokens spent after the trajectory has become unrecoverable. Recent work has shown that early termination is a viable cost-reduction strategy, but existing approaches produce opaque termination decisions that do not support diagnosis or human oversight. In this work we apply closed sequential pattern mining (BIDE+) to K-step prefixes of agent execution traces to produce a small, human-reviewable failure-signature library that organizes into a four-category failure taxonomy with associated repair recommendations. We use a multi-variant evaluation protocol that explicitly removes contamination artifacts (zero-step crashes and trivially separable single-step successes) so that reported detection accuracy reflects behavioral discrimination rather than trace-length distributions. We evaluate our methodology on 1,544 MiniWoB++ traces collected from three open-weight language models, achieving the best F1 at K=3 on the Exclude-errors configuration across eight methods (0.717), recovering 88% of test-set failures within three steps, and supporting an early-termination policy that saves 26.3% of tokens at 92% precision.

papers.title: Is This 3D Asset Usable? Beyond the Beauty Render for Asset Curation
papers.abstract: Large 3D repositories make it easy to collect assets, but difficult to determine whether they can be reused reliably across scene assembly, editing, rendering, game production, and training-data construction. An asset can look plausible in RGB while hiding disconnected geometry, problematic UV organization, or materials that fail to resolve correctly after import. We introduce Diagnostic Rendered Evidence (DRE): aligned beauty, wireframe, and UV-seam-plus-wireframe views scored by pass-specific frozen ViT classifiers and combined through late fusion. On 1,234 human labeled TexVerse assets, nested grouped evaluation achieves 86.36% balanced accuracy and 88.32% bad-asset recall. On a separate, balanced 764 external reference test, DRE achieved 88.9% balanced reference-label accuracy. Our method requires only an imported asset and renderer-derived evidence, without repository identity, creator, popularity, text, or source metadata at inference. Our results support cross-corpus portability and show that purpose built diagnostic views expose defects that just the beauty views can miss. Webpage: https://rbz-99.github.io/is-this-3d-asset-usable/

papers.title: Associahedra are 12-colourable
papers.abstract: We present a proper 12-colouring for all associahedra. This gives the first constant upper bound on chromatic number for this family, and disproves a conjecture of Fabila-Monroy et al. from 2009.

papers.title: A wider state, not wider arithmetic, for single-precision time integration
papers.abstract: Single precision (FP32) halves the memory and data movement of double precision (FP64), and on accelerators is often several times faster. Its rounding errors are harmless except in the stored state. A modified equation for Runge-Kutta methods in Shu-Osher form and linear multistep methods separates the rounding of the stored state, a forcing proportional to $1/\Delta t$, from truncation and from right-hand-side rounding, which sets a $\Delta t$-independent floor. We bound this forcing for strong-stability-preserving schemes and identify two mechanisms that keep its sign fixed, so it accumulates as a bias: past a turnaround step, refining the step increases the error, in FP64 as in FP32. For a model oscillator the analysis predicts the floor and the FP32-to-FP64 ratios of turnaround step and minimum error within 30%. Our remedy needs no FP64 arithmetic: each state variable is stored as the unevaluated sum of two FP32 numbers, updated with error-free transformations, while every right-hand-side evaluation stays in FP32. Unlike compensated summation, it needs no rewriting of the scheme. In model problems from geophysical flow, mechanical dynamics and celestial mechanics, with five Runge-Kutta and multistep schemes, it restores design-order convergence to the floor. In large-eddy simulations of a high-lift airplane wing on three refined grids, up to 544 million cells, with time steps $\Delta t$, $\Delta t/2$ and $\Delta t/4$, FP32 overpredicts the lift by 2.1, 4.5 and 7.7%, while the two-float lift agrees with FP64 within 0.3% on every grid, and on graphics processing units the production solver runs 1.6 to 2.7 times faster than FP64.

papers.title: Canonical Projectivization of Algebraic Varieties in Characteristic Zero
papers.abstract: We construct a canonical projectivization of every smooth proper algebraic variety $X$ in characteristic zero. Once a principalization procedure is fixed, the construction gives a finite sequence of blowups in smooth centers with smooth projective endpoint, natural under semilinear isomorphisms and preserving the quasi-projective core, the intersection of all maximal quasi-projective open subsets. At each stage we select finitely many ideals near the generic points of the image in $X$ of the boundary of a maximal quasi-projective open. Principalizing their product strictly lowers the dimension of that image. The selection is defined intrinsically, without a polarization or a chosen projective modification; a Hilbert scheme argument proves its finiteness. Naturality embeds the automorphism group in that of a smooth projective variety of the same dimension. We then extend the construction to smooth proper integral algebraic spaces, obtaining canonical projectivizations of all compact connected Moishezon manifolds.

papers.title: Rotating two-dimensional Bose--Einstein condensates in power-law traps: collapse, Thomas--Fermi scaling, and the inverse-square endpoint
papers.abstract: In two dimensions, the kinetic and contact energies scale identically under dilation, a trap $V=r^s/s$ as $\lambda^{-s}$. We follow this balance through the power-law family $-2\le s\le4$, $s\neq0$, for both signs of the coupling $g$, with rotation, using scaling bounds, radial solutions, Bogoliubov spectra, and two-dimensional imaginary-time states. Attraction collapses the cloud at the Townes coupling $g_{*}$ in every trap, with width $\ell\propto\delta^{1/(s+2)}$, $\delta=1-|g|/g_{*}$; repulsion spreads it to a Thomas--Fermi (TF) radius $\propto g^{1/(s+2)}$. A rotating collapse leaves the axis once the rotation frequency $\Omega$ exceeds its dipole frequency, which softens only for $s>2$; in a quartic trap this happens at $\delta\simeq0.32\,\Omega^6$, within $3\%$ of the Bogoliubov threshold; it then collapses on the minimum ring of the rotating-frame potential, which also empties a repulsive TF cloud at $\Omega=(3g/\pi)^{1/6}$. For repulsive vortex states the TF energy error splits exactly into a density-gradient and a flow part of comparable or larger size. At $s=-2$ only the cutoff sets a length: the energy is exactly covariant with it, the condensate falls to the center for both signs, and repulsion leaves a halo of density $\propto1/(gr^2)$ whose extent grows exponentially with $g$. Near collapse, split-step imaginary time has a first-order stationary bias invisible to residual tests.

papers.title: An Information Budget for Label-Noise Memorization, and What Statistical Complexity Tracks: A Study with Multilayer Perceptrons
papers.abstract: How much label noise has a network memorized, and when? We study a multilayer perceptron and what statistical complexity adds to a description of its predictions. Standard identities decompose predictive information into signal, memorization, and heterogeneity. The memorization term vanishes in the population under the stated noise-independence condition. A Fano-type bound relates it to training accuracies, but the memorized fraction M provides no upper bound. Across 89 MNIST runs with ten pre-specified hypotheses (five supported, four unsupported, one not testable), normalized memorization information rose with M on training samples, remained near zero on held-out samples with fresh noisy labels, and was close to its Fano bound. Unlike raw M, it has a zero population null under the independence condition and chance correction largely removed this difference. When every label was replaced by an incorrect class, test accuracy fell to 0.5%, yet predictions retained information about the true class. Mean statistical complexity peaked before memorization at corruption rates up to 40%. At higher rates, its peak fell within the memorization phase, near the epoch when mean training confidence reached 0.6 and the two could not be separated. As a stopping rule, it matched established rules only at low noise and detected corrupted samples less well than simple label-free scores. An exploratory extension of 280 runs covering Fashion-MNIST, pair-flip noise, and four training variants yielded similar results under uniform noise, but not pair-flip noise, where complexity peaked within two epochs. Conclusions are limited to this architecture, two small datasets, and synthetic noise.

papers.title: Conjecture B for $X_{10}$ and its genus-two mirror
papers.abstract: We prove Conjecture B of Akhtar--Coates--Corti--Heuberger--Kasprzyk--Oneto--Petracci--Prince--Tveiten unconditionally for the normalized family of maximally mutable Laurent polynomials with prescribed $T$-binomial edge coefficients associated with the degree-10 orbifold del Pezzo hypersurface $X_{10}\subset\mathbb{P}(1,2,3,5)$. An explicit $S$-extended quantum-period calculation determines the affine mirror map $\lambda=a-346$ and proves that the regularized quantum period equals the classical period as a formal power series throughout the family.

papers.title: Are We Just Applying LLMs? What SE Research Studies, Underexplores, and Could Do Next in the LLM Era
papers.abstract: Is AI taking over software engineering research? By 2025, AI appeared in more than half of the research-track papers at ICSE, FSE, and ASE. Yet ubiquity alone cannot show whether AI expanded the publication portfolio, displaced other work, or redirected the intellectual agenda. We investigate this shift through a census of 4,790 research papers (three SE conferences; 2018--2026) and free-form responses from 244 SE researchers discussing the future of the SE research community (ICSE 2026 FoSE survey). We found that while AI is taking over, it is not simply replacing non-AI research; it is unevenly reorganizing SE research around its capabilities. AI accounted for 93.1% of publication growth, but expansion in some venues and problem areas concealed contraction in others. The LLM wave also changed the field's tools more than its problem boundaries: 92.6% of LLM-wave AI papers revisit established SE problems, while most new problems arise from the introduction of LLMs in the SE process themselves. Engagement with AI remains predominantly downstream: 95.7% of AI papers apply AI or evaluate and support its use, while only 4.3% interrogate the paradigm or develop alternatives. The FoSE survey reveals a similar imbalance between recognition and response. AI-driven change was the second-most frequent concern about the field's future 20.2%, yet only 7.0% of responses mentioned AI when researchers were asked to identify one change the community should make. Together, our findings reveal a field reorganizing an inherited agenda around AI faster than it is questioning that reorganization. We discuss how SE can respond by building cumulatively across technological waves, strengthening evaluation and assurance, developing SE-native foundations, and studying software engineering in an AI-transformed world.

papers.title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
papers.abstract: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.

papers.title: Birefringence in non-linear electrodynamics emerging from a Lorentz-symmetry violation scenario
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the classical properties of a non-linear electrodynamics that emerges from one loop effective action for fermions coupled to an antisymmetric background tensor, that breaks the Lorentz symmetry in the model. The conservation laws are obtained through the Belinfante-Rosenfeld energy-momentum tensor in the non-linear electrodynamics that provides the energy density, the Poynting vector, the linear momentum and the stress tensor. In particular, this Lorentz symmetry violation breaks the symmetric index of the energy-momentum tensor, but it preserves the gauge invariance, as we expect. We introduce the prescription of a magnetic background field, that we consider constant and uniform. For propagation effects, the model is linearized by the magnetic background. This prescription allows us investigations of the plane wave propagation in the presence of an external magnetic field. In this context, we obtain the constitutive relations of the material medium, that behaves like an bi-anisotropic medium. Thereby, we calculate the refractive index whose one of the solutions show the total absorption of the wave in the medium. Using the wave equation for linear polarization, we investigate the birefringence phenomenon when the linear wave polarization changes with the magnetic background direction. The birefringence is so related to one of the spatial component of the LSV tensor in which we estimate through the PVLS experiment. We use one of the dispersion relations to obtain the kinematic of the Compton effect in the presence of the LSV parameter.

papers.title: Bright Siren Cosmology Beyond Fisher: DALI Forecasts for Third-Generation Gravitational Wave Observatories
papers.abstract: In this work we assess non-Gaussian extensions of Fisher forecasting based on the Derivative Approximation for Likelihoods (DALI). We simulate ensembles of bright siren catalogs for third-generation observatories, adopting a Cosmic Explorer (CE) and a triangular Einstein Telescope (ET) network, frequency-domain inspiral waveforms, and selection-motivated priors for counterpart detection. We reconstruct approximate likelihoods using Fisher and the first DALI correction (Doublet), and propagate the inferred distance information to cosmological inference in a w0waCDM model. We find that the Doublet approximation provides tighter cosmological constraints than the Fisher approximation, reducing the inferred uncertainties by approximately a factor of two in agreement with non-approximate likelihood (called Exact) results. For our GW network onfiguration, 300 bright-siren detections up to z=1 yield an H0 precision of ~2.7% with the Doublet approximation, compared with ~2.5% for the exact likelihood. The adopted non-Gaussian GW priors induce a systematic displacement of the inferred luminosity distances from the fiducial values, which is also present in the exact GW reconstruction and propagates into the cosmological parameters. Compared with the exact cosmological likelihood, the Doublet results differ by only ~10% on average in the parameter uncertainties, compared with ~195% for the traditional Fisher approximation. The Doublet approximation also substantially reduces the computational cost, by a factor of ~55 for the GW analysis and by ~12 for cosmological likelihood evaluations, yielding an estimated reduction of ~55 in the total computational cost of the combined analysis. Our results show the potential of DALI-based approximations to provide accurate and computationally efficient tools for forecasting in bright siren cosmology.

papers.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
papers.abstract:
We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness.
  Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

papers.title: Black Hole Mass Estimation of a Background Quasar in the Vicinity of the cD Galaxy Holm 15A
papers.abstract: This study analyzes spectra from the central region of the galaxy cluster Abell 85 observed with GTC/OSIRIS, focusing on the cD galaxy Holm 15A and the point-like X-ray source SDSS J004150.75-091824.3, projected $13.74\arcsec$ from Holm 15A. For the latter, we found it is a background quasar with a redshift of $1.56386 \pm 0.00397$, ruling out the possibility of it being a rogue BH gravitationally bound to Holm 15A. In addition, using single-epoch spectroscopy, we report that the quasar J004150 hosts a Supermassive Black Hole (SMBH) with a mass of $\log(M_{\text{BH}}/\mathrm{M_{\odot}}) = 8.72 \pm 0.26$.

papers.title: Singular solutions from simple Euclidean Jordan algebras
papers.abstract: For every finite-dimensional simple Euclidean Jordan algebra $V$ of rank at least three, we realize the function $\operatorname{tr}(x^3)/|x|$ on its traceless subspace $V_0$ as a $C^{1,1}\setminus C^2$ viscosity solution of a uniformly elliptic equation $F(D^2 u)=0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{\operatorname{dim}V_0}$. This unifies and extends earlier constructions from Cartan isoparametric cubics, Hsiang minimal cubics, and traceless real symmetric matrices.

papers.title: Continuum Dirac Theory and Nonlinear Extensions of a Chain of Alternating non-linear springs: an SSH version of the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model
papers.abstract: A mechanical version of the SSH model, made of equal masses joined by two alternating non-linear springs is studied in the continuum limit. Such a non-linear dimerized mechanical chain generates a nonlinear, dispersive, two-field hyperbolic system of Boussinesq type of differential equations, describing coupled acoustic and gapped optical fields. The corresponding Lagrangian density is found, revealing that the acoustic and optical degrees of freedom are coupled through a structure that is formally analogous to a synthetic spin-orbit coupling, where the spatial motion is locked to the internal sublattice degree of freedom. An emergent non-Abelian Berry connection term also appears. Some particular solitary-wave solutions are found using variational theory, as the effective optical field obeys an undamped and unforced cubic-quintic Duffing equation. Near the Brillouin-zone edge, the system becomes a nonlinear Dirac field theory of the Soler type, providing a direct mechanical realization of interacting relativistic solitons. By factoring out fast spatial oscillations, an effective Jackiw-Rebbi Hamiltonian is obtained, with topological zero modes at domain walls. These modes are akin to the electronic flat bands in moire graphene systems associated with superconductivity and charge fractionalization. Finally, we discuss the mechanical rigidity transition and its effects on the fields as the system evolves toward the fully dimerized limit, in which the zero modes are floppy modes.

papers.title: Geometry, Topology, and Confined Spectra Around Anisotropic Cosmic Strings
papers.abstract: We study scalar, Dirac, and electromagnetic test fields on a two-parameter family of static spacetimes, labeled by an angular winding number $k$ and an anisotropy parameter $\alpha$ that shortens one direction of the transverse metric relative to the other. Only the members with $k=1$ and $\alpha<1$ are conical, as for an ordinary straight cosmic string. The remaining members are nonconical and, except in the flat cases, curved and nonvacuum. A common spin-weighted connection Laplacian organizes the local equations, while the curvature coupling, global field conditions, and constraints are fixed separately for each physical field. Explicit frame transitions remove spurious winding dependence in the flat limit. For the nonconical members of the family, isothermal coordinates yield an exact factorization of the indicial equation and determine its monodromy: the indicial exponents are independent of the anisotropy parameter, although the finite-domain eigenvalues are not. We derive variational bounds and a weak-anisotropy selection rule for the scalar spectrum. The electromagnetic equations are obtained from the four-potential in Lorenz gauge, with gauge-invariant transverse-electric (TE) and transverse-magnetic (TM) reductions and an annular transverse-electromagnetic (TEM) mode. Finite-element computations on an annulus, validated against benchmarks, are consistent with the bounds, confirm the selection rule, give MIT bag Dirac and conducting-wall Maxwell spectra, and reproduce the invariance of the transverse-electromagnetic capacity under $k\mapsto2-k$, an exact consequence of a radial inversion of the Dirichlet energy.

papers.title: Mitigating Return Drag and Regime Whipsaws in Sector Rotation: An Asymmetric Downside-Aware Nested Clustered Optimization Framework
papers.abstract: Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. We propose Asymmetric Downside-Risk Nested Clustered Optimization with Sticky Regime Dynamics (Asym-Sticky-NCO) for tactical sector rotation across all 11 S&P 500 GICS sectors. The framework substitutes symmetric covariance with the Bawa-Lindenberg downside semi-covariance matrix across both hierarchical tree clustering and two-stage allocation. Furthermore, we introduce a Sticky Gaussian HMM incorporating a diagonal self-transition persistence prior (\k{appa}) and confidence-adaptive boundaries ({\delta}) to enforce macroeconomic persistence. Strictly non-anticipative walk-forward backtesting across 65 out-of-sample months (August 2020 to December 2025) demonstrates that the architecture elevates CAGR from 10.65% (Plain NCO) to 13.41% (+276 bps/year), delivers a 97.74% total return versus 72.99%, suppresses maximum drawdown to 14.22% (versus 23.93% for the S&P 500), and achieves a Calmar ratio of 0.94 (+38.2% over S&P 500; +84.3% over Baseline Regime-NCO). Crucially, sticky dynamics cut regime whipsaws by 75.0% (from 16 to 4 switches) and reduce monthly turnover from 60.78% to 30.48%, addressing core limitations of machine learning asset allocation.

papers.title: The Min-Max theory of language behavior
papers.abstract: The "Min-Max" theory of language behavior proposes that humans engage simultaneously in minimization of processing effort and maximization of information content, and that this is a primary driver in language evolution (Ring, 2025). This claim seeks to unify observations from language processing (Mahowald et al., 2013; Futrell et al., 2015; Yadav et al., 2020; Hawkins, 2014), interaction (H\"orberg and Sjons, 2023; Tucker et al., 2025; Jaeger and Tily, 2011; Smith and Culbertson, 2025), and corpora (Levshina and Moran, 2021; Levshina, 2023; Newmeyer, 2017), which suggest that considerations of processing efficiency and information content are both implicated in human communication. The interaction between these two processes provides an explanation for human linguistic behavior at various levels (Linders and Louwerse, 2023) and predicts historical developments in language, i.e. related to word order (Ring, 2025). Given that the original formulation of the Min-Max theory is based on observational data, the current paper seeks to validate the theory mathematically. Through a series of experiments that use computational models to investigate the theory's predictions, pretrained and iterated learning models are queried with synthetic data. The experiments show that manipulating the variables of token length and the weight of information content in a tabula rasa model results in word order change, as predicted by the theory. The experiments also identify important differences between computational models and observations of human language data, suggesting that current transformer-based language models may not accurately represent psycholinguistic processes. The overall findings indicate that evolutionary trajectories in language are highly susceptible to minimization of processing and maximization of information content.

papers.title: Terrain-Surface-Area Cover from LiDAR: Inverse-Probability-Weighted Estimation and a Global Cram\'er-von Mises Lack-of-Fit Test
papers.abstract: Canopy cover is normally reported as a fraction of a horizontal map plane. When the domain of inference is the land surface, the appropriate target is the fraction of terrain surface area under canopy. We define this estimand on a C1 graph surface and show that it differs from vertical-projection cover by the planimetric covariance of cover with the area density, divided by the mean area density; the rumple index is a different quantity. A LiDAR pulse is recorded as a canopy return only when detection succeeds, so the naive return fraction estimates cover multiplied by the canopy detection probability. We study an inverse-probability-weighted estimator that uses that probability as the inclusion probability, and a weighted corner-averaged Cram\'er-von Mises lack-of-fit statistic for constant mean surface-area cover under independent canopy returns, calibrated by a parametric bootstrap. Synthetic validation on the flat plane and the Gaussian hill gives a naive bias near -0.40 and a weighted bias near 0.00; at 5000 pulses the test holds size at 0.02-0.06 across the simulated null cells and reaches power 0.79 under surface-uniform and 0.85 under plane-uniform sampling against broad slope-dependent cover, but only 0.12-0.13 against a compact hotspot. The definitions and their exact reductions are machine-checked in Lean 4. No field data yet.

papers.title: The Arc Threshold of the Two-Row Ising Torus: Exact Factorization, an Algebraic Critical Coupling, Uniformity in the Circumference, and the Rate of Convergence
papers.abstract: The Lee-Yang circle theorem places every zero of a ferromagnetic Ising partition polynomial on the unit circle. The arc condition, that every zero lie in the closed left half-plane, turns the circle theorem into a product formula for the characteristic function of the occupation count and makes it usable for local limit theorems. For the two-row periodic Ising torus we give the exact reflection factorization of the row transfer matrix, reduce the crossing at zeta = i to a real cubic, and identify the critical coupling a_c* = 0.8637850566870... as the unique root in (0,1) of an explicit octic. We prove that every a > a_c* satisfies the arc condition simultaneously for all circumferences, that no smaller coupling does, and that the finite thresholds approach a_c* at the rate C/n^2 with an explicit algebraic constant C. The factorization and the 2x2 threshold are formalized in Lean 4 against Mathlib; the zeta = i reduction, uniformity and rate are analysis-level.

papers.title: Iterating logarithms and well-foundedness
papers.abstract:
We prove that there is no sequence $\{ X_n \}_{n\in\omega}$ such that for all $n$, there is an injection from $\mathcal{P}(X_{n+1})$ to $X_n$ under a restricted set of axioms that conforms to the "working mathematician's" intuition (excluding Choice, Replacement, and Foundation).
  We also show such a sequence cannot be defined using a formula either. More precisely, it is inconsistent with Zermelo set theory minus Infinity to have a formula $\Phi(\cdot,\cdot)$ such that for each $n\in\omega$ there are $X$ and $Y$ with $\Phi(n,X)$, $\Phi(n+1,Y)$, and $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ being injectable into $X$.
  We finally show that the theorem fails if we allow infinitely many definitions, one for each term of the sequence, by using Hamkins, Linetsky, and Reitz's pointwise definable extensions of countable models of ZFC.

papers.title: One-Sided Hardy--Littlewood Maximal Operators on Variable Lebesgue Spaces Beyond Log-H\"older Continuity
papers.abstract:
We study the boundedness of the right-sided Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator on variable Lebesgue spaces over the real line. Motivated by the $K_0$ condition for the classical Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator, we introduce a directional condition $K_0^+$ adapted to the geometry of the one-sided maximal operator.
  We characterize $K_0^+$ in terms of the uniform boundedness of a family of one-sided averaging operators and prove that it is a necessary condition for the boundedness of $M^+$ on $L^{p(\cdot)}(\mathbb{R})$. We also establish one-sided analogues of the modular and reverse H\"older estimates associated with the classical $K_0$ condition. These estimates constitute the main local ingredients in the proof of boundedness of $M^+$ under the combined assumptions $K_0^+$ and $N_\infty$.

papers.title: On the Geometric Structure of Hyperbolic Clifford Bundles and Associated Spin Groups
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present the spinor structure associated with the Hyperbolic Clifford algebra of a real $n$-dimensional vector space $V$, which is denoted by $\mathcal{C}l\left(H_{V}\right)$. Unlike the standard Clifford algebra, the Hyperbolic Clifford algebra $\mathcal{C}l(H_V)$ simultaneously accommodates both multiforms and multivectors in a single algebraic structure, making it the natural framework---known as the ``mother algebra''---for the study of superfields in theoretical physics and for generalizing the Clifford bundle formalism to hyperbolic structures arising in gravitational theories. The orthogonal groups and orthogonal transformations associated to the hyperbolic space $H_{V}$ are presented. The Clifford--Lipschitz group and the Pin and Spin groups associated with $\mathcal{C}l\left(H_{V}\right)$ are defined. Then, the frame bundle and spinor structure associated to Hyperbolic Clifford algebra is derived.

papers.title: Chirality rules for optical vortices in rhombohedral graphene multilayers
papers.abstract: Optical zeros are momenta where the interband dipole vanishes. The dipole phase winds around each of them by an integer, so they are vortices of the resonant optical response with a conserved charge. We show that in rhombohedral graphene multilayers one integer, the stacking chirality $N$, fixes their constellation near the $K$ valley: the total charge per linear polarization is $N-1$ and is conserved under trigonal warping and interlayer bias; for $N\ge3$ the $K$ point stays an exact optical zero, the Bernal bilayer being the only exception; warping places the remaining charge on satellites whose radii scale linearly with the warping; and the charge pinned at $K$ is bias independent for $N\ge4$. A quantized interband character counts the enclosed charge as an integer staircase with steps at these radii, and an interlayer bias drives a satellite through the protected $K$ vortex in the trilayer. The rules survive the remote hoppings of the full tight-binding model and, being integer charges, the corrections that reshape the bands. The same integer sets the magnitude of the response: the band-edge shift current grows linearly with $N$.

papers.title: Dynamical Properties of the Multiple Elastic Pendulum
papers.abstract: This article studies the dynamical properties of the multiple elastic pendulum formed by an arbitrary number of point masses connected in a chain by elastic springs. First, using the Lagrangian formulation, the equations of motion governing the system's behavior, accounting for both large-angle displacements and elastic deformations, are derived. It is shown that well-established, low-dimensional systems, such as the classical double elastic pendulum, can be systematically recovered as particular cases directly from the general equations of motion after applying the appropriates particular conditions. The behavior of the system under small oscillations near its stable equilibrium is also investigated. For this case, the linearized equations allow the solution of the eigenvalue problem, demonstrating that in this case uncoupled behavior between the angular displacements and the spring elongations.

papers.title: Weather Adaptive Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Camera object detectors lose recall in rain, fog, snow and sand, and the confidence threshold at which a detector is deployed decides how many objects it misses and how many false alarms it raises. We study how a frozen detector should make this decision in adverse weather. We first reproduce SeqCRC, a conformal object detector whose first step calibrates the confidence threshold by conformal risk control (CRC), and use that step, calibrated separately in each weather condition, as our baseline. With YOLOv8x it keeps the held-out miss fraction within a 20% budget in every DAWN weather bin, where a single global threshold fails in fog, but the false alarms it needs are an output rather than a choice: from 1.6 to 117 per image across DAWN and BDD100K conditions. We then propose a calibrated trade-off dial. One setting, $\lambda$, the number of false alarms accepted to avoid one missed object, selects the expected-cost-optimal decision rule: either one score threshold, or a per-detection rule that keeps a box when its calibrated probability of being a real object, estimated by gradient-boosted trees from the detector's own per-box outputs, is at least $1/(1+\lambda)$. F-score preferences map onto the same dial, and CRC applied to $\lambda$ itself is planned to restore a per-condition miss guarantee. The dial is fitted once on BDD100K train and graded only on BDD100K val and DAWN.

papers.title: Supervised Residual NMPC in Force-Disturbed Quadrotors
papers.abstract: Residual deployment can affect closed-loop tracking. We compare two ways to deploy one supervised acceleration-residual network in nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) of a quadrotor. Cyclewise deployment repeats one correction across the horizon. Stagewise deployment evaluates shifted prediction nodes before the solve. Network parameters remain fixed during control. On prescribed force pulses, both schemes improve average tracking mainly after force removal, but worsen hover; some prediction checks also fail. Seed 1 reinforcement-learning benchmarks add no mean benefit under pulses or prescribed random forces. On 220 conditions, cyclewise and stagewise supervision reduce mean integral absolute position error (IAE) by 4.38% and 7.77%. On a separate 32-condition bank, fixed gain 1.5 lowers IAE by 27.47% relative to stagewise supervision but raises angular-rate root-mean-square error by 10.19%. In one synthetic computational fluid dynamics field, stagewise supervision lowers four-task mean IAE by 2.01% against a same-graph zero-residual control; some secondary metrics worsen. These simulations show that residual deployment affects tracking, with gains and limitations that depend on task and motion metric.

papers.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
papers.abstract: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

papers.title: Algorithmic Non-dimensionalisation of Polynomial Dynamical Systems with CRNNondim
papers.abstract: Although non-dimensionalisation is a fundamental step in modelling, it is rarely obvious, especially for large dynamical systems, how to systematically construct optimal non-dimensionalisations. In this work, we develop a general mathematical framework for non-dimensionalising polynomial ODEs by interpreting them as chemical reaction networks (CRNs) and characterise the space of admissible scalings. Within this viewpoint, admissible scalings of time and species are encoded by Laurent monomials, and we derive exact formulae for the minimal number of multiplicative dimensionless parameters required by the reaction-channel coefficients and by the full initial value problem, together with characterisations of the scale assignments that attain structural lower bounds. These counts are expressed in terms of structural properties of the underlying CRN, and we show that the full initial value problem requires no more parameters than the corresponding Buckingham count. These results lead to constructive algorithms which we analyse rigorously and implement in the open-source Python package CRNNondim, available at https://github.com/georgio-hawi/crnnondim . Given a polynomial system or CRN, CRNNondim determines species and time scalings that bring variables as close to unity as possible while minimising the number of free parameters, and among the admissible scalings it chooses free parameters that result in the corresponding dimensionless system being sparse and simple. We apply CRNNondim to numerous well-known biological and biochemical models, yielding simpler dimensionless systems with fewer free parameters, and interpreting the parameters that govern their dynamics.

papers.title: Non-centered maximal operators over $\ell^q$ balls for exponential and Laguerre-type measures
papers.abstract: We establish the \(L^p\)-boundedness, \(1<p<\infty\), of the non-centered Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator associated with \(\ell^q\) balls, \(1<q<\infty\), for the non-radial exponential measure \[ d\mu(x)=e^{-|x_1|-\cdots-|x_d|}\,dx \] in every dimension \(d\ge1\). This settles the higher-dimensional Euclidean case left open by Nowak, Sasso, Sj\"ogren and Stempak, and extends their results to the full range \(1<q<\infty\). We also prove that these operators are not of weak type \((1,1)\) when \(d\ge2\). Together with the known results for \(q=1\) and \(q=\infty\) for the exponential measure, this gives a complete description of the \(L^p\)-boundedness and weak type \((1,1)\) behavior for all \(1\le q\le\infty\). {We also extend the strong \(L^p\)-boundedness to the Laguerre-type measures \(d\mu_\alpha(x)=\prod_{j=1}^d|x_j|^{\alpha_j}e^{-|x_1|-\cdots-|x_d|}\,dx\) for all \(\alpha_j\ge0\) and \(1\le q\le\infty\), and for the full range \(\alpha_j>-1\) when \(q=\infty\).} {The main arguments rely} on geometric estimates for sections of \(\ell^q\) balls and a slicing argument.

papers.title: Who Is Doing the Thinking? Characterising Human Agency in First-Year Students' AI Interactions
papers.abstract: When students use generative AI to produce their work, the learning process becomes invisible. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. Most prompts (84.2%) carried some student contribution beyond delegation. Agency tracked the development lifecycle. Architecture-discovery prompts dominated the requirements phase (48% of turns) and fell to 5-12% from week 9, while prompts analysing existing systems rose during build and verification (odds ratio 2.88, with turns clustered by student). Two-thirds of the variance in tier lay within students, so agency depended more on the phase of work than on the student. A turn-level rise in delegation in deadline weeks did not hold once turns were clustered by student. Explicitly specifying constraints on the AI's output was rare throughout, which we interpret as a knowledge bottleneck for novices rather than a gap in instruction. We discuss implications for course and assessment design, and for using HADT as a formative lens on how students engage with AI.

papers.title: Path Decompositions of Sparse Graphs via Gaussian Sweeps and Faster Exponential Algorithms
papers.abstract:
Using the bisection bound of Monien and Preis, Fomin and H{\o}ie proved in 2006 that every graph of maximum degree 3 on $n$ vertices has pathwidth at most $n/6+o(n)$. We prove that the pathwidth, bisection width and cutwidth of these graphs are at most $c_3 n+o(n)$, where $c_3=\frac{3}{4\pi}\arccos\frac56\approx0.1398$. For bisection width this improves the bound $n/6+o(n)$ of Monien and Preis (2006) and extends to all such graphs the bound that Lichev and Mitsche (2023) obtained for random cubic graphs. For maximum degree 4, we prove that bisection width and cutwidth are at most $n/3+o(n)$, improving the bound $2n/5+o(n)$ of Monien and Preis for 4-regular graphs, and that pathwidth is at most $0.2458n$, improving the bound $n/3$ of Fomin, Gaspers, Saurabh and Stepanov (2009). We show that every graph with $m$ edges has pathwidth at most $7m/48+o(n)$, improving the bound $13m/75$ of Scott and Sorkin (2007), and we give further bounds of the form $\sum_{d\ge3}a_d n_d+o(n)$ with $a_d<1$, where $n_d$ is the number of vertices of degree $d$. The path decompositions, and linear orderings of the stated cutwidth, can be computed in polynomial time.
  Instead of deriving pathwidth bounds from bisection width, we give each vertex a Gaussian label, a weighted sum of independent standard normal variables over a ball around it, and sweep a threshold through the labels; the bags are frontiers, the vertices above the threshold with a neighbor below it. We bound the probability that a vertex lies in a frontier by comparison with an explicit Gaussian model of a vertex and its neighbors.
  Faster exact algorithms follow: for feedback vertex set and the traveling salesperson problem on graphs of bounded maximum or average degree, and on general graphs for minimum weight dominating set (by branching until the instance is sparse), Max 2-CSP and counting subgraphs with $k$ edges (by the bound in $m$).

papers.title: Statistical analysis of the remaining human life expectancy. Mathematical models of the type Gompertz-Makeham and others
papers.abstract: Many researchers believe that human lifetime on the interval (30,80) years is described by the Gompertz-Makeham distribution. In this work, the task is set to test this hypothesis. We consider a number of distributions: Gompertz-Makeham, Gompertz-Weibull, Logistic Kannisto-Makeham, Logistic Beard-Makeham and Logistic Beard-Weibull, some of which are partially known, for which comparative calculations on real mortality data are performed using the $\chi^2$ criterion. The data were selected for three countries: England \& Wales, Norway and Sweden, cohorts born in 1900. As it turned out, on the interval (30,80) years the Gompertz-Makeham distribution is far from being the best among those listed above. In addition, for the same data, a similar problem was studied for the interval (80,120) years.

papers.title: The Structure of a Non-Isometric Non-Contractive Bijection of a Hereditarily Precompact Quasi-Metric Space
papers.abstract: On a hereditarily precompact quasi-metric space, every bijective non-contractive self-map has the following structure: the quasi-metric splits as $d = \lambda^- + D_0$. The invariant limit register $\lambda^-$ is a quasi-pseudo-metric below $d$ for which the map is an isometry, with totally bounded symmetrization on every orbit, so that the map's rigid shadow is a rotation of a compact monothetic group; the asymmetric limit structure on it, a priori only paratopological, carries the compact topology. The defect $D_0$ lies in a band between a past fee difference and the fee of its source, the fee nondecreasing along orbits and vanishing in the deep past. The defect is zero precisely when the map is an isometry. Deep sources are thus almost rigid: in the deep past the map is an isometry to within any $\varepsilon$, against every target. Every such map that is not an isometry is a toll over its rigid shadow, levied on a forward-invariant zone that sheds into the past. Two further facts are forced: the orbit of the source of any strict pair is infinite and already strict, and the source pays its whole defect on its own backward returns, uniformly on a chain-closed set of displacements. The band is attained at both ends, and beyond it the shape of the defect is not forced: three spirals over the circle show that the toll can depend on the target, that a source carrying a fee can descend for free, and that an ascent can carry defect; no rate of shedding is forced either, and for zone tolls (two-valued descent tolls that are shift-monotone and subadditive along their own routes) the fee reaches zero already at a finite depth, by the ascending chain condition on submonoids of $\mathbb{N}$. The results are machine-checked in Lean, apart from a few statements listed at the end.

papers.title: Charge-Dependent Coordination and Redox Energetics of Actinide Fluoride Complexes in Molten Salts
papers.abstract: Redox control in molten fluoride salt reactors determines actinide solubility and corrosion of structural alloys, but the role of local fluoride coordination in this control remains poorly understood. We use density functional theory with explicit LiF microsolvation to study the coordination chemistry, intrinsic redox energetics, and fluoride-exchange kinetics of Th(IV), U(IV), and U(III) fluoride complexes. The coordination response to solvation primarily follows the formal charge of the complex rather than the actinide at its center: we find that cationic and neutral complexes gain fluoride ligands, most anionic complexes keep their coordination number, and $4-$ complexes lose fluoride. Coordination number then strongly controls the intrinsic U(IV)/U(III) reduction energy. From CN 4 to CN 7, this energy rises by up to $11$ eV and changes sign; a continuum-solvation estimate opposes this trend and therefore establishes the intrinsic value as an upper bound. Fluoride exchange barriers are low, so redox partners of different charge do not keep the same coordination numbers in solvated clusters. Finally, above a threshold between CN 5 and CN 6, single-reference DFT converges to a ligand-reduced U(III) state inconsistent with formal $5f^3$ occupation, however the physical nature of this is still unresolved. Therefore, local coordination is a primary variable in the prediction of redox behavior in molten actinide-fluoride salts.

papers.title: H\"older Duality and Self-Dual Arc Length on $L^p$ Unit Curves
papers.abstract: We study arc length on the first-quadrant unit curve $x^p+y^p=1$, $p>1$, when length is measured with respect to an $L^r$ norm. Denoting this length by $L(p,r)$, we prove the H\"older-duality identity $L(p,r)=L(r^*,p^*)$, where $p^*=p/(p-1)$ and $r^*=r/(r-1)$. The identity is interpreted as a special case of the symmetry of mixed area (equivalently, of the anisotropic perimeter pairing). For the distinguished dual metric $r=p^*$, the length element agrees with the areal angular element: $L(p,p^*)=\int_\gamma (x\,dy-y\,dx)=\frac1p B(1/p,1/p)$. Thus the familiar coincidence between arc length and angular parameter on the Euclidean unit circle is the self-dual case $p=2$ of a more general relation between $L^p$ geometry and its dual metric. As a consequence, the Euclidean arc length of the $L^p$ unit curve admits a dual trigonometric representation.
papers.intro:
The Euclidean unit circle has the familiar property that, on the unit circle, arc length and angular parameter coincide. Equivalently, the arc length of an oriented sector equals twice its swept area. This phenomenon is closely tied to the self-duality of the Euclidean norm.

papers.title: Grid triples, link cobordisms in $\CPbar$ and the computation of Heegaard-Floer TQFT
papers.abstract: We give a combinatorial description of the Heegaard--Floer link-cobordism maps associated with pointed triple grid diagrams in the complement of three $4$-balls in complex projective plane with reverse orientation.  Every contributing index-zero holomorphic triangle decomposes into Euclidean triangular sheets. We characterize the compatible collections of sheets that contribute by an explicit geometric separation criterion, expressed as a lattice-point test, and prove that each has mod-\(2\) count one. Individual sheets may wrap around the torus in the unblocked theory, whereas they are embedded in the blocked theory. In each fixed \(\SpinC\) structure, the map is determined by a finite enumeration. A difference number computed from the triangular regions determines the \(\SpinC\) structure of a Whitney triangle. Together with the topology of the associated surface, this gives an explicit formula for the absolute bigrading of each summand of the cobordism map. After basepoint reduction, the formula determines the Laurent monomial representing any nonzero map on the rank-one torsion-free two-variable knot Floer modules, yielding vanishing and ideal-containment criteria. We apply the construction to an affine family of grid links \(K(n;p,s)\), obtaining explicit cobordisms involving infinite families of torus knots and links, together with closed formulas for the bigradings of their distinguished grid states.
papers.intro:
A recurring theme in Heegaard–Floer theory is the passage from invariants of individual three-manifolds or knots to maps associated with cobordisms. Ozsváth and Szabó’s original construction associated Floer groups to closed three-manifolds and, through knot Floer homology, to knots in three-manifolds [OS04c, OS04b, OS04a]; Rasmussen’s early work provided a closely related viewpoint on the knot filtration [Ras02] and Eftekhary extended the definition to knots that are not null-homologous [Eft05]. The theory rapidly developed into a collection of invariants sensitive to surfaces, concordance, the Thurston norm, and four-dimensional topology; see, for example, [OS03, Ni09]. From this perspective, understanding the maps induced by cobordisms is not secondary to the theory: it is part of the mechanism by which the invariants interact with topology.

A recurring theme in Heegaard–Floer theory is the passage from invariants of individual three-manifolds or knots to maps associated with cobordisms. Ozsváth and Szabó’s original construction associated Floer groups to closed three-manifolds and, through knot Floer homology, to knots in three-manifolds [OS04c, OS04b, OS04a]; Rasmussen’s early work provided a closely related viewpoint on the knot filtration [Ras02] and Eftekhary extended the definition to knots that are not null-homologous [Eft05]. The theory rapidly developed into a collection of invariants sensitive to surfaces, concordance, the Thurston norm, and four-dimensional topology; see, for example, [OS03, Ni09]. From this perspective, understanding the maps induced by cobordisms is not secondary to the theory: it is part of the mechanism by which the invariants interact with topology.

A second fundamental development concerned naturality. Heegaard Floer groups are originally defined from auxiliary Heegaard diagrams, and constructing a TQFT requires canonical control over the identifications associated with changes of diagram. Juhász established functoriality for sutured cobordisms [Juh16], while the naturality problem for Heegaard Floer homology and the associated mapping class group actions was developed systematically by Juhász, Thurston and Zemke [JTZ21] and independently by Alishahi and Eftekhary [AE20b]. More recently, a decoration-independent version of the theory was constructed in [Eft24a], producing a Heegaard–Floer TQFT for oriented link cobordisms in which the auxiliary decoration is no longer part of the final invariant. Geometric Floer constructions, which are by nature deeply analytic, become truly computational only after the analytic data have been translated into sufficiently rigid combinatorial structures. Grid diagrams provide perhaps the most successful example of such a translation. Their use in knot theory goes back well before Floer homology; see, for instance, Cromwell’s work on arc presentations [Cro95]. In Heegaard Floer theory they became the basis of the combinatorial descriptions of knot and link Floer homology developed by Manolescu, Ozsváth, Sarkar, Szabó and Thurston [MOS09, MOST07], and later organized systematically in [OSS15]. In a grid diagram the generators become permutations, the relevant holomorphic disks become empty rectangles, and Maslov and Alexander gradings become finite counting functions. This replacement of analysis by planar combinatorics was strong enough not only to compute the homology but also to support further constructions involving skein triangles, cobordism maps and related operations; see, among others, [LMW08, Man07, Won17a, Won17b]. Sarkar’s polygon index formulas [Sar11] provide another bridge between the analytic and combinatorial sides of the theory, and Eftekhary’s comparison between sign assignments extends the equivalence to the theory with integer coefficients [Eft20].

The question motivating this paper is whether a comparable phenomenon occurs for link-cobordism maps arising from Heegaard triples. Ordinary grids are adapted to pairs of attaching-curve systems and therefore to differentials. Triangle maps require three systems of curves simultaneously. Triple grid diagrams supply precisely such a configuration. Blackwell, Gay and Lambert-Cole used them to construct Lagrangian surfaces in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} [BGLC25]; see also Blackwell’s thesis [Bla22]. Related lattice and hexagonal descriptions of curves and surfaces in ℂ​ℙ2\mathbb{CP}^{2} appear, for example, in [Zup22]. A triple grid consists of three families of curves of slopes 00, ∞\infty and −1-1 on a torus. Any two families form an ordinary grid diagram, while the three families determine the oppositely oriented projective-plane cobordism ℂ​ℙ¯2∖(B4⊔B4⊔B4).\overline{\mathbb{CP}}^{2}\setminus(B^{4}\sqcup B^{4}\sqcup B^{4}). Thus the same elementary diagram simultaneously records three boundary links, an embedded surface joining them, and the Heegaard triple from which the Floer cobordism map is defined. This paper studies the Heegaard–Floer meaning of that diagram.

papers.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
papers.abstract: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.
papers.intro:
A trading desk, a compliance team, and a credit officer all need the same primitive: given a state and a typed question, a probability, not a paragraph. Recent “System-1” decision models (TypeSafe AI, 2026) make this primitive architectural: the model consumes a state and typed questions (choice over options, score on an ordinal scale, noul returning P⁡(yes)P(\mathrm{yes})) and emits calibrated probabilities in one forward pass, at latencies and sizes suitable for production gates. Production deployments exist at exactly this shape (Cloudflare’s clef is a 27B decision model post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B (Cloudflare, 2026); the this-that model serves typed decisions in 30 ms at a millionth of a cent (Cheng et al., 2026)), and a growing open ecosystem (imajev (mohit67890, 2026), strands-decider (strands-labs, 2026), decider (Mapika, 2026), kev (Palmer, 2026)) publishes recipes and leaderboards.

But three questions matter before an institution fine-tunes its own small decision layer, and the open literature answers none of them for the finance domain. (1) What happens to probability quality when the labels come from reality? Decision-model training sets use clean or programmatically-solved labels; financial outcomes are noisy, regime-drifting, and close to unpredictable from standard technical features. (2) What does domain fine-tuning destroy? Narrow SFT is known to erode general capabilities in decision models (mohit67890, 2026); the governance question is how much, at what scale, and whether it can be fixed. (3) How should calibrated probabilities be turned into actions? The gap between P⁡(yes)P(\mathrm{yes}) and an approve/review/reject dispatch is business logic, and needs a measurement discipline (y0usaf, 2026).

papers.title: Robot-Matched Soft Fingers for UMI Data Collection: Lessons from 100 Hours of Pick and Place
papers.abstract: Training robot policies for multi-task pick and place requires demonstrations on many objects, which handheld Universal Manipulation Interfaces (UMIs) can collect quickly and cheaply. However, existing UMIs depend on external base stations, use rigid fingers that give no signal about contact forces, or use parallel-jaw fingers that limit grip strength. We present a battery-powered handheld interface, built on YUBI, whose soft, angled fingers wrap around objects, deform visibly under load as a visual proxy for force, and match the grippers of the robot. With it, we collect a 99.7-hour dataset over 53 objects, train $\pi_{0.5}$ policies on 49 of them, and hold out the other 4 as unseen objects. We find that a top camera raises success by 13 points even when only about half of the data includes it, and that mid-training on our multi-task data raises success after fine-tuning on unseen objects from 35% to 57%. Finger design, dataset, and data processing code: https://lute-corp.github.io/soft-yubi-site/
papers.intro:
General robot policies for multi-task pick and place must handle a wide variety of objects, so they need to be trained on demonstrations with many of them.

General robot policies for multi-task pick and place must handle a wide variety of objects, so they need to be trained on demonstrations with many of them.

The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [4] enables collecting such multi-task datasets quickly and cheaply, without a robot in the loop. Follow-up work mostly changes how the handheld gripper is tracked: with a tracking camera [14], a phone [12], a 360∘ camera [11], head-mounted SLAM [9], self-tracking trackers [6], or VR controllers [7], while EgoMI [13] also captures the operator’s head motion. However, these interfaces either require external base stations [3], use rigid fingers that give the policy no signal about contact forces [7, 9], or use parallel-jaw fingers [4, 14, 12, 6] that touch the object at only two surfaces, which limits grip strength and the range of graspable shapes and breaks the one-to-one mapping to robots with angled grippers [14]. KIWI [11] also uses deformable fingers, but evaluates only capture: its grippers do not match a robot gripper, and it trains no policies.

papers.title: On the lower- and upper bounds of three-colored anti-Ramsey numbers
papers.abstract: In this paper we study a relatively new Ramsey type graph parameter introduced by my Bachelor's thesis supervisor N\'ora Alm\'asi, and her Master's thesis supervisor Maria Axenovich. The parameter $\xi(G)$ denotes the largest natural number $n$, such that there is a red-blue-green edge coloring of $K_n$, such that in the edge coloring all copies of $G$ represent all three colors. After a brief recap on Ramsey numbers, we precisely define $\xi(G)$, and take a look at its relations to the Ramsey numbers. In the third chapter we establish lower bounds on $\xi(G)$, in the cases $G=K_5$ and $G=K_6$, namely $\xi(K_5)\ge 19$ and $\xi(K_6)\ge 31$.

papers.title: A holomorphic Lie-Trotter product formula for nonlinear local semigroup
papers.abstract: We prove a new, holomorphic version of the Lie-Trotter product formula for nonlinear local semigroups with a parameter. We show that the product converges to the solutions of a nonlinear evolutions equation with a parameter. The solution is holomorphic in time on a centered at zero conic set in the complex plane and depends continuously on the parameter, and analytically on the initial data.

papers.title: The Askey-Wilson Function is the Laplace Transform of a Positive Measure
papers.abstract: The Askey-Wilson function $\phi(x, \gamma)$ is a meromorphic continuation of the Askey-Wilson polynomials in their spectral variable off the lattice $\gamma = \tilde{a} q^m, m \in \mathbb{Z}_+$. We show that the analytic part of the Askey-Wilson function $\phi^{an}(x, \tilde{a} q^\gamma)$ is the Laplace transform of a positive measure of total measure $\phi^{an}(x, s_0) < \infty$, under certain conditions on the parameters governing the function. We deduce log-convexity of this function, as well as positive-definiteness and an integral formula for a certain intertwining operator associated with the Askey-Wilson operator $L$. This offers a $q$-analogue of several results, in the trigonometric limit due to Sahi-McSwiggen, and in the rational (i.e. Dunkl) limit due to R\"osler.

This has numerous pleasant consequences, such as log-convexity, a majorization inequality in the style of [mcswiggen_majorization_2026], and positivity for a certain DAHA intertwiner. Our techniques differ from [mcswiggen_opdam-cherednik_2026], as the q→1q\to 1 limit is a crucial part of the argument there in moving from a statement about polynomials to a statement about their analytic continuation. We rely on the so-called expansion formula (18) of Stokman [stokman_expansion_2002], studied in more generality in [stokman_c-function_2014]. Such expansion formulas appear in many similar contexts. For instance, the Jack hypergeometric function introduced in [kaneko_selberg_1993] is defined by such a formula, which is the symmetrization of a formula due to Baker-Forrester [baker_nonsymmetric_1998] expanding the Dunkl kernel in terms of nonsymmetric Jack polynomials. We expect that similar techniques would yield results in those cases, though many of the analytic consequences are already known for the Dunkl kernel; see [rosler_asymptotic_2002], [rosler_generalized_1998], and the aforementioned paper [rosler_positivity_1999] on the positivity of the Dunkl intertwiner. The benefit of our approach using the expansion formula is a completely explicit description of the measure (31) of which ϕa​n​(x,a~​qγ)\phi^{an}(x,\tilde{a}q^{\gamma}) is a Laplace transform; this offers an avenue for more explicit global bounds and a study of the corresponding heat kernel as outlined in [mcswiggen_opdam-cherednik_2026, Section 4.2].

papers.title: Labtune: Treating Lab Organization and Information Sharing as Experimental Variables in LLM-Agent Discovery
papers.abstract:
De-siloing can create groupthink; silos can prevent knowledge sharing and reduce research efficiency. The same tension appears in research systems built with large language model (LLM) agents, yet their organization is usually fixed by design. I propose treating laboratory structure and information sharing as experimental variables.
  I introduce Labtune, an open framework for bounded research workflows with user-selected laboratory organization, communication policy, model configuration and budget. Users can choose among six editable designs, from multidisciplinary silos and transdisciplinary teams to co-leaders, hub-and-spoke structures, flat co-labs and a single scientist. Information sharing can independently vary from none to high detail, with an optional channel for conditional abstractions called wisdom. Sharing is enforced by the controller at phase barriers rather than through unrestricted agent chat, while delegation does not create additional budget or permissions. Development evidence is separated from protected confirmation, and an optional multi-lab layer allows laboratories with different structures to exchange filtered information.
  Labtune is an idea and system-description paper, not a benchmark result. Its contribution is to make laboratory organization and information sharing configurable and measurable under matched budgets. I do not claim that one design or level of sharing is best; the aim is to create a concrete experimental space in which those differences can be tested.
papers.intro:
A research group can fail in two opposite directions. Too little exchange leaves useful knowledge trapped inside silos and allows teams to repeat the same mistakes. Too much exchange can collapse different lines of inquiry into one shared view before the problem has been sufficiently explored. Organizational research has described related tensions between exploration and exploitation [18], between fast convergence and search diversity [14, 19, 37], and between coordination and conformity [13]. Groups also tend to under-share information held by only one member [29], while diversity of approaches can matter as much as individual ability [10]. The useful question is therefore not whether silos or integration are good. It is what should be shared, with whom, and at what point in the search.

LLM-agent research systems already make these choices. Some use a fixed sequence of stages; others generate and debate hypotheses, place a principal-investigator agent above specialists, or let a team discuss its way toward a result [17, 27, 9, 30, 1]. The organization is normally treated as implementation detail rather than as a variable. This is especially important when nominally different roles are instantiated by the same underlying model. Different personas can then share similar priors, blind spots and stylistic tendencies. Generative models can improve individual output while reducing collective diversity [5]; recent work also reports cases in which multi-agent teams hold back an expert member [22] and fail through recurring coordination errors [2]. More communication is therefore not automatically more useful collaboration.

The systems problem I address is simple: if organization and information flow can alter what an artificial research team explores, they should be recorded and varied with the same care as the model, data and budget. Labtune is a concrete attempt to make that possible. It has five commitments: • Selectable organization. Six lab designs are supplied as editable Markdown files with machine-readable front matter describing personas, phases, governance, collaboration forms and delegation defaults (Section 4.2). • Sharing as a controlled policy. Horizontal exchange passes through a controller-owned filter with four detail levels and an independent wisdom channel. Views are published at barriers and constrained by a read budget (Section 5). • Conservation of budget and permissions. A child agent consumes the parent’s allocation and cannot widen the parent’s access (Section 4.3). • Evidence separation. Agents work on development evidence. A fixed candidate is later evaluated on protected confirmation data that does not return to the agents. The user selects frequentist or Bayesian analysis, with a reviewed option for model-assisted prior elicitation (Section 6). • No automatic redesign.
