papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

papers.title: Bounds for Orthogonal Expansion Coefficients via Weighted Primitives
papers.abstract: For trigonometric and polynomial orthogonal expansions, we present coefficient bounds with an explicit numerator determined by the total variation of the function and the largest cumulative signed area of the weighted basis element. This area, denoted by $M_n$, is the sharp constant in the corresponding weighted integral estimate. We calculate or bound $M_n$ for several classical systems, thereby obtaining quantitative inequalities beyond an asymptotic statement of coefficient decay. Integration between consecutive zeros gives a geometric interpretation of the estimate. The comparison includes Chebyshev polynomials of the first three kinds, Legendre, Jacobi, Gegenbauer, and ordinary Laguerre polynomials, with normalization and boundary conditions stated explicitly. Classical estimates and their elementary consequences are organized as Fourier analysis in inequalities. In the controlled distortion application, ideal curves have selected coefficients absent, and restrictions on the variation, corridor width, and number of extrema of admissible departures give explicit guarantees for those coefficients.

papers.title: Structured Clinical Memory as Context for Probabilistic Decision Models: A Synthetic Evaluation with Jev
papers.abstract: Longitudinal clinical context is often distributed across noisy, repetitive forms and narrative records. We study whether a compact structured memory can improve a probabilistic decision model's answers when the underlying patient vignette is already available. We created 30 fully synthetic cases spanning twelve clinical domains, paired each with synthetically generated structured memory, and evaluated 120 typed questions with Jev. The raw-vignette arm achieved 90.0% accuracy (95% normal-approximation confidence interval: 84.6%-95.4%); adding memory achieved 93.3% (88.9%-97.8%). Five questions changed from incorrect to correct and one changed in the opposite direction (exact McNemar $p=0.219$). Choice log loss decreased from 0.258 to 0.175 and binary Brier score from 0.054 to 0.022. Memory added 310 input tokens per call on average, while observed mean latency was unchanged at approximately 0.5 seconds. These results are directionally positive rather than clinically validating: the cases are synthetic, the labels are single-author judgments, and the memory is an oracle upper bound rather than extracted production output. The pilot supports evaluating structured clinical memory as a reusable state interface for decision models.

papers.title: Feynman Propagators on Exponentially Decaying Perturbations of Stationary Spacetimes with Compact Cauchy Surface
papers.abstract: In this paper, we construct Feynman propagators on exponentially decaying perturbations of stationary spacetime with compact Cauchy surface. The propagators are defined as parametrices of the wave operator on exponentially weighted Sobolev spaces defined by complex contours $\Gamma$. We then apply this theory to the computation of indexes of Dirac operators using a continuous Wick-like rotation to relate it to the Riemannian case.
papers.intro:
Motivated by applications to Quantum Field Theories on curved spacetimes, the study of Feynman/anti-Feynman propagators on Lorentzian geometries has flourished in the past years. In layman’s terms these are inverses of wave operators which propagate future directed frequencies forward/backward in time and past directed frequencies backward/forward in time. More succinctly, it propagates them forward/backward along the lifted geodesic flow on phase space. In practice, ensuring this condition exactly is tricky as one first needs an inverse for the wave operator and then obtain exact control on the support of its kernel. Thus, one typically define Feynman(+)/anti-Feynman(-) parametrices Q±FQ_{\pm F} instead, which invert the wave operator up to compact errors. The condition on the propagation of frequencies is then only imposed at high enough frequencies, in which case the propagation is simply given by a choice of direction along the lifted geodesic flow on phase space: propagating along/opposit to the flow gives the Feynman/anti-Feynman condition. This is summarized by the Hadamard condition on their wavefront sets 11 1 For an introduction to the mathematical theory of QFT on curved spacetimes, see [5]. Section 4.3.4 discusses the wavefront set of propagators. In this work, the spaces will be weighted Sobolev spaces depending on contours Γ\Gamma, and can be interpreted as choices of ’boundary conditions’ for the wave equation. Afterwards, we quickly recall the Fourier-Laplace transform and construction of Feynman operators for stationary spacetimes in section 2, then extend the construction to perturbation of stationary spacetimes in section 3 and finally apply it to the computation of the index of Dirac operators in section 4.

papers.title: A transition calculus for 0-pseudodifferential operators with applications to gas giant geometry
papers.abstract: A gas giant Riemannian metric $g$ on a compact $n$-dimensional manifold-with-boundary $M$ blows up at the boundary $\partial M$ at the rate $1/x^\alpha$, for $\alpha \in (0,2)$, where $x \in C^\infty(M)$ is a boundary-defining function. Such metrics arise in the modeling of acoustic waves in gaseous planets. De Hoop-Ilmavirta-Kykk\"{a}nen-Mazzeo [arXiv:2403.05475] showed that, if $\alpha > 2/n$, the Laplace-Beltrami operator $\Delta_g$ is essentially self-adjoint and has discrete spectrum. Moreover, its spectrum is stable under truncations of $M$. The proof leverages the 0-calculus of Mazzeo-Melrose. We extend this theory by introducing a 0-transition calculus for studying families of 0-operators. We demonstrate a parametrix construction for $\Delta_g$ that is stable under truncations. Using this, we study the behavior of the resolvent of $\Delta_g$ under truncation and extend the characterization of the spectrum obtained by de Hoop-Ilmavirta-Kykk\"{a}nen-Mazzeo. In particular, we prove that (on appropriate functional-analytic domains) simple eigenvalues admit asymptotic expansions in the truncation parameter $\epsilon$ and that the corresponding eigenfunctions admit joint asymptotic expansions in $(\epsilon, x)$.

papers.title: It is time for a New Deal for mathematics
papers.abstract: The AI labs' vision is based on extraction (of data, wealth, and political power). Mathematicians must oppose it, moving past personal reflections and towards reforming mathematics' social contract.

papers.title: When Is Fresh AI Stock Analysis Worth It? Allocating a Limited Research Budget Across Price Updates, Deep Forecast Refreshes, and Editorial Reviews of Top Stock Picks
papers.abstract:
Must long-horizon AI investment research be rewritten every time stock prices move? Using 8,120 production reports on the same 203 stocks across four iPulse AI batches, we compare repricing existing targets, guarding them against price shocks, mechanically resetting old forecast growth, and generating fresh multi-agent reports. Ten matched configurations represent seven investment frameworks.
  Our primary economic evaluation selects Top 10 USD portfolios using one-year forecasts. Across two unchanged-model windows, guarded reuse averages 2.25%, versus 1.66% for SPY and 4.77% for fresh reports, after modeled trading costs and reference compute charges on a USD 100,000 account. Guarded reuse beats SPY in all three short windows, including the model-change transition. Extending the first holding window to nearly six months reverses the result: guarded reuse returns -11.26%, fresh reports +9.12%, and SPY +3.46%, motivating the thesis half-life question.
  Supporting quarter-forecast diagnostics show that mechanically re-anchoring old growth paths closes 98% of the MAE improvement over fixed targets, yet Fresh and Reset share only 1-4 of their Top 10 stocks. At Top 30, the unchanged-model portfolio comparison instead favors guarded reuse (4.17% versus 1.88%). Endpoint and concentration tests reveal the influence of horizon choices and exceptional winners. Nine production editions show substantial between-edition turnover, while every final editorial screen retains its own incoming list.
  Measured token workloads connect refresh costs to shared capital and realized break-even budgets. The resulting architecture separates continuous price monitoring from episodic thesis rebuilding and targeted editorial evidence checks.

papers.title: Kaplansky's conjectures fail for torsion-free hyperbolic groups in positive characteristic
papers.abstract: Do Kaplansky's group-ring conjectures hold for torsion-free word-hyperbolic groups? We show that all four fail in positive characteristic. For every prime $p$ there is a finitely presented, torsion-free, word-hyperbolic group $G$ with a finite two-dimensional classifying space and $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_p[G]$ with $ab=1\neq ba$. So, over every field of characteristic $p$, the group algebra of $G$ is not directly finite and has a non-trivial idempotent, zero divisor and unit, and $G$ is neither sofic nor surjunctive. For $p=2$, $G$, $a$ and $b$ come from OpenAI's random construction, and we add that $G$ is hyperbolic with probability $1-o(1)$, as are OpenAI's zero-divisor groups. For odd $p$ the groups are new: they adapt OpenAI's direct-finiteness construction with a signed cancellation, found first by S. V. Ivanov and independently by us, via an exact solution of a colour-balance problem and a Perron certificate. As far as we know, they are the first torsion-free counterexamples to direct finiteness and to the idempotent conjecture in odd characteristic. Hyperbolicity comes from one deterministic criterion: if a labelled graph is pattern-free, the group obtained by coning off its components is aspherical and has a linear isoperimetric inequality. We prove it by running OpenAI's exclusion of reduced spheres on van Kampen discs, an accounting OpenAI used for another complex. For every prime $p$, the existence of $G$, $a$ and $b$ and the failure of all four conjectures are formalized in Lean 4, including existence forms of the random-graph estimates used. In characteristic zero, where the idempotent and direct-finiteness conjectures hold for torsion-free hyperbolic groups, we show that no cancellation built into the vertex types survives the decay estimate that makes the groups torsion-free. OpenAI's characteristic-two counterexample with torsion is a CAT(0) group.

papers.title: Derived Equivalences for Terminal Threefold Flops via Local Index-One Covering Models
papers.abstract: Inspired by the quadratic involutions of Corti-Pukhlikov-Reid and Gavin Brown's description of hypersurface flips via toric GIT, we apply similar symmetries to local covering models of terminal threefold flops. We recover the derived equivalence of their canonical stacks by pullback and pushforward along the fibre product over the canonical stack of the contraction target, revisiting the local picture in Kawamata's work.

papers.title: Inverse powers and 2-adic properties of binary 3 x 3 matrices associated with the Tribonacci sequence
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study binary 3 x 3 matrices with determinant one that generate the Tribonacci recurrence. Starting from a specific generating matrix, we obtain explicit expressions for its powers and inverse powers in terms of the Tribonacci sequence T_n and two associated sequences B_n and R_n. This matrix framework yields identities involving traces, determinants, and products, including addition formulas and Cassini-type relations linking T_n, B_n, and Rn. Moreover, we derive new identities from the matrix representation of inverse powers and establish structural relations between these sequences. As an application, we investigate arithmetic properties of Tribonacci numbers and determine the exact 2-adic valuation of T_2^k for sufficiently large k. Finally, we provide a classification of 3 x 3 matrices associated with the Tribonacci recurrence via similarity over Q.

papers.title: Optical Ceiling on Polaron Mobility in Disordered Molecular Semiconductors: Lessons from Eumelanin
papers.abstract: Polaron hopping in disordered molecular semiconductors such as eumelanin is set by energetic disorder $\sigma$ and reorganization energy $\lambda$. We show that the reduced polaron absorption band encodes this transport problem. Its value at zero energy fixes the mean hop rate, which bounds the mobility in any dimension. For Gaussian disorder and classical vibrations its centroid is $E_\mathrm{op}=\lambda+(1-c)\sigma^2/k_BT$, its variance obeys the Hush relation, and the bound is the Marcus rate at $\lambda\to E_\mathrm{op}$; a 1D lower bound vanishes at $k_BT^*=(1-c)\sigma^2/\lambda$, read from optics.

papers.title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
papers.abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small changes in a policy can alter future observations and amplify into closed-loop task failure. In embodied control, an action error changes the next physical state, modifies the next observation, and may place the policy outside the training distribution. Subsequent errors can therefore compound over the remainder of the trajectory [1, 2].

Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language grounding, and low-level control within a single pretrained policy. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual perception, language grounding, and low-level control within a single pretrained policy. OpenVLA provides an open 7B VLA with tokenized actions and a pretrained vision-language backbone [3]. OpenVLA-OFT later demonstrated that continuous actions, action chunking, and optimized decoding can substantially improve success and inference efficiency [4]. These advances strengthen task acquisition, but do not remove the continual-learning problem: sequential fine-tuning can overwrite behavior required by earlier manipulation skills.

Existing continual-learning strategies offer complementary trade-offs. Replay remains a strong baseline but requires storing or regenerating previous observations. Expansion and routing methods isolate tasks but add modules or routing mechanisms. Parameter-regularization methods preserve a previous solution but can restrict acquisition. Direct update-suppression methods reduce future plasticity according to past update history, but can become too restrictive for large heterogeneous models.

Section III describes the sequential LIBERO evaluation protocol. Section IV motivates the dynamics-risk signal from the compounding-error perspective of imitation learning, and Section V formalizes the replay-free continual learning problem. papers.title: A Wolpert Theorem for shearing coordinates
papers.abstract: A theorem from Wolpert bounds the Weil--Petersson distance from a hyperbolic surface to a maximally noded surface in terms of the lengths of the underlying pants decomposition. We prove analogues for punctured surfaces both in terms of the lambda-lengths and in terms of the shearing coordinates of an ideal triangulation.

papers.title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$\alpha$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.
papers.intro:
Structure prediction is largely solved for proteins with a single well-defined fold [1, 2], yet a substantial fraction of biologically active proteins do not adopt one. Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs), estimated to make up 20–40% of the human proteome [3], instead populate heterogeneous conformational ensembles whose flexibility underlies their function [4, 5], and many human proteins contain both ordered and disordered regions. Modelling these ensembles underpins applications in drug discovery and protein design [6, 7].

Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs), estimated to make up 20–40% of the human proteome [3], instead populate heterogeneous conformational ensembles whose flexibility underlies their function [4, 5], and many human proteins contain both ordered and disordered regions. Modelling these ensembles underpins applications in drug discovery and protein design [6, 7].

While it is tempting to treat the ordered and disordered regimes as endpoints of a continuum, it is more principled to regard them as distinct, as evident in their scaling behaviour (Rg∼NνR_{g}\sim N^{\nu}). Ordered proteins adopt a unique compact native fold, and across the proteome they scale with ν≈1/3\nu\approx 1/3–2/52/5, close to the collapsed-globule limit of a polymer in poor solvent [8]. Disordered proteins instead form polymer-like ensembles governed by excluded volume and conformational entropy, from the θ\theta-regime (ν≈1/2\nu\approx 1/2) for typical sequences to the self-avoiding-walk limit (ν≈0.59\nu\approx 0.59) for highly charged or otherwise expanded ones [9], determined by sequence-dependent physicochemistry such as net charge, charge patterning and hydropathy [10, 5]. Multi-domain proteins, in which folded domains are joined by disordered linkers, reinforce this view rather than softening it: each domain or linker sits in one regime and the protein is their composition.

The experimental methods that underpin structure prediction for folded proteins do not transfer to disorder. Crystallography relies on a well-ordered lattice and single-particle cryo-EM reconstruction requires a small number of alignable states, and as a result the PDB is depleted in proteins with disorder. Instead the probes available for disordered proteins measure ensemble-averaged observables, principally small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) [11] and NMR chemical shifts (CS) [12].

As these observables constrain an ensemble only indirectly, ensembles are more often generated by simulation than inferred from data. For molecular dynamics simulations there is an accuracy–efficiency trade-off: all-atom force fields produce high-fidelity trajectories but at an immense computational cost, while coarse-grained methods provide proteome-scale coverage at reduced resolution [13]. Residue-level models such as CALVADOS [14, 15] are calibrated top-down against experimental SAXS and PRE data, and so are well tuned for global chain dimensions while sacrificing local geometry. An alternative approach is fragment assembly [16], which builds ensembles by stitching together short backbone fragments drawn from structural databases. This method aims for broad coverage and accurate local backbone geometry, but its sampled populations do not follow a Boltzmann distribution.

Recent advances in generative modelling have opened another route, in which models are trained to sample conformational ensembles directly, amortising over sequence so that no simulation is required at inference. For disordered regions, idpGAN [17], idpSAM [18] and STARLING [19] learn from coarse-grained or implicit-solvent simulations. AlphaFlow and ESMFlow [20] fine-tune folded-protein structure predictors with flow matching. BioEmu [21] is trained on all-atom molecular dynamics alongside folded structures. PepTron [22] and IDPFold2 [23] instead target the disordered and multi-domain regimes, drawing on proteome-scale ensembles of the kind described above. Several of these models carry over architectural elements from structure prediction, such as pair representations and structure modules, while SimpleFold [24] shows that folding itself can be learned with general-purpose transformer blocks and no pair representation. A complementary line of work predicts ensemble-averaged quantities directly from sequence, without generating an ensemble [25, 26].

papers.title: Variance Reduction Note 4: The Convergence of SVRG
papers.abstract: Stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) uses a full gradient at a snapshot point to correct inexpensive component gradients. This fourth expository note on variance reduction explains that control variate and gives a self-contained proof of linear convergence for the classical strongly convex finite-sum setting. Each component is assumed convex and smooth, while only their average must be strongly convex. A second-moment bound links the estimator to the objective gaps at the current iterate and the snapshot. Summing a distance recursion over an epoch then yields a geometric decrease and an oracle complexity of order $(n+L/\mu)\log(1/\tau)$ for objective accuracy $\tau$, with the initial gap fixed. The result uses a random snapshot update and counts all full-gradient computations. No new algorithm or rate is claimed.

papers.title: An elementary proof of a tangent-cone identity for rank-one planar Lipschitz maps
papers.abstract: We give an elementary proof of a tangent-cone identity which might be known to specialists in geometric measure theory. It concerns Lipschitz mappings $g$ from the closed unit ball $B\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $x$ be an interior point of differentiability of $g$ at which $Dg(x)$ has rank one. If the upper one-dimensional Hausdorff density of $g(B)$ at $g(x)$ is at most one, then the tangent cone to $g(B)$ at $g(x)$ coincides with the image of $Dg(x)$. This property is used in the proof of rigidity for the four-gradient problem. We provide a detailed, self-contained proof based on differentiability, connectedness and elementary estimates for one-dimensional Hausdorff measure, without using advanced methods from geometric measure theory.

papers.title: A Smooth Shioda-Tate Isomorphism for Elliptically Fibered 4-Manifolds
papers.abstract: This paper studies a subgroup of the mapping class group of an elliptically fibered $4$-manifold $\pi: M\to B$, inspired by number theory. The smooth Mordell-Weil group $\mathrm{MW}(\pi)$ is the group of isotopy classes of smooth sections of $\pi$. We construct a smooth analog of the Shioda-Tate isomorphism, identifying $\mathrm{MW(\pi)}$ with the quotient of $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$ by the trivial lattice of $\pi$. This shows that $\mathrm{MW}(\pi)$ can be computed explicitly from $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$. As an application, we show that the natural inclusion of the holomorphic Mordell-Weil group into the smooth one is an isomorphism if and only if $M$ is a rational elliptic surface. As another application, we show that $\mathrm{MW}(\pi)$ satisfies a strong version of Nielsen realization: any torsion element of $\mathrm{MW}(\pi)$ is represented by a holomorphic translation of $M$ of the same order.

papers.title: Interpretable Social Network Churn Prediction via Ergodic Markov Chains
papers.abstract: Predicting social network churn before it becomes visible in aggregate metrics remains an open challenge, particularly in enterprise settings where heterogeneous usage patterns, sparse data, and deployment constraints preclude standard supervised approaches. We formalize this problem as finite-step engagement projection over contributor-role Markov chains, with a stationary-distribution interpretation for ergodic chains in the long-run limit. For each engagement feature type within a network (e.g., Q&A, communities, articles, etc.), users are classified monthly into four behavioral states and a transition matrix is estimated from six months of history. Six-step propagation yields a label-free projection of the contributor mix; for ergodic chains, the Perron-Frobenius theorem establishes convergence under repeated propagation. Comparing projected future engagement to current engagement produces the Health Ratio, a single score requiring no trained model, no labels, and no infrastructure beyond SQL. Validated across seven rolling prediction windows on 11,500+ tenant-level networks, the Health Ratio achieves mean AUC 0.917 with a 156 times churn-rate gradient across risk tiers, outperforming all single-signal baselines and the growth-adjusted variant previously deployed in production. An ablation study shows that six-step propagation achieves similar churn discrimination to the eigenvector-based score. Deployed on Microsoft Engage since October 2025, the framework powers customer health monitoring and has enabled proactive intervention on at-risk networks before decline becomes visible in traditional metrics.
papers.intro:
Social networks operate on a flywheel: users create content, others consume and react, and those reactions draw creators back. If the flywheel reverses—creators disengage, reactions thin, remaining creators feel unheard—the network can collapse rapidly. Predicting and preventing such reversals is essential to the success of any social platform, and especially so in enterprise settings, where each tenant operates in their own independent network.

Social networks operate on a flywheel: users create content, others consume and react, and those reactions draw creators back. If the flywheel reverses—creators disengage, reactions thin, remaining creators feel unheard—the network can collapse rapidly. Predicting and preventing such reversals is essential to the success of any social platform, and especially so in enterprise settings, where each tenant operates in their own independent network.

Problem. Microsoft Engage is one such platform: each tenant hosts a self-contained social network whose engagement patterns and feature usage vary radically across organizations. Unlike consumer networks with a single global graph, network effects are bounded at the tenant level and churn is per-network rather than platform-wide. This creates a measurement problem across tens of thousands of networks that are all structurally independent: how does one assess network health in a way that is (i) unbiased to usage style, (ii) predictive rather than descriptive, and (iii) actionable enough to identify what specifically must be addressed?

The most common top-down metric, Monthly Active Users (MAU), fails all three criteria. A network with 10,000 passive viewers is fundamentally different from one with 1,000 active creators, yet raw counts conflate the two. By the time systemic MAU decline becomes obvious, it is often too late to intervene. Several constraints compound the difficulty: heterogeneous dynamics across 17 feature types (§5), no ground-truth labels at scoring cadence, sparse data in small networks, limited model-serving infrastructure, and the need for interpretable, actionable outputs that precludes black-box classifiers.

papers.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
papers.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.

papers.title: Diastolic inequalities for the distance function min-max width of spheres
papers.abstract: In this article, we investigate inequalities involving the min-max width associated to the distance function and the area of two-dimensional Riemannian spheres. This geometric invariant naturally arises as min-max methods are applied for the distance function defined on the space of pairs of points. Our methods involve careful constructions of sweepouts that can be performed under the hypothesis that the Riemannian sphere does not contain stable closed geodesics. Improved bounds are obtained under further geometric assumptions (positive curvature, pinching condition, and antipodal symmetry). In the cases of a pinching condition or antipodal symmetry, our inequalities are optimal.
papers.intro:
The pioneering work of Birkhoff [8] introduced a min-max invariant - the Birkhoff width - which is realized by the length of a closed geodesic on every Riemannian 2-dimensional sphere. That was the first proof of the fact that every Riemannian 2-sphere contains at least one non-trivial closed geodesic. Those methods reached great levels of success, specially in the case of minimal hypersurfaces, such as their use by Marques and Neves in the solution to the Willmore Conjecture [15].
